title: MonaVec: A Training-Free Embedded Vector Search Kernel for Edge and Offline AI Systems
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/mona-hq/monavec (PyPI: monavec; crates.io: monavec-core). Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20559587
summary:
We present MonaVec, a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel for edge and offline AI -- settings where server infrastructure, network connectivity, and training data are all unavailable. Existing vector-search systems assume a persistent server, gigabytes of RAM, or a training pass over the corpus; MonaVec instead targets the deployment profile of SQLite: one file, one function call, runs anywhere. Its quantization core is training-free by default and data-oblivious: a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions any input distribution toward N(0,1), so precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8x smaller) with no learned codebook and no data pass. The index persists as a single .mvec file whose embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed makes results reproducible across architectures and byte-identical within a build -- a determinism guarantee that parallel-build graph libraries cannot offer.
  On semantic embeddings (AG News, 45K x 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce reaches 0.960 Recall@10 in 27 MB -- leading float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall -- while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism. A single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends the same data-oblivious pipeline to magnitude-sensitive L2 data, and optional IvfFlat and HNSW backends carry it to million-vector corpora.
  MonaVec is implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar). It targets on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval -- the niche SQLite occupies for relational data: one file, one call, runs anywhere.

AI.tldr: MonaVec is a deterministic, embedded vector-search kernel (like SQLite for vectors) that uses a training-free, data-oblivious quantization scheme based on Randomized Hadamard Transform and precomputed Lloyd-Max tables to achieve 4-bit compression, delivering 0.960 Recall@10 on semantic embeddings in a single-file, single-call deployment model targeting edge/offline AI.
AI.motivation: Existing vector-search systems require server infrastructure, substantial RAM, or a training pass over the corpus — none of which are available in edge, offline, or embedded settings. The authors aim to fill the gap analogous to what SQLite provides for relational data: a zero-dependency, single-file, deterministic vector search kernel that runs anywhere with one function call.
AI.method: MonaVec employs a training-free, data-oblivious quantization pipeline: (1) a Randomized Hadamard Transform (RHDH) conditions arbitrary input distributions toward N(0,1), (2) precomputed Lloyd-Max tables quantize to 4 bits (8× compression) without any learned codebook or data pass, and (3) the index persists as a single .mvec file with an embedded ChaCha20 rotation seed ensuring byte-identical reproducibility across architectures. It supports BruteForce, IvfFlat, and HNSW backends, and a single-pass global standardization (fit()) extends support to magnitude-sensitive L2 data. Implemented in pure Rust with Python bindings and runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX-512/AVX2/NEON/scalar).
AI.result: On AG News (45K × 1024-dim BGE-M3, cosine similarity), MonaVec 4-bit BruteForce achieves 0.960 Recall@10 using only 27 MB, outperforming float32 FAISS-IVF and 8-bit usearch on recall, while trading peak throughput for byte-identical determinism across architectures.
AI.conclusion: MonaVec demonstrates that deterministic, high-recall vector search is achievable at 4-bit precision without training passes or server dependencies, making it suitable for on-device RAG, offline agents, and embedded retrieval — the niche SQLite occupies for relational data.

title: VCG: A Multimodal Retrieval Framework for E-Commerce Video Feeds under Extreme Cold-Start Conditions
summary: The digital commerce landscape is shifting from static, search-driven catalogs to dynamic, immersive video feeds. This transition introduces an ``extreme cold-start'' problem: unlike traditional items, new short-form videos lack the dense interaction history required for collaborative filtering. Furthermore, immersive feeds introduce strong position and duration biases that distort standard engagement signals. In this paper, we demonstrate the Video Candidate Generation (VCG) system, a scalable multimodal retrieval engine designed to solve these challenges in a large-scale e-commerce environment. By leveraging a domain-adapted vision-language model (based on CLIP), we map users and videos into a shared semantic space, enabling zero-shot retrieval based on visual content rather than behavioral history. We detail the system's architecture and present a rigorous evaluation comparing generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings. Our results show that while generative models excel at attribute prediction, they suffer from embedding space collapse in retrieval tasks. Online A/B testing demonstrates that VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases, yielding a 50\% uplift in deep video completion. To showcase the system's capabilities, we present an interactive demonstration featuring three bi-directional retrieval scenarios: Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search.

AI.tldr: A multimodal retrieval engine (VCG) using domain-adapted CLIP embeddings solves extreme cold-start for short-form e-commerce videos, achieving 50% uplift in deep video completion via zero-shot semantic retrieval while avoiding the embedding collapse seen in LLM-based alternatives.
AI.motivation: The shift from static search-driven catalogs to dynamic immersive video feeds creates an "extreme cold-start" problem: new short-form videos lack interaction history for collaborative filtering, and standard engagement signals are distorted by strong position and duration biases in immersive feeds.
AI.method: VCG system employs a domain-adapted vision-language model (CLIP-based) to map users and videos into a shared semantic space for zero-shot retrieval. The paper compares generative (LLM) vs. discriminative (CLIP) embeddings and evaluates through online A/B testing, plus an interactive demo covering Product-to-Video, Video-to-Product, and Zero-Shot Semantic Search scenarios.
AI.result: Discriminative CLIP embeddings outperform generative LLM embeddings, which suffer from embedding space collapse in retrieval tasks. Online A/B testing shows VCG effectively mitigates engagement biases, yielding a 50% uplift in deep video completion.
AI.conclusion: Domain-adapted discriminative vision-language models provide a scalable solution for cold-start video retrieval in e-commerce, outperforming generative alternatives and significantly improving user engagement metrics.

title: Token Factory: Efficiently Integrating Diverse Signals into Large Recommendation Models
summary: Large Recommendation Models (LRMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in industry-scale recommendation tasks. However, holistically integrating traditional signals into these transformer-based architectures effectively and efficiently remains a major challenge. Conventional approaches that "textualize" these signals directly or create discrete item representations often lead to excessively long prompts, substantial memory footprints, and high computational overhead. To overcome these limitations, we propose "Token Factory", a framework designed to transform traditional signals into "soft tokens" that can be directly processed by LRMs. This approach enables efficient integration and compression of heterogeneous input features, preventing prompt length explosion while enhancing model performance. We detail the architecture of Token Factory and present experimental results validating its effectiveness in a production-scale recommendation environment.

AI.tldr: Token Factory introduces "soft tokens" to efficiently integrate traditional recommendation signals into Large Recommendation Models (LRMs), avoiding prompt explosion and computational overhead while improving performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional recommendation signals (e.g., user/item features, behavioral data) are difficult to integrate into transformer-based LRMs. Direct textualization or discrete item representations cause excessively long prompts, large memory footprints, and high computational costs.
AI.method: Proposes "Token Factory," a framework that transforms heterogeneous traditional signals into compact "soft tokens" — continuous vector representations directly consumable by LRMs, enabling efficient feature integration and compression without prompt length explosion.
AI.result: Experimental validation in a production-scale recommendation environment demonstrates the effectiveness of Token Factory in improving model performance while maintaining efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Token Factory offers a practical and scalable solution for holistically integrating traditional signals into LRMs, addressing the key trade-off between representational richness and computational feasibility in industrial recommendation systems.

title: SAFE-Cascade: Cost-Adaptive Vision-Language Routing for Chart Question Answering
comment: Demo paper submitted at CIKM 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful for chart question answering, but invoking a VLM for every query can be unnecessarily expensive when many questions are answerable from OCR text and lightweight language reasoning. We demonstrate SAFE-Cascade, an interactive system for cost-adaptive chart question answering. Given a chart image and a natural-language question, SAFE-Cascade first extracts chart text with OCR, obtains a provisional answer from a text-only language model, and then uses a learned router to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM. The demo exposes this decision process to users: OCR evidence, text-only answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and estimated latency are shown side by side. SAFE-Cascade is designed as a transparent interface for understanding when visual grounding is actually needed. Users can upload or select charts, ask questions, inspect the evidence used by each pathway, compare text-only and VLM answers, and adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost frontier. The system is implemented with Azure Document Intelligence for OCR, gpt-5-mini as the text-only model, gemini-2.5-flash-image as the VLM, and a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features. On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples from a 2,500-example experiment, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared with 67.7% accuracy and 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The observed +1.4 percentage-point difference is statistically uncertain, so we interpret SAFE-Cascade as matching full-VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%. The demonstration shows how selective modality routing can make multimodal knowledge systems more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware.

AI.tldr: SAFE-Cascade is a cost-adaptive chart QA system that uses a learned router to decide whether to answer using OCR + lightweight LM or escalate to a full VLM. It matches full-VLM accuracy (69.1% vs 67.7%) while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and cost by 9.3%, with a transparent UI exposing the routing logic.
AI.motivation: Invoking a VLM for every chart question is computationally expensive and often unnecessary, since many questions can be answered from OCR-extracted text combined with lightweight language reasoning. The work aims to reduce cost and improve transparency by selectively escalating only when visual grounding is truly needed.
AI.method: SAFE-Cascade employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) Azure Document Intelligence extracts chart text via OCR; (2) gpt-5-mini (text-only LM) produces a provisional answer from OCR text; (3) a Random Forest router, trained on inference-time features, decides whether to accept the text answer or escalate to gemini-2.5-flash-image (VLM). The system exposes all intermediate evidence, routing probabilities, costs, and latencies in a side-by-side interface, with a user-adjustable escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost trade-off.
AI.result: On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples (from a 2,500-example experiment), SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, versus a full-VLM baseline of 67.7% accuracy at 100% VLM invocation. The +1.4 pp difference is statistically uncertain, so performance is interpreted as matching the baseline while cutting VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%.
AI.conclusion: Selective modality routing via a learned router can maintain accuracy parity with full-VLM approaches while significantly reducing computational cost. The transparent, tunable interface demonstrates how multimodal systems can be made more cost-aware and interpretable, letting users understand and control when visual grounding is actually required.

title: LLM-Mediated Human-AI Interaction in Search and Rescue: Impact of Expertise on Attentional Allocation
summary: Human-AI teaming (HAT) increasingly involves AI systems that provide real-time, context-aware guidance in complex tasks. While such systems can improve performance, their effectiveness depends on how they shape human cognition and behavior. In particular, AI assistance can introduce cognitive demands and influence attention, planning, and interaction with the task environment, with effects that can vary across levels of expertise. This work investigates these mechanisms in a simulated search and rescue (SAR) environment. We compare human performance under two LLM (Large Language Model)-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline, and analyze interaction at multiple levels, including task performance, eye-tracking measures, and planning behavior. Eye tracking provides fine-grained insight into attention allocation and interaction with AI guidance, while behavioral measures capture how users structure and adapt their decisions over time. Results indicate that LLM guidance enhanced task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but did not increase total victims saved. Eye-tracking data revealed an attention-guidance trade-off, with visual resources shifting to the chat interface alongside increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated this effect: novices exhibited passive AI reliance, whereas experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning. These findings suggest that LLM-mediated teaming efficacy depends on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness.

AI.tldr: LLM guidance in simulated search-and-rescue improved task efficiency (rewards, victims-per-step) but not total victims saved, while eye-tracking revealed an attention-guidance trade-off — visual resources shifted to the chat interface with increased pupil size variability, and expertise moderated reliance patterns: novices showed passive reliance, experts maintained verification loops through environmental scanning.
AI.motivation: To investigate how real-time, context-aware AI guidance shapes human cognition and behavior in complex tasks — specifically, what cognitive demands it introduces and how it affects attention, planning, and task interaction, particularly across different expertise levels.
AI.method: A simulated search-and-rescue (SAR) experiment comparing human performance across two LLM-guided conditions and a no-LLM baseline. Multi-level analysis included task performance metrics, eye-tracking measures (attention allocation, pupil size variability), and behavioral measures of planning and decision adaptation over time.
AI.result: LLM guidance increased task efficiency (higher rewards and victims-per-step) but not total victims saved. Eye-tracking showed an attention-guidance trade-off: visual attention shifted toward the chat interface, with increased pupil size variability. Expertise moderated these effects: novices displayed passive AI reliance, while experts maintained a "verification loop" through persistent environmental scanning to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth.
AI.conclusion: LLM-mediated teaming efficacy hinges on the operator's ability to cross-reference AI guidance with ground truth to maintain situational awareness. The benefits of AI assistance are moderated by expertise, with experts better equipped to integrate guidance without losing environmental awareness.

title: Secure Coding Drift in LLM-Assisted Post-Quantum Cryptography Development: A Gamified Fix
comment: Accepted for 2026 SIGIR Workshop on Vulnerabilities in Generative Systems for Information Retrieval track
summary: The transition to Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) introduces considerable implementation complexity, requiring strict adherence to constant-time execution, side channel resistance, and precise parametrisation. Simultaneously, large language models (LLMs) are heavily embedded in software development workflows, including cryptographic engineering. While LLMs improve productivity, evidence shows that they frequently generate insecure or suboptimal code, particularly in security critical domains. This paper introduces Secure Coding Drift in PQC, a novel socio technical vulnerability model capturing the gradual degradation of secure coding practices due to sustained reliance on LLM-generated code. Unlike prior work that focuses on static vulnerabilities, we conceptualise security risk as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon rising from human AI interaction. To mitigate this, we propose a gamified, LLM augmented secure coding framework that embeds adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into development workflows. Our approach reframes LLMs from passive assistants into active security co-pilots, contributing toward safer PQC implementation in AI mediated environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces "Secure Coding Drift in PQC," a socio-technical vulnerability model where reliance on LLMs gradually degrades secure coding practices in post-quantum cryptography implementations, and proposes a gamified LLM-augmented framework with adversarial evaluation and behavioural feedback to mitigate this drift.
AI.motivation: PQC implementation is inherently complex, demanding constant-time execution, side-channel resistance, and precise parameterization. LLMs are increasingly used in cryptographic engineering but frequently generate insecure code. Existing work focuses on static vulnerabilities, overlooking the longitudinal, behavioural degradation of security practices arising from sustained human-AI interaction.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes "Secure Coding Drift" as a longitudinal behavioural phenomenon. To counter it, the authors propose a gamified, LLM-augmented secure coding framework that integrates adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback loops, and security scoring directly into development workflows, reframing LLMs as active security co-pilots rather than passive assistants.
AI.result: The paper presents a novel vulnerability model and a mitigation framework. As a conceptual/design paper, it does not report empirical quantitative results but articulates the Secure Coding Drift model and the architecture of the proposed gamified framework.
AI.conclusion: Sustained LLM reliance in PQC development risks a gradual erosion of secure coding practices ("Secure Coding Drift"). Embedding adversarial evaluation, behavioural feedback, and security scoring into LLM-augmented workflows can transform LLMs into active security co-pilots, contributing to safer PQC implementations in AI-mediated environments.

title: Exposing the Unsaid: Visualizing Hidden LLM Bias through Stochastic Path Aggregation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit representational and syntactic biases that are difficult to evaluate due to the stochastic nature of text generation. Standard auditing methods rely on a single output inspection or static automated metrics. These approaches obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. This paper introduces TreeTracer, a visual analytics tool designed to evaluate LLM bias through aggregated comparison. Using a systematic perturbation analysis pipeline, the tool replaces ontology-defined terms in each input prompt, aggregates hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical structure, and then performs classification-aware node merging with an auxiliary language model. The resulting structure is visualized through a custom Sankey diagram. By juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees, the workspace enables direct comparison between semantic contexts and supports systematic bias detection. Because any visualization reflects only a subset of the model's learned behavior, the system further applies contrastive inference to compute and directly display counterfactual token probabilities across contexts, reducing the risk of misinterpreting the presence of bias. We validate the workspace through case studies comparing an unaligned baseline model GPT-2 XL against the constitutionally aligned Apertus models. The visual aggregation successfully exposes hidden representational harms, such as counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization of individuals. A preliminary user study confirms that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and effectively supports analysts in detecting systemic biases.

AI.tldr: TreeTracer is a visual analytics tool that aggregates hundreds of LLM text generations into hierarchical Sankey diagrams for systematic bias comparison. It uses ontology-driven perturbation, syntax-aligned tree structures, and contrastive inference to expose hidden representational biases that single-output auditing methods miss.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM bias auditing relies on single-output inspection or static automated metrics, which obscure the underlying probability distributions and fail to capture biases hidden in lower-probability generation branches. A method is needed that reveals the full stochastic landscape of model outputs to detect subtle, systemic representational harms.
AI.method: TreeTracer employs a four-stage pipeline: (1) systematic perturbation analysis replacing ontology-defined terms in prompts; (2) aggregation of hundreds of stochastic generations into a syntax-aligned hierarchical tree structure; (3) classification-aware node merging using an auxiliary language model; (4) visualization via custom Sankey diagrams juxtaposing two ontology-driven trees. Additionally, contrastive inference computes and displays counterfactual token probabilities across contexts to mitigate misinterpretation.
AI.result: Case studies comparing GPT-2 XL (unaligned baseline) against constitutionally aligned Apertus models revealed hidden representational harms including counterfactual pronoun suppression and conversational marginalization. A preliminary user study confirmed that the aggregated comparative interface reduces cognitive load and supports effective systemic bias detection.
AI.conclusion: Aggregated, comparative visual analytics with contrastive inference provides a more robust framework for auditing LLM biases than single-output methods, exposing structural harms that otherwise remain invisible. TreeTracer demonstrates the viability of this approach for responsible model evaluation.

title: Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center
summary: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first formal model of mesh inference, where independent agents with private states exchange only typed observations to collectively derive a conclusion without a central coordinator. Using a coupled free energy framework, the authors prove three key properties—convergence, identification-completeness, and observation-only confidentiality—and show that in the linear-Gaussian regime, the derived answer equals the centralized optimum with O(diam²) latency.
AI.motivation: Current distributed learning and inference systems require sharing weights, gradients, or hidden states, which violates privacy and requires central coordination. The authors are motivated by the conceptual insight that asking a model is fundamentally energy-minimizing inference, leading them to explore whether a population of agents can collectively infer without exposing internals or relying on a coordinator.
AI.method: The authors model mesh inference as a coupled free energy minimization problem, where each agent locally relaxes a free energy functional coupled through admitted observations. They formalize the coupling structure as an M-matrix, analyze information flow through carrier-connected views, and establish the duality between identification and confidentiality. The linear-Gaussian regime is analyzed in detail to characterize convergence properties and latency bounds.
AI.result: Three properties are shown to be governed by a single admission/emission policy: (1) mesh inference always converges to a unique answer regardless of admission symmetry due to the M-matrix property; (2) it is identification-complete, achieving the centralized optimum exactly when contributing views are carrier-connected; (3) it is observation-only—no internal state is transmitted, with content-addressed lineage as the sole global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime, every derived answer equals the centralized optimum with O(diam²) latency, which the authors characterize as the measured price of removing the center.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first formal foundation for mesh inference, demonstrating that center-free collective inference is both feasible and principled. The framework provides architectural guarantees for privacy-preserving distributed inference. The authors identify an open problem: determining when non-linear mesh inference improves rather than corrupts the collective answer, framing one inference round as one turn of a center-free learning loop.

title: Supporting Design Decisions in Rule-Based Model Transformations
summary: Model Driven Engineering relies on model transformations to automate the derivation of target models or source code from source models. However, the design decisions that govern how source elements are mapped to target artifacts typically remain embedded in the transformation source code, limiting flexibility, reusability, and traceability. This paper proposes an approach to explicitly model and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations. Design decisions are separated from transformation implementation through three mechanisms. First, a decision model captures design decisions and their options independently of any source modeling language for a given transformation domain. Second, a binding model connects these decisions to specific metamodel concepts in a given source modeling language, enabling reuse of the same design knowledge across transformations from similar languages. Third, a configuration model records the specific option chosen for each applicable source model element, with defaults pre-selected automatically. During execution, variability points in transformation rules are resolved dynamically according to configured choices. A trace model records which rules and options were applied to produce each target element. We establish a formal mathematical framework that defines the core concepts of variability-based transformations and proves key properties of the resulting transformations. The formal concepts are realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models. We demonstrate practical feasibility by extending an existing embedded domain-specific language for model-driven engineering with variability support and illustrate the approach with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an approach to externalize and manage design decisions in rule-based model transformations using four interconnected models (decision, binding, configuration, and trace), supported by a formal mathematical framework, enabling reuse, flexibility, and traceability of transformation choices.
AI.motivation: Design decisions governing how source model elements map to target artifacts are typically hard-coded within transformation source code, which limits flexibility (cannot easily change decisions), reusability (decisions are language-specific), and traceability (which decision produced which output is opaque).
AI.method: The approach separates design decisions from transformation logic via three mechanisms: (1) a decision model capturing decisions and options independently of any source metamodel; (2) a binding model linking decisions to specific metamodel concepts for cross-language reuse; (3) a configuration model recording per-element option choices with automatic defaults. A formal mathematical framework defines variability-based transformation concepts and proves key properties. The approach is realized in a practical architecture of four interconnected artifact models and implemented by extending an existing embedded DSL for MDE.
AI.result: The paper presents a formal framework with proven properties for variability-based transformations, a practical four-model architecture, and demonstrates feasibility through an extended embedded DSL with a complete ER-to-Relational transformation example.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling design decisions as first-class artifacts — separated from transformation logic, bound to metamodels, and configured per element — improves flexibility, reusability across similar languages, and traceability in model-driven engineering. The formal foundations and practical implementation confirm the approach's viability.

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. To be published in the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Agentic Services which is part of the IEEE Conference on Web Services
summary: Autonomous agentic AI systems driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new class of security, privacy, and compliance challenges: an agent that can invoke tools, manipulate data, install software, and coordinate with peer agents across organizational boundaries must be constrained not just by authentication and access control, but by the full structure of enterprise governance. This includes specifying what agents are permitted and prohibited from doing, what they areobliged to do after certain actions (e.g., notify the CISO), under what conditions a standing obligation may be waived, and which rules take precedence when policies conflict. This governance problem exceeds what current policy engines provide. Systems such as XACML, Rego, and Cedar address only the permit/prohibit subset of this governance structure. They do not provide obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations that waive obligations in specific circumstances, and ontological reasoning over domain class hierarchies commonly found in applications such as healthcare, cybersecurity, or data privacy. We propose AgenticRei, which realizes key governance requirements such as obligations, dispensations, policy conflict resolutions, and reasoning over policies, as well as the basic permit/prohibit constraints. We use a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework, expressed as OWL (Web Ontology Language) and evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations by the agent and agent-to-agent messages. We show through examples that deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that mostly cannot be expressed in current production engines. Our approach composes naturally with industry-standard frameworks like A2AS.

AI.tldr: AgenticRei proposes a deontic policy framework based on OWL and Rei to govern LLM-driven autonomous agents, extending beyond permit/prohibit to include obligations, dispensations, meta-policy conflict resolution, and ontological reasoning—capabilities absent from current policy engines like XACML, Rego, and Cedar.
AI.motivation: LLM-based autonomous agents can invoke tools, manipulate data, and coordinate across boundaries, creating governance challenges that exceed the permit/prohibit scope of existing policy engines (XACML, Rego, Cedar). Missing capabilities include obligation lifecycle management, meta-policy conflict resolution, dispensations, and ontological reasoning over domain hierarchies—all essential for domains like healthcare, cybersecurity, and data privacy.
AI.method: The authors propose AgenticRei, a governance framework using a deontic policy language built on the Rei framework and expressed in OWL. Policies are evaluated at runtime by a high-performance logic engine operating entirely outside the LLM. The same pipeline governs both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages, composing with industry standards like A2A (Agent-to-Agent).
AI.result: Through illustrative examples, the authors demonstrate that their deontic policies capture governance constraints around security and privacy that are largely inexpressible in current production policy engines, covering obligations, dispensations, conflict resolution, and hierarchical domain reasoning.
AI.conclusion: AgenticRei fills a critical gap in agent governance by providing a semantically rich, ontologically grounded policy framework that operates independently of the LLM, enabling enterprise-grade compliance for autonomous agentic systems.

title: Computational Identifiability
summary: Identification conditions describe the computability of a target query or parameter of interest as a function of the type and amount of information available. In causal identification, this information is often expressed in the form of a causal graph, and data are observed or collected for some subset of variables in the graph. Target queries may be for a single effect alone or for a class of effects in a given model. The derivation of an identification algorithm then defines mathematically the process by which the desired causal effect(s) can be uniquely determined, theoretically, in expectation. Identifiability in expectation, or 'theoretical identifiability,' generally assumes asymptotic properties, infinite data, or other mathematically idealized conditions. In this paper, we explore a fundamental distinction between this theoretical, idealized notion of identifiability and a proposed alternative that is computation-bound. The framework we propose - 'computational identifiability' - is to instead define a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator. If this process finds an estimator empirically, within a desired error tolerance, then identifiability is satisfied, conditional on the specified assumptions of the search (i.e., a prior distribution over the parameters) and conditional on the search procedure itself. Through several experiments, we demonstrate how this framework allows us to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions, such as identification with small finite samples, with ambiguous graphical criteria, with mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands. Code is available at https://github.com/lbynum/metadentify.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "computational identifiability," a practical alternative to classical theoretical identifiability that defines identification through a finite computational search procedure for an empirical estimator, conditional on search assumptions and error tolerance.
AI.motivation: Classical theoretical identifiability relies on idealized conditions (asymptotic data, infinite samples, perfect graph specification), which often fail in practical settings with small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, or mixed data types. A computation-bound framework is needed to answer fine-grained, practical identification questions.
AI.method: The authors propose computational identifiability, which defines identification via a finite computational search procedure that seeks an empirical estimator within a specified error tolerance. Identifiability is satisfied if the search empirically finds such an estimator, conditional on prior distributions over parameters and the search procedure itself. The framework is demonstrated through multiple experiments.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the computational identifiability framework successfully addresses identification under small finite samples, ambiguous graphical criteria, mixed observational-interventional data, and across counterfactual data and estimands — scenarios where classical identifiability provides limited practical guidance.
AI.conclusion: Computational identifiability offers a practical, empirically-grounded complement to classical theoretical identifiability, enabling researchers to assess whether causal effects can be estimated under realistic, computation- and data-constrained conditions.

title: Closing the Calibration Gap in Semantic Caching
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures. Source code: https://github.com/aditeyabaral/calibration-gap-semantic-caching ; Models and Datasets: https://huggingface.co/redis
summary: Semantic caching cuts LLM inference costs by serving a cached response to semantically similar queries. Standard practice evaluates these systems using PR-AUC, a metric that only measures how well scores rank and ignores whether they are usable at a fixed threshold. We show this mismatch leads to systematically poor deployment choices, as models with the highest PR-AUC are often the worst in operation. We introduce Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, a cache-aware metric that measures precision across cache utilization levels, and Calibration Retention Rate (CRR), which captures how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. We decompose the operational gap between offline and deployed quality into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component fixed by the dataset's positive rate. Our experiments show that the calibration gap is governed by the training objective rather than data scale, and post-hoc calibration only partially closes it. Ultimately, model selection for semantic caching is a calibration problem, not a ranking one, and measuring it is the first step to closing the gap.

AI.tldr: PR-AUC is a poor metric for selecting models for semantic caching deployment because it only measures ranking quality, not threshold usability. The authors propose P-CHR AUC and CRR to properly evaluate cache-aware precision and calibration retention, revealing that model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem rather than a ranking one.
AI.motivation: The standard metric for evaluating semantic caching systems, PR-AUC, only measures ranking quality and ignores whether similarity scores are usable at a fixed decision threshold. This mismatch causes practitioners to deploy models that rank well but perform poorly in actual operation, creating a systematic gap between offline evaluation and real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors first deconstruct why PR-AUC misleads model selection. They then introduce two new metrics: (1) P-CHR AUC, which measures precision across varying cache utilization levels, and (2) CRR, which quantifies how much offline ranking quality is retained after thresholding at deployment. They further decompose the offline-to-deployment gap into a recoverable calibration component and an irreducible structural component determined by the dataset's positive rate. Experiments examine how training objectives and data scale affect calibration, and whether post-hoc calibration methods can close the gap.
AI.result: Models with the highest PR-AUC are frequently the worst performers under actual deployment conditions. The calibration gap is primarily governed by the training objective rather than the scale of training data, and post-hoc calibration techniques only partially close this gap. The structural component of the gap is irreducible and fixed by the dataset's inherent positive rate.
AI.conclusion: Model selection for semantic caching is fundamentally a calibration problem, not a ranking problem. Proper measurement using cache-aware metrics like P-CHR AUC and CRR is the necessary first step toward closing the offline-to-deployment performance gap.

title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
comment: Pre-Print of a paper to be published at the International Computing Education Research (ICER) conference 2026
summary:
Program visualizations are widely used to support novice programmers, yet students often ignore or resist well-designed visual scaffolds. Research on multiple external representations (MERs) offers cognitive design principles for coordinating views, but less is known about what shapes learners' engagement with available representations.
  We conducted a within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who had completed CS1 and CS2. Students completed think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking while using a multi-representational probe with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views, and Python Tutor, across scope, while loops, and linked lists.
  Gaze analysis showed that students spent nearly half their time focused on code despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior experience anchored even more heavily in code and engaged minimally with metaphor views. Interviews identified three factors shaping selective engagement: agency, as students sought control over cognitive effort rather than simply having it reduced; representational fit, as identical designs differed in whether they felt helpful or overwhelming; and legitimacy, as some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds they perceived as childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
  These findings suggest that multi-representational tools in computing education require attention to affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical considerations include positioning visualizations as verification instruments, offering toggleable abstraction levels, and framing tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. More broadly, the themes help explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage the students they are designed to help.

AI.tldr: A gaze-tracking study with 19 post-CS2 undergraduates reveals that students spend nearly half their time on code despite multi-representational visual scaffolds. Three factors explain selective engagement: agency (desire for cognitive control), representational fit (same design felt helpful or overwhelming), and legitimacy (rejecting "childish" metaphors). Affective and social factors, not just cognitive design, determine whether learners engage with program visualizations.
AI.motivation: Program visualizations are widely deployed to support novice programmers, yet students frequently ignore or resist even well-designed visual scaffolds. While MER research provides cognitive design principles for coordinating views, little is known about what actually shapes learners' selective engagement with available representations. This gap motivates the study.
AI.method: A within-subjects study with 19 undergraduates who had completed CS1 and CS2. Participants used a multi-representational probe (synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views) alongside Python Tutor across three topics (scope, while loops, linked lists). Data collected: think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam-based gaze tracking. Gaze analysis quantified time allocation across views; interviews were analyzed qualitatively for engagement factors.
AI.result: Gaze data showed students spent nearly half their time on code despite available visual scaffolds. Students without prior programming experience anchored even more heavily in code and barely engaged with metaphor views. Qualitative analysis surfaced three factors: (1) agency — students wanted control over cognitive effort, not just reduction; (2) representational fit — identical designs were perceived as helpful by some and overwhelming by others; (3) legitimacy — some students avoided metaphorical scaffolds deemed childish or insufficiently rigorous for university-level work.
AI.conclusion: Multi-representational tools in computing education must attend to affective and social factors alongside cognitive design. Practical recommendations: position visualizations as verification instruments, offer toggleable abstraction levels, and frame tools to signal disciplinary legitimacy. The identified themes explain why cognitively sound visualization tools may fail to engage their intended users.

title: FloatDoor: Platform-Triggered Backdoors in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive settings such as software engineering, where their outputs directly shape downstream artifacts. Recent work has shown that an identical model can produce measurably different outputs depending on the deployment platform, a consequence of non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. We study the security implications of this platform-dependent variability and uncover a novel attack surface on LLM deployments. We introduce FloatDoor, the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against generative LLMs. The compromised model exhibits adversary-chosen behavior when served on a target platform and is otherwise benign. FloatDoor is realized through two lightweight LoRA adapters, one that amplifies inter-platform numerical divergence and one that binds the resulting platform signature to a malicious downstream task, while leaving aggregate model utility largely intact. FloatDoor exploits a pronounced time-of-check, time-of-use gap between model auditing and serving. We demonstrate FloatDoor on Qwen3-4B across a broad range of deployment targets, including NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. As a final case study, we show that FloatDoor reliably induces exploitable code vulnerabilities on a chosen target platform. Our results establish a new class of attacks on LLM deployments and underscore the pressing need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive, LLM-powered applications.

AI.tldr: FloatDoor is the first input-independent, platform-triggered backdoor attack against LLMs, using lightweight LoRA adapters to make a model behave maliciously only when deployed on a specific hardware platform, exploiting floating-point divergence across platforms.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in sensitive settings produce measurably different outputs across platforms due to non-associative floating-point arithmetic and divergent kernel implementations. This variability creates a security vulnerability: an attacker can exploit the gap between model auditing (time-of-check) and serving (time-of-use) to deploy backdoored models that activate only on specific hardware targets.
AI.method: FloatDoor uses two lightweight LoRA adapters: (1) an amplification adapter that magnifies inter-platform numerical divergence to create a robust platform signature, and (2) a binding adapter that links this platform signature to adversary-chosen malicious behavior. The backdoor is input-independent — triggered solely by the deployment platform's floating-point characteristics — while preserving aggregate model utility on non-target platforms.
AI.result: FloatDoor was demonstrated on Qwen3-4B across diverse hardware targets: NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs, AWS Graviton, and Alibaba Yitian-710. The attack reliably induced exploitable code vulnerabilities on the chosen target platform while maintaining benign behavior elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new class of attacks on LLM deployments, highlighting the critical need for trusted model supply chains in sensitive LLM-powered applications, as platform-dependent numerical variability can be weaponized to circumvent standard model auditing.

title: Ensembles of Large Language Models for Identifying EQ-5D Studies in PubMed Based on Their Abstracts
summary: The rapid increase in scientific publications leads to the fact that manual study screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource consuming, inefficient, and inconsistent. Classifying studies that clearly report health-related quality-of-life results, such as EQ-5D data, requires a high level of clinical interpretation and poses challenges for human reviewers. This study investigates the use of Google's Gemini and Gemma large language models (LLMs) in automating EQ-5D detection in the PubMed biomedical database based only on published abstracts. A multi-phase framework is proposed that integrates few-shot prompting, weight ensembling aggregation, and a soft stacking meta-classifier. Nine LLMs are evaluated on a dataset of PubMed studies manually labeled by two experts regarding EQ-5D reporting. The weighted ensemble of gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, and gemma-3-27b obtained a 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, exceeding individually attained results. The ensembling of top-performing models improved the balance between precision and recall compared to individual models, while the soft stacking approach provided greater reliability and interpretability. Feature analysis shows that the probability results from the models are important in guiding the final predictions. The findings suggest that an ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating screening in biomedical research.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a multi-phase framework using Google's Gemini and Gemma LLMs with few-shot prompting, weight ensembling, and soft stacking to automate detection of EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life reporting in PubMed abstracts, achieving 0.74 F1-score and accuracy with a weighted ensemble approach.
AI.motivation: Manual screening in systematic literature reviews (SLRs) is increasingly resource-intensive, inefficient, and inconsistent due to the rapid growth of scientific publications. Classifying studies reporting health-related quality-of-life outcomes (e.g., EQ-5D data) requires high clinical interpretation, posing challenges for human reviewers and motivating automation via LLMs.
AI.method: A multi-phase framework is proposed: (1) few-shot prompting of nine Google Gemini and Gemma LLMs on PubMed abstracts, (2) weight ensembling aggregation combining top-performing models (gemini-2.5-pro, gemma-3-12b, gemma-3-27b), and (3) a soft stacking meta-classifier for final prediction. Evaluation uses a dataset manually labeled by two experts for EQ-5D reporting, with feature analysis of model probability outputs.
AI.result: The weighted ensemble achieved 0.74 weighted F1-score and 0.74 accuracy, outperforming all individual models. Ensembling improved the precision-recall balance over single models, and the soft stacking approach enhanced reliability and interpretability. Probability outputs from constituent models were found to be important features guiding final predictions.
AI.conclusion: An ensemble-based LLM setup is a reliable and scalable approach for automating study screening in biomedical systematic literature reviews, effectively balancing precision and recall while improving interpretability over individual models.

title: SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design
summary: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational. Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD, the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline, by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points, respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points. These results suggest that compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SIGMA-2338/.

AI.tldr: SIGMA proposes a skill-incidence graph framework where agents are dynamically composed as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills, rather than fixed closed-set entities. It predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, constructs agent embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology. Across six benchmarks with three LLMs, it outperforms baselines including CARD by up to 2.36 points and shows robust generalization to unseen skill libraries.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based MAS approaches treat agents as closed-set entities with fixed roles, limiting generalization to tasks requiring novel combinations of capabilities. The authors identify that compositional node construction is an underexplored axis orthogonal to communication topology optimization.
AI.method: SIGMA maintains a skill library and, given a task, predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix indicating which skills compose each agent. Agent node embeddings are built by aggregating embeddings of assigned skills. A communication topology (graph) is then decoded over these dynamically constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to relevant capabilities, operationalizing the incidence structure directly.
AI.result: On six reasoning and coding benchmarks across three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance. It surpasses CARD (the strongest non-compositional topology baseline) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points respectively. Under unseen skill libraries, the average performance drop is only 0.96 points, demonstrating strong robustness.
AI.conclusion: Compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design, orthogonal to communication topology optimization. Dynamically composing agents from reusable skills improves both task performance and generalization to unseen capability combinations.

title: AgentArmor: A Framework, Evaluation, \& Mitigation of Coding Agent Failures
summary: Software engineering and deployment are increasingly being delegated to AI coding agents. The scale of their adoption is surfacing rare, but highly destructive, failure modes. In this paper, we study these failure modes as stemming from three distinct mechanisms: underspecification, where default model behavior is unsafe; capability errors, where the safe action is available but the model does not adhere to it due to bias or capability limitations; and agent harness errors, where the model fails to execute the safe action through the harness. We evaluate these across 8 different evaluations, each inspired by real-life deployment failures, totaling 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. Based on this evaluation, we propose AgentArmor, an agent harness modification, to mitigate these errors. By adding an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a ``3 strikes'' policy, deterministic guardrails, and tools for the agent to edit its own context, we show that AgentArmor is safer across a statistically significant number of samples. Thus, we suggest concrete mitigations for current coding agents and a design philosophy for future agent harness features.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three failure mechanisms in AI coding agents (underspecification, capability errors, agent harness errors) through analysis of real-world deployment failures across 8 evaluations, and proposes AgentArmor — a harness modification with system prompts, command classification, a "3 strikes" policy, deterministic guardrails, and self-editing tools — which demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are being widely deployed for software engineering tasks, but rare yet highly destructive failure modes are emerging. These failures are not well-characterized, and existing agent harnesses lack systematic safeguards against them. The work is motivated by real-life deployment failures that expose gaps in how agents interpret instructions, execute actions, and interact with their execution environment.
AI.method: The authors taxonomize failure modes into three mechanisms: (1) underspecification — default model behavior is unsafe when instructions are ambiguous; (2) capability errors — the model possesses the safe action but fails to select it due to biases or limitations; (3) agent harness errors — the model intends the safe action but the harness fails to execute it properly. They construct 8 evaluations inspired by real deployment incidents, spanning 20 coding environments and 59 synthetic transcript templates. They then design AgentArmor, which integrates an extended system prompt, a separate command classifier, a "3 strikes" policy, deterministic guardrails, and context-editing tools, and evaluate it against baseline harnesses.
AI.result: AgentArmor demonstrates statistically significant safety improvements across the evaluation suite, reducing failures stemming from all three identified mechanisms compared to standard agent harnesses.
AI.conclusion: The three-mechanism taxonomy provides a useful lens for diagnosing and addressing AI coding agent failures. AgentArmor offers concrete, implementable mitigations and establishes a design philosophy for building safer agent harnesses in future systems.

title: Measuring Curriculum Alignment across Topical Coverage, Competency, and Cognitive Depth: A Longitudinal Framework Applied to CS2013 and CS2023
summary: Undergraduate computer science is governed by international curricular guidelines revised about once a decade, yet programs lack a reliable, reproducible way to measure how completely they cover the current guidelines and how that coverage shifts when the guidelines are restructured. We address this with a human-in-the-loop pipeline that measures a program's coverage of an external body of knowledge, applied longitudinally to one accredited BSc in Computer Science against Computer Science Curricula 2013 (CS2013) and 2023 (CS2023). The pipeline represents the program and each guideline as structured corpora, generates candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches by semantic retrieval, and confirms them through human judgment under an explicit coverage definition. Of seven benchmarked retrievers, a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble was strongest, and a reputed long-context model underperformed a small sentence model, so retriever choice must be measured. Both maps were validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's kappa 0.64 for CS2023, 0.69 for CS2013). The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units, near-constant across a decade. Extending the same retrieve-then-confirm design to competency articulation and cognitive depth shows that the program articulates the competency for ~88% of covered units under each guideline, yet delivers it at the recommended depth for 76% of present units under CS2023 against 95% under CS2013, a gap reflecting the newer guideline's raised expectations, not the program. The longitudinal comparison separates persistent structural gaps (parallel and distributed computing, foundations of programming languages, systems fundamentals), uncovered against both guidelines and ABET, from differences that reflect the standard's evolution. The instrument is reusable and available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: A human-in-the-loop pipeline maps an undergraduate CS program to curricular guidelines (CS2013 and CS2023) using semantic retrieval and human confirmation, revealing ~50% knowledge unit coverage that remained stable over a decade, with competency depth gaps emerging under the newer, more demanding CS2023 standard.
AI.motivation: Undergraduate CS programs lack a reliable, reproducible method to measure how completely they cover international curricular guidelines (released roughly decennially) and how coverage shifts when guidelines are restructured. This gap impedes curricular accountability and continuous improvement.
AI.method: A human-in-the-loop pipeline is constructed: (1) the program syllabus and curricular guidelines are represented as structured corpora; (2) candidate course-to-knowledge-unit matches are generated via semantic retrieval — seven retrievers are benchmarked, with a reciprocal-rank-fusion ensemble proving strongest; (3) matches are confirmed by human judgment under an explicit coverage definition; (4) validated by an independent second rater (Cohen's κ); (5) extended to competency articulation and cognitive depth analysis.
AI.result: The program covers 49.7% of CS2023 and 50.9% of CS2013 knowledge units — near-constant across a decade. Competency is articulated for ~88% of covered units under both guidelines, but recommended cognitive depth is met for only 76% (CS2023) vs. 95% (CS2013), reflecting raised expectations in the newer standard. Persistent structural gaps exist in parallel/distributed computing, programming language foundations, and systems fundamentals. Inter-rater agreement reached κ=0.64 (CS2023) and κ=0.69 (CS2013).
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a reusable, validated instrument for longitudinal curricular coverage measurement that distinguishes persistent structural gaps from shifts driven by guideline evolution. Retriever choice matters empirically — a small sentence model outperformed a reputed long-context model. The tool is available on request.

title: When to Trust, How to Distill: Multi-Foundation Model Guidance for Lightweight, Robust Scientific Time Series Forecasting
comment: KDD 2026, paper decision: Accepted, track: AI for Science. total 12 pages including references and appendix
summary: The deployment of Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in physical sciences is hindered by a critical trade-off: while these models encode rich, universal temporal dynamics, they suffer from severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and their computational cost prohibits deployment in edge-computing sensor networks. We address a fundamental challenge: How can we extract latent structural knowledge from misaligned foundation models (FM) to train lightweight, specialized forecasters? We propose Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation (Guard), a novel framework that reframes multiteacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," automatically attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality. We evaluate our proposed lightweight framework on four climate-critical domains: meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids. Our method significantly reduces RMSE relative to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline, successfully distilling knowledge from pretrained FMs (teachers) even when they exhibit suboptimal zero-shot accuracy due to distribution shift between the original and target data domains. We demonstrate that these domain-misaligned teachers can still serve as critical correctives, outperforming the globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. Ultimately, this enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/RupasreeDey/GUARD-KDD2026.

AI.tldr: Guard proposes a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework with adaptive routing and uncertainty-gated temperature to extract useful knowledge from domain-misaligned Time-Series Foundation Models, enabling lightweight, high-precision scientific forecasters deployable on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) capture rich universal temporal dynamics but suffer from two critical limitations in physical sciences: (1) severe distributional misalignment when applied zero-shot to specific scientific domains, and (2) prohibitive computational cost for edge-computing sensor networks. The core challenge is extracting latent structural knowledge from these misaligned FMs to train specialized, lightweight forecasters.
AI.method: Guard (Gated Uncertainty-Aware Routing for Distillation) reframes multi-teacher distillation as an instance-wise decision process with two adaptive mechanisms: (1) a Contextual Router that dynamically selects the most relevant teacher per instance based on local input statistics, exploiting complementarity across diverse foundation models; and (2) an Uncertainty-Gated Temperature mechanism that acts as a "circuit-breaker," attenuating distillation strength when teacher confidence diverges from domain reality.
AI.result: Evaluated on four climate-critical domains (meteorology, ecosystem carbon flux, soil moisture, and energy grids), Guard significantly reduces RMSE compared to a fixed-weight multi-teacher distillation baseline. Domain-misaligned teachers still provide critical corrective value, outperforming globally superior FMs on 28.5% of the hardest instances. The method successfully distills useful knowledge even from teachers with suboptimal zero-shot accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Domain-misaligned foundation models retain valuable structural knowledge that can be effectively extracted via instance-wise adaptive distillation. Guard enables high-precision scientific forecasting suitable for resource-constrained edge deployment, bridging the gap between powerful but misaligned FMs and practical deployment requirements in physical science sensor networks.

title: Stellar: Scalable Multimodal Document Retrieval for Natural Language Queries
summary: Multimodal document retrieval--selecting the most relevant multimodal document from a large corpus to answer a natural language query--plays an essential role in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. State-of-the-art methods represent each document and query with multiple token-level embeddings and use late interaction to achieve high effectiveness. However, such multi-vector representations incur substantial memory overhead during retrieval, leading to poor scalability and hindering real-world deployment. In this paper, we present Stellar, a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that stores token-level document embeddings on disk and loads only a small set of candidate embeddings into memory for late interaction. Stellar comprises two key components: (i) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a sparse encoder to produce high-quality lexical representations, enabling efficient and effective document filtering to significantly reduce the candidate set; (ii) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which designs an on-disk token embedding storage layout guided by a balanced clustering algorithm, and dynamically loads only the necessary token embeddings into memory using a simple yet effective cost model. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks and a newly presented large-scale dataset demonstrate that Stellar reduces memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods without compromising retrieval effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Stellar is a scalable multimodal document retrieval framework that uses on-disk token embeddings with lexical filtering to reduce memory overhead by 1-2 orders of magnitude while maintaining retrieval effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-vector retrieval methods for multimodal documents incur substantial memory overhead (storing all token-level embeddings in RAM), leading to poor scalability and hindering real-world RAG deployment.
AI.method: Stellar introduces two components: (1) Lexical Representation-based Filtering (LRF), which fine-tunes an MLLM as a sparse encoder to produce lexical representations for efficient candidate filtering; (2) Efficient Disk-backed Late Interaction (DLI), which uses balanced clustering to organize on-disk token embeddings and a cost model to dynamically load only necessary embeddings into memory.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmarks and a new large-scale dataset show Stellar reduces both memory overhead and query latency by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to existing methods, with no loss in retrieval effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Stellar enables practical, scalable deployment of high-quality multimodal document retrieval for RAG systems by decoupling storage (disk) from computation (memory) without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Building Drift: Documenting On-Site Construction Adaptations Across Material Lifecycles
summary:
In a circular economy for construction, reclaimed materials carry prior lives of use and go on to have post-lives in future buildings. Yet working with such materials introduces unpredictability that requires on-site improvisation, making their reuse challenging to document and scale across building lifetimes. Without documentation, the on-site adaptations that make construction with reclaimed materials possible leave collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without the information they need to continue, assess, and reuse materials. We call the collective deviation of the physical state from the digital model through these adaptations "building drift." Through a case study, ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion constructed in the forest, we develop a taxonomy for building drift that characterizes the collective deviation across building lifetimes: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities.
  To put our taxonomy for building drift into practice, we present Pentimento, a documentation tool that leverages video documentation and 3D Gaussian Splatting to spatially, temporally, and semantically represent on-site adaptations in relation to the designed model. Pentimento enables each stakeholder to navigate material histories in ways that reduce barriers to material reuse. Together, these contributions open pathways towards computational tools that support the on-site improvisation essential to construction with reclaimed materials, enabling more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "building drift" — the collective deviation between physical state and digital model caused by on-site adaptations when working with reclaimed materials. Through the ReShelter case study, it develops a taxonomy of five drift types and presents Pentimento, a tool using video and 3D Gaussian Splatting to document these adaptations spatially, temporally, and semantically, enabling better material reuse across building lifetimes.
AI.motivation: Reclaimed materials in circular construction carry prior histories and introduce unpredictability requiring on-site improvisation. These ad-hoc adaptations are rarely documented, leaving future collaborators, evaluators, and inheritors without critical information needed to continue, assess, and reuse materials across building lifetimes. This documentation gap fundamentally limits the scalability of sustainable material reuse practices.
AI.method: The authors conduct a case study of ReShelter, a reclaimed timber pavilion built in a forest setting. From this, they develop a taxonomy of "building drift" with five categories: Tending the Site, Foraging for Fit, Interpreting the Material, Marking Measurements, and Coordinating Across Communities. They then design and present Pentimento, a documentation tool that combines video documentation with 3D Gaussian Splatting to capture on-site adaptations spatially, temporally, and semantically in relation to the original digital model.
AI.result: The taxonomy provides a structured vocabulary for characterizing how physical construction deviates from digital models when using reclaimed materials. Pentimento demonstrates a practical computational approach to documenting these deviations, enabling stakeholders to navigate material histories and reducing barriers to reuse.
AI.conclusion: By formalizing building drift and providing computational tools to document it, the work opens pathways toward digital systems that embrace rather than resist the on-site improvisation essential to reclaimed material construction, ultimately supporting more sustainable cycles of recovery, repair, and reuse in the built environment.

title: G-Lox: Group-Adaptive, Privacy-Preserving Bridge Distribution with Two-Party Computation
summary:
We present G-Lox (group-adaptive Lox), a bridge-distribution system that preserves Lox-style distributor blindness while enabling hidden, stateful group-level adaptation. G-Lox places adaptive assignment logic behind a two-server privacy wall, so no single server learns group identifiers or group-to-bridge assignments. Private state access and state-dependent updates use two-server DPF/FSS protocols and secure two-party computation, supporting blockage reporting, transport-aware reassignment, and privacy-preserving group splitting.
  We evaluate G-Lox through system measurements and policy simulation. In our C++/EMP implementation over real TCP sockets, private state access has low client-visible overhead: across state sizes up to 2^16, communication remains in the low-KiB range per iteration. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in about 0.25 s. Simulations with group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration show that G-Lox improves robustness over Lox- and rBridge-like baselines among systems that maintain broad issuance.

AI.tldr: G-Lox extends the Lox bridge-distribution system with privacy-preserving group-level adaptation. It uses a two-server architecture and secure multi-party computation (DPF/FSS, 2PC) to enable group-specific state management — including blockage reporting, transport reassignment, and group splitting — without any single server learning group identities. Evaluated on real TCP sockets, it achieves low overhead (≈2 KiB communication, ~0.25 s per iteration) and improves robustness against Sybil and blocking attacks compared to Lox and rBridge baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing bridge-distribution systems like Lox provide distributor blindness (the distributor cannot link users to assigned bridges) but lack group-level adaptation. This creates a tension: to counter targeted blocking and Sybil attacks, the system needs group-specific state and reassignment logic, yet revealing group identifiers to any single server would undermine privacy. G-Lox addresses this gap by enabling stateful group-adaptive policies while preserving blindness.
AI.method: G-Lox splits adaptive assignment logic across two non-colluding servers behind a "privacy wall." It employs Distributed Point Functions (DPF) and Function Secret Sharing (FSS) for private state access, combined with secure two-party computation (2PC) for state-dependent updates. Key operations include privacy-preserving blockage reporting, transport-aware bridge reassignment, and group splitting — all executed without either server learning group IDs or group-to-bridge mappings.
AI.result: In a C++/EMP implementation over real TCP sockets, private state access incurs low client-visible overhead: communication stays in the low-KiB range for state sizes up to 2^16. At M=1024, the client sends 1,968 bytes, receives 1,280 bytes, and completes an iteration in approximately 0.25 seconds. Policy simulations show G-Lox improves robustness against group-specific blocking and Sybil enumeration compared to Lox and rBridge baselines, all while maintaining broad bridge issuance.
AI.conclusion: G-Lox demonstrates that group-adaptive, stateful bridge distribution is practical without sacrificing distributor blindness. The two-server DPF/FSS + 2PC architecture enables meaningful group-level policies (blockage response, transport reassignment, splitting) at low overhead, yielding improved anti-censorship robustness while preserving the privacy guarantees that distinguish Lox-like systems from less private alternatives.

title: Disentangling Linguistic Relatedness from Task Alignment in Cross-Lingual Transfer
summary: We study cross-lingual transfer by fine-tuning seven large language models (4B--671B parameters) on Arabic and evaluating zero-shot reading comprehension on Semitic languages and non-Semitic controls. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, we find no evidence of Semitic-specific transfer: models with weak baselines improve dramatically across all languages, while strong-baseline models show only marginal gains regardless of language family. A chain-of-thought ablation reinforces this finding -- the same models that benefit most from fine-tuning benefit equally from inference-time reasoning, suggesting both mechanisms address task-format alignment rather than cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
