AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic improves zero-shot reading comprehension universally, not selectively for Semitic languages. Gains are driven by task-format alignment rather than genuine cross-lingual knowledge transfer, as demonstrated by a chain-of-thought ablation yielding equivalent benefits.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether fine-tuning LLMs on Arabic yields cross-lingual transfer benefits specific to genetically related Semitic languages, or whether observed improvements are attributable to more general mechanisms like task-format alignment.
AI.method: Seven LLMs (4B–671B parameters), spanning dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, are fine-tuned on Arabic. Zero-shot reading comprehension is evaluated on Semitic languages and non-Semitic control languages. A chain-of-thought ablation compares inference-time reasoning gains against fine-tuning gains to disentangle cross-lingual transfer from task-format alignment.
AI.result: No evidence of Semitic-specific transfer was found. Weak-baseline models improved dramatically across all languages (Semitic and non-Semitic alike). Strong-baseline models exhibited only marginal gains regardless of language family. The chain-of-thought ablation showed that models benefiting most from fine-tuning also benefited equally from inference-time reasoning, implicating task-format alignment as the operative mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual transfer gains from Arabic fine-tuning reflect task-format familiarization rather than phylogenetic knowledge sharing. Both fine-tuning and chain-of-thought prompting serve to bridge this format gap, with neither mechanism delivering language-family-specific advantages.

title: Blame is easier than praise: Measuring off-ball defensive performance in football
summary: The defensive performance of football players is commonly measured through a limited number of actions like tackles and interceptions while their continuous impact through positional behaviour has hardly been studied before. We formulate this problem as an attribution over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth labels, where event-level changes of expected threat are distributed among individuals. We propose a framework that performs this attribution using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). By computing role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures, we can determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through arbitrary passes. The validity and robustness of this approach are evaluated on a uniquely extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data set, including positional and event data from 64 matches of the men's World Cup, 116 matches of the women's German Bundesliga and 336 matches of the men's German 3. Liga. In the absence of a ground truth, we propose an evaluation protocol that combines multiple relatively weak proxies into robust summary scores. We find a validity score that is improved by around 1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric and demonstrate that many popular measures show limited validity. The "blame" for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric in football to reliably measure positioning errors. All code underlying this work is publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework to attribute defensive responsibility in football by analyzing continuous positional behavior through defensive pressure areas (DPAs), rather than relying solely on discrete actions like tackles. It evaluates involvement scores using role-conditioned baselines and team structure detection, demonstrating improved validity over action-based metrics across extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data.
AI.motivation: Traditional defensive metrics (tackles, interceptions) capture only discrete actions and miss the continuous positional impact of defenders. No prior work reliably quantifies defensive positioning errors from spatiotemporal trajectory data without ground-truth labels.
AI.method: The framework formulates defensive attribution as distributing event-level changes in expected threat across players using involvement scores derived from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). Role-conditioned baselines are computed within automatically detected team formations (via clustering), allowing estimation of each defender's expected responsibility for threat created by passes. Since no ground truth exists, a multi-proxy evaluation protocol combines weak proxies (e.g., external ratings, market values) into robust summary validity scores.
AI.result: The proposed validity score improves by approximately 1 standard deviation over the best action-based metric. The "blame" metric for conceding high-value actions correlates strongly with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric to reliably measure defensive positioning errors. The approach is validated on 518 matches across men's and women's competitions.
AI.conclusion: Continuous positional analysis via DPAs and role-conditioned baselines provides a more valid and robust measure of defensive performance than traditional action-based metrics. The framework is reproducible (code publicly available) and represents the first reliable quantification of defensive positioning errors in football analytics.

title: DynAMO:Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration via Topological Multi-Agent Scheduling
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, 4 algorithms. Evaluated on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark. Code: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO
summary:
While LLM-powered agents offer end-to-end automation for industrial asset lifecycles, real-world Industry 4.0 deployment is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. We present DynAMO (Dynamic Asset Management Orchestration), a deployment-ready engine using a Plan-then-Execute architecture to generate verifiable workflow graphs. DynAMO supports both SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). By dynamically identifying independent tasks, DynAMO preserves structural correctness and safety while significantly improving efficiency through controlled reasoning overlap.
  Across six controlled experiments on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark, DynAMO demonstrates substantial performance and robustness gains. Parallel execution reduces end-to-end latency by a median of 1.6x over sequential orchestration, rising to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows. After instrumenting external tool calls with realistic latencies, a latency decomposition shows that LLM reasoning and orchestration still account for more than 90% of execution time, identifying model inference as the primary system bottleneck. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by approximately 30%, and DynAMO maintains correct functional behaviour (task completion, agent sequencing, and output quality) while exhibiting graceful degradation under controlled fault injection. Reproducibility analysis further confirms stable execution under repeated runs, with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance. These findings establish DynAMO as a practical blueprint for scalable, safe, and latency-aware agent deployment in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines. Code is available at: https://github.com/kushwaha001/DynAMO

AI.tldr: DynAMO is a deployment-ready LLM agent engine for Industry 4.0 that uses Plan-then-Execute architecture with parallel workflow execution to reduce latency by 1.6-1.8x while maintaining safety and correctness under fault conditions.
AI.motivation: Real-world Industry 4.0 deployment of LLM-powered agents is hindered by latency, concurrency instability, and safety risks. Existing approaches lack efficient, verifiable orchestration that balances speed with structural correctness for industrial asset lifecycle automation.
AI.method: DynAMO employs a Plan-then-Execute architecture that generates verifiable workflow graphs supporting two execution modes: SequentialWorkflow (topological execution) and ParallelWorkflow (dependency-aware concurrency). It dynamically identifies independent tasks to enable controlled reasoning overlap. Additional techniques include structured context pruning to reduce inference latency, realistic latency instrumentation for external tool calls, and controlled fault injection for robustness testing. Experiments were conducted across six controlled scenarios on the AssetOpsBench industrial benchmark.
AI.result: Parallel execution achieves median 1.6x end-to-end latency reduction (up to 1.8x on highly parallelizable workflows). LLM reasoning and orchestration account for >90% of execution time. Structured context pruning reduces inference latency by ~30%. DynAMO maintains correct functional behavior (task completion, agent sequencing, output quality) with graceful degradation under fault injection. Reproducibility analysis confirms stable execution with parallel scheduling reducing latency variance.
AI.conclusion: DynAMO provides a practical, scalable, safe, and latency-aware blueprint for deploying LLM agents in Industry 4.0 automation pipelines, with model inference identified as the primary system bottleneck.

title: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized language modeling through autoregressive generation, enabling strong performance across a wide range of tasks. Recently, Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as an alternative paradigm that generates text through iterative denoising rather than next-token prediction, allowing parallel refinement of entire sequences. While numerous diffusion-based architectures have been proposed, differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare their capabilities and understand the trade-offs they offer. In this work, we present a systematic experimental analysis of modern DLMs. Specifically, we evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, and structured problem solving, while explicitly considering both generation quality and computational efficiency. Beyond downstream evaluation, we analyze the impact of key inference-time factors, including denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, and complement large-scale experiments with controlled comparisons of smaller models trained under identical conditions. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of diffusion-based language modeling across different tasks, architectures, and inference budgets. We show that the behavior of DLMs is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, leading to distinct trade-offs between performance and computational efficiency. Overall, our study provides practical insights into the capabilities and deployment characteristics of contemporary DLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic experimental comparison of eight state-of-the-art Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) across eight benchmarks, analyzing the trade-offs between generation quality and computational efficiency, and examining how inference-time design choices (denoising steps, context length, block size, parallel unmasking) impact performance.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of diverse DLM architectures has created a landscape where differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and hyperparameters obscure meaningful comparison. There is a need for a unified, controlled analysis to understand the capabilities, limitations, and practical trade-offs of diffusion-based language modeling relative to autoregressive LLMs.
AI.method: The authors evaluate eight state-of-the-art DLMs across eight diverse benchmarks (reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, structured problem solving). They systematically vary inference-time factors — number of denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies — and conduct controlled comparisons using smaller models trained under identical conditions to isolate architectural effects.
AI.result: DLM behavior is strongly influenced by generation-time design choices, revealing distinct trade-offs between performance and efficiency. The study quantifies these trade-offs across tasks and architectures, highlighting where DLMs excel and where they fall short compared to each other and implicitly to autoregressive baselines.
AI.conclusion: DLMs offer a viable alternative to autoregressive generation with unique parallel refinement capabilities, but their practical deployment requires careful tuning of inference hyperparameters. The paper provides actionable insights for selecting and configuring DLMs based on task requirements and computational budgets.

title: Closing the Social-Semantic Gap: SPSD for Edge-Based Prompt Compression in Cloud LLM Inference
summary: The prefill stage of Large Language Model (LLM) inference is a growing contributor to cloud-scale energy cost. Many consumer-support and conversational prompts contain social scaffolding: politeness markers, apologetic preamble, repetition, and rapport-building language that is important for human communication but carries low marginal information for machine reasoning. We call this discrepancy the Social-Semantic Gap. We present SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation), an edge-based pipeline that compresses user prompts using a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model before transmission to a cloud-deployed LLM. Evaluation on a 248-prompt corpus using Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) as the SLM and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud evaluation model yields a mean input token saving of 99.9 tokens per distilled call, with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. Response quality, assessed by blind LLM-as-judge scoring across 121 pairs, is non-inferior to the raw path within a pre-specified 1-point margin on a 15-point rubric; the judge awarded 43 percent ties, 28 percent distilled wins, and 29 percent raw wins. Cosine similarity is mixed: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1 percent of pairs above the 0.70 reference threshold. Safety-critical domains are conservatively routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Per-call net energy saving is estimated at 70-270 uWh under stated assumptions. SPSD shows that on-device prompt distillation can reduce cloud LLM input-token cost while preserving response quality within a practical non-inferiority margin.

AI.tldr: SPSD uses a quantized small language model on edge devices to distill verbose, socially scaffolded user prompts before sending them to cloud LLMs, saving ~100 input tokens per call with non-inferior response quality.
AI.motivation: User prompts to cloud-deployed LLMs contain substantial "social scaffolding" (politeness markers, apologies, repetition, rapport-building) that is important for human interaction but semantically redundant for machine reasoning. This Social-Semantic Gap wastes cloud inference energy, contributing significantly to operational costs and environmental impact at scale. The authors seek an edge-based compression solution that preserves semantic intent while stripping low-information social content.
AI.method: The SPSD pipeline deploys a 4-bit quantized Small Language Model (Gemma-2-2B-Instruct Q4_K_M) on edge devices to distill user prompts before cloud transmission. The SLM is prompted to remove social scaffolding while preserving core semantic content and sentiment. A 248-prompt corpus is evaluated using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud LLM. Response quality is measured via blind LLM-as-judge scoring on a 15-point rubric with a 1-point non-inferiority margin, plus cosine similarity analysis. Safety-critical domains are protected by rule-based passthrough gates that bypass distillation.
AI.result: Mean input token savings of 99.9 tokens per distilled call; all 146 distilled calls achieved positive savings. Blind LLM-as-judge evaluation (121 pairs): 43% ties, 28% distilled wins, 29% raw wins — non-inferior within the 1-point margin. Cosine similarity: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1% of pairs exceeding the 0.70 threshold. Estimated per-call net energy savings: 70–270 μWh.
AI.conclusion: On-device prompt distillation via a quantized SLM can substantially reduce cloud LLM input-token costs while maintaining response quality within a practical non-inferiority boundary, demonstrating a viable edge-compute approach to narrowing the Social-Semantic Gap and improving cloud inference energy efficiency.

title: PACMS: Submodular Context Selection as a Pluggable Engine for LLM Agents
summary:
Conversational and tool-using LLM agents operate over a context window that fills from several directions simultaneously. As a session proceeds, the agent accumulates user and assistant turns, entries drawn from a persistent memory store, and often largest of all, the verbatim outputs of tool calls such as file reads, search results, and API responses. Once the cumulative context exceeds the model's token budget, the framework must decide what to keep.
  The prevailing mechanism is recency truncation, sometimes paired with periodic summarization. This is topic-blind: a fact established early in a session is discarded simply because it is old, even when the current user query is about exactly that fact; conversely, verbose but irrelevant recent material is retained. Agents that must recall information across many turns, the defining case for memory, are precisely where recency truncation fails.
  Existing alternatives sit outside the agent's assembly step. Retrieval augmented generation fetches external documents into the prompt but does not arbitrate the agent's \emph{already-present} pooled context. Context-compression methods reduce token count by rewriting or pruning text, but operate query-blind and lossily. Neither treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single candidate pool to be selected from by relevance at the moment the prompt is assembled.

AI.tldr: Current LLM agents manage overflowing context windows using recency-based truncation, which discards old but relevant information while keeping recent noise. The authors identify that existing alternatives (RAG and context compression) fail to treat conversation, memory, and tool outputs as a unified pool from which relevance-based selection occurs at prompt assembly time.
AI.motivation: LLM agents face a context window overflow problem as sessions accumulate conversation turns, memory entries, and verbose tool outputs. The dominant solution—recency truncation—is topic-blind: it discards old but query-relevant facts while retaining recent irrelevant material. This is particularly catastrophic for memory-dependent agents that must recall information across many turns. Existing alternatives either operate outside the prompt assembly step (RAG retrieves external documents, not from the agent's already-present context) or are query-blind and lossy (context compression), and none treat all context types as a unified candidate pool for relevance-based selection.
AI.method: This is an abstract only; the paper proposes a framework that, at prompt assembly time, treats memory entries, conversation turns, and tool outputs as a single unified candidate pool and selects what to retain based on relevance to the current query, rather than relying on recency or query-blind compression.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract; the abstract focuses on problem formulation and critique of existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: A relevance-driven, unified selection mechanism operating at prompt assembly time is needed to replace topic-blind recency truncation, addressing the core failure mode of context window management in conversational and tool-using LLM agents.

title: Syndesmoscope: The Power of Invariant Plots\\Linked to Traditional Network Views
summary: Traditional network representations, such as node-link views and adjacency matrices, can show dramatically different visual patterns, depending on the underlying layout or seriation algorithm. In contrast, invariant plots consistently surface the same visual pattern for the same input topology; yet researchers have underexplored them and have not integrated them into visualization systems. We present Syndesmoscope, an interactive system for network exploration that juxtaposes multiple views of the same network. Panes show a familiar a force-directed view alongside three panes with interpretable geometric layouts based on graph-theoretic properties: dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, and spectral bisection. As a secondary contribution, we introduce kSnakes, a new invariant plot based on density decomposition. Syndesmoscope supports two key interactions: leapfrogging, or linked highlighting between different and interpretable visual patterns; and hopscotching, or hop-based traversal that extends data selections through the underlying topology. Through usage scenarios across a corpus of 72 diverse networks, we demonstrate how these interactions reveal network patterns inaccessible through any single view alone. Live demo available at https://syndesmoscope.vercel.app/.

AI.tldr: Syndesmoscope is an interactive network exploration system that juxtaposes force-directed layouts with three invariant geometric layouts (dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, spectral bisection) and introduces kSnakes, a novel invariant plot based on density decomposition. Key interactions — leapfrogging (linked highlighting) and hopscotching (hop-based traversal) — enable discovery of patterns inaccessible through any single view.
AI.motivation: Traditional network visualizations (node-link, adjacency matrices) produce inconsistent visual patterns depending on layout or seriation algorithms. Invariant plots guarantee consistent patterns for the same topology but remain underexplored and unintegrated into practical visualization systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap by combining familiar and invariant views in a unified interactive system.
AI.method: The authors developed Syndesmoscope, a multi-pane system displaying four coordinated views: (1) a force-directed layout, (2) a dense-sparse gradient layout, (3) a geodesic eccentricity layout, and (4) a spectral bisection layout. They also contribute kSnakes, a new invariant plot using density decomposition. The system supports two interaction techniques: leapfrogging (linked cross-pane highlighting to connect patterns across views) and hopscotching (extending selections through the graph topology via hop-based traversal). Evaluation is conducted through usage scenarios on a corpus of 72 diverse networks.
AI.result: Usage scenarios across 72 networks demonstrate that the combination of juxtaposed invariant and traditional views, coupled with leapfrogging and hopscotching interactions, reveals structural network patterns that no single view can expose alone.
AI.conclusion: Invariant geometric layouts, when juxtaposed with traditional views and augmented by cross-view linking and topology-aware selection traversal, significantly enhance network exploration and pattern discovery. The work validates the practical value of integrating underexplored invariant plots into interactive visualization systems.

title: PUFFERDOS: Efficient and Effective Attack String Generation for Regular Expression Denial of Service Vulnerabilities
summary: ReDoS attacks constitute a critical class of resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities. In such attacks, adversaries exploit the pathological worst-case execution behavior of regular expression (regex) engines to induce highly asymmetric computational workloads, ultimately exhausting system resources and degrading service availability. To protect systems against ReDoS attacks, numerous detection techniques have been proposed that simulate the attack process by generating attack strings to proactively exploit ReDoS vulnerabilities at the early development stage and facilitate remediation. Existing techniques broadly fall into two classes: static analyses that search for pathological regex structures, and dynamic exploration methods that synthesize candidate attack strings. However, the generated attack strings are often impractical for real-world exploitation because they usually assume unrealistic input-length budgets and do not validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the attack at the program level. Therefore, many generated strings fail to trigger vulnerable regexes when applied to real-world programs, further limiting the practical utility. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an effective and efficient attack string generator, PUFFERDOS, designed to synthesize attack inputs that are both feasible within realistic length budgets and validated at the program level, enabling effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs. Specifically, we first define three vulnerable patterns based on our observation and formal verification. According to the patterns, PUFFERDOS conducts a synthesis technique to generate attack strings, and then refines and validates the strings with ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to guarantee real-world exploitability.

AI.tldr: PUFFERDOS is an attack string generator for ReDoS vulnerabilities that produces inputs feasible within realistic length budgets and validated at the program level via compositional concolic execution, addressing the practical exploitability gap left by prior static and dynamic techniques.
AI.motivation: Existing ReDoS detection tools generate attack strings assuming unrealistic input-length budgets and fail to validate exploitability at the program level, rendering many generated strings ineffective against real-world programs and limiting practical utility.
AI.method: The authors first define three vulnerable regex patterns through observation and formal verification. PUFFERDOS then synthesizes attack strings based on these patterns and refines/validates them using ReDoS-specific compositional concolic execution to ensure feasibility within realistic length budgets and program-level exploitability.
AI.result: Not explicitly specified in the abstract; the paper claims PUFFERDOS enables effective exploitation of ReDoS vulnerabilities in real-world programs by synthesizing feasible, program-level-validated attack strings.
AI.conclusion: PUFFERDOS bridges the gap between theoretical ReDoS detection and practical exploitation by generating attack strings that respect realistic input-length constraints and are validated at the program level, thereby improving the real-world utility of ReDoS vulnerability detection and remediation.

title: How LLMs Fail and Generalize in RTL Coding for Hardware Design?
summary: Translating sequential programming priors into the parallel temporal logic of hardware design remains a crucial bottleneck for large language models(LLM). To investigate this, we introduce a new error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability, inspired by cognitive theory. Our taxonomy categorizes failures into syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional types. Evaluations reveal a strict empirical ceiling on the VerilogEval benchmark, as frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate. These plateaus are defined by unsolvable functional errors, exposing persistent knowledge gaps immune to test time compute scaling. Furthermore, we expose a striking surface convergence gap: optimization readily eliminates syntax errors but concurrently exacerbates deeper functional failures. Our findings demonstrate that alignment techniques merely teach models to compile. While repeated sampling strategies can patch solvable errors, register-transfer level(RTL) coding capacity remains strictly bounded by pretraining knowledge. Addressing challenges in the current LLM based hardware generation pipeline requires more studies in model reasoning rather than alignment interventions.

AI.tldr: LLMs plateau at ~90.8% pass rate on VerilogEval due to unsolvable functional errors rooted in pretraining knowledge gaps. Alignment techniques only teach models to compile, while optimization for syntax inadvertently worsens functional correctness. True progress requires reasoning improvements, not alignment interventions.
AI.motivation: Translating sequential programming knowledge into hardware description languages (HDLs) like Verilog requires reasoning in parallel temporal logic, a skill LLMs struggle with. The authors aim to systematically diagnose why frontier models hit a performance ceiling on hardware design benchmarks, moving beyond superficial metrics to understand the nature and origins of failures.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability (inspired by cognitive theory), categorizing failures into four types: syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional. Using this taxonomy, they evaluate frontier LLMs on the VerilogEval benchmark, analyzing pass rates, error distributions, and the effects of test-time compute scaling, alignment techniques, and repeated sampling strategies.
AI.result: Frontier models plateau at a 90.8% initial pass rate on VerilogEval. This ceiling is driven by unsolvable functional errors that are immune to test-time compute scaling. A "surface convergence gap" emerges: optimization eliminates syntax errors but concurrently worsens deeper functional failures. Repeated sampling can patch solvable errors, but RTL coding capacity remains fundamentally bounded by pretraining knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Alignment techniques merely teach models to produce compilable code without ensuring functional correctness. Addressing the hardware generation bottleneck requires advancing model reasoning capabilities rather than relying on alignment interventions or compute scaling alone.

title: Human-like autonomy emerges from self-play and a pinch of human data
summary: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500x fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and full source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.

AI.tldr: A self-play RL method for autonomous driving that uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations as a regularizer, achieving human-compatible driving policies trained on a single GPU in 15 hours — 2500× less data than imitation learning approaches.
AI.motivation: Pure self-play RL for driving policies produces effective but "alien" driving behaviors incompatible with human drivers. Prior mitigations (reward engineering, domain randomization) are brittle and labor-intensive. The authors seek a sample-efficient way to align self-play policies with human driving conventions without requiring massive human demonstration datasets.
AI.method: The method uses a minimal safe goal-reaching reward as the base RL objective and adds human demonstrations as a regularization term — treating the small amount of human data as a "spice" rather than the main ingredient. This contrasts with pure imitation learning and pure self-play, combining the strengths of both.
AI.result: The resulting policies coordinate successfully with held-out human trajectories, using only 30 minutes of human demonstrations (2500× less than comparable imitation learning methods). Training completes in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU.
AI.conclusion: A small amount of human demonstration data used as regularization (rather than as the primary learning signal) is sufficient to align self-play RL driving policies with human conventions, dramatically reducing data requirements while preserving the benefits of simulation-based self-play training.

title: Bistable by Construction: Wall-Clock-Calibrated State Monitors Have No Moment-Detection Regime at Agent Cadence
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Sequel to arXiv:2606.04296. Pre-registered; falsification clauses honored (H5 unsupported; H7 strict band 16/20) repo:https://github.com/2025eb1100268-tech/intervention-timing-saturation-trap
summary: Runtime monitors for autonomous agents commonly threshold an accumulated internal state - a behavioural baseline, a drift statistic, or, in our prior work, a modelled affective state. We previously reported a State Saturation Trap: threshold-on-state triggers over a continuous affect engine become near-constant alarms on SWE-bench debugging agents (Modgil 2026). A post-release audit found the engine received dt=0 between actions, so its exponential decay never operated: the published trap is a pure-accumulator result. We correct the record (erratum, v2) and treat the flaw as an experiment. The key variable it exposes is whether a monitor's dynamics are calibrated in sample time (per observation, as in CUSUM) or wall-clock time (half-lives in seconds, as in affect models and EMA baselines). On fixed-rate streams these coincide; on agent streams, where inter-action time varies by orders of magnitude, they do not. A pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt in {0..600}s) on 20 trajectories shows the wall-clock level trigger has two regimes: at dt<=1s a constant alarm (20/20; median 18 firings); at dt>=60s silent. Every critical dt lies in (1,30]s. Real agent runs measure latency at median 1.53s (p90 2.33s); real coding cadence sits inside the trap regime, vindicating the empirical finding under a corrected mechanism. The structure is a property of the calibration class, not the engine: a minimal wall-clock accumulator over the raw error stream reproduces the same cliff, while a sample-time CUSUM over the identical stream is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). A rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0-3 times per trajectory in every condition. We conclude that wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime in which they act as moment detectors on agent streams; transition detection escapes the trap at every cadence, but does not recover human intervention timing.

AI.tldr: A prior paper reported a "State Saturation Trap" where threshold-based monitors on affect engines triggered near-constant alarms. An audit revealed the engine received dt=0 between actions (no decay), making it a pure accumulator. The corrected experiment shows wall-clock-calibrated monitors (exponential decay in seconds) exhibit a critical dt regime (1–30s) where they either constantly alarm or go silent, matching real agent latencies (~1.53s median). In contrast, sample-time methods like CUSUM are dt-invariant, and rising-edge triggers with hysteresis remain stable. The trap is a property of calibration class, not the specific engine.
AI.motivation: To correct a prior erroneous finding (Modgil 2026) where a runtime monitor exhibited a "State Saturation Trap," and to systematically investigate why wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors fail on autonomous agent streams with variable inter-action times, distinguishing sample-time vs. wall-clock-time calibration as the root cause.
AI.method: Post-release audit identifying the dt=0 bug; pre-registered sweep over uniform intervals (dt ∈ {0…600}s) across 20 trajectories testing the wall-clock level trigger; comparison of three monitor types: (1) wall-clock leaky integrator over raw error, (2) sample-time CUSUM over identical stream, and (3) rising-edge trigger with hysteresis; real agent latency measurement (median 1.53s, p90 2.33s).
AI.result: Wall-clock level trigger shows two regimes: dt ≤ 1s → constant alarms (20/20 trajectories, median 18 firings); dt ≥ 60s → silent. All critical dt values lie in (1, 30]s. Real agent latency (median 1.53s) falls within the trap regime. A minimal wall-clock accumulator reproduces the same cliff; sample-time CUSUM is exactly dt-invariant (20/20). Rising-edge trigger with hysteresis fires 0–3 times per trajectory across all conditions.
AI.conclusion: Wall-clock-calibrated leaky-integrator monitors admit no regime where they function as moment detectors on agent streams with variable inter-action times. Transition detection escapes the trap at all cadences but cannot recover human intervention timing. The failure is structural to the calibration class, not specific to any engine.

title: Hidden Anchors in Multi-Agent LLM Deliberation
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation, where agents exchange and revise answers over several rounds, is increasingly used to improve reasoning and accuracy, yet how and why it works is rarely modelled. Such deliberation mirrors how humans reach decisions. As social animals we are pulled both by the group, the herd effect that classical opinion-dynamics models such as DeGroot and Friedkin--Johnsen capture, and by our own internal belief, which they do not. We model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system in which each agent carries a hidden internal belief, its anchor, that continually pulls its opinion regardless of its neighbours. We show this anchor can be recovered from the deliberation alone, and that it explains a behaviour classical consensus rules forbid: an agent's confidence in the correct answer can climb past where any agent started, escaping the space (convexhull) formed by the initial beliefs. Checking whether the recovered anchor also predicts held-out runs (generalizes) gives a simple test for when a model is truly driven bysuch an anchor. Across three open-weight model families this is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing. All anchors' influence are about equally strongly, but they differ in where the anchor sits, and only when it sits far from the initial opinions does deliberation escape the hull and need the full closed-loop model.

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-agent LLM deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal "anchor" belief that continually pulls its opinion. This anchor can be recovered from deliberation data and explains why agent confidence can exceed the initial belief convex hull. The model generalizes classical opinion-dynamics models (DeGroot, Friedkin-Johnsen) and provides a test for when anchor-driven behavior is present.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM deliberation improves reasoning and accuracy, but the underlying mechanism is poorly understood. Classical opinion-dynamics models like DeGroot and Friedkin-Johnsen capture the "herd effect" (conformity to group), but fail to model an agent's persistent internal belief — analogous to humans being pulled both by group consensus and personal conviction. The authors aim to formalize this dual pull to explain emergent behaviors like confidence surpassing initial beliefs.
AI.method: The authors model multi-agent deliberation as a closed-loop dynamical system where each agent has a hidden internal belief ("anchor") that exerts a constant pull on its expressed opinion, independent of neighbors. The anchor is recovered from deliberation trajectories alone. They test whether the recovered anchor generalizes to held-out runs as a diagnostic for genuine anchor-driven behavior. Experiments span three open-weight LLM families, examining whether deliberation escapes the convex hull of initial beliefs and requires the full closed-loop model.
AI.result: The anchor can be reliably recovered from deliberation data. Anchor-driven behavior is a spectrum across model families, not all-or-nothing. All anchors exert roughly equal influence strength, but differ in where they sit. Only when the anchor sits far from initial opinions does deliberation escape the convex hull and require the full closed-loop model. The recovered anchor successfully predicts held-out runs when anchor-driven dynamics are genuinely present.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM deliberation can be effectively modeled as anchor-driven closed-loop dynamics, extending classical opinion-dynamics models. The anchor recovery method provides a principled test for when this mechanism is active. The spectrum of anchor influence across model families suggests deliberation quality depends on where internal anchors are positioned relative to initial beliefs.

title: Performance Analysis and Optimization of 3D Generative Diffusion Models across GPU Architectures
summary: Diffusion models have become essential for high-fidelity 3D MRI synthesis, yet their deployment remains constrained by substantial GPU resource demands arising from hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and a highly heterogeneous kernel behavior. This paper performs a comprehensive performance analysis of the state-of-the-art medical diffusion model, Med-DDPM, across three generations of NVIDIA architectures to study kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. We show that training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels, with inefficiencies arising from memory-access patterns, tensor-layout conversions, and limited Tensor Core utilization. Guided by these insights, we evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations TF32 Tensor Core activation and a 3D channels-last layout and demonstrate that they reduce SM cycles by up to 100x, cut dynamic instructions by 100x, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45 to 9.98x, and increase IPC by 7% on A100, all without degrading synthesis quality.

AI.tldr: A performance analysis of the Med-DDPM 3D MRI diffusion model across three NVIDIA GPU generations reveals that training is dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels with inefficiencies in memory access and Tensor Core utilization. Architecture-aware optimizations (TF32 Tensor Core activation and 3D channels-last layout) yield up to 100× reduction in SM cycles and dynamic instructions, a ~7× increase in Tensor Core utilization, and 7% IPC improvement on A100, without degrading synthesis quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models for 3D MRI synthesis produce high-fidelity results but are prohibitively expensive in GPU resources due to hundreds of U-Net evaluations per sample and heterogeneous kernel behavior. Understanding the low-level performance bottlenecks across GPU architectures is essential to make these models more deployable in clinical and research settings.
AI.method: The authors perform a comprehensive performance analysis of Med-DDPM across three NVIDIA GPU generations (V100, A100, H100), examining kernel-level runtime breakdowns, instruction-mix characteristics, memory system utilization, warp-level activities, and profiler priority-score estimates. Based on these insights, they evaluate two architecture-aware optimizations: enabling TF32 Tensor Core acceleration and converting tensors to a 3D channels-last memory layout.
AI.result: Training is overwhelmingly dominated by cuDNN convolution and implicit-GEMM kernels. The optimizations reduce SM cycles by up to 100×, cut dynamic instructions by 100×, raise Tensor Core utilization from 1.45× to 9.98×, and increase IPC by 7% on the A100, all while preserving synthesis quality.
AI.conclusion: Architecture-aware, low-level profiling reveals substantial inefficiencies in medical diffusion model training that can be mitigated with targeted optimizations, dramatically improving GPU efficiency without compromising output quality. This underscores the value of kernel-level analysis for deploying diffusion models in resource-constrained environments.

title: Generative Engine Optimization at Scale: Measuring Brand Visibility Across AI Search Engines
summary:
People increasingly get answers straight from AI search engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini rather than scrolling search results. Brands that once focused on search engine optimization (SEO) must now optimize for how these engines represent, cite, and recommend them -- a shift variously called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), and AI Search Visibility. We treat AEO and AI Visibility as part of GEO, and study how to measure brand visibility across AI engines: what they value when they cite a brand, which sources they rely on, and what content large language models surface. The hard case is everyone outside the already-authoritative top brands -- SMEs, D2C brands, creators, and early-stage startups.
  We analyze 100K+ prompt responses across 100+ brands tracked on Ranqo between March and May 2026. First visibility runs form a clear three-tier brand-stature ladder: global household names (e.g., Stripe, Nike) appear in 73% of relevant AI answers on their first run; established mid-market and regional brands (e.g., Olipop, Klaviyo) in 44%; niche and small brands in just 11% -- about 30 percentage points per step. When engines cite sources, about 78% go to corporate websites; among non-corporate sources YouTube leads, ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. The highest-leverage page is the ranked "best-of" listicle, the most-cited content format at about 21% of all citations. Sentiment is the unstable signal: whether a brand is framed positively or negatively flips about 6.7 times more often than whether it is mentioned at all.
  These findings provide a first large-scale baseline for measuring GEO: AI brand visibility can be measured, differs by platform, and varies strongly by brand maturity. We close by proposing seven v1.1 protocols to test whether specific recommendations can causally improve AI visibility.

AI.tldr: A large-scale analysis of 100K+ AI search engine responses across 100+ brands reveals a three-tier visibility ladder (73% for household names, 44% for mid-market, 11% for niche brands). Corporate websites dominate citations (78%), "best-of" listicles are the most-cited format (21%), and sentiment is far more volatile than mention frequency. The paper proposes seven protocols for causally testing GEO strategies.
AI.motivation: As users shift from traditional search to AI engines (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini), brands need to understand how to optimize for AI-driven visibility. This is especially critical for non-authoritative brands — SMEs, D2C companies, creators, and startups — who lack the built-in authority of household names.
AI.method: The authors analyzed over 100,000 prompt responses across 100+ brands using the Ranqo tracking platform between March and May 2026. They measured brand mention rates, citation sources, content formats, and sentiment stability, stratifying brands by market stature to construct a visibility framework.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) A clear three-tier visibility hierarchy with ~30 percentage-point gaps between tiers. (2) Corporate websites receive ~78% of all citations; YouTube leads non-corporate sources ahead of Reddit, editorial media, and Wikipedia. (3) "Best-of" listicles are the single most-cited content format at ~21%. (4) Sentiment fluctuates ~6.7× more frequently than brand mentions, making it an unreliable signal.
AI.conclusion: AI brand visibility is measurable, platform-dependent, and strongly correlated with brand maturity. The authors propose seven v1.1 protocols as a framework for causally testing GEO interventions, establishing a baseline for the emerging field of Generative Engine Optimization.

title: Vibe Coding for Visualization Implementation: An Empirical Study of Practices and Challenges
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Short paper under review
summary: Data visualization is essential for data analysis and communication, yet creating expressive visualizations remains labor-intensive. Recent AI-driven ``vibe coding'' tools enable users to generate visualizations through natural language interaction, lowering the barrier to entry. However, visualization implementation requires precise alignment between user intent and visual representation, which may differ from general software development practices. We present an empirical study with 16 participants of varying expertise to examine how users employ vibe coding tools for visualization implementation. Participants completed two visualization tasks and a semi-structured interview. Our findings characterize the diverse practices users adopt across prompting, evaluation, and iteration, and surface the challenges they encounter throughout the process.

AI.tldr: An empirical study with 16 participants examines how users with varying expertise employ AI-driven "vibe coding" tools for data visualization, characterizing practices across prompting, evaluation, and iteration while surfacing key challenges.
AI.motivation: Creating expressive data visualizations is labor-intensive. While AI-driven "vibe coding" tools lower the entry barrier via natural language interaction, visualization implementation demands precise alignment between user intent and visual representation — a requirement that may diverge from general software development practices. Understanding how users actually employ these tools for visualization is thus critical.
AI.method: The authors conducted an empirical study with 16 participants of varying expertise levels. Participants completed two visualization implementation tasks using vibe coding tools, followed by semi-structured interviews to capture their experiences, practices, and challenges.
AI.result: The study characterizes diverse user practices across three key phases: prompting strategies, evaluation of generated output, and iterative refinement. It also surfaces the challenges users encounter throughout the visualization implementation process with vibe coding tools.
AI.conclusion: Vibe coding tools show promise for democratizing visualization creation, but the unique demands of visualization — particularly intent-to-representation alignment — require distinct interaction patterns and reveal gaps in current tool support that warrant further research and design attention.

title: A Layered Security Framework Against Prompt Injection in RAG-Based Chatbots
comment: Submitted in ICCK Transactions on Information Security and Cryptography
summary: Prompt injection is ranked as the most critical vulnerability in large language model (LLM) deployments by the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, yet existing defenses operate at isolated pipeline stages and remain incomplete. Input filters cannot inspect retrieved documents, while output monitors cannot prevent malicious payloads from reaching the model. Consequently, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbots remain vulnerable to indirect injection, where a poisoned knowledge-base document compromises every user whose query retrieves it. We present a three-layer framework that intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection throughout the inference pipeline. Layer 1 screens user input using a rule-based pattern library and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier. Layer 2 enforces a provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly, preventing retrieved content from overriding operator policy. Layer 3 audits model output using a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector before delivery. A continuous audit loop aggregates structured logs and supports retraining to adapt the classifier to emerging attack patterns. The framework is model-agnostic and deploys as middleware without modifying the underlying LLM. Evaluation on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B shows that the framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 71.4\% to 11.3\%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 percentage points and a published guardrail system by 23.8 percentage points, while maintaining a 4.8\% false positive rate and a median latency overhead of 61.2 ms. Ablation studies confirm that all three layers provide complementary protection and that their combined effect exceeds the sum of individual contributions.

AI.tldr: A three-layer middleware framework that intercepts both direct and indirect prompt injection attacks across the LLM inference pipeline, reducing Attack Success Rate from 71.4% to 11.3% while maintaining low false positive rate and latency overhead.
AI.motivation: Prompt injection is the top OWASP vulnerability for LLM applications, yet existing defenses are fragmented: input filters miss retrieved document attacks, and output monitors cannot block malicious payloads from reaching the model. This leaves RAG chatbots especially vulnerable to indirect injection via poisoned knowledge-base documents.
AI.method: A three-layer, model-agnostic middleware framework: (1) input screening using rule-based pattern matching and a fine-tuned semantic anomaly classifier; (2) provenance-based instruction hierarchy during context assembly to prevent retrieved content from overriding operator policy; (3) output auditing via a policy rule engine and semantic drift detector. A continuous audit loop aggregates logs and supports classifier retraining against emerging attacks.
AI.result: Evaluated on 5,080 samples across GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Mistral 7B, the framework reduced ASR from 71.4% to 11.3%, outperforming the best single-layer baseline by 27.3 pp and a published guardrail system by 23.8 pp, with a 4.8% false positive rate and 61.2 ms median latency overhead. Ablation studies confirmed all layers provide complementary, synergistic protection.
AI.conclusion: The three-layer defense-in-depth approach effectively mitigates both direct and indirect prompt injection attacks across multiple LLMs without model modification, demonstrating that complementary pipeline-stage defenses achieve greater protection than any single mechanism alone.

title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
summary: We present a preview version of DeepSeek-V4 series, including two strong Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models -- DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated) -- both supporting a context length of one million tokens. DeepSeek-V4 series incorporate several key upgrades in architecture and optimization: (1) a hybrid attention architecture that combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) to improve long-context efficiency; (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) that enhance conventional residual connections; (3) and the Muon optimizer for faster convergence and greater training stability. We pre-train both models on more than 32T diverse and high-quality tokens, followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline that unlocks and further enhances their capabilities. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max, the maximum reasoning effort mode of DeepSeek-V4-Pro, redefines the state-of-the-art for open models, outperforming its predecessors in core tasks. Meanwhile, DeepSeek-V4 series are highly efficient in long-context scenarios. In the one-million-token context setting, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache compared with DeepSeek-V3.2. This enables us to routinely support one-million-token contexts, thereby making long-horizon tasks and further test-time scaling more feasible. The model checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.

AI.tldr: DeepSeek-V4 introduces two MoE models (Pro: 1.6T/49B activated; Flash: 284B/13B activated) with 1M-token context. Key innovations include hybrid CSA/HCA attention, manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC), and the Muon optimizer. The Pro-Max reasoning mode sets new SOTA for open models, while achieving drastic efficiency gains: 27% inference FLOPs and 10% KV cache versus V3.2 at 1M-token contexts.
AI.motivation: To push the frontier of open-source large language models by improving long-context efficiency and reasoning capability, while addressing the computational bottlenecks (FLOPs, KV cache) that make million-token contexts impractical in prior architectures like DeepSeek-V3.2.
AI.method: (1) Hybrid attention: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) combined with Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) for long-context efficiency. (2) Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) to enhance residual connections. (3) Muon optimizer for faster, more stable training. Both MoE models are pre-trained on 32T+ tokens, followed by a comprehensive post-training pipeline. A maximum reasoning effort mode (Pro-Max) is introduced for DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Max achieves state-of-the-art results among open models on core tasks. At 1M-token context, DeepSeek-V4-Pro uses only 27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache compared to DeepSeek-V3.2, making long-horizon tasks and test-time scaling practically feasible.
AI.conclusion: The DeepSeek-V4 series represents a significant advancement in open-source MoE language models, combining architectural innovations (CSA, HCA, mHC) with training optimizations (Muon) to deliver both superior reasoning performance and breakthrough long-context efficiency at million-token scale.

title: Interpretable and Verifiable Hardware Generation with LLM-Driven Stepwise Refinement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in software development. However, they are susceptible to hallucinations, meaning that they can introduce subtle semantic and logical errors. Due to the high stakes in chip design and manufacturing, hardware engineers are still reluctant to rely on LLMs for register-transfer level (RTL) generation. In this paper, we propose a hardware generation framework that combines the creativity and broad knowledge of LLMs with the explainability and mathematical rigor of formal methods. Specifically, we devise a set of transformation rules that cover various design decisions and hardware features. By iteratively applying these rules, an LLM agent can convert a design specification into an RTL program with guaranteed correctness. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the framework.

AI.tldr: A framework combining LLMs with formal methods for verified RTL hardware generation, using iterative transformation rules to guarantee correctness.
AI.motivation: LLMs are prone to hallucinations and subtle errors, making them unreliable for safety-critical RTL generation in chip design, where correctness is paramount.
AI.method: A transformation-rule-based framework where an LLM agent iteratively applies a set of formal transformation rules (covering design decisions and hardware features) to convert a specification into a correct-by-construction RTL program.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and efficiency for verified RTL generation.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM creativity with formal method rigor via iterative rule-based transformations yields a practical and trustworthy hardware generation workflow.

title: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
summary: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

AI.tldr: DeXposure-Claw is an agentic supervision system for DeFi that uses a graph time-series foundation model (DeXposure-FM) to forecast exposure networks, then applies deterministic monitors and confidence gates to generate auditable, low-false-alarm supervisory tickets. It is evaluated with DeXposure-Bench, a regulator-aligned benchmark with a false-intervention rate metric.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM agents are ill-suited for DeFi supervision because they over-interpret weak signals, recommend disproportionate high-stakes interventions, and lack regulator-aligned evaluation frameworks to measure false alarms. There is a need for a structured, forecast-grounded system that produces auditable, calibrated supervisory actions.
AI.method: DeXposure-Claw routes LLM decisions through a three-stage pipeline: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future credit exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios convert forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation, producing auditable tickets with rationales. Evaluation uses DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis harness with a decision axis scoring tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate.
AI.result: Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support the proposed system, demonstrating its effectiveness over general-purpose LLM agents in the DeFi supervisory setting.
AI.conclusion: Structurally grounding LLM-based supervision in forecast networks, deterministic monitors, and confidence gating yields a regulator-compatible DeFi oversight system with auditable decisions and controlled false-intervention rates.

title: Information Lattice Learning as Probabilistic Graphical Model Structure Learning
summary: Information lattice learning (ILL) learns interpretable rules of a signal by alternately projecting the signal onto a partition lattice that encodes a hierarchy of abstractions and lifting selected rules back to the signal domain. When the signal is a probability mass function, we show the probabilistic rules learned by ILL admit a natural probabilistic graphical model (PGM) interpretation and develop this interpretation in detail. A partition in ILL induces a deterministic quotient variable, and a rule is the marginal law of that quotient variable. A rule set is therefore a collection of marginal constraints over interpretable abstractions. General lifting is the feasible family of all joint distributions satisfying those constraints, while special lifting chooses a maximum-ignorance reconstruction, implemented in ILL by an L2 uniformity principle closely related to maximum entropy. Under a Shannon-entropy lifting, the same constraints yield a log-linear factor graph whose factors are indexed by learned abstractions. The information lattice itself, however, is not a Bayesian network: its edges encode refinement and coarsening of abstractions, not conditional dependence. Thus ILL is best viewed as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables. This view clarifies how ILL relates to graphical models and maximum entropy models, while suggesting new directions for inference, identifiability, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning.

AI.tldr: Information Lattice Learning (ILL) learns interpretable probabilistic rules via partition lattice projections. The paper shows these rules correspond to marginal constraints on quotient variables, with lifting operations yielding factor graphs under maximum-entropy principles, establishing ILL as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs rather than Bayesian networks.
AI.motivation: To establish a formal probabilistic graphical model interpretation for Information Lattice Learning, clarifying how its learned rules, lattice structure, and lifting operations relate to existing frameworks like factor graphs, maximum entropy models, and Bayesian networks.
AI.method: The authors map ILL components onto PGM concepts: partitions induce deterministic quotient variables; rules correspond to marginal laws (constraints); general lifting defines the family of joint distributions satisfying those constraints; special lifting with an L2 uniformity principle (akin to maximum entropy) selects a maximum-ignorance reconstruction. Under Shannon-entropy lifting, constraints yield a log-linear factor graph whose factors are indexed by learned abstractions. The lattice edges encode refinement/coarsening, not conditional dependence.
AI.result: ILL is best characterized as structure learning for interpretable constraint-based factor graphs over quotient variables, not as a Bayesian network. This framing clarifies ILL's relationship to graphical models and maximum entropy models.
AI.conclusion: The factor-graph interpretation opens new directions for inference, identifiability analysis, and hybrid symbolic-probabilistic learning within the ILL framework.

title: ScholarQuest: A Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark for Agentic Academic Paper Search in Open Literature Environments
summary: Academic paper search is a core step in scientific research, and LLM-based search agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for iterative, intent-driven literature exploration. However, existing benchmarks are insufficient for systematically evaluating agentic academic search under realistic open literature environments. We propose ScholarQuest, a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for agentic academic paper search. ScholarQuest is constructed from over 1,000 computer science topics and four representative research intents, including method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, and scope-controlled queries. It further provides scalable answer construction and a shared retrieval backend ScholarBase for reproducible evaluation. Benchmarking results show that agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent only achieves 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All, indicating substantial room for improvement. In addition, analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases further highlight the benchmark's ability to provide multi-dimensional evaluation signals for academic paper search agents.

AI.tldr: ScholarQuest is a large-scale, taxonomy-guided benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agentic academic paper search across four research intents, revealing that even the best agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100, indicating substantial room for improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks lack the capacity to systematically evaluate LLM-based search agents under realistic, open-domain academic literature settings. There is a need for a reproducible, intent-driven, and scalable evaluation framework that captures the iterative nature of agentic academic search.
AI.method: Constructed ScholarQuest from over 1,000 CS topics and four research intents (method-oriented, setting-anchored, comparison-based, scope-controlled). Features scalable answer construction, a shared retrieval backend (ScholarBase) for reproducibility, and multi-dimensional evaluation metrics including Recall@K, search efficiency, and intent-level robustness.
AI.result: Agentic methods outperform single-shot retrieval baselines, yet the best-performing agent achieves only 0.314 Recall@100 and 0.355 Recall@All. Analyses of search efficiency, intent-level robustness, and failure cases provide multi-dimensional diagnostic signals.
AI.conclusion: Agentic academic search shows promise over static retrieval but remains far from solved. ScholarQuest provides a reproducible, fine-grained benchmark that exposes key failure modes and efficiency bottlenecks, guiding future research toward more robust and efficient academic search agents.

title: Designing for Interconnected Islamic Learning: A Qualitative Study of Muslim Women's Experiences with Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah Apps
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
summary: Islamic learning often depends on reading the Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah together, yet digital tools typically separate these sources across apps, screens, and search pathways. We examine this as a human-computer interaction problem through five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Participants described a recurring tension: they wanted Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah context at the point of reading, but only when contextual expansion remained trustworthy, optional, and did not interrupt reading. Interpreting the interviews through gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning, we identify five themes concerning contextual understanding, authenticity, interface clutter, study modes, and guidance features. We introduce layered contextuality as an HCI account of this domain: contextual expansion must be balanced with interpretive accountability, devotional flow, and continuity across devices and study intensities.

AI.tldr: Muslim learners need Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah integrated contextually while reading, but only when trustworthy, optional, and non-disruptive. The paper introduces "layered contextuality" as an HCI framework balancing contextual expansion with devotional flow and interpretive accountability.
AI.motivation: Islamic learning requires interconnected reading of Qur'an, Hadith, and Seerah, yet existing digital tools fragment these sources across separate apps and interfaces. This creates a human-computer interaction problem where users must constantly switch contexts, disrupting both learning and devotional experience.
AI.method: Five semi-structured interviews with Muslim women recruited from an online Islamic learning community. Data interpreted through three analytical lenses: gendered digital religion, epistemic trust, and seamless learning theory. Thematic analysis identified five key themes.
AI.result: Five themes emerged: (1) contextual understanding — learners desire Qur'an-Hadith-Seerah integration at the point of reading; (2) authenticity — contextual expansion must be trustworthy and epistemically sound; (3) interface clutter — information must remain optional and not interrupt reading flow; (4) study modes — varying intensities of study require different levels of contextual support; (5) guidance features — users want continuity across devices and learning sessions. These tensions informed the concept of layered contextuality.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes "layered contextuality" as a novel HCI construct: design for Islamic digital learning tools must enable contextual expansion that is trustworthy, optional, and non-interruptive while maintaining devotional flow and ensuring continuity across devices and study intensities.

title: When Global Gating Is Enough: Admission-Time Hubness Control in Anisotropic Vector Retrieval Systems
summary: Vector hubness, where a few points become nearest neighbors of many queries, creates a poisoning risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): one injected document can influence unrelated requests. Existing defenses use periodic reverse-kNN scans, leaving an exposure window and repeated corpus-wide work. We study admission-time control, scoring each candidate against sentinel queries and quarantining hub-like documents before insertion. Across two 100,000-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker and defender query sets, a global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point (>=0.92 across the effective range) and 0.91 +/- 0.07 on HotFlip attacks, with 1% false positives on general documents. A per-topic gate provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, with corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. On HNSW, admission adds about 3.1% to ingestion latency, scoring remains flat to 10^6 vectors, and 1.2% of decisions flip under approximate indexing, none involving attacks. Provenance complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an admission-time gating mechanism to defend against vector hubness poisoning in RAG systems, where a few injected documents become nearest neighbors to many queries. A global gate using sentinel queries achieves near-perfect recall (≈0.92–1.0) in detecting hub-like documents before insertion, with low false positives (~1%) and minimal overhead (~3.1% added ingestion latency on HNSW). Per-topic gates prove unreliable due to anisotropy. The approach eliminates the exposure window inherent in periodic reverse-kNN scanning defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against hubness-based poisoning in RAG rely on periodic reverse-kNN scans, which leave an exposure window between scans and incur repeated corpus-wide computational cost. The authors aim to shift defense from periodic detection to admission-time control—intercepting and quarantining hub-like documents before they enter the index, thereby eliminating the vulnerability window and reducing ongoing overhead.
AI.method: The method introduces admission-time gating: each candidate document is scored by querying a fixed set of sentinel queries against the existing index, measuring how often the candidate appears in top-k results. Documents exceeding a hubness threshold are quarantined pre-insertion. Two gating strategies are evaluated: (1) a global gate using a single corpus-wide threshold, and (2) per-topic gates with topic-specific thresholds. Thresholds are maintained incrementally, yielding corpus-size-independent insertion cost and amortized deletion cost. Evaluation spans two 100k-document corpora, five encoders, and disjoint attacker/defender query sets, including HotFlip adversarial attacks. Approximate indexing (HNSW) impact is also measured.
AI.result: The global gate achieves recall 1.0 at the decisive embedding-space point and ≥0.92 across the effective operating range. Against HotFlip attacks, recall is 0.91 ± 0.07. False positive rate on benign documents is ~1%. Per-topic gating provides no reliable benefit, consistent with anisotropy coupling local and global visibility. Admission adds ~3.1% to HNSW ingestion latency; scoring cost remains flat up to 10^6 vectors. Only 1.2% of admission decisions flip under approximate indexing, with none involving attack documents. Provenance tracking complements the gate for natural or tight-domain hubs.
AI.conclusion: Admission-time gating is a practical, low-overhead defense against hubness poisoning in RAG, effectively eliminating the exposure window of prior approaches. The global gate is both accurate and efficient, while per-topic gating is unnecessary due to anisotropy. The method scales well with corpus size and degrades minimally under approximate indexing, making it suitable for production retrieval systems.

title: Where to Place the Query? Unveiling and Mitigating Positional Bias in In-Context Learning for Diffusion LLMs via Decoding Dynamics
summary: While In-Context Learning (ICL) is extensively studied in Autoregressive (AR) LLMs, its mechanism within Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) remains largely unexplored. Unlike AR models restricted by unidirectional causal masking, dLLMs intrinsically utilize bidirectional attention, offering extensive spatial flexibility for query placement. Unfortunately, current practices conventionally inherit AR-style trailing-query templates, often overlooking the structural paradigm shift. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis unveiling that query position is actually a first-order variable in dLLMs. Through empirical decoupling, we demonstrate that positional variance impacts generation quality on par with example semantic quality. Internally, this positional sensitivity stems from a spatial ``Recency Effect'' in attention flow and task-dependent shifts in decoding trajectories. To mitigate this instability without ground-truth labels, we reveal that traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$) fails in dLLMs. Instead, we propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), a novel metric tracking the iterative decoding process. By establishing the foundational spatial ICL baselines, we introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement, robustly approaching oracle performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that query position is a critical first-order variable in Diffusion LLMs for In-Context Learning, stemming from a spatial "Recency Effect." The authors propose Average Confidence, a novel decoding metric, and Auto-ICL, an adaptive routing strategy that dynamically optimizes query placement without training.
AI.motivation: Current ICL practices for Diffusion LLMs blindly inherit AR-style trailing-query templates, ignoring the fundamental structural differences: dLLMs use bidirectional attention rather than unidirectional causal masking. The impact of query placement in dLLMs' ICL remains unexplored, motivating a systematic investigation of whether and how query position affects generation quality.
AI.method: The authors conduct empirical decoupling experiments to isolate positional effects from semantic effects. They analyze internal mechanisms, identifying a spatial "Recency Effect" in attention flow and task-dependent decoding trajectory shifts. To address instability without ground-truth labels, they propose Average Confidence ($\overline{C}$), which tracks the iterative decoding process rather than relying on traditional single-step confidence ($C_{decoded}$). Finally, they introduce Auto-ICL, a training-free adaptive routing strategy that dynamically selects optimal query positions.
AI.result: Query position is shown to be a first-order variable, impacting generation quality comparably to example semantic quality. Traditional single-step confidence fails as a selection metric in dLLMs. Auto-ICL robustly approaches oracle performance across heterogeneous reasoning and perception tasks by dynamically optimizing query placement.
AI.conclusion: Query position fundamentally matters in dLLMs' ICL due to bidirectional attention and the spatial Recency Effect. Average Confidence enables reliable position selection without labels, and Auto-ICL provides a practical, training-free solution that bridges the gap to oracle performance, establishing foundational spatial ICL baselines for diffusion language models.

title: Before the Pull Request: Mining Multi-Agent Coordination
comment: 9 pages, 2 tables. LNCS format. Code, dataset, and mining toolkit: https://github.com/neul-labs/grite
