summary: Autonomous coding agents now open millions of pull requests, yet large-scale studies find their PRs are produced faster but accepted less often - a coordination and trust gap that pull-request-level telemetry cannot explain. We argue the missing signal lives before the PR, in how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. We study this process through grite, our open-source coordination substrate that needs no central server and stores its records inside git itself, so its append-only, signed event log captures the coordination process directly. We show that (i) this shared substrate reduces duplicate and conflicting work at bounded overhead - the share of work that merely re-does a teammate's task falls from 78% to 0% while useful throughput more than triples; (ii) every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, where a file-based tracker loses concurrent writes; and (iii) the log is a mineable artefact from which concrete failure modes - conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close - are automatically recoverable with provenance, several invisible in pull-request history. We release the dataset, harness, and mining toolkit.

AI.tldr: Autonomous coding agents generate PRs faster but suffer lower acceptance rates due to coordination failures invisible at the PR level. The authors present grite, a git-native, serverless coordination substrate with an append-only signed event log that eliminates duplicate work (78%→0%), triples useful throughput, ensures log convergence across agents, and enables automatic recovery from failure modes (conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close) that PR-level telemetry cannot detect.
AI.motivation: Existing large-scale studies show autonomous coding agents produce pull requests faster but with lower acceptance rates, revealing a coordination and trust gap. PR-level telemetry alone cannot explain why, because the critical failures occur before the PR is filed—during how concurrent agents claim, divide, and collide over shared work. A mechanism to capture, analyze, and mitigate this pre-PR coordination process is needed.
AI.method: The authors build grite, an open-source coordination substrate that is fully decentralized (no central server) and stores its records directly inside git as an append-only, cryptographically signed event log. This log captures the entire coordination process—task claiming, division of labor, and collision events—making it auditable and automatically mineable. They evaluate grite by measuring (i) reduction in duplicate/conflicting work, (ii) log convergence properties (comparing against file-based trackers that lose concurrent writes), and (iii) the log's capacity as a mineable artifact for recovering provenance of failure modes.
AI.result: (i) The share of work that merely redoes a teammate's task drops from 78% to 0%, while useful throughput more than triples. (ii) Every agent's copy of the log converges to the same state with no write silently dropped, unlike a file-based tracker that loses concurrent writes. (iii) Concrete failure modes—conflicting edits, lock starvation, redundant rediscovery, race-to-close—are automatically recoverable with full provenance from the log, several of which are invisible in conventional PR history.
AI.conclusion: Pre-PR coordination is the missing link in understanding and improving autonomous coding agent collaboration. grite demonstrates that a git-native, decentralized, append-only event log eliminates duplicate work, ensures consistent state across agents, and surfaces recoverable failure modes that PR-level telemetry misses. The authors release all artifacts—dataset, harness, and mining toolkit—to enable further research.

title: Beyond the GUI Paradigm: Do Mobile Agents Need the Phone Screen?
summary: Recent advances in mobile agents are dominated by the GUI paradigm, in which agents perceive UI information and emit screen interactions. However, mobile platforms also expose a command-line interface (CLI) that provides direct access to device services and data. We argue CLI deserves first-class consideration alongside GUI. We evaluate three coding agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld without any mobile-specific post-training, comparing against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Claude Code (Opus 4.7) reaches 71.8\% and 51.9\%, outperforming every reproducible GUI baseline (69.3/68.1/57.8\% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3\% on MobileWorld), while every other CLI configuration remains competitive. To establish the paradigm's ceiling, we provide oracle CLI solutions that reach 88.8\% on AndroidWorld (103/116 tasks CLI-solvable) and 86.3\% on MobileWorld (101/117 tasks CLI-solvable), indicating substantial room for future improvement. To cover everyday user intents beyond the GUI scope, we introduce the \textbf{CLI-Advantage Task Suite}, comprising 45 templates across five categories: bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, and hidden device state. Every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline in all five categories, with substantially fewer steps per task (10.7 vs.\ 18.6). To support future research on mobile CLI agents, we will open-source agent implementations, oracle solutions, the CLI-Advantage suite, and evaluation infrastructure.

AI.tldr: The paper advocates for mobile CLI agents as a first-class paradigm alongside GUI agents. Evaluating three coding agents on AndroidWorld and MobileWorld, Claude Code (Opus 4.7) achieves 71.8% and 51.9%, outperforming all reproducible GUI baselines. Oracle CLI solutions reach 88.8% and 86.3%, revealing significant headroom. A new CLI-Advantage Task Suite (45 templates across 5 categories) demonstrates CLI agents consistently outperform GUI baselines with fewer steps.
AI.motivation: Current mobile agent research is dominated by the GUI paradigm, yet mobile platforms also expose command-line interfaces (via ADB/shell) that provide direct, programmatic access to device services and data. The CLI approach has been neglected despite its potential advantages for structured, multi-step, and data-intensive tasks that are cumbersome or impossible through GUI manipulation alone.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three coding-based CLI agents (Claude Code, Terminus-2, mini-swe-agent) across four model APIs on two standard benchmarks (AndroidWorld and MobileWorld), without any mobile-specific post-training. They compare against three reproducible GUI baselines (GUI-Owl-1.5-32B, MAI-UI, Qwen3-VL-32B). Oracle CLI solutions establish the paradigm's upper bound. Additionally, they introduce the CLI-Advantage Task Suite with 45 templates covering bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, aggregation, cross-app workflows, and hidden device state.
AI.result: Claude Code (Opus 4.7) reaches 71.8% on AndroidWorld and 51.9% on MobileWorld, surpassing every GUI baseline (69.3/68.1/57.8% on AndroidWorld; 43.2/26.3/13.3% on MobileWorld). Other CLI configurations remain competitive. Oracle CLI solutions achieve 88.8% (103/116 solvable) and 86.3% (101/117 solvable). On the CLI-Advantage suite, every CLI agent outperforms every GUI baseline across all five categories, averaging 10.7 steps per task versus 18.6 for GUI agents.
AI.conclusion: CLI-based mobile agents represent a viable, competitive, and complementary paradigm to GUI-based approaches. They excel particularly at structured, multi-step tasks and offer substantial headroom for improvement toward oracle performance. The authors commit to open-sourcing agents, oracle solutions, the CLI-Advantage suite, and evaluation infrastructure to foster further research.

title: LLM Doesn't Know What It Doesn't Know: Detecting Epistemic Blind Spots via Cross-Model Attribution Divergence on Clinical Tabular Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to structured clinical data, yet whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge on such tasks remains unexplored. We study this question through the lens of cross-model attribution divergence with the goal of reducing epistemic uncertainty for structured tasks, comparing Qwen 2.5 7B and XGBoost on a prediction task via attribution divergence analysis. We report four findings. First, LLM verbalized confidence is epistemically vacuous, it outputs a near-constant (0.856-0.937) regardless of whether accuracy is 49% or 75.3%, tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. Second, the LLM exhibits an inverse difficulty effect: accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is 99% correct, but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) when it is moderately uncertain. Third, few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions: they reduce the Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) from 1.54 to 0.38 and improve accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. Fourth, a cross-model calibrator that determined LLM reliability using attribution divergence signals reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080, replacing uninformative verbalized confidence with patient-specific reliability estimates, without accessing model internals or requiring repeated inference. We frame these findings as a cold start problem for LLMs on structured data and outline a path toward genuine epistemic self-awareness.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit poor epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical data — their verbalized confidence is near-constant and uninformative. The paper introduces cross-model attribution divergence analysis (LLM vs. XGBoost) to detect when the LLM is unreliable, proposes interventions (few-shot + SHAP evidence) that are super-additive, and builds a cross-model calibrator that reduces calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080 without accessing model internals.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed on structured clinical prediction tasks, but whether they can recognize the limits of their own knowledge (epistemic self-awareness) is unknown. The authors aim to characterize and mitigate epistemic uncertainty in LLMs on structured data through cross-model attribution divergence analysis, framing this as a "cold start problem."
AI.method: The study compares Qwen 2.5 7B with XGBoost on a clinical prediction task. Key methods include: (1) measuring LLM verbalized confidence against actual accuracy; (2) computing an Attribution Disagreement Score (ADS) between LLM and XGBoost attributions to quantify epistemic uncertainty; (3) testing few-shot examples and SHAP-derived feature evidence as interventions, both individually and combined; (4) building a cross-model calibrator that uses ADS signals to produce patient-specific reliability estimates without requiring model internals or repeated inference.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) LLM verbalized confidence is nearly constant (0.856–0.937) regardless of accuracy (49%–75.3%), tracking prompt format rather than prediction quality. (2) An inverse difficulty effect: LLM accuracy drops to 64.8% when XGBoost is highly accurate (99%), but matches XGBoost (73.8% vs. 73.1%) under moderate uncertainty. (3) Few-shot examples and SHAP evidence are orthogonal, super-additive interventions — together they reduce ADS from 1.54 to 0.38 and boost accuracy from 49% to 75.3% without training. (4) The cross-model calibrator reduces expected calibration error from 0.254 to 0.080.
AI.conclusion: LLMs suffer from a fundamental lack of epistemic self-awareness on structured clinical tasks, producing overconfident, uninformative confidence estimates. Cross-model attribution divergence provides a practical signal for detecting unreliability. The proposed calibrator offers a lightweight path toward patient-specific confidence without model internals or repeated inference, outlining a framework for genuine epistemic self-awareness in LLMs applied to structured data.

title: Weibull Weight-Scale Parameter Evolution under AdamW Training Dynamics
summary: Building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, we study why the Weibull weight-scale parameter $λ$ grows, overshoots, and then relaxes during AdamW training. We derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update: an alignment force measuring the correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction, an injection force from adaptive step magnitude, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, contributing 88-94% of the absolute force budget across four random seeds and remaining robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the transition from weight-scale growth to relaxation. These force dynamics directly govern the squared-norm component underlying $λ(t)$; the remaining RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset is measurable and decomposes into bridge and integration components, totaling approximately 5-6% in densely sampled regions. To extend the analysis to real models where optimizer moments are unavailable, we introduce a spline displacement method that recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints with approximately 92-94% accuracy, about twice the naive two-point baseline. We further observe that the peak value of $λ(t)$ varies with training-data coherence in our experiments, suggesting a data-dependent component of weight-scale growth that we leave to a controlled follow-up study. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes AdamW training dynamics through a Weibull distribution framework, decomposing weight norm evolution into three forces (alignment, injection, decay). Alignment force dominates weight-scale growth (88-94%), while alignment-decay equilibrium explains saturation and relaxation. A spline method recovers optimizer moments from sparse checkpoints with ~92-94% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Prior work established a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions, but the dynamical mechanism behind the characteristic growth, overshoot, and relaxation of the Weibull scale parameter λ during AdamW training remains unexplained. Understanding these dynamics is essential for linking optimizer behavior to emergent weight structure.
AI.method: The authors derive a leading-order three-force decomposition of the squared weight norm from the AdamW update rule: (1) an alignment force (correlation between weights and adaptive update direction), (2) an injection force (adaptive step magnitude), and (3) a decay force (decoupled weight decay). They validate this on self-trained Pythia-70M models with ground-truth optimizer moments, analyze the RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset (decomposed into bridge and integration components), and introduce a spline displacement method to recover alignment forces from sparse checkpoints when optimizer states are unavailable.
AI.result: Alignment dominates the rise phase (88-94% of absolute force budget across four seeds) and is robust to super-weight removal. Near saturation, alignment and decay approach balance, explaining the λ overshoot-to-relaxation transition. The RMS-to-Weibull reconstruction offset totals ~5-6% in densely sampled regions. The spline displacement method recovers alignment force from sparse checkpoints with ~92-94% accuracy, roughly double the naive two-point baseline. Peak λ(t) varies with training-data coherence.
AI.conclusion: The three-force decomposition provides a mechanistic account of Weibull scale parameter dynamics under AdamW, with alignment force as the primary driver of weight-scale growth. The spline method enables retrospective analysis on real models lacking optimizer states. Data-dependent variation in peak λ suggests a connection to data coherence, motivating further controlled study.

title: ELVA: Exploring Ranking-Driven Universal Multimodal Retrieval
summary:
Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) via contrastive learning has become a mainstream paradigm for improving the performance of Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR). However, previous works have ignored the grain blindness when adapting the contrastive paradigm into retrieval tasks. Grain blindness refers to the tendency of the model to overlook grain-level information contained in the query, which is crucial for effectively handling complex queries. This stems from contrastive learning treating samples as a binary classification (positive/negative), while ignoring the different information carried by each negative sample. To address this, we argue that negatives should be treated differently according to their similarity to the positive sample, enabling the model to learn distinct grain information from each negative. In this paper, we introduce a simple but effective framework, called ELVA, a novel rule-based RL framework that mitigates grain blindness through ranking-driven MLLMs. 1) Instead of relying on reward models, we extend Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
  (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, allowing the model to explore new ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels. 2) By utilizing rule-based rewards, our approach jointly optimizes the ranking of negative samples while enlarging the similarity gap between positive and negative. To more precisely measure grain blindness, we further introduce MRBench, a new benchmark specifically designed for multi-grain query scenarios. ELVA achieves state-of-the-art results across standard retrieval benchmarks, and its notable 13.1% improvement on MRBench further demonstrates its effectiveness in alleviating grain blindness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ELVA, a rule-based reinforcement learning framework that addresses "grain blindness" in multimodal retrieval — the failure to leverage granular information from negative samples. By extending RLVR to retrieval and using rule-based rewards to differentially weight negatives, ELVA achieves SOTA results, including a 13.1% gain on the newly introduced MRBench for multi-grain queries.
AI.motivation: Existing contrastive learning approaches for Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR) treat all negative samples uniformly (binary positive/negative classification), causing "grain blindness" — the model's inability to capture fine-grained, grain-level information from the query that is essential for handling complex retrieval scenarios.
AI.method: ELVA (a rule-based RL framework) introduces two key components: (1) Extending Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to retrieval tasks, enabling exploration of ranking behaviors without explicit ranking labels; (2) Employing rule-based rewards that jointly optimize negative sample ranking while maximizing the similarity gap between positives and negatives based on each negative's relative similarity to the positive. Additionally, MRBench is introduced as a new benchmark for evaluating multi-grain query scenarios.
AI.result: ELVA achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard retrieval benchmarks. Notably, it demonstrates a 13.1% improvement on MRBench, validating its effectiveness in mitigating grain blindness.
AI.conclusion: Treating negatives differently according to their similarity to the positive, rather than as a homogeneous class, effectively alleviates grain blindness. The proposed rule-based RL approach (ELVA) provides a simple yet powerful framework for this, with strong empirical validation across benchmarks.

title: MemGUI-Agent: An End-to-End Long-Horizon Mobile GUI Agent with Proactive Context Management
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress on short-horizon tasks, yet remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks that require retaining intermediate facts across many steps and app transitions. We attribute this limitation to ReAct-style prompting, which passively accumulates per-step records, leading to prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts. To address this, we introduce MemGUI-Agent, an end-to-end long-horizon mobile GUI agent with proactive context management. MemGUI-Agent is built on Context-as-Action (ConAct), which casts context management as first-class actions emitted by the same policy that selects UI actions. Instead of passively appending history, ConAct maintains three structured context fields: folded action history, folded UI state, and recent step record, preserving critical UI facts while keeping context compact. To make proactive context management learnable across model scales, we construct MemGUI-3K, a 2,956-trajectory dataset with full ConAct annotations for supervised training and offline analysis. Training an 8B model on MemGUI-3K produces MemGUI-8B-SFT, an 8B MemGUI-Agent that achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://memgui-agent.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MemGUI-Agent introduces proactive context management (Context-as-Action) for long-horizon mobile GUI agents, maintaining structured context fields instead of passively accumulating history. An 8B model trained on the MemGUI-3K dataset achieves state-of-the-art open-data performance on MemGUI-Bench and generalizes to MobileWorld.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based mobile GUI agents using ReAct-style prompting fail on long-horizon tasks because passive accumulation of per-step records causes prompt explosion and dilution of critical cross-app facts. There is a need for agents that can selectively retain and manage context across many steps and app transitions.
AI.method: The authors propose MemGUI-Agent, built on Context-as-Action (ConAct), which treats context management as first-class actions alongside UI actions. Rather than appending raw history, ConAct maintains three structured context fields: (1) folded action history, (2) folded UI state, and (3) recent step record. This preserves critical UI facts while keeping context compact. They also construct MemGUI-3K, a 2,956-trajectory dataset with full ConAct annotations for supervised fine-tuning. An 8B model is trained via SFT to produce MemGUI-8B-SFT.
AI.result: MemGUI-8B-SFT achieves the best open-data 8B performance on MemGUI-Bench and successfully generalizes to the out-of-distribution MobileWorld benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Proactive context management via ConAct is an effective paradigm for enabling MLLM-based agents to handle long-horizon mobile GUI tasks. Structured, compact context fields overcome the limitations of passive history accumulation, and the approach is learnable via supervised fine-tuning on a modestly sized annotated dataset.

title: SafeSpec: Fast and Safe LLM via Dynamic Reflective Sampling
summary: Speculative inference accelerates large language model (LLM) decoding but provides no inherent safety guarantees. Existing safety defenses are largely incompatible with speculative inference: they either introduce additional computation or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating acceleration benefits. This reveals a fundamental incompatibility between current safety methods and speculative decoding. We propose SafeSpec, a safety-aware speculative inference framework that integrates risk estimation directly into the verification process. SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model to jointly evaluate semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass. When unsafe generations are detected, SafeSpec applies rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations rather than terminating generation. We model jailbreak attacks as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase the probability of harmful continuations without eliminating safe ones. Under this model, SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process. Across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks, SafeSpec achieves a substantially improved safety-efficiency trade-off. On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads, demonstrating that speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized.

AI.tldr: SafeSpec integrates lightweight safety evaluation into speculative inference's verification pass, using rollback and reflective multi-sampling to recover safe continuations when harmful generations are detected, achieving a 15% reduction in attack success rate while maintaining 2.06x speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety defenses are fundamentally incompatible with speculative inference — they either add computational overhead or disrupt the draft-verify mechanism, negating the acceleration benefits. Meanwhile, speculative decoding itself provides no inherent safety guarantees. This creates a pressing need for safety mechanisms that coexist with speculative acceleration.
AI.method: SafeSpec attaches a lightweight latent safety head to the target model, enabling joint evaluation of semantic validity and safety in a single forward pass during verification. When unsafe continuations are detected, instead of terminating generation, SafeSpec performs rollback and safety-guided reflective multi-sampling to recover safe trajectories. Jailbreak attacks are modeled as distributional shifts over generative trajectories, where adversarial prompts increase harmful continuation probability without eliminating safe ones. SafeSpec performs risk-aware trajectory recovery within the speculative decoding process.
AI.result: On Qwen3-32B, SafeSpec reduces attack success rates by 15% while preserving a 2.06x inference speedup on benign workloads. The safety-efficiency trade-off is substantially improved across multiple models and adversarial benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Speculative acceleration and inference-time safety can be jointly optimized rather than being mutually exclusive. SafeSpec demonstrates that integrating risk estimation directly into the verification process enables effective safety guarantees without sacrificing the speed benefits of speculative decoding.

title: Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on LLM Reasoning. 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

AI.tldr: CAP is a training-free pruning method that uses causal attribution scores of attention heads to guide fine-grained weight pruning, outperforming correlation-based methods like Wanda on reasoning benchmarks at moderate sparsity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are costly for multi-step reasoning inference. Existing pruning methods (magnitude-based, activation-based) rely on correlation rather than causation, missing each head's true functional contribution to reasoning tasks.
AI.method: CAP masks each attention head on a small calibration set of reasoning problems, measures expected performance degradation (causal score), propagates head-level scores to weight-level importance in projection matrices, then prunes the lowest-importance weights to the target sparsity.
AI.result: CAP achieves up to 61% relative accuracy gain over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct across GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge, CAP outperforms Wanda at 10–20% sparsity, with especially large gains for Llama-3 on ARC-Challenge.
AI.conclusion: Causal attribution at the attention-head level better preserves reasoning performance than correlational pruning. However, CAP's benefit diminishes at 50% sparsity due to coarse MLP attribution limitations.

title: Exit-and-Join Dynamics for Decentralized Coalition Formation
summary: This paper studies coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process driven by unilateral exit-and-join decisions. Agents evaluate local moves using the Aumann-Dreze value, so payoffs are computed within the agent's current coalition rather than through a globally negotiated coalition structure. The resulting model links cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior: a terminal partition is precisely a coalition structure with no admissible, individually profitable exit-and-join deviation. We establish equilibrium characterizations, identify conditions under which the dynamics admit scalar Lyapunov or exact-potential representations, and analyze how switching and acceptance costs shape local stability. Numerical experiments test finite-time stabilization, cost sensitivity, and a special convex-game benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper models coalition formation as a decentralized dynamical process where agents make unilateral exit-and-join decisions based on the Aumann-Drèze value, linking cooperative payoff allocation with noncooperative best-response behavior. It provides equilibrium characterizations, identifies conditions for Lyapunov/potential representations, analyzes the role of switching and acceptance costs, and validates findings through numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: Traditional coalition formation models often rely on globally negotiated outcomes (e.g., the Shapley value or core over the entire coalition structure). This paper seeks to bridge cooperative and noncooperative game theory by studying how decentralized, myopic, self-interested moves by individual agents—evaluated locally within their own coalitions—can lead to stable coalition structures, thereby providing a more realistic model of emergent coalitional dynamics.
AI.method: The authors model coalition formation as a dynamical system where in each step, a single agent evaluates a unilateral exit from its current coalition and potential join to another, with payoffs determined by the Aumann-Drèze value (a restriction of the Shapley value to the agent's current coalition). A terminal partition is defined as a coalition structure admitting no such individually profitable deviation. They characterize equilibria, derive conditions under which the dynamics admit a scalar Lyapunov function or an exact potential function, incorporate switching and acceptance costs, and conduct numerical simulations to assess finite-time convergence, cost sensitivity, and performance on convex games.
AI.result: Equilibrium characterizations are established linking stable partitions to the absence of profitable unilateral deviations under the Aumann-Drèze value. The authors identify conditions guaranteeing that the dynamics possess a Lyapunov or exact-potential representation, ensuring convergence. Switching and acceptance costs are shown to affect local stability and the set of reachable equilibria. Numerical experiments demonstrate finite-time stabilization, quantify sensitivity to cost parameters, and validate behavior on a convex-game benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The decentralized exit-and-join process under the Aumann-Drèze value provides a meaningful bridge between cooperative solution concepts and noncooperative adaptive dynamics. The existence of Lyapunov/potential structures under certain conditions guarantees convergence, while switching and acceptance costs serve as tuning parameters that shape stability and equilibrium selection. The framework offers a tractable model for studying emergent coalition structures in multi-agent systems.

title: Execution-bound advisory automation for agentic AI: a reproducible AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework
summary: A protocol driven framework is presented that binds SBOM and AIBOM artefacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed from declared artefacts, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay. Evaluation uses approximately 10000 component entries across synthetic Agentic AI workloads 50 to 5000 components, incorporating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets.

AI.tldr: A framework that links SBOM/AIBOM artifacts with runtime telemetry to compute exploitability, generate signed CSAF VEX advisories, and validate via deterministic replay, tested on Agentic AI workloads with up to 5000 components.
AI.motivation: Current vulnerability management lacks a unified, verifiable link between declared software/AI bills of materials and actual runtime behavior, making exploitability assessment imprecise and advisory generation non-reproducible.
AI.method: A protocol-driven framework binds SBOM and AIBOM artifacts to deterministic environment capture and structured runtime telemetry. Exploitability is computed by correlating declared components, observed activation conditions, and enforced execution policies. CSAF VEX advisories are then generated from combined static and runtime evidence, cryptographically signed, and validated through deterministic replay of the captured environment.
AI.result: Evaluation across approximately 10,000 component entries using synthetic Agentic AI workloads (50–5000 components) integrating OSV, GitHub Advisory, KEV, and EPSS datasets demonstrates the framework's ability to produce verifiable, evidence-backed VEX advisories at scale.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic binding of SBOM/AIBOM artifacts to runtime telemetry enables reproducible, cryptographically verifiable exploitability assessment and VEX advisory generation, advancing supply chain security assurance for both traditional and AI software components.

title: REVEAL++: Differentiable Phenotypic Grouping for Vision-Language Retinal Modeling of Alzheimer's Disease Risk
summary: The retina offers a noninvasive window into neurodegenerative disease, capturing subtle structural patterns associated with a risk of future cognitive decline. Vision-language alignment frameworks such as REVEAL have shown that pairing retinal fundus images with structured clinical risk narratives improves early prediction of Alzheimer's disease (AD). A key design choice in these approaches is the use of phenotypic grouping, where individuals with similar risk profiles are treated as multi-positive pairs during contrastive learning. However, existing methods operationalize phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct, relying on hard group assignments that impose rigid supervision and decouple group formation from representation learning. We propose a continuous formulation of phenotypic structure within contrastive learning. Rather than assigning samples to fixed clusters, we model inter-subject similarity as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embedding similarities in both retinal images and risk profiles. These weights define soft multi-positive relationships through a continuous aggregation operator, enabling graded supervision that reflects the spectrum nature of disease risk. We further introduce a soft-target contrastive objective that jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure in an end-to-end manner. Evaluated on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident AD prediction, the proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines. By treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule, our approach provides a principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes replacing discrete phenotypic grouping in vision-language contrastive learning with a continuous, learnable similarity formulation. Instead of hard cluster assignments, inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function derived from intra-modality embeddings, enabling soft multi-positive relationships. A soft-target contrastive objective jointly learns cross-modal alignment and phenotypic structure end-to-end, outperforming discrete group-based methods on UK Biobank Alzheimer's disease prediction from retinal images and clinical risk profiles.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language alignment methods like REVEAL use phenotypic grouping to pair retinal images with clinical risk narratives for AD prediction, but they treat phenotypic similarity as a discrete construct with hard group assignments. This imposes rigid supervision and decouples group formation from representation learning, failing to capture the continuous, spectrum nature of neurodegenerative disease risk.
AI.method: The authors propose a continuous phenotypic structure formulation: (1) inter-subject similarity is modeled as a differentiable weighting function based on intra-modality embedding similarities from both retinal images and risk profiles; (2) these weights define soft multi-positive relationships via a continuous aggregation operator; (3) a soft-target contrastive objective jointly learns cross-modal alignment and the phenotypic structure end-to-end, treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently outperforms discrete group-based contrastive learning and standard vision-language baselines on UK Biobank retinal imaging data for incident Alzheimer's disease prediction.
AI.conclusion: Treating phenotypic similarity as a learnable, continuous signal rather than a fixed grouping rule provides a more principled and robust foundation for population-scale neurodegenerative risk modeling from multi-modal retinal and clinical data.

title: Zero-Inflated Gaussian Distributions Enable Parameter-Space Sparsity in Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms
summary: Estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs) are a powerful class of evolutionary methods for black-box optimization, especially when little is known about the structure of the objective. Whereas classical evolutionary algorithms rely on hand-designed mutation and crossover operators, hard to devise for unknown problem structures, and a source of bias, EDAs sidestep operator design entirely: they fit a probability distribution to the best individuals and sample the next generation from it. EDAs are well established on continuous parameter spaces, but they have not previously been generalized to sparse ones, in which most coefficients of a good solution are exactly zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers therefore reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level schemes alternating between support set and active values, zeroing thresholds, and other baked-in assumptions. We close this gap by proposing multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as EDA sampling laws. A latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and the interactions between the two, so sparsity patterns and active values are optimized jointly, hierarchy-free. We show that the latent parameters of this model are identifiable from observed samples, unlike in the missing-data settings where related constructions originate, and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators for them. The estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures, and on the Lunar Lander benchmark the resulting ZIG-EDA converges faster and reaches higher final returns than a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while finding controllers with only a small fraction of parameters active.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions as sampling laws for estimation-of-distribution algorithms (EDAs), enabling EDAs to natively operate on sparse parameter spaces without hand-crafted sparsity operators. The proposed ZIG-EDA jointly optimizes sparsity patterns and active values, and is shown to outperform both dense and ad-hoc sparse baselines on the Lunar Lander benchmark.
AI.motivation: EDAs avoid hand-designed operators by fitting distributions to elite individuals, but have not been generalized to sparse optimization problems where most coefficients are zero. Existing sparse black-box optimizers reintroduce exactly what EDAs were designed to avoid: hand-crafted sparsity operators, bi-level alternating schemes, and zeroing thresholds. The gap is a native probabilistic model for sparse continuous optimization within the EDA framework.
AI.method: The authors propose multivariate zero-inflated Gaussian (ZIG) distributions, a latent Gaussian model with separate indicator and value dimensions that jointly represents sparsity patterns, correlations among active parameters, and interactions between the two. They prove identifiability of latent parameters from observed samples (unlike related missing-data models) and introduce practical amortized inversion-based estimators. The ZIG distribution serves directly as the sampling law in an EDA, eliminating hierarchy and hand-crafted operators.
AI.result: The amortized estimators accurately recover latent correlation structures. On the Lunar Lander benchmark, ZIG-EDA converges faster and achieves higher final returns compared to a dense Gaussian EDA, a hand-crafted sparse evolutionary algorithm, and an ad-hoc sparse EDA, while discovering controllers with only a small fraction of active parameters.
AI.conclusion: ZIG distributions provide a principled, hierarchy-free probabilistic model for sparse continuous black-box optimization within EDAs, successfully closing the gap between EDA methodology and sparse problem domains without resorting to hand-designed sparsity mechanisms.

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.

AI.tldr: G2Rec is a scalable generative recommendation framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization, enabling models to capture semantically grounded user interest prototypes without ground-truth labels.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods struggle with two key limitations: (1) graph-based integration approaches (serialization, GNNs) either lack scalability or capture only local graph information; (2) semantic tokenization methods rely on heuristics without explicit supervision, yielding inaccurate semantic representations. A unified approach addressing both issues simultaneously is needed for industrial-scale deployment.
AI.method: G2Rec proposes a unified framework combining holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with supervised semantic tokenization. It leverages global graph structural information to derive user interest prototypes and integrates semantic signals into item tokenization with explicit supervision, overcoming the locality and heuristic limitations of prior work.
AI.result: G2Rec demonstrates superior performance over existing methods, validated through online deployment across product surfaces at industrial scale and extensive offline experiments on public datasets.
AI.conclusion: G2Rec effectively addresses the dual challenges of holistic user context modeling and accurate semantic tokenization in generative recommendation, offering a scalable, semantically grounded solution suitable for industrial sequential recommendation systems.

title: MobileForge: Annotation-Free Adaptation for Mobile GUI Agents with Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization
summary: MLLM-based mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in UI understanding and action execution, but adapting them to real target apps remains costly because mobile apps are numerous, frequently updated, and hard to cover with human-written tasks, demonstrations, or reward labels. Existing annotation-free GUI learning reduces manual supervision, yet lacks a unified substrate connecting target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and feedback, while policy optimization often relies on isolated rollouts and coarse rewards that are hard to convert into reliable improvement signals. We present MobileForge, an annotation-free adaptation system for mobile GUI agents. MobileForge consists of MobileGym, which grounds task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interaction, and Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which turns trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO updates. Using only automatically generated annotation-free adaptation data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld, close to the closed-data GUI-specialized GUI-Owl-1.5-8B base model at 69.0%. The MobileForge-adapted ForgeOwl-8B further reaches 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent in our evaluation. Code, data, and trained models will be released at https://mobile-forge.github.io/.

AI.tldr: MobileForge is an annotation-free adaptation system for MLLM-based mobile GUI agents that combines target-app exploration, curriculum mining, rollout evaluation, and hierarchical feedback-driven policy optimization (HiFPO) to achieve state-of-the-art results without manual supervision.
AI.motivation: Adapting MLLM-based GUI agents to real target apps is costly due to the sheer number and frequent updates of mobile apps, making human-written tasks, demonstrations, and reward labels impractical. Existing annotation-free methods lack a unified framework that integrates exploration, curriculum mining, rollout execution, and fine-grained feedback for reliable policy improvement.
AI.method: MobileForge comprises two components: (1) MobileGym, which grounds automatic task generation and rollout evaluation in real mobile app interactions, and (2) Hierarchical Feedback-Guided Policy Optimization (HiFPO), which converts trajectory outcomes, step-level process feedback, and corrective hints into hint-contextualized step-level GRPO updates for fine-grained policy optimization.
AI.result: Using only automatically generated annotation-free data, MobileForge adapts Qwen3-VL-8B to 67.2% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld (vs. 69.0% for the closed-data GUI-Owl-1.5-8B). The adapted ForgeOwl-8B achieves 77.6% Pass@3 on AndroidWorld and 41.0% success on the out-of-domain MobileWorld GUI-only split, setting a new SOTA for open-data mobile GUI agents.
AI.conclusion: MobileForge demonstrates that annotation-free adaptation with hierarchical feedback-driven policy optimization can produce mobile GUI agents competitive with or surpassing closed-data models, establishing the strongest open-data mobile GUI agent and offering a scalable path for adapting agents to diverse real-world apps.

title: DISARM: Target Electronic Device Informed Mitigation of Software Runtime Side-Channel Vulnerabilities
summary: Program runtime or timing attacks exploit variations in a program's execution times to extract sensitive information from the program (e.g. encryption keys, sensitive variable data, intellectual property). State-of-the-art solutions to runtime side-channel attacks attempt to balance the execution time of the sensitive code for different control flow paths to eliminate the timing leakage. However, during the mitigation process, most techniques do not consider the underlying hardware or device on which the target program is supposed to run on. This can lead to over-fixing (unnecessary extra operations), under-fixing (not solving the imbalance properly), and even failures. We propose DISARM, a joint hardware-software methodology (unlike any existing solution) for mitigating runtime side-channel vulnerabilities that utilizes timing values from real embedded devices to generate targeted software fixes. We implement DISARM to support C, C++, and Java source codes and validate it across 22 standard benchmarks. DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions such as PENDULUM and DifFuzzAR in terms of execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness on five different embedded or edge devices.

AI.tldr: DISARM is a joint hardware-software methodology that uses real timing measurements from embedded devices to generate targeted mitigations for runtime side-channel vulnerabilities, outperforming existing solutions across multiple metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime side-channel mitigation techniques (e.g., program balancing) fail to account for the underlying hardware, leading to over-fixing, under-fixing, or outright mitigation failures. A hardware-aware approach is needed.
AI.method: DISARM employs a joint hardware-software methodology that collects timing values from real embedded/edge devices and uses them to generate targeted software fixes for C, C++, and Java source code, ensuring that mitigation is tailored to the specific hardware platform.
AI.result: Validated across 22 standard benchmarks on five different embedded/edge devices, DISARM outperforms state-of-the-art solutions (PENDULUM, DifFuzzAR) in execution time overhead, code size overhead, and correctness.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware, measurement-driven mitigation (DISARM) is more effective than hardware-agnostic approaches for eliminating runtime side-channel timing leakage on embedded systems.

title: Detecting Hallucinations for Large Language Model-based Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning infers new knowledge from existing facts and is widely applied in question answering, recommendation, and decision support. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks have become increasingly popular by leveraging retrieved KG information. However, hallucinations in LLMs remain a critical issue. Even when relevant KG knowledge is incorporated, models may still generate incorrect outputs, leading to misinformation and unreliable decisions. Existing hallucination detection methods either focus on LLM internal states or verify consistency with retrieved contexts, but both overlook the structural information in KGs, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this gap, we propose LUCID, the first halLUcination deteCtIon method for LLM-based knowleDge graph reasoning frameworks. LUCID jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information. Specifically, it extracts node and edge features from attention scores and semantic similarities, and integrates them with KG structure using a graph neural network. We also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation. Experiments on nine datasets show that LUCID achieves state of the art performance compared to 15 baselines.

AI.tldr: LUCID is a hallucination detection method for LLM-based KG reasoning that jointly leverages LLM attention scores, KG semantics, and structural information via a graph neural network, achieving SOTA across 9 benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs hallucinate even when provided with relevant KG knowledge during reasoning, and existing hallucination detection methods overlook the structural information inherent in KGs, leading to suboptimal detection performance.
AI.method: LUCID extracts node and edge features from LLM attention scores and semantic similarities, then integrates these with KG structural information using a graph neural network (GNN) for hallucination detection. The authors also construct manually annotated benchmark datasets for evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate that LUCID achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to 15 baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating KG structural information via GNNs significantly improves hallucination detection in LLM-based KG reasoning frameworks. LUCID represents the first dedicated solution to this problem.

title: Library-Aware Doubles and Iterative Repair for Large Language Model-Generated Unit Tests in OpenSIL Firmware
summary: Validating changes in low-level C firmware is expensive because unit tests (UTs) are fragile under strict build constraints, where missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. This study introduces an automated UT authoring workflow for the Open-Source Silicon Initialization Library (openSIL) firmware codebase maintained by Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) that reduces manual effort through a large language model (LLM) guided multi-agent pipeline. The workflow combines automated generation of test scaffolds, library-aware creation or reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes, and an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop driven by build logs and line-coverage feedback. We evaluate the approach using compilation success, repair iterations, dispatch success, and line coverage, with time, cost, and token usage as secondary measures. Across 76 functions under test, the workflow generated compilable UTs for 73 functions. In a configuration without line coverage guidance or retrieval augmentation, mean line coverage reached 73.9%. On a 48-function subset evaluated under both configurations, mean line coverage reached 98.8% with line-coverage guidance alone and reached 94.7% when combined with vector-database retrieval. Results show that automated generation-and-repair pipelines can substantially improve UT creation efficiency and coverage for constrained firmware environments while reducing manual debugging effort.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-guided multi-agent pipeline that automates unit test generation for low-level C firmware (AMD's openSIL), using iterative compile-dispatch repair loops driven by build logs and coverage feedback. Across 76 functions, 73 produced compilable tests, with mean line coverage reaching 98.8% when using coverage guidance.
AI.motivation: Unit testing low-level C firmware is expensive and fragile due to strict build constraints—missing headers, unresolved symbols, and dependency mismatches frequently prevent compilation and linking. Manual effort to create test scaffolds, stubs, mocks, and fakes is substantial, motivating automation.
AI.method: An automated multi-agent pipeline leveraging LLMs: (1) automated generation of test scaffolds; (2) library-aware creation/reuse of stubs, mocks, and fakes; (3) an iterative compile-dispatch repair loop informed by build logs and line-coverage feedback. Evaluated with and without line-coverage guidance and vector-database retrieval augmentation.
AI.result: Of 76 functions under test, 73 yielded compilable UTs. Without coverage guidance or retrieval, mean line coverage was 73.9%. On a 48-function subset, coverage-guided repair achieved 98.8% mean line coverage; combining with vector-database retrieval yielded 94.7%. Secondary measures included time, cost, and token usage.
AI.conclusion: Automated generation-and-repair pipelines substantially improve UT creation efficiency and line coverage for constrained firmware environments, significantly reducing manual debugging effort.

title: DevOps and General Developers: Insights from Stack Overflow's 2023 Survey
comment: 17 pages, 11 tables, research paper based on the 2023 Stack Overflow Developer Survey data analysis
summary:
Purpose: To investigate the distinct roles of DevOps specialists and general software developers, examining their varying use of tools, technologies, methodologies, and demographics in the current software development environment. In addition, to differentiate these two professional groups regarding their unique contributions and challenges in the field.
  Design/Methodology/Approach: The research uses a quantitative approach to analyze data from the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey. It focuses on a comparative analysis of technological preferences, demographic information, and professional experiences between DevOps specialists and general developers, highlighting key trends and differences. The data analysis was conducted using Python's Pandas library for data analysis.
  Findings: The research indicates no significant difference in the tool and technology preferences between DevOps specialists and general software developers, highlighting their complementary roles. DevOps specialists and general software developers use tools like Docker and Kubernetes, emphasizing efficiency and automation. While general developers employ diverse tools for various role demands, demographic trends show younger general developers and mid-career DevOps professionals. This age range reflects growing experience in DevOps, and both groups are adapting to remote and hybrid work models in the evolving tech industry.
  Practical Implications: This research offers perspectives on the dynamic roles within software development, emphasizing the growing importance of DevOps. It is a valuable resource for academic and industry professionals to understand the evolving dynamics in software development roles.
  Originality/Value: This research fills a significant gap in the existing literature regarding the evolving dynamics of software development roles.

AI.tldr: This study compares DevOps specialists and general software developers using Stack Overflow 2023 survey data, finding no significant differences in tool/technology preferences but revealing demographic distinctions—younger general developers versus mid-career DevOps professionals—with both groups adapting to remote/hybrid work models.
AI.motivation: To fill a gap in existing literature by systematically distinguishing DevOps specialists from general software developers in terms of tool usage, methodologies, demographics, and professional contributions, thereby clarifying their unique and complementary roles in modern software development.
AI.method: A quantitative comparative analysis of the Stack Overflow 2023 Developer Survey data, using Python's Pandas library to examine technological preferences, demographic distributions, and professional experiences between the two groups.
AI.result: No significant difference in tool/technology preferences was found between groups; both use Docker and Kubernetes heavily. Demographic analysis shows general developers skew younger while DevOps specialists are mid-career, reflecting the experience required for DevOps roles. Both groups are increasingly adopting remote and hybrid work arrangements.
AI.conclusion: DevOps specialists and general developers serve complementary rather than divergent roles, sharing similar tool ecosystems. The research provides valuable insights for academia and industry on evolving software development role dynamics, with the demographic patterns underscoring DevOps as a career progression path requiring accumulated experience.

title: Emergent Alignment
summary: Can Large Language Models (LLMs) discern when their own outputs are misaligned with human ethics? And can they self-correct? We endow an LLM with a conscience step that reviews its own reasoning and outputs, and we extend the training loss with an alignment component using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to steer the model away from non-ethical outputs. The result is an online technique to align models in a wide range of applications: training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot learning. It does not require a weaker or stronger judge, relying instead on a frozen copy of itself. In previous work, the Emergent Misalignment scenario showed a range of emergent unethical behaviors from fine-tuning the model to hack code. Instead, we empirically show how to achieve Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question steers training toward an ethical model under the same code hacking scenario.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "conscience step" where an LLM reviews its own outputs for ethical alignment, combined with DPO training, enabling self-correction of unethical outputs without external judges. The method achieves "Emergent Alignment" — a single introspective question steers the model toward ethical behavior, countering the previously observed Emergent Misalignment phenomenon.
AI.motivation: Prior work demonstrated Emergent Misalignment, where fine-tuning LLMs on tasks like code hacking produced unethical behaviors. The authors aim to address whether LLMs can detect their own ethical misalignment and self-correct, eliminating reliance on external weaker/stronger judges.
AI.method: The approach adds a "conscience step" where the model reviews its own reasoning chain and outputs. An alignment component is added to the training loss using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), steering the model away from non-ethical outputs. The method uses a frozen copy of the model as its own reference, operating online across training, fine-tuning, adversarial prompting, and zero-shot settings.
AI.result: Under the same code-hacking scenario that previously induced Emergent Misalignment, the method empirically demonstrates Emergent Alignment: a single high-level introspective question successfully steers training toward an ethical model.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can discern their own ethical misalignment and self-correct using an internal conscience mechanism paired with DPO, achieving Emergent Alignment without external judges, across diverse application scenarios.

title: Cost-Optimal LLM Routing with Limited User Feedback under User Satisfaction Guarantees
summary: Inference costs for large language model (LLM) applications are rapidly growing, driven by surging demand and rising infrastructure cost. Users expect high-quality responses, and in commercial settings this is formally codified in Service Level Agreements (SLAs), creating a fundamental tension between cost and quality. Recent progress on cost-aware LLM request routing has shown potential to resolve this tension, but existing approaches rely on complete feedback signals, offline training, extensive per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity. We introduce SLARouter, an online routing algorithm that learns a cost-optimal policy from the sparse, one-sided user feedback available in production systems. SLARouter provides theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance. Experiments across a wide range of LLM benchmarks show that SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without the need for per-benchmark tuning, reducing operating cost by up to 2.2x over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: SLARouter is an online routing algorithm for LLM applications that learns a cost-optimal policy from sparse, one-sided user feedback while providing theoretical guarantees for both cost optimality and strict SLA compliance, achieving up to 2.2x cost reduction over baselines without per-benchmark tuning.
AI.motivation: LLM inference costs are surging due to high demand and infrastructure expenses, while users expect high-quality responses codified in SLAs. Existing cost-aware routing methods require complete feedback, offline training, and per-workload tuning, and most lack SLA guarantees or inference-time adaptivity.
AI.method: SLARouter is an online learning-based routing algorithm that operates using only sparse, one-sided user feedback (implicit signals available in production systems). It jointly optimizes for cost and SLA compliance at inference time, with formal theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: Across diverse LLM benchmarks, SLARouter satisfies SLA constraints without any per-benchmark tuning and reduces operating costs by up to 2.2x compared to existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: SLARouter demonstrates that cost-optimal LLM routing with strict SLA guarantees is achievable using only the sparse feedback naturally available in production, eliminating the need for offline training and per-workload customization while significantly lowering operational costs.

title: AI Conversational Interviewing: Scaling Up Semi-Structured and In-depth Interviews
summary: Public opinion research has long faced a trade-off between depth and scale: standardized surveys enable large-scale measurement but restrict respondents to researcher-defined categories, obscuring the diversity of unexpected considerations that underlie public sentiment. More conversational interviews provide richer insights through open-ended probing, but their reliance on trained human interviewers has kept them difficult to scale. This study introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a method for collecting open-ended public opinion data at scale, pursuing three objectives: to demonstrate the analytical value of conversational text data for questions beyond the reach of closed-ended items; to assess the method's practical viability through participants' own evaluations; and to inform implementation by experimentally comparing voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice interview modes. We conducted a study combining an AI-led interview with a standardized survey on migration policy among 571 respondents recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel. The findings establish AI Conversational Interviewing as a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit. The conversational transcripts surface considerations and reasoning that a comprehensive standardized battery does not capture such as markedly different mental models of migration among subgroups with similar attitudes levels. Among respondents who completed the interview, evaluations of the AI interview were at or above those of the standardized survey across modes, although completion itself varied by condition. By releasing open data and open-source pipeline materials, the study contributes to a growing literature on harnessing artificial intelligence to expand the methods of public opinion measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AI Conversational Interviewing as a scalable method for collecting open-ended public opinion data, demonstrating through a study on migration policy (n=571) that conversational AI interviews surface reasoning missed by standardized surveys, achieve comparable or better respondent evaluations, and vary in completion rates across voice, chat, and free-choice modes.
AI.motivation: Public opinion research faces a persistent trade-off: standardized surveys offer scale but constrain respondents to researcher-defined categories, while conversational interviews yield richer insights but are difficult to scale due to reliance on trained human interviewers. The authors seek to resolve this tension by leveraging AI to conduct open-ended interviews at scale.
AI.method: The authors conducted a study with 571 respondents (recruited via Prolific and Payback Panel) combining an AI-led conversational interview with a standardized survey on migration policy. They experimentally compared three interview modes—voice-based, chat-based, and free-choice—to assess practical viability. Analysis focused on: (1) the unique analytical value of conversational transcripts versus closed-ended items, (2) participant evaluations of the AI interview experience, and (3) mode-dependent differences in completion and engagement.
AI.result: Conversational transcripts revealed considerations and mental models (e.g., divergent framings of migration among subgroups with similar attitude levels) that a comprehensive standardized battery failed to capture. Respondent evaluations of the AI interview matched or exceeded those of the standardized survey across all modes among completers. Completion rates, however, varied significantly by condition (voice, chat, free-choice).
AI.conclusion: AI Conversational Interviewing is a viable and valuable addition to the social-science toolkit, enabling scalable collection of open-ended public opinion data that surface reasoning beyond the reach of closed-ended items. The authors contribute open data and open-source pipeline materials to support further development of AI-augmented methods in public opinion research.

title: Heterogeneous LLM Debate Under Adversarial Peers: Honest Gains, Replacement Costs, and Resilience
summary: Heterogeneous LLM debate is motivated by the promise that diverse peers correct one another, but the same exchange that carries correction also carries adversarial influence. We measure which dominates by tracking how a heterogeneous peer changes the honest agents' revision behavior: how often they change their answer, and whether the change is corrective or harmful. We compare matched panels (homogeneous baseline, honest-mixed, and adversarial-mixed) and contaminated panels in which a malicious same-family peer is already present, spanning four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. An honest heterogeneous peer sharply lowers harmful revision, and an adversarial one reverses it. For Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the honest-slot harmful-revision rate falls from 89% in the homogeneous panel to 35% with an honest peer, and an adversarial peer returns it to 90%. The conditional rate hides this damage on weak defenders, but the end-of-debate flip rate exposes it. The pattern keeps its sign across families and benchmarks while its magnitude varies with the defender-benchmark regime. We also measure the effects when an adversarial same-family peer is already present: an honest heterogeneous peer lowers both harmful revision and the rate at which initially-correct answers are lost. On the same Llama-3.1-70B setting, the added honest peer cuts the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% under a same-family adversary to 6%. Heterogeneity is therefore not only an attack surface but, when an adversary is already present, also a defense.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how heterogeneous LLMs in debate panels affect revision behavior, finding that an honest heterogeneous peer sharply reduces harmful corrections, while an adversarial one reverses this benefit. When a malicious same-family peer is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer serves as an effective defense, cutting the loss rate of initially-correct answers dramatically.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous LLM debate offers the promise that diverse models correct each other's errors. However, the same mechanism that enables correction also opens the door to adversarial influence. The paper aims to disentangle these two forces by measuring which one dominates in practice — corrective benefit vs. adversarial harm — when peers from different model families interact.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled experimental framework comparing multiple panel configurations: (1) homogeneous baselines (same-family peers), (2) honest-mixed panels with a heterogeneous honest peer, (3) adversarial-mixed panels with a heterogeneous adversarial peer, and (4) contaminated panels where a malicious same-family peer is already present. They track two key metrics: how often honest agents change their answers, and whether each change is corrective or harmful. Experiments span four model families (including Llama-3.1-70B) and three reasoning benchmarks (notably MATH-hard).
AI.result: An honest heterogeneous peer sharply reduces harmful revision: for Llama-3.1-70B defenders on MATH-hard, the harmful-revision rate drops from 89% (homogeneous) to 35% (with honest heterogeneous peer). An adversarial heterogeneous peer reverses this back to 90%. On weak defenders, conditional rates mask the damage, but end-of-debate flip rates expose it. Critically, when an adversarial same-family peer is already present, adding an honest heterogeneous peer reduces the flip rate on initially-correct items from 31% to 6%. The sign of the pattern is consistent across model families and benchmarks, though magnitude varies by defender-benchmark regime.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneity in LLM debate is a double-edged sword: it is an attack surface exploitable by adversarial peers, but it also serves as a defense mechanism. When an adversary is already embedded within a same-family panel, introducing an honest heterogeneous peer provides substantial robustness, preserving initially-correct answers that would otherwise be lost. This reframes heterogeneity as not merely a vulnerability but a practical mitigation strategy.

title: Sign-Language Datasets at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey on Resources, Benchmarks, and Annotation Standards
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Sign languages are expressive visual languages used by Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) communities. Despite substantial progress in sign-language recognition, translation, and production, advances remain constrained by fragmented datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited linguistic coverage. Existing benchmarks often fail to reflect real-world communication needs, and systematic analyses of these limitations remain limited. In this survey, we present a comprehensive index of sign-language datasets, covering 120 resources across 35 sign languages. We analyze key challenges such as modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias, and outline considerations for future dataset design. We also introduce a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet and release a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/Ginqwerty/Open-Sign-Language) to support standardized documentation and reproducible evaluation. Overall, our work provides a unified and practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey indexing 120 sign-language datasets across 35 sign languages, analyzing challenges like modality imbalance, annotation granularity, and signer bias. Introduces a standardized 24-field datasheet and public repository to guide future dataset design and reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing sign-language datasets are fragmented, inconsistently annotated, and limited in linguistic coverage, hindering progress in recognition, translation, and production. Current benchmarks often misalign with real-world communication needs, and systematic analysis of these shortcomings is lacking.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale survey and indexing of 120 sign-language datasets spanning 35 sign languages. They systematically analyzed key challenges (modality imbalance, annotation granularity, signer bias) and proposed a 24-field Sign-Language Datasheet for standardized documentation, accompanied by a public GitHub repository for reproducible evaluation.
AI.result: The survey catalogs 120 datasets, identifies pervasive issues in modality balance, annotation quality, and demographic representation, and provides a structured datasheet template plus an open-source repository to facilitate more consistent, transparent, and reproducible sign-language research.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a unified, practical foundation for developing inclusive, robust, and scalable sign-language technologies by addressing dataset-level weaknesses and promoting standardization through the datasheet and repository framework.

title: JustDiag!: A Diagnostic Justification Engine for Accountable Root Cause Analysis
summary: Large language models can produce fluent root cause analyses, but fluent final answers alone are insufficient evidence for accountability in high-stakes operations. In real incident response, engineers need to know what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were considered, where contradictions remained, and whether the system resolved the case or preserved uncertainty. We address this gap with JustDiag, a diagnostic justification engine for RCA that maintains an explicit process state over evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. We evaluated the system on 66 real-world incidents using a two-layer protocol that separately scores final-answer quality and process quality. Relative to a matched control without diagnostic justification, JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores, while accepting slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure. These results suggest that accountable RCA requires explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not only fluent final answers.

AI.tldr: JustDiag is a diagnostic justification engine for root cause analysis (RCA) that maintains explicit process state over evidence, hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. Evaluated on 66 real-world incidents, it outperformed a matched control on both outcome and process quality, though with slightly lower terminal completion due to more calibrated non-closure — demonstrating that accountable RCA requires justification artifacts beyond fluent final answers.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate fluent RCA outputs, but fluency alone cannot establish accountability in high-stakes incident response.
