Engineers need transparency into what evidence supported a diagnosis, which alternatives were ruled out, where contradictions remain, and whether uncertainty was preserved or prematurely resolved. Existing systems lack this explicit diagnostic justification capability.
AI.method: JustDiag maintains an explicit process state tracking evidence, findings, competing hypotheses, conflicts, and next checks. Evaluation used a two-layer protocol on 66 real-world incidents, separately scoring final-answer quality and process quality, with a matched control group lacking diagnostic justification.
AI.result: JustDiag achieved stronger outcome and process scores relative to the control. Terminal completion was slightly lower, attributed to more calibrated non-closure — the system appropriately refrains from closing cases when evidence is insufficient rather than forcing a fluent but potentially incorrect resolution.
AI.conclusion: Accountable RCA demands explicit diagnostic justification artifacts and process-aware evaluation, not merely fluent final answers. Systems should preserve uncertainty, document evidential reasoning, and expose their diagnostic process for scrutiny.

title: ITNet: A Learnable Integral Transform That Subsumes Convolution, Attention, and Recurrence
summary: Convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers each encode different inductive biases -- locality, sequential memory, and content-dependent pairwise interaction -- and have remained mathematically distinct since their inception. We show that this fragmentation reflects not a fundamental diversity in how signals should be processed, but rather incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object: a learnable integral transform. We introduce the Integral Transform Network (ITNet), a unified architecture built around a learnable kernel that depends jointly on positions and features. This kernel is implemented as a small neural network, specifically an MLP, that models pairwise interactions, enabling the model to adapt its behavior from data. We show that convolution, self-attention (including multi-head), and autoregressive recurrence (including LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba) arise as special cases under appropriate parameterizations, and that ITNet is a universal approximator of continuous operators. To make this practical, we develop tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization, enabling efficient and scalable computation. A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K , GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA\,v2 and NLVR2. The results demonstrate that a single learned interaction mechanism can recover the behavior of all three architectural families from data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Integral Transform Networks (ITNet), a unified architecture showing that convolutions, self-attention, and recurrent networks are all special cases of a learnable integral transform with a joint position-feature kernel, implemented via an MLP. ITNet matches or surpasses specialized models across vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Convolutional networks (locality), recurrent networks (sequential memory), and transformers (content-dependent pairwise interaction) have remained mathematically distinct. The authors argue this fragmentation stems from incomplete views of a single underlying mathematical object — a learnable integral transform — rather than fundamental differences in signal processing.
AI.method: ITNet is built around a learnable integral transform with a kernel that depends jointly on positions and features, implemented as a small MLP modeling pairwise interactions. Convolutions, multi-head self-attention, and autoregressive recurrence (LSTM, GRU, S4, Mamba) are derived as special parameterizations. For practical scalability, the authors introduce tiled kernel fusion, importance-weighted Monte Carlo integration, and learned low-rank factorization.
AI.result: A single ITNet architecture with a shared operator and lightweight modality-specific encoders matches or exceeds specialized baselines on ImageNet-1K (vision), GLUE (language), ModelNet40 (3D), VQA v2, and NLVR2 (multimodal).
AI.conclusion: A single learned interaction mechanism — the integral transform kernel — can recover the behaviors of all three major architectural families (convolutional, recurrent, transformer) directly from data, demonstrating their mathematical unification under ITNet.

title: ProMUSE: Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty-guided Staged Evidential Alzheimer Disease Classification
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a fatal disorder that destroys memory and cognitive skills in the elderly population. Most treatments for AD are effective in the early stage, leading to an increasing demand for early AD diagnosis. AD diagnosis increasingly relies on multimodal data such as clinical assessments, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging. However, MRI and PET acquisition remain costly and not universally accessible, making full-modality inference impractical in real-world clinical workflows. We propose ProMUSE, a Progressive Multi-modal Uncertainty Guided Staged Evidential Network that adaptively determines when additional modalities are necessary, helping reduce the overall cost of data acquisition while maintaining accuracy. ProMUSE first performs evidential classification using low-cost clinical data and quantifies uncertainty via a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, ProMUSE progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty through Dempster-Shafer theory to obtain a calibrated multimodal prediction. This staged acquisition strategy enables accurate diagnosis while minimizing reliance on expensive imaging. Experiments on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks demonstrate that ProMUSE achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to full-modality baselines while reducing MRI/PET usage by 50-90%, yielding substantial cost savings. These results highlight ProMUSE as a practical, uncertainty-aware, and resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening.

AI.tldr: ProMUSE is a staged evidential network that uses clinical data first, quantifies uncertainty, and only requests costly MRI/PET when needed—achieving competitive AD diagnosis accuracy while reducing imaging usage by 50–90%.
AI.motivation: MRI and PET are expensive and not universally accessible, making full-modality AD diagnosis impractical in real-world clinical workflows. Current methods lack a principled way to decide when additional costly modalities are actually necessary.
AI.method: ProMUSE performs evidential classification on low-cost clinical data using a Dirichlet-based subjective logic model to quantify uncertainty. When uncertainty exceeds a learned threshold, it progressively incorporates MRI or PET features, fusing modality-wise belief and uncertainty via Dempster-Shafer theory for calibrated multimodal prediction.
AI.result: On ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS datasets across CN-AD, CN-MCI, and MCI-AD tasks, ProMUSE matched or exceeded full-modality baselines while cutting MRI/PET usage by 50–90%, yielding substantial cost savings.
AI.conclusion: ProMUSE offers a practical, uncertainty-aware, resource-efficient solution for real-world AD screening by adaptively determining when expensive imaging is necessary without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy.

title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Cold-start Recommendation
summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems due to its accessibility and generality, yet it usually presents noisy samples (e.g., clickbait, position bias). Meanwhile, recommenders inevitably face the item cold-start problem due to the continuous influx of new items. We identify that cold items are more prone to noisy samples due to the aforementioned factors, and researchers often overlook the significance of denoising implicit feedback for cold items. Previous denoising studies usually identify noisy samples based on heuristic patterns, such as higher loss values, and mitigate noise through sample selection or re-weighting. However, these methods have limited adaptability and are ineffective in cold-start scenarios. To achieve denoising implicit feedback for cold-start recommendation, we propose a model-agnostic denoising method called DIF. First, user preferences for content remain stable, which allows us to infer pseudo-labels indicating whether a user is interested in a cold item through content-similar warm items. Furthermore, to improve pseudo-label accuracy, we model the confidence of pseudo-labels based on the content similarity between the cold item and warm items, and then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels for each sample. Finally, we explicitly estimate the uncertainty of the noisy sample label by considering its relative entropy and the cold-start status of the item, which adaptively guides the role of pseudo-labels to correct the noisy labels at the sample level. DIF's superiority is supported by both theoretical justification and extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The method has been deployed on a billion-user scale short video application Kuaishou and has significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIF is a model-agnostic denoising method for cold-start recommendation that leverages content-similar warm items to generate pseudo-labels, models pseudo-label confidence via content similarity, and uses relative entropy to estimate label uncertainty, thereby adaptively correcting noisy implicit feedback for cold items. Deployed at Kuaishou, it significantly improved commercial metrics.
AI.motivation: Implicit feedback in recommender systems is noisy (clickbait, position bias), and cold items are disproportionately affected by this noise. Existing denoising methods rely on heuristic patterns (e.g., high loss) and lack adaptability, performing poorly in cold-start scenarios where interaction data is sparse and unreliable.
AI.method: DIF operates in three stages: (1) Infer pseudo-labels for cold items by leveraging stable user content preferences and content-similar warm items. (2) Model pseudo-label confidence based on content similarity between cold and warm items, then aggregate multiple pseudo-labels per sample. (3) Estimate the uncertainty of noisy sample labels using relative entropy and the item's cold-start status, which adaptively weights pseudo-labels to correct noisy labels at the sample level.
AI.result: The method is theoretically justified and validated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets. It has been deployed on Kuaishou, a billion-user short-video platform, and significantly improved various commercial metrics within cold-start scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DIF effectively addresses the overlooked problem of denoising implicit feedback specifically for cold items. By using content-similar warm items to generate confidence-weighted pseudo-labels and adaptively correcting noisy labels based on uncertainty estimation, it outperforms prior heuristic denoising methods and demonstrates real-world industrial impact at scale.

title: Editorial Alignment: A Participatory Approach to Engaging Editorial Expertise in LLM-mediated Knowledge Dissemination
summary: The emergence of LLM-driven information services is reshaping the conditions under which public knowledge institutions operate, threatening to absorb the editorial function these institutions exist to exercise. While LLMs offer powerful new affordances for knowledge dissemination, editorial authority is challenged by pretrained LLMs that arrive already aligned with the values and dissemination strategies of their commercial developers. This paper investigates editor participation in re-aligning LLM interfaces to editorial standards through design workshops, in a case study where we design and implement an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface with a Nordic public knowledge institution. We introduce editorial alignment as a design practice within Participatory AI, framing AI alignment as a design process and positioning the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation. Last, we discuss how editorial alignment can create space for ongoing participation and give editors agency in LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "editorial alignment" as a Participatory AI design practice, demonstrated through a case study with a Nordic public knowledge institution where editors participated in designing an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface to realign pretrained models with institutional editorial standards.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven information services threaten to absorb the editorial function of public knowledge institutions by imposing the values and dissemination strategies of commercial developers. There is a need to investigate how editors can participate in realigning LLM interfaces to uphold institutional editorial authority and standards.
AI.method: A case study employing design workshops with editors from a Nordic public knowledge institution. Researchers and editors collaboratively designed and implemented an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface, using "editorial alignment" — framing the editorial standard as a design artefact that translates editorial practice and values into alignment objectives for technical implementation.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that editorial alignment, as a Participatory AI practice, enables editors to reassert agency over LLM-mediated knowledge dissemination. The editorial standard serves as a boundary object bridging editorial values and technical alignment objectives, and the participatory process creates ongoing space for editor involvement.
AI.conclusion: Editorial alignment offers a viable design practice for public knowledge institutions to reclaim editorial authority in LLM-mediated contexts. By treating alignment as a participatory design process rather than a purely technical one, institutions can create durable mechanisms for ongoing editor participation and value translation.

title: Low-Cost Multi-Precision Systolic Arrays for Accelerating FHE NTTs on AI ASICs
summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) ensures robust data privacy but suffers from prohibitive computational overhead. Accelerating FHE on AI hardware like Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) is promising, yet fundamentally limited by a precision mismatch: TPUs are optimized for 8-bit arithmetic, whereas FHE and its critical parts such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), demand high precision. Current approaches bridge this gap using matrix decomposition to execute NTT computations on low-precision matrix engines. However, reconstructing the full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that does not match the dataflow of matrix multiplication. This forces offloading full-precision reconstruction from matrix engines to vector processors that disrupts the matrix multiplication dataflow, creating significant performance bottleneck. To resolve this limitation, we propose a minimally modified multi-precision systolic array that performs full-precision output reconstruction natively within the array in sync with low-precision matrix multiplication under a uniform dataflow. Synthesized at 7nm with OpenRoad, our design incurs negligible hardware overhead. Cycle-accurate simulations using SCALE-Sim demonstrate that natively executing NTTs on the proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33x speedup, for transform sizes 2^12 to 2^16 on 128x128 matrix engines, successfully enabling standard AI hardware to support high-precision FHE acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-precision systolic array that natively performs full-precision output reconstruction within the array, eliminating the bottleneck caused by offloading reconstruction to vector processors. The design achieves at least 1.33× speedup for NTT on TPU-like hardware with negligible hardware overhead.
AI.motivation: FHE requires high-precision arithmetic, but AI accelerators (TPUs) are optimized for low-precision (8-bit). Existing solutions use matrix decomposition for NTT on low-precision matrix engines, but reconstructing full-precision results requires shift-and-add accumulation that disrupts the systolic dataflow, forcing offloading to vector processors and creating a severe performance bottleneck.
AI.method: A minimally modified multi-precision systolic array design that integrates full-precision output reconstruction natively within the systolic array, synchronized with low-precision matrix multiplication under a unified dataflow. The design is synthesized at 7nm using OpenRoad and evaluated via cycle-accurate simulation with SCALE-Sim.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves at least 1.33× speedup for NTT transform sizes ranging from 2^12 to 2^16 on 128×128 matrix engines, with negligible hardware overhead confirmed by 7nm synthesis.
AI.conclusion: By minimally extending the systolic array to natively support full-precision reconstruction, standard AI hardware can efficiently support high-precision FHE acceleration without disrupting the matrix multiplication dataflow, enabling practical FHE deployment on existing AI accelerators.

title: Quantifying Aleatoric Uncertainty of In-Context Learning for Robust Measure of LLM Prediction Confidence
summary: In-Context Learning (ICL) allows LLMs to adapt to new tasks from a few demonstrations, but its reliability remains a concern: predictions are highly sensitive to both prompt design and the model's ability to understand the context, obscuring whether failures arise from data properties or model limitations. Uncertainty decomposition-separating aleatoric from epistemic sources-is particularly crucial in this setting, yet existing methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL. To address this, we introduce a concept of self-function vectors, built upon Bayesian views and the mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal model representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, thereby enabling a direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework and circumventing the reliance on brittle input or decoding manipulations. Given the lack of established benchmarks and suitable evaluation protocols, we also propose the first and rigorous evaluation protocol, in which data is manipulated in controlled ways so as to quantify aleatoric uncertainty precisely and separately from epistemic uncertainty. With this new evaluation framework, initially grounded in synthetic tasks for conceptual development and subsequently extended to real-world datasets, we show that our proposed methodology can measure uncertainty of LLM predictions made under ICL more reliably than existing alternative methods. Moreover, we show it can be used as a practical tool for trustworthy-related applications, such as hallucination detection. Our findings pave a new direction for connecting the quantitative view of uncertainty with the mechanistic understanding of model behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "self-function vectors" - a Bayesian framework using internal model representations to decompose uncertainty in In-Context Learning, addressing the failure of existing uncertainty methods. It also proposes the first rigorous evaluation protocol with controlled data manipulation, demonstrating superior reliability over alternatives and practical applications like hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: In-Context Learning (ICL) reliability is compromised by high sensitivity to prompt design and model understanding, making it unclear whether failures stem from data properties (aleatoric uncertainty) or model limitations (epistemic uncertainty). Existing uncertainty decomposition methods, designed for standard generation tasks, fail to capture the unique dynamics of ICL, creating a need for a tailored approach and a rigorous evaluation benchmark.
AI.method: The authors propose self-function vectors grounded in Bayesian principles and mechanistic interpretability of ICL. These vectors leverage internal LLM representations to model the latent concept learned during in-context prompting, enabling direct estimation of aleatoric uncertainty within a Bayesian framework without relying on brittle input or decoding manipulations. They also introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that manipulates data to precisely quantify aleatoric uncertainty separately from epistemic uncertainty, tested first on synthetic tasks and then on real-world datasets.
AI.result: The proposed self-function vector methodology measures uncertainty in ICL predictions more reliably than existing methods. The approach also proves practical for trustworthy applications such as hallucination detection, bridging quantitative uncertainty estimation with mechanistic model understanding.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new direction connecting quantitative uncertainty quantification with mechanistic interpretability of model behavior. The self-function vector framework and accompanying evaluation protocol offer a principled, reliable way to decompose and estimate uncertainty in ICL, with demonstrated practical utility for trustworthiness applications.

title: ScaffoldAgent: Utility-Guided Dynamic Outline Optimization for Open-Ended Deep Research
summary: Open-ended deep research (OEDR) requires systems to acquire knowledge through multi-round retrieval and generate coherent long-form reports. The outline plays a central role as a structural scaffold that coordinates retrieval, evidence organization, and generation. However, existing methods either fix the outline before writing or refine it with local heuristics, leading to scaffold drift under continuous information accumulation and delayed feedback for evaluating outline modifications. We propose ScaffoldAgent, a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for OEDR. ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three operations: Expansion, Contraction, and Revision, enabling controlled updates to the report scaffold. It further introduces a utility-guided feedback mechanism that estimates the downstream value of each outline operation from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. The resulting utility signal guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference. Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym show that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves long-form report generation and factual grounding over existing deep research agents.

AI.tldr: ScaffoldAgent introduces a utility-guided dynamic outline optimization framework for open-ended deep research, modeling outline evolution through Expansion, Contraction, and Revision operations with a feedback mechanism that estimates downstream value from retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing open-ended deep research systems suffer from "scaffold drift" — the outline becomes misaligned with accumulated information over time because methods either lock the outline before writing or refine it with only local heuristics, lacking timely global feedback on whether outline modifications improve the final report.
AI.method: ScaffoldAgent models outline evolution as a structured decision process with three atomic operations (Expansion, Contraction, Revision) for controlled scaffold updates. A utility-guided feedback mechanism estimates the downstream value of each operation by evaluating retrieval gain, structural coherence, and trial-generation quality. This utility signal then guides node selection, operation scheduling, and termination during inference.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearch Gym demonstrate that ScaffoldAgent consistently improves both long-form report generation quality and factual grounding compared to existing deep research agents.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, utility-guided outline optimization with global feedback effectively mitigates scaffold drift in open-ended deep research, enabling more coherent and factually grounded long-form report generation.

title: OpenRath: Session-Centered Runtime State for Agent Systems
summary: Modern agent systems often suffer from fragmented runtime state: transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, and replay evidence are recorded separately and become difficult to inspect or reproduce. OpenRath addresses this issue with a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent, multi-session systems. The analogy concerns the role of a central first-class runtime abstraction, not tensor computation. Its core abstraction is Session, the runtime value passed between agents and workflows. A Session is branchable, inspectable, replayable, backend-aware, and composable. It records conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence, while defining where memory interactions enter the runtime record. Since this state is carried by the same value used in program execution, fork, merge, and replay become explicit runtime operations rather than states reconstructed from external traces. OpenRath further defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector, with Selector turning control flow into runtime-routed decisions. This report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and evidence protocol. Its claims are limited to controlled runtime properties, while broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are left for follow-on evaluation. The central thesis is that Session provides agent systems with a first-class runtime value for auditable composition.

AI.tldr: OpenRath introduces a PyTorch-like programming model for multi-agent systems centered on a first-class runtime abstraction called Session, which unifies fragmented runtime state (transcripts, tool effects, memory, lineage) into a branchable, inspectable, and replayable value, enabling explicit fork/merge/replay operations rather than external trace reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Modern agent systems record runtime state (conversation transcripts, tool effects, memory events, workspace placement, branch provenance, replay evidence) in fragmented, disparate locations, making inspection and faithful reproduction difficult. There is a need for a unified runtime abstraction that consolidates these scattered artifacts into a single, auditable value.
AI.method: OpenRath proposes a programming model analogous to PyTorch's central tensor abstraction, but applied to agent runtime state. Its core abstraction, Session, is a first-class runtime value that carries conversation chunks, sandbox placement, lineage metadata, token usage, pending work, and tool evidence while defining memory interaction boundaries. Session supports explicit fork, merge, and replay as runtime operations. The model also defines Sandbox, Tool, Agent, Memory, Workflow, and Selector — the latter transforming control flow into runtime-routed decisions.
AI.result: The report presents the programming model, architecture, audited milestones, and an evidence protocol. Claims are strictly scoped to controlled runtime properties; broad quantitative comparisons, live-provider quality, optional-backend availability, and memory quality are deferred to follow-on evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The central thesis is that Session, as a first-class runtime value, provides agent systems with auditable composition, addressing the fragmentation problem by making state an intrinsic, operable part of program execution.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
summary: Recent position papers argue that the classical aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty framework is insufficient for interactive large language model (LLM) agents and call for underspecification-aware, decomposed, and communicable uncertainty representations that can unlock new agent capabilities such as proactive clarification seeking and shared mental-model building. Practical deployment constraints -- black-box APIs, interactive latency budgets, and the absence of labeled trajectories -- rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based estimation as the most viable family for surfacing such signals at deployment time. We answer this call with a simple prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u), enabling the agent to ask for clarification when the task specification is ambiguous. To evaluate it, we introduce two clarification-augmented benchmarks (WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified, and systematically compare the proposed decomposition against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B) on these variants together with the standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL benchmarks for fault detection. Averaged across the five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM, and leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, indicating that the gains generalize beyond a single LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-based method that decomposes LLM agent uncertainty into action confidence and request uncertainty, enabling proactive clarification-seeking when task specifications are ambiguous. Evaluated on two new underspecified benchmarks across five LLM backbones, it significantly outperforms existing uncertainty estimation methods (ReAct+UE, UAM) on clarification F1.
AI.motivation: Existing aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty frameworks are insufficient for interactive LLM agents. Deployment constraints (black-box APIs, latency budgets, no labeled trajectories) rule out logprob-based, multi-sampling, and training-based methods, leaving prompt-based uncertainty estimation as the only viable approach. There is a need for underspecification-aware, decomposed, communicable uncertainty representations that support proactive clarification seeking.
AI.method: A prompt-based decomposition that separates action confidence from request uncertainty (u). When request uncertainty is high — indicating an ambiguous task specification — the agent proactively asks for clarification. Two new benchmarks are introduced: WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification, where 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified. The method is systematically compared against ReAct+UE and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM) across five LLM backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B), tested on these augmented benchmarks plus standard WebShop, ALFWorld, and REAL for fault detection.
AI.result: Averaged across five backbones, the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and by 36% over UAM. It leads clarification F1 on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and on four of five backbones on ALFWorld-Clarification, demonstrating generalization beyond a single LLM.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based decomposition of uncertainty into action confidence and request uncertainty is an effective, deployment-viable strategy for enabling LLM agents to recognize underspecified tasks and proactively seek clarification, with consistent gains across diverse model backbones.

title: cAPM: Continual AI-Assisted Pace-Mapping with Active Learning
summary: Ventricular tachycardia is a life-threatening rhythm disorder and a major cause of sudden cardiac death. Pace-mapping is a clinical procedure for identifying the intervention target during catheter ablation of VT. It requires clinicians to pace different sites in the ventricles and rapidly interpret the resulting electrocardiograms to determine where to pace next or whether a target site has been identified. Active learning AI models have been proposed to guide clinicians to the next pacing site, showing promise in reducing the number of pacing sites and improving the efficiency of pace-mapping. Existing methods require retraining each target without the ability to transfer knowledge across multiple VTs within the same patient or across patients. We introduce cAPM for continuous AI-assisted pace-mapping to capture and transfer knowledge accumulated from past pace-mapping data to reduce the number of pace-mapping data needed for future target VTs. This is made possible by a task-agnostic surrogate neural network that learns the mapping from pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, an active-learning strategy that refines this surrogate model by selecting the most informative pacing site for each target, and a continual learning strategy to do so sequentially while retaining knowledge from prior targets. Evaluated on an in-silico testbed consisting of sequentially-presented localization tasks across different physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, cAPM with and without replay of past data samples achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (5 mm accuracy) using 4.5 pace-mapping sites, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving 38% probability using 13.7 pacing sites. These results provide a strong basis for preparing cAPM towards in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies where it can be used to guide pace-mapping.

AI.tldr: cAPM is a continual active-learning framework for pace-mapping that transfers knowledge across sequential ventricular tachycardia (VT) localization tasks, achieving 81% localization probability within 5 mm using only 4.5 pacing sites versus 38% with 13.7 sites for prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-assisted pace-mapping methods require retraining from scratch for each VT target, failing to leverage knowledge accumulated from prior pace-mapping procedures within the same patient or across patients. This inefficiency demands a solution that can transfer and build upon past experience to reduce the number of pacing sites needed.
AI.method: cAPM combines three components: (1) a task-agnostic surrogate neural network mapping pacing sites to 12-lead ECG morphology, (2) an active-learning strategy selecting the most informative next pacing site for each target, and (3) a continual learning strategy enabling sequential knowledge retention across targets. Evaluation used an in-silico testbed with sequentially-presented localization tasks across varied physiological conditions and ventricular geometries, tested with and without replay of past data samples.
AI.result: cAPM achieved an 81% probability of localizing within clinical tolerance (≤5 mm) using only 4.5 pace-mapping sites on average, compared to the state-of-the-art active-learning method achieving only 38% probability while requiring 13.7 pacing sites.
AI.conclusion: Continuous learning substantially improves the data efficiency of AI-assisted pace-mapping by transferring knowledge across VT targets. The strong in-silico results provide a solid foundation for advancing cAPM toward in-vivo preclinical and clinical studies.

title: Organizing in the Digital Age: Understanding Community, Challenges, and Consequences in Digitally-facilitated Labor Organizing
summary: The contemporary American labor force is highly dispersed, necessitating the use of digital communication tools to bridge spatial and temporal gaps in union organizing. This study provides an in-depth analysis of how workers within various labor unions utilize digital, text-based communication platforms -- including Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack -- for labor organizing. Through 17 qualitative interviews, we examine the challenges and opportunities presented by digital organizing, identifying both technical and social obstacles. Our findings reveal that although digital tools are integral to contemporary labor successes, they also introduce new complexities, such as navigating technical security, managing information overload, and building trust and consensus. Based on these insights, we draw connections to broader understandings of digital organizing and the role of digital tools in unions.

AI.tldr: This qualitative study (n=17 interviews) investigates how American labor unions use text-based digital platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing. While digital tools are essential to modern union successes, they introduce challenges around security, information overload, and trust-building.
AI.motivation: The American workforce is increasingly geographically dispersed, creating spatial and temporal gaps that hinder traditional union organizing. Digital communication tools have become necessary to bridge these gaps, yet their specific affordances and challenges for labor organizing remain underexamined.
AI.method: The study employs 17 qualitative semi-structured interviews with workers across various labor unions who use digital, text-based communication platforms (Discord, WhatsApp, Slack) for organizing activities.
AI.result: Digital tools are integral to contemporary labor organizing successes but introduce three key complexities: (1) navigating technical security concerns, (2) managing information overload, and (3) building trust and consensus in text-based environments. Both technical and social obstacles were identified.
AI.conclusion: The findings connect to broader understandings of digital organizing, highlighting a dual-edged dynamic: digital platforms enable geographically dispersed worker coordination but simultaneously create novel socio-technical challenges that unions must strategically navigate.

title: FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
summary: Existing safety benchmarks target general adversarial scenarios but miss finance-specific risks. Financial LLMs face regulatory compliance violations, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion that require targeted evaluation. We introduce FinRED, an expert-guided red-teaming framework for financial LLM safety evaluation developed with financial experts. FinRED uses a novel two-level taxonomy mapping global standards (e.g., FATF and EU DORA) to threats ranging from regulatory evasion to complex fraud, integrated with a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into context-rich red-teaming Behavioral Prompts (seeds) through an expert-defined schema. Rigorous expert validation confirms seed plausibility and realism for meaningful LLM safety evaluation. We also provide an expert-validated, finance-specific rubric that goes beyond disclaimer checks, aligns more closely with human experts than static one-size-fits-all rubrics, and reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12. Aligned with internationally adopted risk-management and information-security standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 27001), FinRED is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI) regulatory sandbox for generative AI security evaluation in real financial services. To mitigate dual-use risks, the dataset, generation pipeline, prompt template, and evaluation framework are gated for qualified researchers at https://github.com/selectstar-ai/FinRED-paper and https://huggingface.co/datasets/datumo/FinRED.

AI.tldr: FinRED is an expert-guided red-teaming framework for evaluating financial LLM safety, featuring a two-level threat taxonomy aligned with global standards (FATF, EU DORA), a document-to-prompt generation pipeline, and a finance-specific evaluation rubric that significantly reduces false negatives. It is deployed in South Korea's FSI regulatory sandbox.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks overlook finance-specific risks such as regulatory non-compliance, fraud facilitation, and systemic trust erosion. Financial LLMs require targeted, context-rich evaluation grounded in real financial regulations and expert knowledge.
AI.method: FinRED employs: (1) a two-level threat taxonomy derived from global standards (FATF, EU DORA) and mapped to threats like regulatory evasion and complex fraud; (2) a scalable pipeline that converts real financial documents into Behavioral Prompts (seeds) via an expert-defined schema; (3) a finance-specific evaluation rubric validated by experts that moves beyond simple disclaimer detection and better aligns with human judgment.
AI.result: The expert-validated rubric reduces critical false negatives from 28 to 12 compared to static, one-size-fits-all rubrics. The framework is deployed in South Korea's Financial Security Institute regulatory sandbox for real-world generative AI security evaluation in financial services.
AI.conclusion: FinRED provides a rigorous, standards-aligned, and practically deployed solution for financial LLM safety evaluation. Its expert-driven design, real-document grounding, and improved rubric offer a meaningful advance over generic benchmarks, with gated access to mitigate dual-use risks.

title: Granularity-Regulated Adaptive Computational Efficiency for Optimal Verification in Test-Time Scaling
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs) by investing additional compute at inference time. A central component of TTS is the \emph{verifier}, which selects or scores candidate solutions to guide the search process. While prior work has explored the benefit of verification, a fundamental question remains underexplored: \emph{what is the optimal granularity of verification under a given compute budget?} Coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) and fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) represent two extremes, yet neither alone achieves compute-optimality across all regimes. In this paper, we establish a unified theoretical framework, called \textbf{GRACE} (\underline{G}ranularity-\underline{R}egulated \underline{A}daptive \underline{C}omputational \underline{E}fficiency), that characterizes the optimal verification granularity as an explicit function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget. We prove that there exists a phase transition: fine-grained verification dominates when either the compute budget is large or the problem is hard, whereas coarse-grained verification is preferred in the low-budget, easy-problem regime. Our theory unifies Best-of-$N$, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality framework, and motivates an adaptive granularity strategy that provably achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME benchmarks corroborate all four theoretical claims, with our adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1\% accuracy at matched compute.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GRACE, a theoretical framework that determines the optimal granularity of verification (coarse-grained ORMs vs. fine-grained PRMs) in test-time scaling for LLMs. The authors prove a phase transition: fine-grained verification is optimal under large compute budgets or hard problems, while coarse-grained verification wins in low-budget, easy-problem regimes. An adaptive strategy is derived that achieves the compute-performance Pareto frontier, with up to 3.1% accuracy gains over fixed-granularity baselines.
AI.motivation: Prior work uses either coarse-grained outcome reward models (ORMs) or fine-grained process reward models (PRMs) for verification in test-time scaling, but a fundamental question is unanswered: what is the optimal verification granularity given a compute budget? Neither ORMs nor PRMs alone are compute-optimal across all regimes. The authors seek to formally characterize the optimal granularity as a function of problem difficulty, verifier accuracy, and compute budget.
AI.method: The authors propose GRACE, a unified theoretical framework that models verification granularity as a continuum between ORMs and PRMs. They formally analyze the expected utility of different granularities under varying problem difficulty, verifier error rates, and compute budgets. The framework unifies Best-of-N, beam search, and step-level MCTS within a single Pareto-optimality analysis. They prove a phase transition theorem and derive an adaptive granularity strategy that dynamically selects the optimal granularity per problem instance to achieve the Pareto frontier.
AI.result: The theory predicts four claims: (1) a phase transition exists where fine-grained verification dominates with large budget/hard problems and coarse-grained dominates with low budget/easy problems; (2) the optimal granularity is a monotonic function of budget and difficulty; (3) the adaptive strategy achieves Pareto optimality; (4) the framework unifies existing search strategies. Empirical results on MATH-500, GSM8K, and AIME confirm all four claims, with the adaptive strategy outperforming fixed-granularity baselines by up to 3.1% accuracy at matched compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: There is no universally optimal verification granularity — it depends on the compute budget and problem difficulty. The GRACE framework provides a principled way to select granularity adaptively, achieving the compute-performance Pareto frontier. This motivates moving beyond one-size-fits-all verifiers toward budget-aware, difficulty-aware verification strategies in test-time scaling.

title: RACL: Reasoning-Agent Control Layers for Continuous Metaheuristic Learning
summary: This paper introduces RACL, a Reasoning-Agent Control Layer for metaheuristics. RACL places a reasoning agent above an existing optimizer. The agent does not replace the optimizer and does not modify business constraints. Instead, it controls the optimizer's internal search behavior by observing operational memory, reasoning over past behavior, formulating bounded hypotheses, testing interventions, evaluating outcomes, applying guardrails, consolidating useful policies and explaining its decisions. The experiment uses vehicle routing as a testbed, but the contribution is not a new routing solver, a particular ALNS configuration or a specific set of routing rules. The contribution is the RACL method: a way for a reasoning agent to discover, validate, consolidate and explain algorithmic control rules for a metaheuristic. In the current experimental setting, RACL improves or ties the Operational Memory Policy in 21 of 21 feasible cases and improves or ties a non-reasoning Stagnation-Triggered Policy in 18 of 21 feasible cases, with an average RACL vs STP cost delta of -0.641%. In the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL improves average cost by -8.337% versus Fixed and -1.605% versus STP without showing material computational overhead. During the proof-of-concept, Codex was used as an in-the-loop reasoning agent observing executions, interpreting logs and proposing live bounded interventions. The policy proxy was later used only to make quantitative evaluation reproducible.

AI.tldr: RACL introduces a reasoning-agent control layer that sits above existing metaheuristic optimizers, autonomously observing, reasoning, and intervening in the search process without modifying core algorithms or constraints. Tested on vehicle routing, it demonstrates consistent cost improvements over baseline policies with negligible computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Metaheuristics often rely on hand-tuned control policies that are brittle and fail to adapt to diverse problem instances. The authors aim to replace static, human-designed control logic with an autonomous reasoning agent capable of observing search behavior, formulating hypotheses, testing interventions, and consolidating useful policies — all without altering the underlying optimizer or business constraints.
AI.method: RACL consists of a reasoning agent (Codex during proof-of-concept) operating in-the-loop with an existing optimizer. The agent: (1) observes operational memory of the running metaheuristic, (2) reasons over past behavior to formulate bounded hypotheses, (3) tests interventions in live search, (4) evaluates outcomes, (5) applies guardrails for safety, (6) consolidates successful policies, and (7) explains its decisions. The method is optimizer-agnostic and was validated on vehicle routing problems using ALNS. For reproducibility, a policy proxy later replaced the live LLM agent.
AI.result: RACL matched or outperformed the Operational Memory Policy in all 21 feasible cases (21/21) and the Stagnation-Triggered Policy (STP) in 18/21 feasible cases, with an average cost reduction of -0.641% vs STP. On the Sevilla-9/10 runtime sample, RACL achieved -8.337% average cost improvement over Fixed and -1.605% over STP, without material computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: RACL demonstrates that a reasoning agent can effectively serve as a control layer for metaheuristics, discovering and consolidating algorithmic control rules autonomously. The contribution is the general method — not any specific routing solver or rule set — enabling adaptive, explainable, and transferable control policies without modifying the underlying optimizer.

title: FAPO: Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization of Multi-Step LLM Pipelines
summary: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail through interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, so prompt-only optimization can miss bottlenecks in the chain. We present FAPO (Fully Autonomous Prompt Optimization), a framework that lets Claude Code optimize an LLM pipeline inside a standardized codebase. FAPO evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants repeatedly to optimize against a score function. It first tries prompt edits and, only when prompt optimization appears insufficient, changes chain structure within the permitted scope when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the baseline GEPA in 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. In 11 model-benchmark comparisons, FAPO wins with non-overlapping mean $\pm$ trial-standard-deviation ranges, and the mean FAPO-GEPA gain is +14.1 pp. In the six HoVer and IFBench comparisons where prompt-first search escalated to structural changes, FAPO wins all six with a mean gain of +33.8 pp. FAPO also improves performance on security tasks: on CTIBench-RCM, a security CVE-to-CWE task, prompt-only FAPO lifts test accuracy by +4.0 pp on GPT-5, +7.1 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, and +2.0 pp on Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning. These results position FAPO as a state-of-the-art pipeline optimization technique for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks.

AI.tldr: FAPO is an autonomous LLM pipeline optimization framework that alternates between prompt editing and structural changes to the chain. It outperforms the GEPA baseline across 15 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons, with particularly large gains (+33.8 pp) when structural changes are needed.
AI.motivation: Multi-step LLM pipelines fail due to interactions among retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps. Prompt-only optimization methods miss structural bottlenecks that arise from these interactions, motivating a framework that can autonomously diagnose and fix both prompt-level and structural issues.
AI.method: FAPO operates inside a standardized codebase using Claude Code. It iteratively evaluates a pipeline, inspects intermediate steps, diagnoses failures, proposes scoped changes, and validates variants. It first attempts prompt edits; only when attribution identifies a structural bottleneck does it escalate to modifying the chain structure within a permitted scope, all optimized against a score function.
AI.result: FAPO beats GEPA in 15/18 model-benchmark comparisons across six benchmarks. It wins 11 comparisons with non-overlapping mean ± trial-SD ranges, with a mean gain of +14.1 pp. In six HoVer and IFBench comparisons requiring structural changes, FAPO wins all six (mean gain +33.8 pp). On CTIBench-RCM security tasks, prompt-only FAPO improves accuracy by +4.0 pp (GPT-5), +7.1 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct), and +2.0 pp (Foundation-Sec-8B-Reasoning).
AI.conclusion: FAPO represents state-of-the-art pipeline optimization for both general-purpose and security-focused tasks, demonstrating that autonomous, attribution-driven optimization combining prompt and structural changes yields substantial and reliable performance gains.

title: Analyzing the Narration Gap in LLM-Solver Loops
summary: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how LLM-solver hybrid pipelines lose formal soundness guarantees during the narration step—when a solver's verified output is translated into natural language for users. Through formal modeling and empirical evaluation, the authors show that prompt injection attacks can invert verified conclusions, and hardened prompts only partially mitigate this vulnerability.
AI.motivation: While SAT/SMT solvers embedded in LLM reasoning pipelines provide sound, verifiable answers, the soundness guarantee can break during the interaction between the solver and the language model. Prior work has studied formalization and decision steps but neglected the narration step—how the solver's formal output is translated into the user-facing answer. This gap represents a critical security vulnerability in safety-critical applications.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure, (2) evaluate five open-source models under prompt injection attacks, introducing "certificate gating" to preserve solver verdict soundness, and (3) test mitigation strategies using hardened prompts against both static and adaptive adversarial attacks.
AI.result: Certificate gating successfully preserves solver verdict soundness. However, an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across different phrasings and communication channels. Hardened prompts significantly reduce injection success but cannot eliminate it entirely, and the defense still fails under adaptive attack scenarios.
AI.conclusion: In LLM-solver loops, robustness does not extend to the final answer the user reads. The narration step is a critical weak link where formal soundness guarantees are lost, highlighting the need for stronger defenses at the interface between formal tools and language model outputs.

title: Protein Representation Learning with Secondary-Structure and Energy-Filtered Hydrogen-Bond Graphs
summary: Graph-based representations are widely used in protein modeling, yet many existing approaches rely primarily on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially reflect the principles governing protein folding. Proteins instead adopt complex three-dimensional conformations organized around secondary structure elements, such as $α$-helices and $β$-sheets, which encode recurring local motifs and stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions. In this work, we introduce a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning. Residue-level node representations are augmented with secondary structure assignments, and graph edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by their energetic strength. This design enables the model to capture both local structural context and long-range couplings that are central to protein stability and function. We evaluate the proposed approach on commonly used protein benchmarks and observe consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods. In addition, the resulting graph representations offer enhanced biological interpretability, as the learned connectivity aligns with established structural motifs. These findings suggest that incorporating secondary structure and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The code is released at https://github.com/mohamedmohamed2021/SSProNet

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a secondary-structure-aware graph neural network for protein representation learning that augments residue-level node features with secondary structure assignments and constructs graph edges based on energetically filtered hydrogen-bond interactions, achieving consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods on standard protein benchmarks while offering enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based protein models rely on sequence adjacency or geometric proximity, which only partially capture the principles of protein folding. Proteins adopt 3D conformations organized around secondary structure elements (α-helices, β-sheets) with stabilizing hydrogen-bond interactions that encode recurring local motifs and long-range couplings critical to stability and function — these are inadequately leveraged by current approaches.
AI.method: The proposed model, SSProNet, is a graph neural network where each residue is a node augmented with secondary structure assignments. Edges are constructed from hydrogen-bond interactions filtered by energetic strength, rather than relying solely on sequence adjacency or spatial proximity. This design captures both local structural context and long-range couplings. The model is evaluated on commonly used protein benchmarks against existing graph-based methods.
AI.result: The secondary-structure-aware GNN achieves consistent improvements over existing graph-based methods across standard protein benchmarks. The learned graph connectivity aligns with established structural motifs, providing enhanced biological interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating secondary structure information and energy-filtered hydrogen-bond topology provides an effective inductive bias for protein representation learning. The approach demonstrates that grounding graph construction in physically meaningful interactions — rather than heuristic proximity measures — yields both better performance and more interpretable representations aligned with known folding principles.

title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
summary: The decentralized deployment of LLM agents with diverse capabilities across diverse tasks motivates infrastructure for knowledge sharing across heterogeneous agent populations. Just as search engines index human-generated artifacts to support human problem solving, retrieval systems can organize agent-generated artifacts for reuse across agent populations. We extend retrieval-augmented generation - which demonstrates the value of human-authored artifacts to individual agents - to retrieval of agent-generated artifacts supporting a population of agents. In particular, agent trajectories encode reusable procedural knowledge, yet these artifacts are typically discarded after a single use or retained only by the producing agent, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover existing solutions. We propose Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. We focus on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena), where trajectories are long and encode especially rich procedural structure. Our experiments demonstrate that retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps without coordination or joint training. These results position MATM as a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: MATM is a framework enabling populations of LLM agents to share and retrieve agent-generated trajectories from a communal repository, improving downstream task performance and reducing interaction steps in complex environments without requiring coordination or joint training.
AI.motivation: Agent-generated trajectories encode valuable reusable procedural knowledge but are typically discarded after single use or siloed within individual agents, forcing newly instantiated agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions. The paper draws an analogy to how search engines index human artifacts for human problem-solving, proposing analogous infrastructure for agent populations.
AI.method: MATM introduces a shared repository where producer agents contribute full interaction trajectories and consumer agents retrieve relevant past trajectories during task execution. The framework is evaluated on interactive environments (ALFWorld and WebArena) characterized by long, procedurally rich trajectories. Retrieval is performed without requiring explicit coordination or joint training between agents.
AI.result: Retrieving trajectories from MATM consistently improved downstream task performance and reduced the number of interaction steps needed across both ALFWorld and WebArena benchmarks, demonstrating the efficacy of population-level experience sharing.
AI.conclusion: MATM establishes a design pattern for population-level experience sharing in open agent ecosystems, extending retrieval-augmented generation from human-authored artifacts to agent-generated ones and validating the value of communal agent memory infrastructure.

title: DataMagic: Transforming Tabular Data into Data Insight Video
summary: Data videos integrate dynamic charts, voice narration, and synchronized animations to communicate data insights as temporal narratives, making them an effective medium for improving data consumption efficiency in the data management lifecycle. However, producing high-quality data videos requires expertise spanning data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing approaches fall short: static visualization tools (e.g., BI dashboards) lack narrative logic and animation; authoring tools require users to pre-prepare visualizations rather than working from raw data; pixel-level video generation models cannot guarantee data fidelity or provenance. We demonstrate DataMagic, an end-to-end interactive system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into narrative data-insight videos. To ensure data fidelity, DataMagic introduces the declarative specification DVSpec, which binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields through data-driven semantic references. To address the combinatorial explosion of the design space, DataMagic adopts a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then optimizes narrative coherence through global orchestration. Leveraging DVSpec's decoupling of logic and rendering, the system further supports three interaction modes and structured provenance-based data Q&A, transforming one-way videos into explorable interactive data interfaces. Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of the DataMagic. Homepage: https://datamagic-home.github.io/

AI.tldr: DataMagic is an end-to-end system that transforms raw tabular data and natural language queries into interactive data-insight videos, using a declarative specification (DVSpec) to ensure data fidelity and a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture to handle design complexity.
AI.motivation: Producing high-quality data videos requires combined expertise in data analysis, narrative design, and video production. Existing tools are inadequate: static dashboards lack narrative and animation, authoring tools cannot start from raw data, and pixel-level video generation models fail to guarantee data fidelity or provenance.
AI.method: DataMagic introduces (1) DVSpec, a declarative specification that binds visual and animation elements to underlying data fields via data-driven semantic references, ensuring data fidelity; (2) a Generate-then-Orchestrate multi-agent architecture that generates candidate scenes in parallel and then globally optimizes narrative coherence; and (3) three interaction modes plus structured provenance-based data Q&A, leveraging DVSpec's logic-rendering decoupling to transform one-way videos into explorable interfaces.
AI.result: Evaluation on 109 real-world samples validates the effectiveness of DataMagic.
AI.conclusion: DataMagic successfully bridges the gap between raw data and narrative video production by combining declarative specification, multi-agent orchestration, and interactive exploration, making data video creation accessible without requiring multi-domain expertise.

title: AutoTam: Specifying Secure Protocol Implementations with Tamarin Model Generation
summary:
Formal verification is a challenging but important task for ensuring the security of cryptographic protocols. While modern protocol verification tools significantly reduce verification effort, modelling remains challenging to practitioners without a background in formal verification. In addition, transferring verification results to a concrete protocol implementation requires expert knowledge.
  In this paper, we present a novel language-first method for verification of trace properties using a domain-specific language for protocol implementations. We target the Tamarin prover for verification, and we prove that verified universal trace properties translate back to the implementation. We additionally integrate symbolic execution in order to analyse the memory safety of protocol implementations. We use our tool to implement and generate accurate models for a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol, and for the WireGuard VPN protocol. Our WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when using our interpreter, and achieves acceptable performance. We formally prove our implementations secure using a combination of symbolic execution and verification of the generated Tamarin models.

AI.tldr: A language-first approach using a domain-specific language for cryptographic protocol implementations that automatically generates Tamarin prover models, enabling formal verification of trace properties with results that translate back to the implementation. The method also incorporates symbolic execution for memory safety analysis, demonstrated on a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard VPN.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of cryptographic protocols remains challenging for practitioners without formal methods backgrounds. Two key pain points: (1) modelling protocols for verification tools like Tamarin requires expertise, and (2) transferring verification results to concrete implementations demands expert knowledge, creating a gap between verified models and running code.
AI.method: The authors propose a language-first methodology centered on a domain-specific language (DSL) for writing protocol implementations. From DSL programs, they automatically generate Tamarin models for formal verification of trace properties. They prove a preservation theorem showing that verified universal trace properties in the Tamarin model translate back to the concrete implementation. Additionally, they integrate symbolic execution to verify memory safety of implementations. The approach is validated through case studies on signed Diffie-Hellman and WireGuard.
AI.result: The tool successfully generates accurate Tamarin models for both a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and the WireGuard VPN protocol. The WireGuard implementation is interoperable with existing implementations when run through their interpreter and achieves acceptable performance. Both protocols are formally proven secure via the combination of symbolic execution (memory safety) and Tamarin verification (trace properties).
AI.conclusion: The language-first approach effectively bridges the gap between formal verification and practical protocol implementation, making verification accessible to non-experts. The methodology ensures verification results are meaningful for the actual implementation, not just the abstract model, representing a significant step toward integrating formal methods into real-world cryptographic protocol development.

title: Trustworthy Multi-Agent Systems: Mitigating Semantic Drift with the Argent Signaling Protocol
summary:
When multi-agent LLM systems produce bad answers, not all failures are equal: some answers are grounded in the right material but incomplete, while others are simply ungrounded and should be stopped. Current retry strategies treat both cases identically (try again and hope for the best), leaving human supervisors unable to tell whether a retry was warranted or whether the system should have halted instead.
  We introduce the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header that accompanies every AI-generated response with structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index that classifies the evidentiary basis of each claim. These signals enable a controller to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures and route each case differently.
  We evaluate ASP in two modes. In standalone mode, a 27-question document-grounded QA benchmark over the Array BioPharma/Ono license agreement compares baseline prompts against ASP-instrumented controller actions across three local GGUF models. On Qwen~(0.8B), ASP improves pass rate from 11.1% to 33.3% and mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; on Dobby~(8B), ASP produces 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; on SmolLM3~(3B), ASP alternates between repair and containment per question. Aggregate improvement is meaningful (12/81 to 21/81 passes). In multi-agent mode, an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent; the sidecar blocks 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from reaching the downstream agent (24/27 blocked, 0 ungrounded propagations).

AI.tldr: The Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP) adds structured quality signals (@C, @G, @S, and an assumption index) to LLM outputs, enabling controllers to distinguish repairable failures from containment failures. Evaluated on a document-grounded QA benchmark, ASP improved pass rates across multiple models and, in multi-agent mode, blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs from propagating downstream.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems treat all failures identically with naive retry strategies, failing to distinguish between incomplete-but-grounded answers (repairable) and ungrounded answers (should be halted). This leaves human supervisors unable to determine whether retrying is appropriate or whether the system should have stopped entirely.
AI.method: The authors propose the Argent Signaling Protocol (ASP), a compact machine-readable header carrying four structured quality signals: certainty (@C), grounding (@G), stochasticity (@S), and an assumption index classifying each claim's evidentiary basis. A controller uses these signals to route failures into repair (retry) or containment (halt) pathways. Evaluation occurs in two modes: (1) standalone mode, comparing baseline vs. ASP-instrumented QA on a 27-question benchmark over a legal contract using three local GGUF models (Qwen 0.8B, Dobby 8B, SmolLM3 3B); (2) multi-agent mode, where an ASP sidecar sits between a retrieval agent and a downstream decision agent, blocking ungrounded upstream outputs.
AI.result: In standalone mode: Qwen (0.8B) pass rate improved from 11.1% to 33.3%, mean term coverage from 36.7% to 65.4%; Dobby (8B) achieved 4 fail-to-pass recoveries, raising pass rate from 33.3% to 44.4%; SmolLM3 (3B) alternated between repair and containment. Aggregate improvement: 12/81 to 21/81 passes. In multi-agent mode, the ASP sidecar blocked 100% of ungrounded upstream outputs (24/27 blocked, zero ungrounded propagations to the downstream agent).
AI.conclusion: ASP provides an effective, lightweight mechanism for distinguishing failure modes in LLM outputs, enabling intelligent routing between retry and halt decisions. This improves overall system reliability and prevents ungrounded information from propagating through multi-agent pipelines.

title: A Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization
comment: Presented at the 17th Workshop on Optimization and Learning in Multiagent Systems (OptLearnMAS, https://optlearnmas.github.io), co-located with the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
summary: Many decision-making problems in computing and networking systems can be naturally formulated as cost-minimization problems under performance constraints. In dynamic environments, reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to solve such problems at runtime by embedding both costs and constraint violations into a single scalar reward through weighted penalty terms, following a Lagrangian-inspired formulation. However, in this context the behavior of the learned policy critically depends on the choice of these weights, which are typically selected manually. This makes it difficult to identify an appropriate trade-off between optimizing the primary objective and effectively avoiding constraint violations, particularly in non-stationary environments where their relative importance may change. This paper presents MAMO (Multi-Agent system for Multi-Objective constrained optimization), an approach to tackle this balancing problem through multi-agent RL. MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by formulating the selection of reward weights as a learning problem, providing a !rst step towards more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization problems in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: MAMO proposes a multi-agent RL framework that automatically learns the reward weights for balancing cost minimization and constraint satisfaction, replacing manual tuning in Lagrangian-based RL for constrained optimization in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: In Lagrangian-inspired RL for constrained optimization, the learned policy's behavior is highly sensitive to manually chosen penalty weights, making it difficult to strike the right balance between objective optimization and constraint avoidance—especially in non-stationary environments where this trade-off shifts over time.
AI.method: MAMO decouples task execution from objective design by using a multi-agent RL setup: one agent (or set of agents) focuses on solving the primary cost-minimization task, while another agent learns to dynamically select the reward weights (penalty coefficients) that shape the cost-minimizing agent's reward signal, effectively framing weight selection as a learning problem.
AI.result: The paper presents MAMO as a first step toward more autonomous and robust RL-based solutions for constrained optimization, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling task execution from reward-weight design via multi-agent RL offers a promising path toward autonomous adaptation of the cost–constraint trade-off in dynamic, constrained optimization settings.

title: StaminaBench: Stress-Testing Coding Agents over 100 Interaction Turns
summary: We introduce StaminaBench, a benchmark that measures the stamina of coding agents: how many consecutive interaction turns (change requests) they can handle before failing. Unlike the prevailing fraction-of-tasks-solved metric, this matches real vibe-coding where sessions run dozens or hundreds of turns. In StaminaBench, agents implement a REST API server and modify it across a tunable number of procedurally generated follow-up change requests - 100 in our experiments, resulting in codebases of up to 6,000 lines. Tests are generated fully programmatically without LLM involvement, ensuring reproducibility and reliability; change sequences are drawn from either a hardcoded or LLM-driven sampler, both constrained to a structured action space to ensure changes are valid. The agent and the server run in an isolated environment and communicate with the benchmark through HTTP, making testing fully black-box and language-agnostic. We evaluate six agent harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs across 20 scenarios of 100 turns each and find that: (1) all the tested models fail within 5-6 turns, confirming that vibe-coding-style programming without thorough testing produces bugs; (2) passing test feedback back to the agent and allowing it to retry improves passed turn count by up to 12x; and (3) a good harness is required for strong performance: stronger models exhibit up to a 6x gap between their best and worst harness, while weaker models fail with any harness. We release the benchmark and the generated tasks to enable further research into multi-turn coding agent behavior. Benchmark code and data: github.com/amazon-science/StaminaBench.

AI.tldr: StaminaBench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents' ability to handle long sequences of incremental change requests, revealing that without test feedback, all models fail within 5-6 turns, while test-feedback loops and good harness design dramatically improve multi-turn performance.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks measure fraction-of-tasks-solved, which fails to capture real-world "vibe-coding" sessions where agents must handle dozens or hundreds of consecutive modification requests without breaking the codebase.
AI.method: StaminaBench tasks agents with implementing and iteratively modifying a REST API server over 100 procedurally generated turns. Change sequences are produced by either hardcoded or LLM-driven samplers constrained to a structured action space. Tests are generated programmatically (no LLM) for reproducibility. The agent and server communicate via HTTP in an isolated, black-box, language-agnostic environment. Six harnesses paired with seven open-source LLMs were evaluated across 20 scenarios.
AI.result: (1) All models fail within 5-6 turns without test feedback. (2) Providing test feedback with retry capability improves passed turn count by up to 12×. (3) Harness quality significantly impacts performance: stronger models show up to a 6× gap between best and worst harness, while weaker models fail regardless of harness.
