AI.conclusion: Multi-turn coding stamina is a distinct and challenging dimension of agent capability. Test-feedback loops and robust harness design are critical for sustained performance. The benchmark and tasks are publicly released to spur further research.

title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why
summary: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5\% of extractions, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80\% to 99\%.

AI.tldr: ACIE is an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline deployed at University Medicine Essen that addresses the metadata gap in clinical documents. It reasons over complete patient contexts with source-grounding, achieving 96.5% clinician acceptance across 7,326 extraction judgments in a lymphoma registry study.
AI.motivation: Patient records contain hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, but critical document-level metadata for AI retrieval and triage is missing or incomplete. Standard RAG fails due to poor temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and absent metadata. A system is needed that can reason over complete patient contexts while providing source-level verification for clinicians.
AI.method: The authors deploy ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction), an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline. The system reasons over entire patient contexts and grounds every extracted answer in specific source passages, enabling clinician verification. Evaluation is conducted via an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study where nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources.
AI.result: Across 7,326 extraction judgments, clinicians accepted 96.5% of all extractions. Per-type acceptance rates ranged from 80% to 99%, demonstrating robust but variable performance across different extraction categories.
AI.conclusion: The metadata gap in clinical documents is a significant barrier to effective RAG in healthcare. ACIE demonstrates that agentic architectures with explicit source-grounding can achieve high clinician trust (96.5% acceptance), but the variation in per-type performance (80–99%) indicates residual challenges in certain extraction categories.

title: Physics-Informed Discovery of Yield Functions in Plasticity via Convex Neural Representations
summary: Identifying anisotropic yield functions remains challenging since yielding is not directly observed in full-field mechanical measurements, directional calibration can require many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for discovering yield functions from full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed parametric yield function. The framework identifies the yield function as a mechanically constrained constitutive component inside elastoplastic stress integration, rather than through direct stress-space supervision. The yield function is represented by a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one while imposing the assumed tension-compression symmetry, and this neural yield function is trained with a differentiable stress update and a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. The proposed framework is validated using finite element (FE) benchmark studies with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions, assessing yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment. This study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while keeping the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a physics-informed framework that discovers anisotropic yield functions directly from full-field displacement and reaction force data using convex neural networks, without requiring stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or a pre-specified parametric yield function form. The neural yield function is trained within a differentiable elastoplastic stress integration scheme, validated on von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Identifying anisotropic yield functions is challenging because yielding is not directly observable in full-field measurements, directional calibration demands many loading directions, and selecting an appropriate analytical form is nontrivial. Existing methods typically require stress-space supervision or pre-specified parametric forms, limiting their applicability when only displacement and force data are available.
AI.method: The framework represents the yield function as a convex neural network that enforces convexity and positive homogeneity of degree one, with assumed tension-compression symmetry. This neural yield function is embedded as a constitutive component within elastoplastic stress integration and trained using a differentiable stress update alongside a physics-informed force equilibrium loss across multiple loading cases. Training uses only full-field displacement data and reaction force data, without stress observations, plastic strain measurements, or direct yield surface data.
AI.result: The framework was validated on finite element benchmarks with von Mises, Hill 1948, and Yld2000-2d yield functions. Assessments covered yield contour agreement, displacement-noise sensitivity, identifiability through plastically active stress states, epistemic uncertainty, and polynomial-surrogate deployment, all demonstrating the method's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a mechanics-constrained pathway for discovering anisotropic yield functions from displacement and force data while preserving the identified component within the structure of elastoplastic stress integration, eliminating the need for stress measurements or pre-specified parametric forms.

title: When Does Streaming Tool Use Help? Characterizing Tool-Intent Stabilization in Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Streaming Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Streaming RAG) reduces user-perceived latency by issuing tool queries in parallel with ongoing user input, before the utterance is complete. Reported gains are aggregate, yet the mechanism's benefit is fundamentally query-intrinsic: speculation can only help when the correct tool query becomes determinable before the user stops speaking or typing. We isolate and measure this property -- tool-intent stabilization, the point in the input stream at which a speculative query's retrieval converges to the answer-bearing result. On the CRAG benchmark (1371 validation questions) we (i) measure the distribution of stabilization, (ii) derive a model-agnostic bound H on the portion of tool latency that can be hidden behind the user's remaining input, as a function of tool latency L and input cadence δ, (iii) validate against a working streaming pipeline that realized savings meet or exceed this bound, and (iv) identify which query properties predict early versus late stabilization. The study requires no model training and runs on commodity CPU hardware. We find that at a realistic operating point (L=600ms, δ=3w/s, θ=0.8), 73.9% of queries across the full benchmark admit substantial latency hiding -- a blended figure that mixes sufficiency stabilization on the 21.3% of questions where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable (95.2% streamable on this favorable slice) with a grounding-free top-1-settling fallback on the remainder. On the favorable slice, φ_suf is bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] by exact and relaxed grounding -- both early. Question type produces a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, epsilon^2=0.04), directly informing when a learned speculative trigger is worth its cost.

AI.tldr: This paper measures when tool queries stabilize during streaming user input, finding that at realistic latencies ~73.9% of queries can hide significant tool latency behind ongoing typing/speaking, with stabilization occurring early for queries where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable.
AI.motivation: Streaming RAG claims latency reduction by issuing tool queries before the user finishes speaking, but the actual benefit depends on *when* the correct query becomes determinable. No prior work isolates or quantifies this "tool-intent stabilization" property, leaving practitioners without guidance on when speculative querying is worthwhile.
AI.method: The authors define and measure "tool-intent stabilization" — the point in an input stream where a speculative retrieval query converges to the final answer-bearing result. Using the CRAG benchmark (1371 questions), they: (i) compute the empirical distribution of stabilization points; (ii) derive a model-agnostic upper bound H on hidable latency as a function of tool latency L, input cadence δ, and a sufficiency threshold θ; (iii) validate against a working streaming RAG pipeline; and (iv) analyze which query properties (e.g., question type) predict early vs. late stabilization. No model training is required; all experiments run on commodity CPU.
AI.result: At L=600ms, δ=3 words/s, θ=0.8: 73.9% of all CRAG queries admit substantial latency hiding. On the 21.3% "favorable slice" where gold evidence is verbatim-present and BM25-retrievable, 95.2% are streamable, with φ_suf (stabilization proportion) bracketed to [0.26, 0.281] via exact and relaxed grounding — both early. Question type yields a significant but coarse early/late split (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.017, ε²=0.04), informing when learned speculative triggers are cost-effective.
AI.conclusion: Tool-intent stabilization is measurable, early for a substantial fraction of queries, and predictable from query properties — providing a principled, training-free framework for deciding when speculative retrieval in streaming RAG yields genuine latency savings.

title: A Measurement Study of Cryptographic Misuse in Embodied AI Mobile Applications
summary: Embodied AI (EAI) mobile applications are evolving from auxiliary user interfaces into active control-path components, directly linking mobile-side cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust. Despite this shift, existing security research predominantly focuses on embodied AI devices and cloud infrastructures, leaving the mobile control layer largely unexplored as a critical attack surface. To bridge this gap, we present the first large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse within the EAI mobile ecosystem. We construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world applications across six EAI domains, and employ an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to measure the prevalence and characteristics of five major cryptographic failure modes. Our measurement yields 12,975 misuse findings (with an evaluated precision of 80.74\%), revealing that these cryptographic failures are driven by EAI-specific engineering constraints rather than random developer errors. We uncover structural security trade-offs: latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport protection, while the heavy reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs exacerbates the local hardcoding of authentication credentials. Through real-world case studies, we demonstrate how these mobile-side cryptographic flaws bypass nominal network protections, enabling adversaries to intercept command channels and hijack the physical control of EAI entities. Ultimately, our findings highlight that mobile applications have become a fragile, yet overlooked, cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale measurement study of cryptographic misuse in Embodied AI mobile apps. Analyzing 507 apps across 6 EAI domains, researchers found 12,975 misuse instances (80.74% precision), revealing that EAI-specific engineering constraints — not random errors — drive systematic cryptographic failures, enabling command interception and physical hijacking of EAI entities.
AI.motivation: Existing security research on Embodied AI focuses on devices and cloud infrastructure, neglecting the mobile control layer as a critical attack surface. As mobile apps evolve from passive interfaces into active control-path components linking cryptographic security to cyber-physical trust, this gap represents a significant and unexamined vulnerability.
AI.method: The authors construct EAIAppZoo, a benchmark of 507 real-world EAI mobile applications spanning six domains. They develop an automated semantic-aware analysis pipeline to systematically detect and characterize five major cryptographic failure modes across the dataset.
AI.result: The measurement yielded 12,975 cryptographic misuse findings at 80.74% precision. Two structural trade-offs were identified: (1) latency-sensitive control paths systematically weaken transport-layer protection, and (2) reliance on offline device provisioning and legacy IoT SDKs drives widespread hardcoding of authentication credentials. Real-world case studies demonstrated that these flaws enable adversaries to bypass nominal network protections, intercept command channels, and hijack physical control of EAI entities.
AI.conclusion: Mobile applications have become a fragile yet overlooked cryptographic trust boundary in cyber-physical systems. The cryptographic failures are systematic and driven by domain-specific engineering constraints rather than developer negligence, necessitating targeted interventions for the EAI mobile ecosystem.

title: Characterizing Narrative Content in Web-scale LLM Pretraining Data
comment: 8 pages of main content, 28 total pages. 30 figures
summary: The narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored even though narrative is a fundamental mode of human communication. We present the first fine-grained study of narrative features in Dolma, a 3-trillion-token open pretraining corpus. Drawing on narrative theory, we design a framework spanning three core narrative elements (agency, setting, and events) operationalized as 11 interpretable dimensions. After sampling and annotating a diverse set of 400 passages, we finetune and validate NarraBERT, a RoBERTa-based model for fine-grained narrative prediction. We apply NarraBERT to 3M passages, resulting in a new dataset, NarraDolma. We find (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous data, (ii) we uncover a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlying web text, and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics in ways that current curation practices neither measure nor account for. Our framework, dataset, and analyses provide a foundation for understanding how narrative qualities are distributed in LLM pretraining data and for studying how data composition affects narrative reasoning tasks. We publicly release NarraDolma and NarraBERT.

AI.tldr: First fine-grained study of narrative features in the Dolma pretraining corpus, introducing NarraBERT—a RoBERTa-based model for predicting 11 narrative dimensions (agency, setting, events)—applied to 3M passages. Reveals measurable, multidimensional narrative structure that is unequally distributed across sources and topics, with publicly released NarraDolma dataset.
AI.motivation: Despite narrative being a fundamental mode of human communication, the narrative composition of web-scale LLM pretraining corpora remains largely unexplored. Current data curation practices neither measure nor account for narrative qualities, creating a gap in understanding how pretraining data composition affects downstream narrative reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors design a framework grounded in narrative theory spanning three core elements—agency, setting, and events—operationalized into 11 interpretable dimensions. They sample and manually annotate 400 diverse passages from Dolma (a 3-trillion-token open corpus), then fine-tune NarraBERT (RoBERTa-based) on these annotations for fine-grained narrative prediction. The model is applied at scale to 3 million passages to produce the NarraDolma dataset.
AI.result: Three key findings: (i) narrative structure is measurable at scale across extremely heterogeneous web data; (ii) a continuous, multidimensional narrative structure underlies web text; and (iii) narrative qualities are unequally distributed across pretraining sources and topics—inequalities that current curation practices fail to capture or address.
AI.conclusion: The framework, NarraBERT model, and NarraDolma dataset establish a foundation for understanding narrative quality distribution in LLM pretraining data and for investigating how data composition influences narrative reasoning tasks. All artifacts are publicly released.

title: Phoenix: Safe GitHub Issue Resolution via Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: We present Phoenix, a multi-agent LLM system that resolves GitHub issues from triage through pull-request creation, combining seven layered safety controls with a baseline-aware test evaluation strategy. Phoenix decomposes the work across six specialized agents. Planner, reproducer, coder, tester, failure analyst and Pull Request (PR) agent, all coordinated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Every change is checked against a baseline test run before a pull request is opened. On a 24-instance slice of SWE-bench Lite. run on the production webhook path, Phoenix oracle-resolves 75% of instances with no pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs; this curated slice is not directly comparable to full-split leaderboard results, and we discuss the limits of the comparison. A complementary pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories yields 100% correctness preservation (CP; mean 122s on the hard tier). Manual inspection shows that about half of the resulting pull requests are well-targeted fixes. The other half place code at incorrect paths, a planner localization limitation we are addressing with retrieval. We also report the deployment failure modes (WAF filtering, token expiry, permission boundaries, flaky CI) that motivated each safety mechanism.

AI.tldr: Phoenix is a multi-agent LLM system with seven safety controls that resolves GitHub issues from triage to PR creation. On a curated 24-instance SWE-bench Lite slice, it oracle-resolves 75% with no regressions; a pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repos achieves 100% correctness preservation.
AI.motivation: Automated end-to-end GitHub issue resolution is challenging due to safety risks (e.g., flaky CI, token expiry, permission boundaries, WAF filtering) and the need for correctness preservation. Existing systems lack robust safety mechanisms and baseline-aware evaluation, motivating the design of a controlled multi-agent pipeline.
AI.method: Phoenix employs six specialized agents (Planner, Reproducer, Coder, Tester, Failure Analyst, PR Agent) orchestrated by a label-based GitHub webhook state machine. Seven layered safety controls are integrated, including baseline test comparisons before any PR is opened — every change is checked against a baseline test run to prevent pass-to-pass regressions.
AI.result: On a 24-instance curated slice of SWE-bench Lite (production webhook path): 75% oracle-resolved, zero pass-to-pass regressions on successful runs. A pilot on 42 real issues across 14 repositories: 100% correctness preservation (CP), mean 122s on the hard tier. Manual inspection shows ~50% of PRs are well-targeted fixes; the remainder exhibit incorrect code path placement due to planner localization limitations.
AI.conclusion: Phoenix demonstrates that layered safety controls and baseline-aware evaluation enable robust automated issue resolution. Key failure modes (planner localization errors) are being addressed with retrieval. The curated evaluation slice limits direct comparability to full leaderboard results.

title: Which Pairs to Compare for LLM Post-Training?
summary: Preference-based post-training has become a central paradigm for aligning language models. A common data-collection strategy is to generate a small set of completions for each prompt and label the resulting comparison pairs. However, human preference labels are often much more expensive than generating additional completions, suggesting a different use of the same labeling budget: generate a larger pool of completions, but label only the most informative comparison pairs. This paper studies which pairs should be compared in preference-based post-training. We formulate comparison curation as a sampling-design problem and evaluate designs by the quality of the final policy under the preference-based post-training objective. We instantiate this framework for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), analyzing how the choice of labeled pairs propagates through DPO training to downstream policy performance. Our main results provide matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap of the DPO-trained policy. The bounds show that comparison selection affects downstream performance through a single design-dependent information matrix, which links label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality. This yields an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation and motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large generated completion pools. Experiments on synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks show that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes comparison pair selection in preference-based post-training (specifically DPO) as a sampling-design problem. It establishes matching upper and lower bounds showing that the choice of labeled pairs affects downstream policy performance through a design-dependent information matrix, yielding an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation. The proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over standard heuristics in both synthetic and LM post-training benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Human preference labels are far more expensive than generating additional completions. Current practice typically generates few completions per prompt and labels all resulting pairs, but a smarter allocation of a fixed labeling budget would generate many completions and label only the most informative comparison pairs. The paper addresses the open question of *which* pairs should be compared to maximize downstream policy quality.
AI.method: The authors frame comparison curation as a sampling-design problem, evaluating designs by the quality of the final DPO-trained policy. They derive matching upper and lower bounds on the post-training optimality gap, revealing that comparison selection influences performance through a single design-dependent information matrix. This matrix connects label allocation to parameter estimation error and policy suboptimality, yielding a principled optimization criterion for selecting which pairs to label under a budget constraint.
AI.result: The derived bounds provide an explicit optimization criterion for budgeted comparison curation, which motivates practical sampling designs for selecting informative pairs from large completion pools. Experiments on both synthetic settings and language-model post-training benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed designs consistently improve sample efficiency over common comparison-selection heuristics.
AI.conclusion: Comparison curation should be treated as a principled sampling-design problem rather than relying on naive heuristics. By optimizing the design-dependent information matrix, one can significantly improve the sample efficiency of preference-based post-training under a fixed labeling budget.

title: Creating Multilingual Mental Health Dialogue Datasets: Limits of Persona-Based Localization via Nationality and Language
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the 2026 Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026), co-located with ACL 2026
summary: AI and large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools to address global mental health challenges. Despite the global nature of these challenges, there remains a critical shortage of high-quality datasets for training and evaluating such systems. To mitigate this gap, researchers increasingly generate synthetic clinical personas to simulate user data and test digital mental health support systems. However, most validated personas rely on English-centric contexts. This paper investigates whether similar persona-based methods can be used to generate multilingual mental health datasets. We modified nationality and language parameters in personas to generate clinical dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi. We then examined how different LLMs perform when evaluating the depression severity of these generated multilingual datasets against the baseline in English. Our findings indicate that just adding nationality and language parameters in personas might not be adequate, as it can introduce clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judge models often exhibit inaccuracies in assessing depression severity in non-English texts, with performance varying across different models. This exposes the systemic limitations of applying English-centric personas to multilingual contexts. Ultimately, our work highlights the urgent need for culturally responsive data generation to ensure equitable mental health systems globally.

AI.tldr: Simply adding nationality and language parameters to English-centric clinical personas is insufficient for generating multilingual mental health data; LLM evaluations of depression severity become inaccurate across Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi, exposing systemic cultural biases.
AI.motivation: Address the global shortage of high-quality multilingual mental health datasets and test whether existing English-centric persona-based generation methods can be straightforwardly adapted to non-English languages (Mandarin, Bengali, Hindi).
AI.method: Modified nationality and language parameters in clinical personas to generate synthetic mental health dialogues in Mandarin, Bengali, and Hindi; evaluated depression severity assessments from multiple LLM judge models and compared performance against an English baseline.
AI.result: Adding only nationality and language parameters introduced clinical inconsistency across languages. LLM judges showed variable and often inaccurate depression severity assessments on non-English texts compared to the English baseline.
AI.conclusion: English-centric persona generation methods do not transfer reliably to multilingual contexts. Culturally responsive data generation approaches are urgently needed for equitable global mental health AI systems.

title: Accelerating Trust Convergence in IIoT: A ML Approach for Dynamic Network Conditions
summary: In Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, trust management plays a vital role in securing systems, especially when dealing with resource-constrained devices. Traditional trust models often overlook the impact of fluctuating network quality, leading to slower trust convergence and inaccurate assessments. In this paper, we propose a dynamic trust management solution, known as the Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach, which integrates Machine Learning (ML) to accelerate trust convergence under poor network conditions. Our model predicts the number of time units needed for trust convergence based on key network metrics and dynamically adapts transition probabilities in the trust model to enhance convergence speed. Using a simulation framework that incorporates realistic Wi-Fi channel conditions based on the IEEE 802.11 standard, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the TCA-based approach, achieving up to a 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging conditions. Furthermore, the proposed solution exhibits resilience in scenarios involving malicious nodes, improving trust evaluation accuracy. This work provides a scalable and adaptive trust framework for IIoT systems in dynamic industrial environments, ensuring robust performance under varying network conditions.

AI.tldr: A dynamic trust management approach (TCA) leveraging ML to accelerate trust convergence in IIoT under poor network conditions, achieving up to 28.6% reduction in convergence time while improving accuracy against malicious nodes.
AI.motivation: Traditional trust models in IIoT ignore fluctuating network quality, causing slow trust convergence and inaccurate assessments, especially for resource-constrained devices. There is a need for a trust framework that adapts to dynamic network conditions.
AI.method: The Trust Convergence Acceleration (TCA) approach uses ML to predict time units needed for trust convergence from network metrics and dynamically adjusts transition probabilities in the trust model. Evaluation uses a simulation framework with realistic IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi channel conditions.
AI.result: TCA achieves up to 28.6% reduction in trust convergence time under challenging network conditions and demonstrates resilience against malicious nodes, yielding improved trust evaluation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: TCA provides a scalable, adaptive trust framework for IIoT that ensures robust performance across varying network conditions in dynamic industrial environments.

title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models Across Agreement, Consistency, and Bias
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for language models, but judge validation in practice relies on exact-match agreement, a metric that does not correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. We present the largest systematic evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge to date: 21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments. Four findings emerge, consistent across the full cohort, including the April 2026 frontier: kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is universal (33--41 pp on MT-Bench), judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, high test--retest reliability (>0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) in two production-deployed judges (instantiating a consistency--bias paradox), and verbosity bias is small (<0.011) across our cohort under a single pairwise rubric. We distill these into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study of 21 LLM judges across three benchmarks reveals that exact-match agreement overstates judge quality; Cohen's kappa deflation is universal (33–41 pp), judge rankings shift dramatically across benchmarks, and a consistency–bias paradox exists where high test-retest reliability coexists with severe position bias. The authors propose a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge is the dominant evaluation paradigm, yet judge validation relies on exact-match agreement—a metric that fails to correct for chance and systematically overstates discriminative ability. The paper seeks to rigorously quantify this problem and establish more robust validation practices.
AI.method: 21 judges from nine providers evaluated on MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit), totaling 118 runs and ~541,000 individual judgments. Metrics compared include exact-match agreement, Cohen's kappa, test-retest reliability, position bias, and verbosity bias.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) kappa deflation between exact match and Cohen's kappa is 33–41 pp universally on MT-Bench; (2) judge rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks; (3) a consistency–bias paradox: test-retest reliability >0.95 coexists with position bias >0.10 in two production judges; (4) verbosity bias is small (<0.011) under a single pairwise rubric.
AI.conclusion: Exact-match agreement is an insufficient validation metric for LLM judges. The field should adopt chance-corrected metrics like Cohen's kappa, multi-benchmark evaluation, and explicit bias audits. The authors distill findings into a Minimum Viable Validation Protocol for standardizing judge assessment.

title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

AI.tldr: Evaluator biases in LLM-based multi-agent systems propagate between agents. Using a 3-agent controlled experiment, the authors introduce Contagion Networks to quantify this spread, finding consistent propagation (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]), identifying three spectral-radius-governed regimes, and demonstrating that increasing evaluator committee size from 1 to 3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.motivation: When LLMs act as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases do not remain isolated—they propagate through the agent network. Prior work observed strong cross-model contagion (γ ≈ 0.85–1.3), but the dynamics within homogeneous-model systems and potential mitigation strategies remained unexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation. They conduct a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based). The Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ₃ is measured, and propagation regimes are characterized by the spectral radius ρ(Γ_N). Mitigation is tested by varying the evaluator committee size k from 1 to 3.
AI.result: Evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (γ ∈ [0.157, 0.352]) even within the same underlying model. Three propagation regimes governed by ρ(Γ_N) are identified: homogeneous-model agents fall into the suppression regime, with contagion coefficients 3–5× weaker than cross-model coefficients (MM-EPC: γ ≈ 0.85–1.3). Increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%.
AI.conclusion: Bias propagation in LLM multi-agent systems is both measurable and mitigable. The Contagion Networks framework provides a principled approach to diagnosing propagation regimes, and committee-based evaluation offers a practical, high-impact mitigation strategy. The experimental framework is released open-source.

title: Prompt Quality and Pull Request Outcomes: A Stage-Based Empirical Study of LLM-Assisted Development
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering workflows, yet little is known about how prompt structure influences downstream pull request (PR) outcomes. Prior studies primarily examine conversational helpfulness, productivity, or coarse-grained adoption metrics, leaving the role of prompt structure in collaborative integration behavior insufficiently understood. We analyze 265 manually validated developer-ChatGPT interactions derived from self-admitted ChatGPT usage in open-source pull requests. Building on prior research on developer-facing artifacts and prompt engineering, we operationalize prompt structure using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification. We first evaluate whether LLM-assisted annotation can reliably reproduce human judgments of prompt structure, finding substantial variation across dimensions and workflow contexts. Specificity shows the most stable agreement with human judgments; Context is systematically under-scored by the LLM; and Verification remains difficult to assess consistently, motivating a hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy. Using this validated framework, we then examine how prompt structure influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth across AI-assisted PR workflows. Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerges as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth is most strongly associated with Context. Overall, our findings show that prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream adoption and integration through contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 265 developer-ChatGPT interactions in open-source PRs to examine how prompt structure — operationalized along Context, Specificity, and Verification dimensions — influences actionable code generation, code adoption, and integration depth. Findings reveal stage-dependent effects: Specificity and Context drive code generation, Verification predicts adoption, and Context shapes integration depth.
AI.motivation: While LLM-powered tools like ChatGPT are increasingly used in collaborative software engineering, prior work focuses narrowly on conversational quality or coarse adoption metrics, leaving a gap in understanding how the structural properties of prompts themselves influence downstream PR outcomes such as code generation, adoption, and integration.
AI.method: The authors collected and manually validated 265 developer-ChatGPT interactions self-admitted in open-source pull requests. Prompt structure was operationalized along three dimensions: Context (background information provided), Specificity (precision of the task description), and Verification (evaluability cues). A hybrid human-LLM annotation strategy was developed after evaluating LLM reliability across dimensions. Regression analyses then examined how each dimension predicts (1) actionable code generation, (2) code adoption likelihood, and (3) integration depth.
AI.result: LLM-assisted annotation reliability varied by dimension: Specificity achieved the strongest human-LLM agreement, Context was systematically underscored by the LLM, and Verification was inconsistently assessed. In downstream analyses, Specificity and Context were most strongly associated with actionable code generation; Verification emerged as the primary predictor of code adoption; and integration depth was most strongly associated with Context.
AI.conclusion: Prompt characteristics exert distinct, stage-dependent effects across AI-assisted software engineering workflows. Contextual grounding, task specificity, and evaluability cues each play differentiated roles at different stages — generation, adoption, and integration — highlighting the need for prompt design strategies tailored to specific workflow phases.

authors: Antonio de Sousa Leitão Filho; Allan Kardec Duailibe Barros Filho; Fabrício Saul Lima; Selby Mykael Lima dos Santos; Rejani Bandeira Vieira Sousa
title: Toten: Knowledge-Based Ontological Tokenization Of Physical Quantities And Technical Notation In Brazilian Portuguese
summary: Byte-Pair Encoding tokenization is statistically efficient for vocabulary compression, but semantically blind to structured technical entities, fragmenting physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions into lexically arbitrary subwords. We present TOTEN, a knowledge-based ontological tokenization framework that replaces statistical derivation with declarative classification grounded in a formal ontology of engineering entities (OEE). We formalize TOTEN as the triple <O, classify, {inst_tau}>: the ontology gathers types, structural principles, composition relations, and preservable invariants; the classification function maps raw text into typed regions; and the instantiator family yields a self-descriptive structured representation. Robustness derives from deterministic coupling with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional), Unicode Character Database (typographic), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Intrinsic evaluation covers four properties verifiable by construction -- ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction -- over an internal, physically validated benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1771 eligible cases). We also report detection recall, distinguishing coverage from conditional atomicity. Against eight state-of-the-art baselines, TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts and numerical reconstruction of 0.775-0.904 on external corpora, vs. 0.627-0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. Differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms concurrent validity of the control benchmark. Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, the oracle from which the system inherits dimensional authority.

AI.tldr: TOTEN is a knowledge-based tokenization framework that replaces statistical Byte-Pair Encoding with ontology-grounded classification, preserving physical quantities, numbers, units, and symbolic expressions as atomic, semantically coherent tokens, achieving significantly superior numerical reconstruction and unit atomicity over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization is vocabulary-efficient but semantically blind: it fragments structured technical entities such as physical quantities, units, numbers, and symbolic expressions into arbitrary subword pieces. This undermines downstream tasks in scientific and engineering NLP that require coherent numerical and dimensional reasoning. The motivation is to replace statistical subword segmentation with a principled, ontology-driven tokenization that preserves the integrity of technical entities by construction.
AI.method: TOTEN is formalized as a triple: (1) an ontology of engineering entities (OEE) defining types, composition relations, structural principles, and invariants; (2) a classification function that maps raw text into typed regions; and (3) an instantiator family producing self-descriptive structured representations. The framework couples deterministically with three external oracles: Pint (dimensional analysis), the Unicode Character Database (typographic classification), and RSLP (Portuguese morphology). Evaluation is intrinsic, measuring four verifiable properties — ontological atomicity, dimensional equivalence, typographic robustness, and numerical reconstruction — on an internal benchmark (EngQuant, N=800) and four Brazilian Portuguese external corpora (N=1,771 eligible cases), with statistical significance assessed via McNemar test with Holm correction and concurrent validity via Spearman rank correlation.
AI.result: TOTEN achieves unit ontological atomicity in all contrasts against eight baselines. For numerical reconstruction on external corpora, TOTEN scores 0.775–0.904 vs. 0.627–0.703 for the best baseline (Quantulum3); on EngQuant, 0.780 vs. 0.340. All differences are statistically significant (McNemar with Holm correction). Dimensional equivalence shows statistical parity with Pint, from which TOTEN inherits dimensional authority. Spearman correlation between internal and external rankings confirms the concurrent validity of EngQuant as a control benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-grounded tokenization, as realized in TOTEN, decisively outperforms statistical tokenization on preserving structured technical entities. By construction, it guarantees ontological atomicity and dimensional coherence, validated through oracle coupling and rigorous intrinsic evaluation. The framework demonstrates that declarative, knowledge-based tokenization is a viable and superior alternative to statistical subword methods for scientific and engineering text processing.

title: Emyx: Fast and efficient all-atom protein generation
summary: Computational enzyme design requires generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands, a task that demands both geometric accuracy and structural diversity from the underlying generative model. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction, leading to high training costs and limited sample diversity. We argue that much of this complexity is unnecessary for generators, which condition on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich co-evolutionary signals. Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that concentrates capacity within standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity. We additionally derive an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, bridging flow matching training efficiency with state-of-the-art sampling methods designed for diffusion models without retraining. Despite being the smallest model, Emyx outperforms both Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 against the AME enzyme design benchmark across success rate under strict evaluation requiring both global fold recovery and catalytic geometry accuracy, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity, while training in just $682$ GPU-hours, roughly $4\times$ less than RFdiffusion3.

AI.tldr: Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model for computational enzyme design that outperforms larger competitors on the AME benchmark while training 4× faster. It uses lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity instead of heavy structure-prediction architectures, and bridges flow matching with EDM noise-level sampling via an exact reparametrisation.
AI.motivation: Current all-atom generative models for enzyme design inherit expensive, complex architectures from structure prediction (e.g., IPMs, diffusion backbones), designed for rich co-evolutionary signals. However, enzyme design only requires conditioning on sparse geometric constraints (catalytic residues and ligands), making this complexity unnecessary and costly in both training and sample diversity.
AI.method: Emyx is a 140M-parameter conditional flow matching model that (1) replaces heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditional representations and sparse connectivity, concentrating capacity in standard transformer blocks; (2) derives an exact reparametrisation of the flow matching interpolant into the EDM noise-level framework, enabling state-of-the-art diffusion sampling methods without retraining.
AI.result: On the AME enzyme design benchmark, Emyx outperforms Proteína-Complexa and RFdiffusion3 across success rate (strict evaluation requiring global fold recovery + catalytic geometry accuracy), structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and geometric validity. Training requires only 682 GPU-hours, approximately 4× less than RFdiffusion3.
AI.conclusion: Simpler, flow-matching-based architectures with lightweight conditioning suffice for enzyme design constrained by sparse geometric specifications. The exact reparametrisation into the EDM framework demonstrates that flow matching and diffusion models can be unified without retraining, offering both training efficiency and high-quality sampling.

title: Beyond Uniform Forgetting: A Study of Sequential Direct Preference Optimization Across Preference Settings
summary: Aligning language models with human preferences often requires optimising multiple behavioural objectives. A practical approach is to apply these objectives sequentially using preference optimisation methods such as Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO), but it remains unclear whether later training uniformly degrades preferences learned earlier or whether the effect depends on the relationship between objectives. We study sequential DPO across four preference settings covering distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, we evaluate all objectives after every stage with a fixed base-model reference. We find that sequential DPO does not produce a single forgetting pattern; preference change ranges from partial degradation to stability, pair-level redistribution, or positive transfer depending on objective relationship, signal strength, and training order. Pair-level analysis using length-normalised policy margins shows that aggregate metrics can mask heterogeneous changes across preference pairs, whereas quartile decomposition reveals that high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve depending on the setting. Mechanistic diagnostics show that Stage~2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective across all settings, providing little evidence that direct gradient opposition is the primary driver. These findings suggest that future sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength, rather than assuming that later objectives affect earlier preferences uniformly.

AI.tldr: Sequential DPO does not uniformly degrade earlier preferences; effects range from degradation to stability or positive transfer depending on objective compatibility, signal strength, and training order. Aggregate metrics mask heterogeneous pair-level changes, and gradient opposition is not the primary driver of forgetting.
AI.motivation: Prior work on aligning LMs with multiple objectives via sequential preference optimisation (e.g., DPO) leaves unclear whether later training uniformly degrades earlier-learned preferences or whether the effect depends on inter-objective relationships. The paper aims to systematically characterise forgetting patterns in sequential DPO across diverse objective pairings.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled experimental study using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA adapters, evaluating four preference settings: distributional conflict, multi-attribute interaction, strong safety signal, and compatible response-quality objectives. All objectives are evaluated after each training stage with a fixed base-model reference. Analysis employs length-normalised policy margins, pair-level redistribution analysis, quartile decomposition of confidence levels, and mechanistic diagnostics comparing Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates to the previous objective's direction.
AI.result: Sequential DPO exhibits no single forgetting pattern: outcomes include partial degradation, stability, pair-level redistribution, and positive transfer. Aggregate metrics conceal heterogeneous pair-level changes. Quartile analysis reveals high-confidence pairs can either degrade or improve context-dependently. Stage 2 gradients and adapter updates are near-orthogonal to the previous objective, indicating gradient opposition is not the primary cause of forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Sequential alignment pipelines should account for objective compatibility and signal strength rather than assuming uniform degradation of earlier preferences. Orthogonal gradient dynamics suggest forgetting arises from mechanisms other than direct gradient interference.

title: GNSS Spoofing Threat for V2X communications
comment: 2026 IEEE\@. Personal use of this material is permitted. summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) constitute a core technology for delivering crucial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services in the Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) domain, where they are indispensable for generating Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that uphold network reliability and vehicular safety. Yet, GNSS signals are acutely exposed to spoofing, an advanced attack in which an adversary transmits crafted signals that replicate legitimate satellite characteristics, misleading the receiver into computing a false position. This work presents a methodology for conducting physical spoofing with inexpensive Software Defined Radio (SDR), describing a coordinate generation pipeline that employs Haversine-based distance calculations, temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity, and linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a low-cost GNSS spoofing attack against V2X OnBoard Units (OBUs) and RoadSide Units (RSUs) using HackRF One SDR, demonstrating that forged GPS signals at various vehicle speeds (90, 145, 200 km/h) can degrade V2X services without detection.
AI.motivation: GNSS is critical for V2X Cooperative Awareness Messages (CAM) that ensure vehicular safety and network reliability, yet GNSS signals are vulnerable to spoofing. The authors aim to expose that V2X communications are not secured against such attacks, highlighting a practical security gap in real-world deployments.
AI.method: A physical-layer spoofing methodology using low-cost SDR (HackRF One). The coordinate generation pipeline includes: (1) Haversine-based distance calculations for trajectory synthesis, (2) temporal discretization to emulate constant velocity motion, and (3) linear interpolation to produce high-fidelity GPS baseband signals. The attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices across three speed scenarios: 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h.
AI.result: The spoofing attack successfully misled both OBU and RSU devices across all three tested speed scenarios. The key finding is that V2X communications suffer service degradation due to GNSS spoofing without any detection by the victim systems, confirming that V2X security mechanisms fail to identify such physical-layer attacks.
AI.conclusion: V2X communications are not secured against GNSS spoofing attacks. The demonstrated susceptibility to low-cost SDR-based spoofing reveals a critical vulnerability in V2X systems, where undetected position manipulation can degrade PNT-dependent services and potentially compromise vehicular safety.

title: LaViSA: A Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity Benchmark
summary: Structural ambiguity arises when a single sentence admits multiple valid interpretations due to its syntactic structure, posing a fundamental challenge for language understanding. Visual scenes serve as useful cues for resolving such ambiguity, and Vision and Language Models (VLMs) need to be capable of deriving possible semantic interpretations from visual scenes. We introduce Language and Vision Structural Ambiguity (LaViSA), a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of VLMs to resolve structural ambiguity leveraging visual scenes. LaViSA consists of ambiguous sentences, their disambiguated sentences, and corresponding images of these disambiguated sentences across seven ambiguity categories. Using LaViSA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of diverse VLMs, including both proprietary and open-source models with varying parameter scales and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that although recent VLMs can leverage visual scenes to resolve structural ambiguity to a some extent, they still struggle with certain ambiguity types and visually subtle semantic distinctions, indicating remaining limitations in resolving structural ambiguity using visual scenes.

AI.tldr: LaViSA is a benchmark evaluating VLMs' ability to resolve syntactic structural ambiguity using visual scenes across seven categories. Experiments show VLMs can leverage visuals to some extent but struggle with subtle semantic distinctions and specific ambiguity types.
AI.motivation: Structural ambiguity — where a sentence has multiple valid syntactic interpretations — is a fundamental challenge for language understanding. While visual scenes can serve as disambiguating cues, it is unclear how well current Vision and Language Models (VLMs) can exploit visual context to resolve such ambiguity.
AI.method: The authors introduce LaViSA, a benchmark comprising ambiguous sentences paired with their disambiguated counterparts and corresponding images, spanning seven ambiguity categories. They evaluate a diverse set of VLMs — both proprietary and open-source, varying in parameter scale and reasoning capabilities — on their ability to resolve structural ambiguity by leveraging visual scenes.
AI.result: Recent VLMs demonstrate some capacity to use visual scenes for structural ambiguity resolution, but performance remains limited on certain ambiguity types and on cases requiring fine-grained visual semantic distinctions.
AI.conclusion: Despite progress, current VLMs still exhibit notable limitations in fully resolving structural ambiguity through visual cues, highlighting a gap between human-level disambiguation and model capabilities.

title: AI4SE and SE4AI Exploration: A Decade Looking Back and Forward
summary: The March 2020 INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and Systems Engineering (SE) became the most downloaded issue in the publication's history and launched a research community that now draws over 250 registrants to its annual workshop. In this article, we trace the progress in AI and SE across three phases (labeled here foundational, applied, and LLM inflection) based on the authors' reading of the field's core papers, and describe our opinions of where the community has converged and where critical gaps remain. Separately, a human-AI agreement literature review leveraging both human expertise and six AI models was performed to assess the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications. The results identify five critical research gaps and offer guidance for practitioners navigating AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE. We share the agreement data and the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application so readers can compare their own relevance judgments with the human and AI raters.

AI.tldr: The article traces the evolution of AI and Systems Engineering (SE) integration across three phases—foundational, applied, and LLM inflection—based on core literature. It also presents a human-AI agreement study analyzing 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications to assess relevance, revealing five critical research gaps and offering practical guidance for AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation in SE.
AI.motivation: The INCOSE INSIGHT special issue on AI and SE sparked significant community interest, yet the field lacks a structured understanding of its own progress and remaining gaps. The authors aim to map the trajectory of AI4SE/SE4AI research and systematically identify critical research gaps to guide both researchers and practitioners.
AI.method: The work combines two approaches: (1) a qualitative synthesis tracing AI/SE progress across three historical phases (foundational, applied, LLM inflection) through expert reading of core papers, and (2) a human-AI agreement literature review where human experts and six AI models independently assessed the relevance of 1,712 INCOSE INSIGHT articles and 889 SERC publications, with results made available via the AI4SE/SE4AI Explorer web application.
AI.result: Five critical research gaps were identified in the intersection of AI and SE. The human-AI agreement analysis yielded relevance judgments across the full corpus, revealing patterns of convergence and divergence between human and AI raters. The agreement data and explorer tool were publicly released for further analysis.
AI.conclusion: The AI4SE/SE4AI community has matured through distinct phases and is now at an LLM-driven inflection point. Despite progress, five research gaps persist that require attention. Practitioners need structured guidance for AI adoption, assurance, and workforce transformation, and the shared data/tool enables ongoing collaborative assessment of relevance in this domain.

title: A Hybrid GNN-FEM Framework for Phase-Field Fracture Simulation. Physics-Preserving Hybridization for Generalizable Surrogate Modeling
summary: Scientific machine learning (SciML) has emerged as a promising approach for accelerating simulations of complex physical systems, yet achieving physically consistent and generalizable predictions for nonlinear, history-dependent problems remains a central challenge. In this study, we propose a hybrid GNN--FEM framework for efficient and generalizable phase-field fracture modeling. While phase-field approaches provide a robust variational framework for simulating complex crack evolution, their high computational cost limits practical applications because they require solving coupled, nonlinear, and history-dependent systems within an incremental finite element procedure. To address this challenge, a graph neural network surrogate is integrated into the conventional staggered scheme, replacing the phase-field update at each load increment while retaining the FEM-based displacement solver to enforce mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. By preserving the incremental solution structure, the framework remains consistent with history-dependent fracture evolution without requiring the surrogate to approximate the full solution trajectory. This selective surrogate strategy emphasizes the identification of a physically meaningful and incrementally structured learning target, rather than relying on brute-force data generation to learn the full fracture process. The proposed framework achieves strong generalization across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations through dimensionless feature design, a graph-based formulation on mesh-based domains, and a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field equation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the hybrid approach reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy compared with conventional FEM, and exhibits robust predictive performance across diverse problem settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid GNN-FEM framework that replaces the phase-field update in staggered fracture simulations with a graph neural network surrogate, while retaining FEM for displacement solves. Achieves strong generalization across geometries, loads, materials, and discretizations using dimensionless features and physics-informed loss, reducing computational cost without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.motivation: Phase-field fracture modeling is computationally expensive because it requires solving coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent systems incrementally. Existing SciML approaches often struggle with physical consistency and generalization for such history-dependent problems. The authors aim to accelerate simulations while maintaining the incremental structure and physical fidelity of the conventional staggered scheme.
AI.method: A graph neural network (GNN) surrogate is integrated into the staggered FEM scheme: the GNN replaces the phase-field update at each load increment, while FEM continues to solve the displacement field, enforcing equilibrium and boundary conditions. Key design choices include: (1) preserving the incremental solution structure rather than learning full trajectories; (2) dimensionless feature design; (3) graph-based formulation on mesh domains; and (4) a physics-informed loss derived from the governing phase-field PDE.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show the hybrid GNN-FEM framework reduces computational cost compared to conventional FEM while maintaining accuracy. It exhibits robust predictive performance across varying geometries, loading conditions, material properties, and discretizations.
AI.conclusion: Selectively replacing only the phase-field update with a GNN, while retaining FEM for mechanics, yields an efficient, generalizable, and physically consistent surrogate for phase-field fracture. The incremental structure preservation and physics-informed learning are critical to achieving generalization without brute-force data generation.

title: Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring
summary: LLMs can personalize education, although current static-prompt tutoring systems struggle to adapt to diverse academic disciplines. We develop and test a system with subject-aware prompting, based on 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) extracted from raw transcripts. We first train a prompt routing model in a simulation environment, and then deploy it for online adaptation with actual high-school students. The simulation benchmark shows the router outperforming two static baselines ($0.694$ vs. $0.647$ and $0.64$, $p<0.001$). A/B testing ($N=656$ conversations from 359 students) shows sim-to-real transfer where the model switches from analytical to scaffolding learning strategies. Our adaptive prompt selection mechanism improves instructional efficiency, maintains pedagogical quality and reduces interactions by around 3 turns ($p=0.007$). While a greedy router achieves a comparable exercise conversion rate with the baseline ($19.1\%$ vs. $19.6\%$), a stochastic router that samples strategies leads to a higher conversion rate ($28.1\%$).

AI.tldr: An adaptive tutoring system using subject-aware prompt routing based on 14 pedagogical features outperforms static baselines in simulation and real-world A/B testing with high-school students, with a stochastic router achieving the best exercise conversion rate (28.1%).
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based tutoring systems rely on static prompts that fail to adapt across diverse academic disciplines, motivating the development of a subject-aware, adaptive prompt selection mechanism that can personalize instruction dynamically.
AI.method: The authors (1) extracted 14 pedagogical features (e.g., tutor scaffolding, student understanding) from raw transcripts; (2) trained a prompt routing model in a simulation environment; (3) deployed it for online adaptation with high-school students; (4) evaluated via simulation benchmarks and A/B testing (N=656 conversations, 359 students), comparing a greedy router and a stochastic router against two static baselines.
AI.result: In simulation, the router significantly outperformed two static baselines (0.694 vs. 0.647 and 0.64, p<0.001). Real-world A/B testing demonstrated successful sim-to-real transfer, with the model shifting from analytical to scaffolding strategies. The adaptive mechanism maintained pedagogical quality while reducing interactions by ~3 turns (p=0.007). The greedy router achieved comparable exercise conversion (19.1% vs. 19.6% baseline), but the stochastic router substantially improved conversion to 28.1%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, subject-aware prompt routing can improve instructional efficiency and pedagogical quality in LLM-based tutoring. A stochastic sampling strategy for prompt selection yields significantly better learning outcomes (higher exercise conversion) than both static baselines and a greedy router, suggesting that exploration in prompt strategy selection benefits student engagement.

title: TrustMix: How to Mix Messages in a Mobile Ad-hoc Network
summary:
Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party.
  In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities.
  We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.

AI.tldr: TrustMix is a decentralized mix network protocol for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) that provides anonymity without any central trusted party. It operates through group-based message shuffling and enforces rate limits via linkable ring signatures, with provable security in the random oracle model and demonstrated practicality on Android devices.
AI.motivation: Traditional mix networks are designed for infrastructure settings and cannot be directly applied to MANETs. Existing MANET anonymity solutions either require advance knowledge of network topology or rely on a trusted central party — both assumptions impractical in decentralized, dynamic mobile environments. There is a need for a fully decentralized mix protocol tailored to MANET constraints.
AI.method: TrustMix organizes participants into groups. Users forward messages to a nearby trusted party's group, where all group members collectively shuffle messages before forwarding to subsequent groups. This multi-group forwarding ensures unlinkability between original and forwarded messages. Linkable ring signatures enforce per-party rate limits without identity disclosure. The protocol's security is proven in the random oracle model, anonymity is evaluated via simulation, and a proof-of-concept Android implementation demonstrates practical throughput.
AI.result: Simulation results show TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. The Android proof-of-concept achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices, demonstrating real-world feasibility.
AI.conclusion: TrustMix successfully provides a decentralized mix protocol for MANETs, eliminating reliance on central authorities or prior topology knowledge. It robustly protects anonymity even when some participants are adversarial — anonymity is only compromised if an entire group colludes. The combination of formal security proofs, simulated anonymity gains, and practical mobile implementation validates the approach.

title: A BART-based approach with hierarchical strategy for Vietnamese abstractive multi-document summarization
summary: In this technical report, we focus on solving the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, introduced in the International Workshop on Vietnamese Language and Speech Processing (VLSP) 2022. We choose to follow the popular hierarchical approach, i.e. condensing each document followed by aggregation and summarization. We propose a novel yet simple strategy to shorten documents that is driven by the golden summary, thus ensuring high correlation between stages of the hierarchical approach. Our method achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP's public test set, and can produce fluent and concise summaries. Additionally, we utilize external sources for extra data, which greatly enhances the quantity of data for Vietnamese multi-document summarization. The additional data is made available for the community.

AI.tldr: A technical report proposing a novel document-shortening strategy for Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization, using a golden-summary-driven hierarchical approach. Achieves 0.2468 ROUGE2-F1 on the VLSP 2022 benchmark and releases additional training data.
AI.motivation: Addressing the challenge of Vietnamese multi-document abstractive summarization introduced at VLSP 2022, where existing methods struggle with long input documents and limited training data for Vietnamese.
AI.method: Follows a hierarchical approach: (1) condense each individual document, (2) aggregate and summarize. The key novelty is a simple document-shortening strategy guided by the golden summary to maximize cross-stage correlation. External data sources are also leveraged to augment the training corpus.
AI.result: Achieves a ROUGE2-F1 score of 0.2468 on the VLSP 2022 public test set and produces fluent, concise summaries. The additional training data is publicly released.
AI.conclusion: The golden-summary-driven document shortening effectively improves hierarchical multi-document summarization for Vietnamese, and data augmentation from external sources provides substantial benefit to the low-resource setting.

title: Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective
summary: Electronic design automation (EDA) is inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy. Design artifacts, flow scripts, and engineering decisions cross tool, session, and organizational boundaries before final implementation, signoff, or release. Each transfer carries explicit and implicit requirements that may not be fully captured by stage-local checks. LLM-based agents now invoke EDA tools directly, embed retrieved knowledge in executable scripts, and hand off state across sessions and stages. Once their outputs condition downstream engineering decisions, the transferred object must satisfy a handoff contract and meet the assumptions of its next consumer. This survey introduces handoff validity as its organizing principle. A handoff is valid when the transferred object satisfies the consumer's acceptance conditions and carries sufficient context, evidence, and provenance for downstream use. We review 82 systems and classify them into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems establish validity within a single EDA stage or bounded verification task. Flow-Bound systems preserve coherent workflow state across tools, invocations, and sessions. Organization-Bound systems maintain source grounding, provenance, scope, and admissibility across knowledge and authority boundaries. For each class, we analyze handoff contracts, handoff objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions. These analyses motivate a five-layer EDA agent communication protocol (EACP), covering the agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security and IP protocols. We aim to provide a common vocabulary and research agenda for trustworthy agentic EDA.

AI.tldr: This survey proposes "handoff validity" as a framework for evaluating LLM-based agents in EDA. It classifies 82 systems into Stage-Bound, Flow-Bound, and Organization-Bound categories based on boundary scope, analyzes handoff contracts/objects/coordination mechanisms for each, and proposes a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) to standardize trustworthy multi-agent EDA workflows.
AI.motivation: EDA workflows are multi-stage with frequent handoffs across tools, sessions, and organizations. Each handoff carries explicit and implicit requirements that stage-local checks may miss. As LLM-based agents increasingly automate EDA tasks — invoking tools, generating scripts, and passing state downstream — there is no established framework to ensure that transferred objects satisfy consumer acceptance conditions or carry sufficient context, evidence, and provenance. This gap motivates a systematic treatment of handoff validity.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured survey of 82 LLM-based EDA systems. They introduce "handoff validity" as an organizing principle — a handoff is valid when the transferred object meets the consumer's acceptance conditions with adequate context, evidence, and provenance. Systems are classified into three boundary classes: (1) Stage-Bound (validity within a single EDA stage), (2) Flow-Bound (coherent state across tools and sessions), and (3) Organization-Bound (source grounding and provenance across knowledge/authority boundaries). For each class, handoff contracts, objects, coordination mechanisms, and open questions are analyzed. Based on these analyses, a five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) is proposed.
AI.result: The survey classifies 82 systems into three boundary classes. Stage-Bound systems handle isolated verification tasks; Flow-Bound systems maintain coherence across tool chains; Organization-Bound systems address provenance and authority across organizational lines. Each class exhibits distinct handoff contract structures, coordination mechanisms, and unresolved challenges. The proposed EACP spans five layers: agent discovery, agent message, tool invocation, workflow orchestration, and security & IP protocols, providing a standardized communication stack for trustworthy agentic EDA.
AI.conclusion: Handoff validity offers a unifying lens for designing and evaluating LLM-based EDA agents. The three boundary classes reveal fundamentally different trust and coordination requirements. The five-layer EACP provides a concrete protocol architecture to address these needs, aiming to establish a common vocabulary and research agenda for building trustworthy, multi-agent EDA systems that preserve provenance, context, and correctness across stage, flow, and organizational boundaries.

title: BrainG3N: A Dual-Purpose Tokenizer for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
