summary: Three-dimensional (3D) brain MRI is central to clinical neurology and neuro-oncology, where generative models could augment under-represented cohorts, simulate disease trajectories, and support privacy-preserving data sharing. Latent diffusion has been the go-to solution for modeling imaging data, but it places two competing demands on the tokenizer: encoder embeddings must retain the clinical information that downstream tasks act on, and the decoder must reconstruct anatomically faithful volumes. Existing reconstruction-driven tokenizers achieve the second at the expense of the first. To address this, we introduce a fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) based tokenizer for 3D brain MRI latent diffusion, decoupling encoder and decoder: a frozen 3D MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of those embeddings. We pretrain the encoder on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts spanning four modalities, ten disease categories, and 200+ acquisition sites, and demonstrate its dual utility in two settings. First, on a 23-task linear-probing benchmark, the encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (i.e., BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, and MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 tasks. Second, a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on these clinically informative embeddings supports both conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Together these results establish a single 3D brain-MRI embedding space capable of both downstream clinical tasks and controllable generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 3D brain MRI tokenizer for latent diffusion that decouples encoder and decoder: a frozen MAE encoder produces clinically informative embeddings, while a separate CNN decoder handles reconstruction. This single embedding space supports both state-of-the-art downstream task performance (21/23 tasks) and conditional generation/longitudinal forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing latent diffusion models for 3D brain MRI face a trade-off: reconstruction-driven tokenizers produce anatomically faithful volumes but sacrifice the clinical utility of encoder embeddings needed for downstream tasks. The authors aim to resolve this tension by decoupling the two objectives.
AI.method: A fully volumetric masked-autoencoder (MAE) encoder is pretrained on 35,309 volumes from 18 public cohorts (4 modalities, 10 disease categories, 200+ sites) and frozen. A dedicated CNN decoder reconstructs voxels from a linear projection of MAE embeddings, decoupling encoding from reconstruction. The embeddings are then used to train a conditional diffusion transformer (DiT) supporting generation conditioned on six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting. Evaluation uses a 23-task linear-probing benchmark.
AI.result: The MAE encoder outperforms or matches SOTA models (BrainIAC, BrainSegFounder, MedicalNet) on 21 of 23 downstream tasks. The conditional DiT trained on these embeddings successfully performs conditional generation across six variables and patient-specific longitudinal forecasting.
AI.conclusion: A single 3D brain MRI embedding space derived from a decoupled MAE tokenizer can simultaneously serve both clinically meaningful downstream task performance and controllable generative modeling, overcoming the traditional trade-off in latent diffusion approaches.

title: How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural
summary:
Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs) are often treated as nonlinear stores of computation, yet how nonlinear a trained FFN block actually is has rarely been measured. We treat each FFN as a position-wise input-to-output map and split it into the exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance the closed-form linear map explains defines a block's linear recoverability (R^2_lin), an optimiser-free measure of its linearity.
  Across all twelve blocks of GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and llama-160m, R^2_lin is highly heterogeneous and non-monotone with depth, ranging from near-linear (>0.99) to strongly nonlinear (<0.3) between adjacent blocks, and is not set by the activation function: same-width GELU models GPT-2 and Pythia-160m have sharply different profiles, so recoverability is a learned property of individual trained blocks, not an architectural one. A low-rank bilinear probe of the residual recovers only a few points of R^2, with gain uncorrelated with residual nonlinearity: the unrecovered computation is not a single position-wise product but higher-order or distributed structure.
  The measurement also serves as a targeted compression signal: recoverable blocks admit large single-layer replacements (GPT-2's early FFN at 8x fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity), while low-recoverability blocks flag where this is unsafe. It further exposes a methodological pitfall: trained linear baselines can badly under-converge on ill-conditioned transformer activations, so we report the exact closed-form least-squares ceiling throughout.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces R²_lin, a closed-form measure of how linear each FFN block in a transformer is, by computing the variance explained by the optimal least-squares linear approximation. Applied to GPT-2, Pythia-160m, and Llama-160m, R²_lin reveals heterogeneous, non-monotone, and strongly depth-dependent linearity profiles that are learned rather than architecturally determined. The measure also guides targeted FFN compression and exposes under-convergence pitfalls in trained linear baselines.
AI.motivation: Transformer FFNs are widely considered nonlinear computational stores, but the actual degree of nonlinearity in trained FFN blocks has rarely been quantitatively measured. The authors aim to fill this gap with a principled, optimizer-free metric.
AI.method: Each FFN block is treated as a position-wise map and decomposed into its exact least-squares linear approximation plus a residual. The held-out variance explained by that linear map defines R²_lin. A low-rank bilinear probe is also used to test whether the residual is a simple position-wise multiplicative interaction. The closed-form solution avoids issues of training linear baselines on ill-conditioned activations.
AI.result: R²_lin varies dramatically across blocks (from <0.3 to >0.99) with a non-monotonic depth profile. Same-width GELU models (GPT-2 vs. Pythia-160m) show sharply different profiles, indicating linearity is learned, not architectural. The bilinear probe recovers little of the residual, suggesting higher-order structure. Highly recoverable blocks can be compressed (e.g., GPT-2's early FFN at 8× fewer params, +0.77 PPL), while low-R² blocks flag unsafe compression. Trained linear baselines often under-converge on ill-conditioned activations.
AI.conclusion: FFN linearity in transformers is a heterogeneous, learned property that varies sharply across blocks and models. R²_lin provides a reliable, closed-form signal for both interpretability and targeted model compression, while also revealing a methodological flaw in training-based linear baselines for such analyses.

title: Apparent Psychological Profiles of Large Language Models are Largely a Measurement Artifact
summary: Psychological instruments designed for humans are increasingly used to assign large language models (LLMs) stable psychological profiles that affect their usability, safety assessment, and use as proxies for human participants in research. Using a formal psychometric framework, we show that these profiles are largely a measurement artifact. Administering a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments spanning self-reports and behavioral tasks to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples, we report four findings. First, differences between models are driven not by the traits an instrument targets but by a directional response bias, a tendency to respond toward one end of the scale, or one labeled option, regardless of item content; a variance decomposition attributes 81-90% of between-model variation to this bias, against 9-16% in humans. Second, the bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated by it. Third, because bias rather than trait drives responding, an instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality, a term we coin for the proportion of items for which trait and bias point in opposite directions. Fourth, the profile a model appears to have shifts with the items used and can be manufactured through item selection. These results demonstrate that the apparent psychological profiles of LLMs are artifacts of the instrument used to measure them, not properties of the models themselves. As instruments borrowed from human psychology are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, we call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

AI.tldr: LLMs' apparent psychological profiles are largely a measurement artifact driven by directional response bias (81-90% of between-model variance) rather than genuine traits. Bias declines with model capability but persists, and profiles can be manufactured through item selection.
AI.motivation: Human psychological instruments are increasingly used to assign stable personality/risk-preference profiles to LLMs for usability, safety, and human-proxy purposes. The authors question whether these profiles reflect genuine model properties or measurement artifacts.
AI.method: Administered a battery of personality and risk-preference instruments (self-reports and behavioral tasks) to 56 instruction-tuned LLMs alongside large human reference samples. Applied formal psychometric framework including variance decomposition to partition between-model variation into trait-driven vs. response-bias-driven components. Introduced "response orthogonality" as a novel metric.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Directional response bias accounts for 81-90% of between-model variation vs. 9-16% in humans; (2) Bias declines with model capability but is not eliminated; (3) An instrument's apparent reliability is almost entirely predicted by its response orthogonality; (4) Model profiles shift with item selection and can be deliberately manufactured.
AI.conclusion: Apparent LLM psychological profiles are artifacts of measurement instruments, not model properties. Since human-psychology instruments are rarely fully orthogonal and may inherently lack validity for LLMs, the authors call for dedicated assessments centered on response orthogonality.

title: Quantization as a Malicious Task: Removing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors via Task Arithmetic
summary: Model quantization is widely adopted to reduce memory usage and inference cost when deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, recent studies have revealed a new security threat known as Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs), where a model behaves normally in full precision but activates malicious behavior only after quantization. Existing defenses typically modify quantization procedures or correct activation statistics, often introducing additional computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. Here, we present QVec, a parameter-space perspective for defending against QCBs. We observe that the weight difference between a full-precision model and its quantized counterpart encodes a structured behavioral shift, which can be interpreted as a malicious task vector rather than random quantization noise. Based on this insight, QVec counteracts this malicious direction through controlled parameter correction prior to deployment. QVec requires no retraining, no trigger samples, and only a single quantization pass to estimate the parameter shift, together with a lightweight hyperparameter search. Extensive experiments across image classification benchmarks and multiple Large Language Model (LLM) attack scenarios demonstrate that QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance.

AI.tldr: QVec is a parameter-space defense against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) that interprets the weight shift from quantization as a malicious task vector and neutralizes it via parameter correction, requiring no retraining or trigger samples.
AI.motivation: Existing QCB defenses modify quantization procedures or activation statistics, incurring computational overhead or relying on specific quantization settings. A lightweight, general-purpose defense is needed.
AI.method: QVec computes the weight difference between full-precision and quantized models via a single quantization pass, interprets this as a malicious task vector, and applies a controlled parameter correction (with lightweight hyperparameter search) to counteract the malicious direction before deployment.
AI.result: QVec consistently suppresses backdoor activation while preserving clean performance across image classification benchmarks and multiple LLM attack scenarios.
AI.conclusion: QVec provides an effective, retraining-free, and trigger-agnostic defense against QCB attacks by operating purely in parameter space through malicious task vector neutralization.

title: Where Does Social Reasoning Come From? Capability Provenance in Language Models
summary: We use training-data attribution as an interpretable tool for capability discovery, mapping which regions of the pretraining corpus support social-reasoning versus STEM-reasoning in OLMo3-7B. Training-data attribution measures how strongly each training document influences a model's predictions on a benchmark, but document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities, and prior work has emphasized factual knowledge rather than reasoning. We compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set drawn from the de-duplicated Dolma3 mix, aggregate influence across WebOrganizer's 24-format x 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins), and contrast benchmark pairs in a 2x2 design that varies domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge): SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, and the contrast is sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Targeted machine unlearning provides partial causal validation: forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, and we open-source all code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints.

AI.tldr: This paper uses training-data attribution to map which regions of a pretraining corpus support social reasoning vs. STEM reasoning in OLMo3-7B. By aggregating gradient-based influence scores across a 576-bin topic-format taxonomy and contrasting benchmark pairs, the authors find that social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with partial causal validation via targeted machine unlearning.
AI.motivation: Prior work using training-data attribution has focused on factual knowledge rather than reasoning, and document-level scores are too noisy to identify which corpus regions support which capabilities. The authors aim to develop a more interpretable, structured method for capability discovery—mapping how different regions of pretraining data contribute to distinct reasoning abilities (social vs. STEM).
AI.method: The authors compute gradient-based attribution (TrackStar via Bergson) over a working set from the deduplicated Dolma3 mix. Influence scores are aggregated across WebOrganizer's 24-format × 24-topic taxonomy (576 bins). They use a 2×2 contrastive design varying domain (social vs. STEM) and capability type (reasoning vs. knowledge), comparing SocialIQA and MMLU Social Sciences against ARC-Challenge and MMLU STEM. Targeted machine unlearning is performed on high-attribution topic bins as partial causal validation.
AI.result: Social and STEM reasoning draw on qualitatively distinct corpus regions, with the contrast sharper at the reasoning level than at the knowledge level. Forgetting high-attribution topic bins (e.g., Literature for SocialIQA) degrades the aligned benchmark more than within-bin random baselines, providing partial causal support for the attribution mapping.
AI.conclusion: Training-data attribution, when aggregated across a structured taxonomy and used contrastively, can effectively map which corpus regions support specific reasoning capabilities. All code, sampling manifests, the bin-level influence matrix, and unlearning checkpoints are open-sourced.

title: The Hidden Environmental Cost of Poor Coding Practices in TensorFlow and Keras Applications: A Study on Resource Leaks and Carbon Emissions
summary: Efficiency and sustainability are critical considerations in the development and deployment of machine learning (ML) applications. Among the factors influencing sustainability, resource leaks in ML code can introduce hidden inefficiencies that elevate energy consumption and CO2 emissions. Despite this, empirical evidence quantifying their environmental impact remains limited. This emerging results paper presents an initial empirical investigation of two common resource-leak smells, namely Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR), and their impact on energy consumption and CO2 emissions in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Controlled experiments were conducted for each smell by executing identical training tasks while comparing against a smell-free baseline. Our preliminary results show that both smells consistently increase estimated electricity usage and carbon emissions. IMR and UTR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32% and 46%, respectively, with proportional increases in CO2 emissions. Paired statistical tests indicate that these differences are systematic and statistically significant, providing initial empirical evidence that resource-leak smells may degrade ML energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. These findings suggest that resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and sustainability, emphasizing the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development.

AI.tldr: An empirical study quantifying how two resource-leak code smells (Improper Model Reuse and Unreleased Tensor References) in TensorFlow/Keras increase energy consumption by 32% and 46% respectively, with proportional CO₂ emission increases, providing statistically significant evidence that resource leaks degrade ML sustainability.
AI.motivation: While efficiency and sustainability are critical for ML deployment, empirical evidence quantifying the environmental impact of resource leaks in ML code remains limited. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing quantitative data on how specific resource-leak smells affect energy consumption and carbon emissions.
AI.method: Controlled experiments were conducted for two resource-leak smells — Improper Model Reuse (IMR) and Unreleased Tensor References (UTR) — in TensorFlow and Keras workloads. Each smell was tested by executing identical training tasks and comparing against a smell-free baseline. Paired statistical tests were applied to assess the significance of observed differences in electricity usage and CO₂ emissions.
AI.result: IMR increased electricity consumption by approximately 32%, while UTR increased it by approximately 46%, with proportional increases in CO₂ emissions. Paired statistical tests confirmed these differences are systematic and statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: Resource-leak smells pose measurable risks to both software quality and environmental sustainability. The findings underscore the importance of integrating resource-lifecycle management and energy-efficiency considerations into ML development practices.

title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: VERITAS is a zero-shot framework that improves LLM-based theorem proving by routing rich verifier feedback (beyond binary pass/fail) into a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling followed by critic-guided MCTS that uses Phase 1 failures as negative examples, achieving 40.6% on miniF2F and exposing the limits of unguided sampling on a new combinatorics benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLM-based formal provers typically discard rich intermediate verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) by reducing them to a binary pass/fail bit. This wastes valuable feedback that could guide proof search, especially in settings requiring iterative recovery of correct lemma names from verifier feedback.
AI.method: VERITAS employs a two-phase zero-shot protocol: (1) Best-of-N sampling to generate candidate proofs, then (2) a critic-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples, routing every verifier signal back into proof search. Phase 2 is designed so that it preserves all theorems solved in Phase 1, making additional solves attributable to feedback-driven exploration.
AI.result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. Best-of-5 at 36.9% and Portfolio at 26.2%). On the newly released VERITAS-CombiBench (55 combinatorics theorems), VERITAS reaches 7.3% while Best-of-5 falls to 1.8% (below Portfolio's 3.6%), demonstrating that unguided sampling fails when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback.
AI.conclusion: Rich verifier feedback, when properly routed back into proof search via critic-guided MCTS with negative examples, yields significant gains over binary-feedback baselines. The poor performance of unguided sampling on combinatorics problems highlights the necessity of feedback-driven exploration for complex theorem-proving tasks.

title: Your Mouse and Eyes Secretly Leak Your Preference: LLM Alignment using Implicit Feedback from Users
summary: To align a Large Language Model (LLM), most existing methods collect explicit human feedback and train a reward model to predict the human preference based on the response text. These existing methods have two key limitations. First, the users rarely provide explicit feedback for LLM responses, which makes the high-quality preference annotation expensive to collect. Second, the methods do not leverage implicit human feedback, which has proven vital to the economic moats of Internet giants. To quantify the value of implicit feedback, we build a new dataset called IFLLM, which collects 1336 multi-turn questions from the 59 Mechanical Turk workers, their mouse trajectories, and eye gazing points to the LLMs' responses from their webcams. IFLLM shows that the users have very diverse types of gazing behavior and mouse trajectories. Our reward model based on the implicit user feedback boosts the accuracy of the text-based reward model from 55% to 64% and nearly triples the relative response quality improvements after applying the DPO to eight LLMs, demonstrating the value of implicit feedback in the wild. Our data collection website, dataset, and codes can be found at https://github.com/themehulpatwari/llm-implicit-feedback/.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IFLLM, a dataset capturing implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories, eye gaze) during LLM interactions, and shows that incorporating such implicit signals into reward modeling significantly boosts preference prediction accuracy and downstream DPO alignment performance across eight LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM alignment methods rely on explicit human feedback, which is expensive to collect and overlooks the rich implicit feedback signals (e.g., gaze, mouse movement) that major internet platforms already leverage. The authors aim to quantify the value of implicit feedback for LLM alignment.
AI.method: The authors built IFLLM, a dataset of 1,336 multi-turn questions from 59 MTurk workers, recording their mouse trajectories and webcam-based eye gaze while they read LLM responses. They then train a reward model that fuses text-based and implicit-feedback-based signals, and evaluate it via preference prediction accuracy and DPO-based alignment improvements on eight LLMs.
AI.result: Implicit-feedback-augmented reward models improve text-only reward model accuracy from 55% to 64%. After applying DPO with the combined reward signal, relative response quality improvements nearly triple compared to using text-based rewards alone, across eight LLMs. The data also reveals diverse, user-specific patterns in gazing and mouse behavior.
AI.conclusion: Implicit human feedback (mouse trajectories and eye gaze) carries substantial signal for LLM alignment, complementing explicit textual feedback. Integrating these signals meaningfully boosts reward model accuracy and downstream alignment quality, demonstrating that implicit feedback is a valuable and underutilized resource in the wild.

title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

AI.tldr: NRT-Bench introduces a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. Adaptive attacks cause 8.7–12.1% of sessions to lose a critical safety function, with vulnerabilities nearly disjoint across models. Defenses are model-dependent, sometimes backfiring.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical supervisory roles, but their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure is poorly understood. Existing red-teaming lacks objective, non-LLM-judged harm signals in multi-turn, bounded settings with real safety constraints.
AI.method: The authors built NRT-Bench: a simulated nuclear power plant with a five-role LLM agent operator team managing six critical safety functions (CSFs). Adversaries inject messages over four channels in multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is objectively defined — the run terminates when any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Four frontier models were evaluated under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, with guardrail stacks and safety-advisor agents tested as defenses.
AI.result: Adaptive multi-turn attacks caused 8.7–12.1% of attack sessions to lose a CSF across four models. Despite similar aggregate rates, failures barely overlapped: of 149 sessions, none defeated all four models, while one-third defeated at least one. Defenses were strongly model-dependent — the same guardrail or safety advisor could lower attack success for one model while raising it for another.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent vulnerabilities under adversarial pressure are largely disjoint across models, meaning aggregate robustness metrics obscure per-model weaknesses. Defenses cannot be assumed to transfer across models and may backfire. The benchmark and tooling are released for reproducible safety evaluation.

title: Before the Labels: How Dataset Construction Shapes Suicidality Detection in Clinical Text
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology (CLPsych 2026)
summary: Clinical NLP increasingly relies on electronic health record (EHR) data to detect suicidal behaviors, treating clinical documentation as more reliable ground truth than social media. We argue that this framing obscures how EHR-based suicidality datasets encode a particular operationalization of suicidality, shaped by who authors the data, how episodes are bounded, and how ambiguity is resolved. We ground this argument in a case study of the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. We show how governance constraints, ICD-based cohort selection, single-annotator labeling, and hospital-stay-level aggregation produce labels that reflect clinician-documented judgments, treat suicidality as a bounded episode, and assume that intent can be reliably inferred from documentation. A linguistic analysis demonstrates that identical labels subsume heterogeneous clinical framings differing in temporality, negation, and uncertainty. We argue that clinical NLP should examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before interpreting their labels as ground truth.

AI.tldr: Clinical NLP treats EHR-derived suicidality labels as ground truth, but this paper argues those labels encode specific operational assumptions. Using the ScAN dataset (MIMIC-III) as a case study, the authors demonstrate how dataset construction choices—ICD-based cohort selection, single annotators, stay-level aggregation—embed clinician-authored framings, and show that identical labels mask heterogeneous linguistic expressions of temporality, negation, and uncertainty.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing assumption in clinical NLP that EHR-based suicidality annotations constitute more reliable ground truth than social media data. It aims to expose how dataset construction practices implicitly operationalize suicidality in ways that go unexamined, potentially leading models to learn reified, clinically-shaped definitions rather than capturing the full phenomenology of suicidal behavior.
AI.method: A case study of the ScAN dataset (suicide attempt classification from MIMIC-III clinical notes). The authors analyze governance constraints, ICD-code-driven cohort selection, single-annotator labeling protocols, and hospital-stay-level aggregation. They then conduct a linguistic analysis of the annotated texts, examining heterogeneity in temporality (past vs. current), negation (denied vs. affirmed), and uncertainty (hedged vs. certain) within identical label categories.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) ICD-based cohort selection constrains the population to those already clinically recognized, missing undetected cases. (2) Single-annotator labeling collapses annotation into clinician-documented judgment rather than independent verification. (3) Hospital-stay-level aggregation treats suicidality as a bounded episode, erasing longitudinal trajectories. (4) The linguistic analysis reveals that identical labels subsume heterogeneous framings: past vs. present events, negated mentions, and uncertain language all receive the same classification.
AI.conclusion: Clinical NLP should critically examine the assumptions embedded in suicidality datasets before treating their labels as ground truth. The operationalization of suicidality in EHR data is not neutral—it reflects clinical workflows, documentation practices, and institutional constraints. Failure to interrogate these assumptions risks building models that reproduce narrow, clinician-centric definitions of suicidality rather than capturing its full complexity.

title: CoRaCommit: A VS Code Extension for Commit Message Generation with Exemplar Retrieval
comment: 17 pages, 6 images, 3 tables, Manuscript submitted to a Journal (2026)
summary: Commit messages are essential textual artifacts that describe the intent behind code changes, and play a critical role in version control, code review, and historical tracking. However, in practice, commit messages are primarily authored manually, which is time-consuming and often results in inconsistent quality and non-uniform expression. Existing VS Code extensions for commit message generation typically directly invoke large language models based on the code diff, without leveraging similar commit exemplars as references, and rarely support user feedback-driven LLM recommendation. To address these limitations, this paper presents CoRaCommit, a VS Code extension that enhances commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as prompt context, invoking multiple LLMs in parallel for candidate commit message comparison, and dynamically recommending LLMs based on user feedback. Experimental results on 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset show that CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions across BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented context for commit message generation.

AI.tldr: CoRaCommit is a VS Code extension that improves commit message generation by retrieving similar commit exemplars as context, running multiple LLMs in parallel, and dynamically recommending the best LLM based on user feedback, outperforming existing extensions on standard NLG metrics.
AI.motivation: Manual commit message authoring is time-consuming and leads to inconsistent quality. Existing VS Code extensions rely solely on code diffs fed directly to a single LLM, lacking retrieval of similar exemplars as references and lacking user feedback mechanisms for LLM recommendation.
AI.method: CoRaCommit employs three key strategies: (1) retrieval of similar commit exemplars to serve as prompt context, (2) parallel invocation of multiple LLMs to generate candidate commit messages for comparison, and (3) dynamic LLM recommendation based on user feedback. Evaluation uses 945 commits from the ApacheCM dataset.
AI.result: CoRaCommit outperforms existing VS Code extensions on BLEU, CIDEr, METEOR, and ROUGE-L metrics across the 945-commit ApacheCM evaluation set.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-augmented context is effective for commit message generation. Combining exemplar retrieval with multi-LLM comparison and user feedback-driven recommendation yields superior performance over single-LLM, diff-only approaches.

title: Thermodynamic Signatures of Reasoning: Free-Energy and Spectral-Form-Factor Diagnostics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) is deployment-critical, and recent work shows that the spectrum of attention-derived graph Laplacians carries strong signal about reasoning quality. Prior spectral diagnostics, however, summarize the Laplacian spectrum by a handful of eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, leaving most of its structure unused. We propose Free-Energy Signatures (Fes), a spectral descriptor that treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and extracts its thermodynamic potentials partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity together with the random-matrix-theory (RMT) spectral form factor. We prove three results: (i)~Lipschitz stability of Fes under attention perturbation; (ii)~an expressiveness result showing that Fes enriches finite spectral summaries and approximates moment-derived spectral functionals under explicit regularity and grid-resolution assumptions; and (iii)~a finite-sample PAC bound on the AUROC of a training-free detector built from Fes. Empirically, across six open-weight LLMs and six benchmarks, a lightweight probe on Fes descriptors achieves the strongest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by $+6.5$ AUROC points and over GoR-4 by $+2.4$ points on average, while requiring no update to the underlying LLM. In the fully unsupervised setting, an RMT-deviation score achieves mean AUROC $0.71$, providing a label-free but weaker detector. A complementary RMT analysis shows that correct generations exhibit more Wigner-Dyson like spectral statistics, whereas hallucinations exhibit more Poisson-like statistics. The anonymized code and config are provided in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: Fes (Free-Energy Signatures) is a spectral descriptor that treats attention Laplacians as Hamiltonians, extracting thermodynamic potentials and RMT spectral form factors for hallucination detection in LLMs. It outperforms existing attention-spectral baselines by +2.4–6.5 AUROC points, with theoretical guarantees on stability, expressiveness, and PAC bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior spectral diagnostics for LLM hallucination detection summarize the Laplacian spectrum using only a few eigenvalues or hand-picked scalars, discarding most structural information. The authors aim to capture richer spectral structure to improve detection accuracy.
AI.method: Fes treats each layer's attention Laplacian as a Hamiltonian and computes thermodynamic potentials: partition function, free energy, spectral entropy, heat capacity, plus the random-matrix-theory spectral form factor. A lightweight probe is trained on these descriptors. The authors prove Lipschitz stability, expressiveness (enriching finite spectral summaries), and a finite-sample PAC bound on AUROC. An unsupervised variant uses RMT-deviation scoring.
AI.result: Across 6 open-weight LLMs and 6 benchmarks, Fes achieves the highest aggregate AUROC among attention-spectral baselines, improving over LapEig by +6.5 and over GoR-4 by +2.4 AUROC points on average. The unsupervised RMT-deviation detector reaches mean AUROC 0.71. RMT analysis reveals correct generations follow Wigner-Dyson statistics while hallucinations follow Poisson statistics.
AI.conclusion: Fes provides a principled, training-free (for the LLM), and theoretically grounded spectral descriptor for hallucination detection that substantially outperforms prior spectral methods by leveraging the full thermodynamic and RMT structure of the attention Laplacian spectrum.

title: Multi-View Decompilation for LLM-Based Malware Classification
summary: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Providing LLMs with pseudo-C output from two decompilers (Ghidra and RetDec) instead of one improves malware classification recall and F1, because different decompilers make complementary errors that offer richer evidence for triage.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based malware classification pipelines assume a single decompiler view, ignoring that decompilers are lossy and heuristic-driven. Different decompilers can reveal distinct artifacts from the same binary, so relying on just one may miss signals critical for identifying malicious code.
AI.method: The authors curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning diverse threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Multiple LLMs from major model families are then evaluated under single-decompiler and dual-decompiler prompting conditions, with agreement analysis between decompiler outputs.
AI.result: Dual-decompiler prompting improves malicious-class F1 across LLMs, primarily via increased recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses confirm that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, providing complementary evidence rather than redundant information.
AI.conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free strategy that enhances LLM-based malware triage in practical settings by exploiting the complementary nature of decompiler outputs.

title: MiqraBERT: Regression-Based Sentence-BERT Finetuning for Biblical Hebrew Parallel Detection
summary: Textual reuse pervades the Hebrew Bible, yet the computational methods used to detect it still rest largely on lexical overlap, and they falter once a parallel involves paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. This paper introduces MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model finetuned from AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) for verse-level semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew. The training set comprises 1,650 labeled verse and half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels drawn from the Chronicles synoptic material and from foundational studies of poetic parallelism, balanced against 825 randomly sampled negatives. Through cosine-similarity regression, the model learns an embedding space in which parallel verses cluster together and unrelated verses move apart. We evaluate separation with distribution-based metrics, Wasserstein distance and the overlap coefficient, across ten random seeds. MiqraBERT improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from roughly 24% to about 6%. Narrative synoptic parallels reach a recall@10 of 87.1%; poetic parallels remain difficult, below 9%. This genre-dependent asymmetry confines the model's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. MiqraBERT is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/davidmsmiley/MiqraBERT

AI.tldr: MiqraBERT is a Sentence-BERT model fine-tuned from AlephBERT for detecting semantic similarity in Biblical Hebrew verses. Trained on 1,650 labeled verse pairs, it improves distributional separation 2.7-fold over baselines, achieving 87.1% recall@10 for narrative parallels but under 9% for poetry, limiting its reliable scope to narrative textual reuse.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods for detecting textual reuse in the Hebrew Bible rely on lexical overlap and fail when parallels involve paraphrase, lexical substitution, or syntactic reworking. A semantic similarity model tailored to Biblical Hebrew is needed to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune AlephBERT (a Modern Hebrew encoder) into MiqraBERT, a Sentence-BERT model for verse-level semantic similarity. Training uses 1,650 labeled verse/half-verse pairs: 825 true parallels (from Chronicles synoptic material and poetic parallelism studies) balanced with 825 random negatives. Cosine-similarity regression learns an embedding space where parallel verses cluster. Evaluation uses Wasserstein distance and overlap coefficient across ten random seeds.
AI.result: MiqraBERT achieves a 2.7-fold improvement in distributional separation over the pre-trained baseline and reduces the ambiguous overlap region from ~24% to ~6%. Narrative synoptic parallels yield 87.1% recall@10, but poetic parallels remain below 9%.
AI.conclusion: The genre-dependent performance asymmetry — strong on narrative, weak on poetry — confines MiqraBERT's reliable scope to narrative textual reuse. The model is publicly released on HuggingFace.

title: JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines
summary: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.

AI.tldr: JamSet and JamBench are the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on the Godot engine, sourced from Game Jam competitions. The benchmark defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated via compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a dramatic capability cliff as project scale grows (runtime pass rates drop from 80.4% to 5.7%), and Code Agents improve compilation but not runtime quality, indicating the bottleneck is architectural design. JamSet also proves effective as training data.
AI.motivation: Current AI-driven game development has advanced in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based coding, but project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains unexplored due to the lack of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. Game Jam competitions provide a rich source of open-source, complete game projects that can fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors leverage the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode to build a deterministic verification pipeline covering file integrity and runtime behavior. They collected over 240,000 repositories from Game Jams, distilled 8,133 verified projects (JamSet), and manually curated 300 into JamBench. JamBench defines two tasks: theme-driven generation and code completion. Evaluation uses compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Nine frontier models and Code Agents are evaluated, and JamSet is tested as training data via fine-tuning.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals a severe capability cliff: runtime pass rates drop from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large projects (Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates but produce no gains in runtime behavioral quality. Fine-tuning on JamSet yields improvements, validating its utility as training data. The bottleneck is architectural design, not syntactic correctness.
AI.conclusion: Project-level game code generation on professional engines remains a formidable challenge for frontier models, with scale being the primary failure factor. Code Agents alone cannot bridge the gap, as the core bottleneck is architectural reasoning. JamSet and JamBench provide the community with essential resources to advance research in this domain.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Predictive Validity for the Evaluation of LLM Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks are growing fast, but no single benchmark touches more than four or five of the dimensions that deployment exposes. This paper aggregates the largest coordinated deep-dive of one MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark to date: fourteen parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including a multi-modal visual extension), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation-methodology probes. Consolidating those studies with seven prior agent benchmarks, we argue that aggregate-score leaderboards systematically underspecify deployed-agent evaluation. Rankings derived from aggregate scores do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings; recent public-to-hidden competition retrospectives provide direct empirical evidence of this rank instability. We propose ranking configurations by predictive validity, the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample rank, rather than in-sample mean, and report a twelve-tier measurement apparatus that exposes the deployment-relevant dimensions HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. The position is operationalized through three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds; existing evidence partly supports it but is too thin to confirm. We close with a pre-registered pilot design and a field-level vision for what the next generation of agentic benchmarks should report.

AI.tldr: Current agent benchmarks aggregate across too few dimensions and produce leaderboard rankings that fail to transfer to out-of-distribution deployment settings. The paper reports 14 parallel implementation studies using an MCP-based industrial-agent benchmark, demonstrates rank instability in aggregate scores, and proposes evaluating configurations by predictive validity (in-sample to out-of-sample rank correlation) using a twelve-tier measurement framework.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks (including HELM and successors) collapse deployment-relevant dimensions into aggregate scores, producing leaderboard rankings that are underspecified and unstable. No single benchmark covers more than four or five deployment dimensions, yet real-world deployment exposes many more. The authors aim to expose this gap and propose a more valid evaluation paradigm.
AI.method: The authors conducted 14 parallel implementation studies covering new asset classes (including multi-modal visual extensions), alternative orchestrations, retrieval strategies, reasoning modes, infrastructure optimizations, and evaluation methodology probes. These are consolidated with seven prior agent benchmarks. They analyzed rank instability using public-to-hidden competition retrospectives and proposed ranking by predictive validity — the correlation between in-sample and out-of-sample ranks. A twelve-tier measurement apparatus is introduced to capture deployment-relevant dimensions. Three falsifiable out-of-distribution criteria with explicit thresholds are proposed.
AI.result: Aggregate-score leaderboard rankings do not transfer to out-of-distribution settings, as evidenced by direct empirical data from competition retrospectives. The twelve-tier measurement apparatus reveals dimensions that HELM and its agent-era successors collapse. Existing evidence partially supports the authors' position but remains too thin for confirmation.
AI.conclusion: The field should shift from aggregate-score leaderboards to predictive-validity-based ranking configurations. The authors provide a pre-registered pilot design and outline a vision for what next-generation agentic benchmarks should report, emphasizing multi-dimensional evaluation with out-of-distribution validity.

title: FlexLAM: Resolving the Bottleneck Trade-off in Latent Action Learning
summary: Latent actions provide a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making, yet existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. We identify a bottleneck trade-off: overly tight codes can discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while overly loose codes preserve additional transition variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrowly distributed. FlexLAM replaces this fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout, yielding prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, without new architectures or losses. A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and under a low-return single-task alignment stress test, indicating that FlexLAM is not merely adjustable at inference time but learns a better latent-action interface at the same token budgets. The same model supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining, and FlexLAM improves Ego4D transition reconstruction. These results suggest that variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces.

AI.tldr: FlexLAM introduces variable-length latent actions via nested dropout, replacing the fixed-capacity bottleneck in Latent Action Models. This yields prefix-valid codes that capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed, matching or surpassing fixed-capacity LAMs across token budgets without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Existing Latent Action Models (LAMs) force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck, creating a trade-off: tight codes discard transition cues needed for action alignment, while loose codes preserve excess variation that is hard to resolve with scarce or narrowly distributed alignment labels. The authors aim to resolve this bottleneck trade-off.
AI.method: FlexLAM replaces the fixed-capacity latent code with variable-length latent actions trained using nested dropout. Nested dropout produces prefix-valid codes: earlier tokens capture the most compact, essential transition structure, and subsequent tokens add progressively finer detail. The model requires no new architectures or auxiliary losses. At inference time, the token budget can be adjusted without retraining.
AI.result: A single FlexLAM matches or surpasses separately trained fixed-capacity LAMs at every evaluated token budget under standard scarce-label supervision and a low-return single-task alignment stress test. FlexLAM also improves transition reconstruction on Ego4D and supports inference-time token-budget adjustment without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Variable-length latent actions are an architecture-free, drop-in upgrade to the fixed-capacity bottleneck in latent action models, latent-action world models, and video-pretrained action interfaces. FlexLAM learns a fundamentally better latent-action interface, not merely an adjustable one.

title: Image Encryption Algorithm Based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Dynamic S-Box Generation
summary: The paper proposes a dynamic approach to image encryption, combining the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and classical cryptography to improve the security and flexibility of image encryption. The main concept is to create adaptive Substitution boxes (S-boxes) based on characteristics that are learned by a trained CNN. The CNN-based S-boxes can be relied on for more non-linearity, uniqueness, and input image dependence than the conventional fixed S-boxes because they are susceptible to the linear and differential attacks. This dynamic behaviour enhances the confusion property and makes it more resistant to statistical and structural attacks. The encryption algorithm consists of CNN-based feature extraction and the creation of a personalised S-box to replace the pixels. Entropy, histogram analysis, correlation, NPCR, and UACI enable security assessment of generated S-boxes based on the CNN, indicating that the scheme is more resilient and flexible than traditional ones.

AI.tldr: A dynamic image encryption scheme using CNN-generated adaptive S-boxes that outperform fixed S-boxes in non-linearity, uniqueness, and attack resistance.
AI.motivation: Conventional fixed S-boxes used in image encryption are vulnerable to linear and differential cryptanalysis. A dynamic, content-adaptive approach is needed to enhance confusion properties and resist statistical and structural attacks.
AI.method: A CNN is trained to extract image features, which are then used to generate personalized, input-dependent Substitution boxes (S-boxes). These adaptive S-boxes replace traditional fixed S-boxes in the encryption algorithm for pixel substitution. Security is evaluated via entropy, histogram analysis, correlation coefficients, NPCR, and UACI.
AI.result: The CNN-based adaptive S-boxes demonstrate superior non-linearity, uniqueness, and input dependence. The encryption scheme exhibits strong resilience against statistical and structural attacks, with favorable security metrics.
AI.conclusion: Combining CNN-driven S-box generation with classical cryptography yields a more secure, flexible, and attack-resistant image encryption framework compared to traditional fixed S-box approaches.

title: Repository-Level Solidity Code Generation with Large Language Models: From Prompting to Fine-Tuning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in general-purpose code generation, but their effectiveness in specialized software domains remains underexplored. Solidity smart contracts represent a high-stakes domain where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks and metrics remain insufficient for repository-level Solidity generation, where models must synthesize complete contracts from natural language requirements. To address this gap, we introduce SolidityBench, a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts paired with natural language descriptions. We also propose SolidityScore, a Solidity-aware semantic metric that emphasizes domain-critical constructs such as security modifiers, contract declarations, and Solidity-specific keywords. Using this benchmark, we evaluate representative code LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama, across zero-shot prompting, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and supervised fine-tuning. The results show that general-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. Among non-parametric methods, retrieval-augmented generation performs best, while in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. Supervised fine-tuning achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive benchmark for repository-level Solidity code generation and shows that high-quality domain data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts.

AI.tldr: SolidityBench introduces a benchmark of 5,470 repository-level Solidity smart contracts with natural language descriptions, paired with SolidityScore, a domain-aware semantic metric. Evaluating various LLMs across multiple prompting and fine-tuning strategies reveals that supervised fine-tuning with high-quality domain data most effectively addresses the systematic structural deficiencies of general-purpose models in Solidity code generation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose code LLMs are underexplored in specialized, high-stakes domains like Solidity smart contracts, where generated code must satisfy strict language-level, security, and software-engineering constraints. Existing benchmarks are insufficient for repository-level generation from natural language requirements.
AI.method: The authors construct SolidityBench (5,470 repository-level Solidity contracts with NL descriptions) and SolidityScore (a Solidity-aware semantic metric emphasizing security modifiers, contract declarations, and domain-specific keywords). They evaluate Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder, and CodeLlama under zero-shot, Chain-of-Thought, in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
AI.result: General-purpose models exhibit systematic structural deficiencies in repository-level Solidity generation. RAG performs best among non-parametric methods; in-context learning degrades beyond two examples due to context saturation. SFT achieves the largest improvement by internalizing Solidity-specific constraints into model parameters.
AI.conclusion: High-quality domain-specific data combined with supervised fine-tuning is the most effective strategy for improving the reliability of LLM-generated smart contracts. The benchmark and metric provide a comprehensive evaluation framework for repository-level Solidity code generation.

title: GLARE: A Natural Language Interface for Querying Global Explanations
summary: While global explanations are crucial for understanding vision models across datasets, classes, and decision contexts, their complex and monolithic nature often hinders practical exploration. Because users typically seek targeted answers to specific questions rather than static artifacts, we present an LLM-based interactive interface that provides natural language access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers. The system's core LLM acts as a mediator, translating natural language questions into structured SQL queries over local explanation data. This enables flexible aggregation without exposing users to low-level representations. For each query, the interface outputs statistics-augmented natural language responses, supporting local explanations, and intent-aligned visualizations. We evaluate the system on intent interpretation, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors. Our results demonstrate that LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based interactive interface that translates natural language questions into SQL queries over local explanation data, enabling flexible, targeted access to global explanations for black-box image classifiers with statistics-augmented responses and visualizations.
AI.motivation: Global explanations are monolithic and difficult for users to explore practically; users need targeted answers to specific questions rather than static explanatory artifacts, yet no existing system provides flexible natural language querying over global explanation data.
AI.method: An LLM mediates between users and structured local explanation data by translating natural language questions into SQL queries, then aggregating results into statistics-augmented natural language responses paired with intent-aligned visualizations. The system is evaluated on intent interpretation accuracy, query mapping accuracy, generalization to novel queries and datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors.
AI.result: LLM-mediated querying substantially improves the accessibility and usability of global explanations for human-centered XAI, demonstrating accurate intent interpretation, reliable query mapping, generalization across novel queries/datasets, and robustness to linguistic errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-based interactive interface successfully bridges the gap between monolithic global explanations and practical user needs, offering a more accessible and usable paradigm for human-centered explainable AI.

title: Spectral DPPs via NEPv: A Scalable Continuous Relaxation of Determinantal MAP for Diversity-Aware Data Selection
summary: Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a massive pool of candidates is a recurring primitive in modern machine learning -- data curation and coreset selection for training and fine-tuning large models, active-learning batch acquisition, prompt and exemplar selection for in-context learning, retrieval diversification, and experimental design. Determinantal Point Processes (\DPP s) give a principled, well-calibrated notion of diversity for this task, but their \emph{MAP} objective -- pick a size-$k$ subset $S$ maximizing $\logdet(L_S)$ -- is NP-hard, and the standard greedy and sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in the ground-set size $n$. This cost is prohibitive precisely in the data-centric regime where diversity matters most, where $n$ ranges over millions to billions of candidate examples, features, or embeddings. We recast \DPP-MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold, and show that its first-order optimality conditions form a \emph{Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency} (\NEPv) of a previously unstudied form. This \NEPv\ admits a self-consistent field (\SCF) iteration with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, giving a principled iterative solver where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, \OurMethod, requires only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in time $O\!\big((ndk+nk^2)\,t\big)$ for a small number of iterations $t$, scaling near-linearly in $n$ and integrating directly with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML. This paper focuses on the relaxation, solver, and scaling analysis; full real-data benchmarking is left to a planned empirical study.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts the NP-hard DPP MAP inference problem (selecting a size-k subset maximizing log-determinant) as a continuous optimization over the Stiefel manifold, revealing a novel Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). A self-consistent field (SCF) iteration with spectral-gap contraction guarantees yields an algorithm that scales near-linearly in the ground-set size n, requiring only matrix-vector products.
AI.motivation: DPP MAP inference is a fundamental primitive for diverse subset selection in modern ML (data curation, active learning, prompt selection, retrieval diversification). However, exact MAP is NP-hard and standard greedy/sampling algorithms scale superlinearly in n, which is prohibitive when n is in the millions to billions — precisely the data-centric regime where diversity matters most.
AI.method: The authors recast DPP MAP as a continuous optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold. They derive first-order optimality conditions that form a Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problem with eigenvector dependency (NEPv) of a novel form. They propose a self-consistent field (SCF) iterative solver with a spectral-gap-based local contraction guarantee, where the diversity objective drives an eigenvector-dependent operator. The resulting algorithm, called OurMethod, uses only matrix-vector products with the kernel and runs in O((ndk + nk²)·t) time for t iterations.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves near-linear scaling in the ground-set size n, integrates naturally with low-rank and feature-map kernels common in ML, and comes with theoretical convergence guarantees via spectral-gap contraction. Full real-data benchmarking is deferred to a planned empirical study.
AI.conclusion: The continuous relaxation via Stiefel manifold optimization and the SCF-based NEPv solver provide a principled, scalable approach to DPP MAP inference. The near-linear time complexity makes diversity-based subset selection feasible at the billion-scale regime. Empirical validation on real data is planned for future work.

title: Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly rely on language-model components to interpret instructions, process external data, invoke tools, and coordinate with other agents. These capabilities make prompt-injection and jailbreak attacks more consequential, especially as attackers adopt model-guided automation to scale probing, prompt refinement, and response evaluation. This work analyzes the resulting attack-defense setting through a probabilistic model of a target system, its defense mechanism, and the attacker's automated judge. Our analysis shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses can allow attacker success rate (ASR) to approach one as the query budget grows, since predictable refusals provide useful feedback to automated search. We then examine detect-and-misdirect, where detected malicious interactions receive controlled, non-operational responses designed to induce false-positive errors in the attacker's judge. This strategy reduces the positive predictive value of attacker-selected candidates and yields a bounded asymptotic ASR. We evaluate a proof-of-concept realization of this strategy through Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), a lightweight conversational misdirection method designed to replace predictable refusal text with safe but strategically misleading responses in automated jailbreak settings. On jailbreak benchmarks, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz attack runs.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the security dynamics of prompt-injection/jailbreak attacks on LLM-based agents under automated, model-guided attack frameworks. It shows that conventional detect-and-block defenses asymptotically drive attacker success rate (ASR) toward 1 as query budget increases, because predictable refusals leak useful gradient-like feedback. The authors propose "detect-and-misdirect" — replacing refusal responses with strategically misleading content — which mathematically bounds asymptotic ASR, and implement Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement (CMPE), demonstrating up to 100× reduction in ASR upper bounds and near-elimination of verified attack success against PAIR and GPTFuzz.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems integrate LLMs for instruction interpretation, tool use, and multi-agent coordination, making prompt-injection and jailbreak threats more severe. Attackers increasingly use automated, model-guided search (iterative probing, refinement, evaluation) to scale attacks. The core gap is that existing detect-and-block defenses create a predictable, information-leaking signal (the refusal) that automated optimizers can exploit, enabling ASR to asymptotically approach 1 given sufficient query budget. A defense strategy is needed that deprives the attacker of reliable success/failure signal.
AI.method: The authors formalize the attack-defense interaction as a probabilistic model with three components: a target system, a defense mechanism, and an attacker's automated judge. They analyze detect-and-block (where malicious queries receive a refusal) and detect-and-misdirect (where malicious queries receive controlled, non-operational but misleading responses designed to cause false-positive errors in the attacker's judge). They derive asymptotic ASR bounds for both strategies. They then implement CMPE (Contextual Misdirection via Progressive Engagement), which generates safe but strategically misleading responses that appear superficially cooperative while providing no operational payoff, progressively degrading the attacker judge's precision.
AI.result: Analytically, detect-and-block allows ASR→1 as query budget→∞ because predictable refusals enable the attacker judge to learn a reliable success/failure discriminator. Detect-and-misdirection bounds asymptotic ASR by reducing the positive predictive value (PPV) of attacker-selected candidates. Empirically, CMPE reduces estimated ASR upper bounds by up to two orders of magnitude on jailbreak benchmarks and nearly eliminates verified attack success in end-to-end PAIR and GPTFuzz automated attack runs.
AI.conclusion: Detect-and-block is fundamentally insufficient against automated model-guided attacks due to information leakage through predictable refusals. Detect-and-misdirect, realized via CMPE, offers a principled alternative with bounded asymptotic ASR by corrupting the attacker's evaluation feedback loop. This represents a paradigm shift from binary accept/reject to strategic engagement with attackers.

title: From 50K to 8.2 Million in 24 Hours: Vozinha's Algorithmic Consecration and the Multilingual Making of World Cup Visibility
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; v0.1 pilot preprint. Dataset and evidence package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20722235
summary: We present a multilingual computational discourse analysis of how language constructed the algorithmic consecration of Vozinha, the 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper, after Spain 0-0 Cape Verde at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The study contributes a multilingual corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French; a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based frame annotation; a reproducible annotation pipeline combining LLM-assisted suggestion with human validation; and an analysis of cross-lingual narrative diffusion across discourse phases. We treat the platform follower count itself, narrated as "50k to 8M", as a linguistic object: a circulating and narratable proof of visibility rather than a mere measurement. The follower-growth timeline is used only as contextual metadata: we reconstruct a conservative phase structure, not a continuous API-native series, and type every datapoint by value class, confidence, and evidence type. The only exact primary scraper anchor is 8,235,652 followers at 2026-06-16 15:47 UTC; all other figures are reported as estimated ranges or thresholds, including an estimated pre-match baseline of 45k-56k. Findings suggest that distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilization, Spanish crisis, English nation-making, and a shared platform-metric spectacle through which peripheral athletic performance became globally visible. As a v0.1 pilot, the paper releases the corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline, while flagging full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement as planned work.

AI.tldr: A multilingual discourse analysis of how Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French media narratively framed the viral rise of Cape Verdean goalkeeper Vozinha after a 2026 World Cup draw, introducing a nine-frame taxonomy and LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, with the follower-count trajectory treated as a linguistic-narrative object rather than mere social media metric.
AI.motivation: To understand how distinct languages construct divergent narrative frames around the same algorithmic consecration event — a peripheral athlete's sudden global visibility — and to model cross-lingual narrative diffusion using a reproducible, cue-based frame annotation methodology.
AI.method: Construction of a multilingual corpus (Portuguese, Spanish, English, French); development of a nine-frame narrative taxonomy with cue-based annotation; a reproducible hybrid annotation pipeline combining LLM-suggested frame labels with human validation; reconstruction of a conservative discourse-phase structure from follower-growth metadata classified by value class, confidence, and evidence type; cross-lingual diffusion analysis across phases.
AI.result: Distinct languages carried distinct frames: Portuguese discourse emphasized mobilization, Spanish discourse centered on crisis, English discourse foregrounded nation-making, and all languages converged on a shared platform-metric spectacle framing. The follower count functioned narratively as circulating proof of visibility ("50k to 8M") rather than as a neutral measurement.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the viability of multilingual frame analysis for algorithmic consecration phenomena and releases corpus schema, frame taxonomy, annotation guidelines, hashed visual-evidence log, and typed timeline as a v0.1 pilot, with full double annotation and inter-annotator agreement planned as future work.

title: Beyond Static Endpoints: Tool Programs as an Interface for Flexible Agentic Web Services
summary: In the agentic web era, LLM-based agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, yet most interfaces remain \emph{static endpoints} that poorly express long-horizon workflows with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. We present ToolPro, which represents an agent's tool intent as an \emph{executable tool program} that compactly encodes multi-step service interactions with explicit effect types. ToolPro combines constraint-guided program construction, effect-aware replay for exactly-once state-modifying calls, and a profile-driven policy that decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. We instantiate ToolPro over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing and evaluate it on diverse workflows of real-world applications. ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4\% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1\%, with larger gains under higher network latency and workflow complexity.

AI.tldr: ToolPro introduces an executable tool program abstraction for LLM agents that encodes multi-step web service interactions with loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. It reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% and client-side traffic by up to 96.1% compared to stepwise tool calling.
AI.motivation: In the agentic web era, LLM agents increasingly invoke web services as tools, but most interfaces are static endpoints that poorly express long-horizon workflows requiring loops, conditionals, joins, and retries. Stepwise calling leads to high latency and excessive client-server round-trips, especially under network constraints and complex workflows.
