AI.method: ToolPro represents agent tool intent as an executable tool program with three core components: (1) constraint-guided program construction that compiles multi-step service interactions into compact programs; (2) effect-aware replay ensuring exactly-once semantics for state-modifying calls; and (3) a profile-driven policy that dynamically decides when program execution outperforms stepwise calling. The system is instantiated over MCP-style services with WebAssembly sandboxing.
AI.result: ToolPro achieves up to 53.4% reduction in end-to-end latency and up to 96.1% reduction in client-side traffic compared to stepwise calling. Gains are amplified under higher network latency and greater workflow complexity.
AI.conclusion: Compiling agent tool interactions into executable programs with effect-aware replay and adaptive dispatch policies significantly outperforms traditional stepwise API calling, enabling more efficient long-horizon agentic workflows in the agentic web.

title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, yet its black-box nature remains a key roadblock to deployment and scientific diagnosis. Standard interpretability tools, such as Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), are ill-equipped for NCO, whose decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack proper concept vocabulary definition. To close this gap, we introduce Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), to our knowledge, the first framework for interpreting NCO policies by distilling black-box NCO models into human-readable program portfolios. EPB employs an LLM to autonomously evolve a bank of programs, where each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. EPB works through an iterative framework: Block I fixes program bank capacity and introduces a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme that couples numerical gradients for student router updates and textual gradients for LLM-based program revision; Block II dynamically adapts bank capacity via fault-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate EPB's effectiveness and broad applicability, where the distilled program portfolios largely match original performance. EPB also reveals that NCO behavior shifts across optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising tool for interpreting sequential decision-making models.

AI.tldr: EPB distills black-box neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) models into interpretable program portfolios using LLM-driven evolution, combining hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent for program revision with dynamic capacity adaptation, achieving near-original performance while revealing that NCO behavior approximates compositions of classical heuristic variants.
AI.motivation: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) models suffer from a black-box nature that hampers deployment and scientific understanding. Existing interpretability tools like Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) fail for NCO because NCO decisions are dynamic, state-dependent, and lack a well-defined concept vocabulary. There is a pressing need for an interpretability framework tailored to sequential decision-making in combinatorial optimization.
AI.method: The authors propose Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks (EPB), which distills black-box NCO policies into human-readable program portfolios. EPB operates in two alternating blocks: (1) Block I uses a hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent scheme — numerical gradients update a student router that selects among programs, while textual gradients guide an LLM to revise individual programs; each program's per-step action distribution serves as the bottleneck. (2) Block II dynamically adapts the program bank's capacity through fault-targeted expansion (adding programs where errors occur) and redundancy pruning (removing overlapping programs). The LLM autonomously evolves the program bank throughout this iterative process.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that distilled program portfolios largely match the original black-box NCO performance. EPB also reveals key insights: NCO behavior shifts across different optimization stages and can be approximated as a composition of classic heuristic variants, demonstrating both the practical and diagnostic value of the approach.
AI.conclusion: EPB is the first framework for interpreting NCO policies via programmatic distillation, establishing a promising paradigm for interpreting sequential decision-making models. It bridges the gap between performance and interpretability in NCO, offering both deployment-ready transparent policies and scientific insights into black-box optimization behavior.

title: Spectral Retrieval-Augmented Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting leverages historical patterns to predict future values, but traditional methods face challenges when dealing with complex, non-stationary patterns that are difficult to memorize during training. Retrieval-augmented approaches have emerged as promising solutions by retrieving similar historical patterns to enhance predictions. However, existing retrieval methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: spectral blindness, which overlooks critical frequency-domain characteristics that capture underlying periodic structures, and temporal recency, which treats all historical data equally without emphasizing recent, more relevant patterns. In this paper, we propose SpecReTF, a novel retrieval method that addresses these issues by converting time series into windowed frequency representations, measuring similarity with a combined metric that captures both amplitude and phase information. To balance recency and historical context, we apply an exponential moving average weighting scheme that emphasizes recent windows. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SpecReTF outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy across diverse, non-stationary time series.

AI.tldr: SpecReTF introduces a retrieval-augmented time series forecasting method that converts sequences into windowed frequency-domain representations, uses a combined amplitude-phase similarity metric, and applies exponential moving average weighting to prioritize recent patterns, outperforming time-domain retrieval baselines on non-stationary benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) spectral blindness — they operate purely in the time domain and fail to capture frequency-domain characteristics that reveal underlying periodic structures; and (2) temporal recency neglect — they treat all historical data equally without emphasizing more recent, contextually relevant patterns. These shortcomings degrade performance on complex, non-stationary time series.
AI.method: SpecReTF proposes three core technical components: (1) converting time series into windowed frequency representations via spectral transformation, explicitly capturing amplitude and phase spectra; (2) a combined similarity metric that jointly measures alignment in both amplitude and phase domains to retrieve structurally similar historical windows; and (3) an exponential moving average (EMA) weighting scheme applied over retrieved windows to emphasize recency, balancing historical context with temporal relevance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SpecReTF consistently outperforms time-domain retrieval methods, achieving superior forecasting accuracy, particularly on diverse, non-stationary time series where periodic structures and recency dynamics are critical.
AI.conclusion: SpecReTF demonstrates that incorporating frequency-domain awareness and recency-sensitive weighting into retrieval-augmented forecasting significantly improves predictive performance on non-stationary time series, addressing fundamental weaknesses of prior retrieval-based approaches.

title: A-COMPASS: Formal Foundations for Anonymity Analysis in Microdata
summary: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.

AI.tldr: A-COMPASS extends the COMPASS language to operate on standard one-record-per-person microdata tables instead of preprocessed grouped tables. It adds anonymization action execution, formal syntax and semantics with proven determinism and compositionality, and a verification mechanism for anonymity properties like k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.motivation: Formal verification of data privacy models is underexplored, even for basic models. The existing COMPASS language operates on preprocessed tables (one record–one group) rather than raw microdata (one record–one person), limiting practical applicability. There is a need for a language that works directly on standard microdata while retaining formal verifiability of privacy guarantees.
AI.method: The authors modify the COMPASS language to create A-COMPASS, designed for standard microdata tables. They define formal syntax and semantics for the new language and prove key semantic properties: determinism (each program has a unique outcome) and compositionality (semantics of compound constructs derive from their parts). They also implement a verification mechanism for anonymity properties including k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.result: A-COMPASS successfully extends COMPASS to operate on one-record-per-person microdata tables. It supports both checking pre-existing anonymity conditions and executing anonymization actions—a new feature. The formal semantics are proven deterministic and compositional. The language can verify standard anonymity properties such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.
AI.conclusion: A-COMPASS provides a formally grounded, practically applicable language for privacy verification and enforcement on standard microdata, advancing the formal verification landscape for data privacy models.

title: SAGE-OPD: Selective Agent-Guided Intervention for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves student models by training them on trajectories induced by their own policy, making it a promising approach for mitigating exposure bias in agent training. However, most OPD studies focus on single-turn settings, while realistic LLM agents interact with environments over multiple turns. In this regime, early errors can alter future observations and compound across the trajectory, and standard dense token-level OPD becomes brittle, as it may over-penalize semantically valid alternatives, reinforce local degeneracies such as repeated actions, and propagate unreliable teacher supervision on off-distribution histories. We propose SAGE-OPD, a verifier-free selective intervention framework specifically designed for multi-turn OPD. Instead of applying teacher supervision uniformly across all turns, SAGE-OPD first observes environment feedback and uses teacher judgment to decide whether each student response should be skipped or intervened on. To further address compounding errors, SAGE-OPD weights token-level distillation by teacher confidence, reducing the influence of uncertain teacher distributions on corrupted or ambiguous histories. Finally, SAGE-OPD applies loss normalization to preserve the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting. Experiments on agent tasks show that SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines, achieving up to a 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies further demonstrate that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization provide complementary benefits. Our results suggest that effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is necessary and reliable.

AI.tldr: SAGE-OPD is a selective intervention framework for multi-turn on-policy distillation that uses teacher judgment to decide which student turns to intervene on, weights distillation by teacher confidence, and normalizes loss to maintain scale — achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement on ALFWorld over standard OPD.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) with dense token-level supervision fails in multi-turn agent settings because early errors compound across trajectories, semantically valid alternatives get over-penalized, local degeneracies (e.g., repeated actions) are reinforced, and teacher supervision becomes unreliable on off-distribution histories.
AI.method: SAGE-OPD introduces three components: (1) turn-level selective intervention — after observing environment feedback, teacher judgment determines whether to skip or intervene on each student response; (2) teacher confidence weighting — token-level distillation is weighted by teacher confidence to reduce influence on corrupted/ambiguous histories; (3) loss normalization — preserves the overall loss scale of standard OPD while retaining selective turn-level weighting.
AI.result: SAGE-OPD consistently improves over baselines on agent tasks, achieving up to 13.3% relative improvement in ALFWorld unseen success rate over standard OPD. Ablation studies confirm that turn-level intervention, teacher confidence weighting, and loss normalization each provide complementary benefits.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-turn OPD should remain on-policy, but teacher supervision should be selectively allocated to turns where intervention is both necessary and reliable, rather than applied uniformly.

title: When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
summary: As LLM agents increasingly select tools autonomously, their choices among tools with different privileges become safety-relevant. However, prior tool-selection studies focus on safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving privilege-sensitive choices underexplored. To address this gap, we study over-privileged tool selection, in which an agent selects or escalates to a higher-privilege tool despite a sufficient lower-privilege alternative. We introduce ToolPrivBench to evaluate whether agents choose higher-privilege tools despite sufficient lower-privilege alternatives, measuring both initial selection and escalation after transient tool failures. Across eight domains and five recurring risk patterns, we find that over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is further amplified by transient failures. We further find that general safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege tool choice, while prompt-level controls provide only limited mitigation under transient failures. We therefore introduce a privilege-aware post-training defense that teaches agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools and escalate only when necessary. Our mitigation experiments show that this defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.

AI.tldr: LLM agents frequently choose higher-privilege tools when lower-privilege alternatives suffice, a problem amplified by transient failures. The authors introduce ToolPrivBench to benchmark this behavior across 5 risk patterns and 8 domains, then propose a privilege-aware post-training defense that substantially reduces unnecessary privilege escalation while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain autonomy in tool selection, over-privileged tool choices pose safety risks (e.g., accessing sensitive data or performing destructive actions when unnecessary). Prior work only examines safety-agnostic metadata preferences, leaving the safety-critical question of least-privilege tool selection unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors construct ToolPrivBench, a benchmark spanning 8 domains and 5 recurring risk patterns, measuring both initial over-privileged selection and privilege escalation after transient tool failures. They evaluate mainstream LLM agents and test two mitigation approaches: prompt-level controls and a novel privilege-aware post-training defense that fine-tunes agents to prefer sufficient lower-privilege tools.
AI.result: Over-privileged tool selection is common among mainstream LLM agents and is amplified by transient failures. General safety alignment fails to transfer to least-privilege tool choice. Prompt-level controls offer only limited mitigation under failure conditions. The proposed privilege-aware post-training defense substantially reduces unnecessary high-privilege tool use while preserving general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Over-privileged tool selection is a prevalent and underexplored safety problem in autonomous LLM agents. Privilege-aware post-training offers an effective mitigation strategy, outperforming both generic safety alignment and prompt-level interventions.

title: A Comparative Study of Pretrained Transformer Models for Quranic ASR: Speech Representations, Label Formats, and Dataset Composition
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to International Journal of Speech Technology
summary: Quran Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) aims to convert Quranic recitation into text, enabling applications such as aided memorisation tools and Quranic search engines. However, existing ASR models often exhibit high Word Error Rates (WER) on user-recited verses and lack full coverage of the Quranic corpus. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of domain-specific fine-tuning of pretrained Transformer-based models for Quranic ASR, using advanced speech feature extraction methods: Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, and XLS-R. These models apply self-supervised learning by masking portions of input audio and using Transformer architectures to learn context-aware speech features. The pretrained models are fine-tuned on a filtered Quranic dataset exceeding 870 hours of professional and user recitations. Through comprehensive ablation studies across feature extractors, output label formats, training strategies, and clip durations, we identify the key factors that affect transcription accuracy in this domain. Our best-performing configuration achieves a WER of 0.08 on the EveryAyah subset and 0.11 on the combined EveryAyah+Tarteel setting, representing roughly a five-percentage-point gain over the Citrinet baseline (WER = 0.163) while reducing combined-model training time from 140 hours to 40 hours. Arabic text without diacritics yields the best fine-tuning results, and Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides the strongest overall representation. Future work includes improving dataset quality and developing phoneme-aware models to extract deeper speech feature representations for Tajweed-sensitive applications.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning self-supervised Transformer models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on 870+ hours of Quranic recitation achieves state-of-the-art WER of 0.08–0.11, substantially outperforming the Citrinet baseline while reducing training time by ~70%.
AI.motivation: Existing Quranic ASR systems suffer from high Word Error Rates on user-recited verses and incomplete Quranic corpus coverage, limiting practical applications like memorisation aids and search engines.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study fine-tuning pretrained self-supervised Transformer models (Wav2Vec2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) on a filtered 870+ hour Quranic dataset. Ablation studies examine feature extractors, output label formats (with/without diacritics), training strategies, and clip durations. Models use masked audio input and context-aware speech feature learning.
AI.result: Best configuration: WER 0.08 (EveryAyah subset), 0.11 (EveryAyah+Tarteel combined). ~5 percentage point improvement over Citrinet baseline (WER 0.163). Training time reduced from 140 to 40 hours. Non-diacritized Arabic text yields best results; Wav2Vec2-XLSR-53 provides strongest representation.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning of XLS-R with non-diacritized text output significantly advances Quranic ASR. Future work targets improved dataset quality and phoneme-aware models for Tajweed-sensitive recognition.

title: Does Text Actually Help? Uncovering and Resolving Text Collapse in Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
summary: Multimodal time series forecasting, which pairs numerical sequences with domain-relevant textual reports, promises to inject world knowledge into forecasting pipelines. However, we uncover a critical failure mode in existing frameworks that we term text collapse: the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal regardless of the input description. We argue that text collapse is a consequence of a fundamental asymmetry in time series forecasting: the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant, while the text branch, despite carrying complementary and often critical information, is insufficiently utilized, leading to its systematic underexploitation. To address this, we propose \textbf{REST-TS} (\textbf{R}esidual-\textbf{E}xclusive \textbf{S}upervision for \textbf{T}ext in \textbf{T}ime \textbf{S}eries), which turns the asymmetry into a design principle: the numerical backbone produces its own independent numerical forecast, and the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual, the prediction gap that numbers cannot explain. Because no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch must extract genuine content from the input description. Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence that supervising the text branch on the residual compels it to extract genuine content from the input.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "text collapse" in multimodal time series forecasting, where the text branch learns content-independent representations. The authors propose REST-TS, which supervises the text branch exclusively on the residual (the part of the forecast unexplained by the numerical backbone), forcing it to extract genuine textual content and achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Multimodal time series forecasting pairs numerical sequences with textual reports to inject world knowledge, but existing frameworks suffer from "text collapse": the text branch converges to a content-independent transformation, contributing negligible discriminative signal. This stems from a fundamental asymmetry where the numerical input is strongly autocorrelated with the output, making the numerical backbone inherently dominant while the text branch is systematically underexploited.
AI.method: REST-TS (Residual-Exclusive Supervision for Text in Time Series) transforms the asymmetry into a design principle. The numerical backbone independently produces its own forecast, while the text branch is exclusively supervised to predict the structured components of the residual — the prediction gap that numbers alone cannot explain. Since no numerical pathway can reduce these losses, the text branch is compelled to extract genuine content from the input description.
AI.result: Evaluated across diverse real-world domains and backbone architectures, REST-TS achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance and consistently demonstrates greater text-branch utilization than existing frameworks, providing strong empirical evidence for the approach.
AI.conclusion: Supervising the text branch exclusively on the residual effectively mitigates text collapse, forcing the text encoder to extract meaningful, content-dependent representations. The residual-exclusive supervision design turns the inherent asymmetry of multimodal time series into a principled advantage.

title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing the Limits of Fine-Tuning LLMs for Vulnerability Detection in Systems Software
summary: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: CWE-Trace is a Linux kernel vulnerability detection benchmark (834 samples, 74 CWEs) with strict temporal splits to test whether LLMs truly reason about security or merely exploit data contamination. Results show contamination provides no advantage, models exhibit persistent directional biases impervious to fine-tuning, and no model exceeds 52.1% detection accuracy — confirming LLMs lack genuine security reasoning for systems software.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses an unresolved question: do LLMs that perform well on vulnerability benchmarks actually reason about security, or do they merely exploit data contamination and pattern matching? Existing benchmarks fail to disentangle these possibilities due to temporal leakage and lack of diagnostic metrics.
AI.method: The authors construct CWE-Trace, a framework comprising 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples covering 74 CWEs. Key design elements: (1) a strict temporal split — pre-2025 historical data vs. post-cutoff leakage-free data; (2) context-aware vulnerable–patched pairs; (3) two novel diagnostic metrics: Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). Eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants are evaluated across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification tasks.
AI.result: (1) Data contamination provides no measurable advantage: 84% of nominally contaminated samples lack usable memorization (vulnerable functions absent or cross-mapped), and ~31% carry CWE misclassification. (2) Backbone directional priors dominate: DFI ranges from -85.5 to +94.8 pp and persists across temporal splits, unchanged by fine-tuning. Fine-tuning shifts output thresholds without altering decision policies — calibration without comprehension. Detection and CWE understanding are decoupled (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 performs worst at detection but gains most in classification). Best detection is 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE Top-1 accuracy remains below 1.3%.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems-level software. Benchmark contamination is not the core problem; rather, models exhibit systematic directional failure modes rooted in backbone priors that fine-tuning cannot correct. The decoupling of detection and classification capabilities further underscores the absence of genuine comprehension.

title: CacheWeaver: Cache-Aware Evidence Ordering for Efficient Grounded RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factual grounding, but it also lengthens prompts and raises prefill cost. Prefix caching in serving engines such as vLLM reduces this cost only when requests share the same token prefix. In grounded generation, however, adjacent queries may retrieve overlapping evidence in different orders, so set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap. We present CacheWeaver, a lightweight prompt-layer method for cache-aware evidence ordering. The method keeps a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences and uses a greedy walk to place the most reusable prefix first, while leaving the serving engine and retrieved evidence set unchanged. Across three vLLM configurations, the method lowers median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by about 20-33 percent relative to retrieval-order prefix caching, without hurting answer quality in our QA tests. The greedy policy reaches 97.5 percent of the median TTFT gain from oracle ordering, indicating that most reusable prefix locality can be recovered by a simple scheduling layer between retrieval and inference.

AI.tldr: CacheWeaver reorders retrieved evidence chunks before sending them to the LLM, maximizing prefix cache reuse in serving engines like vLLM. This reduces time-to-first-token by 20–33% without degrading answer quality, achieving 97.5% of oracle-level gains.
AI.motivation: RAG improves factual accuracy but inflates prompt length and prefill cost. While prefix caching (e.g., vLLM) amortizes this cost for shared prefixes, grounded generation queries often retrieve overlapping evidence sets in different orders, so semantic overlap fails to translate into cache-reusable prefix overlap. The gap between evidence overlap and prefix overlap motivates a scheduling intervention.
AI.method: CacheWeaver maintains a prefix tree over recently served evidence sequences. Given a new set of retrieved evidence chunks, it performs a greedy walk over the tree to order chunks such that the longest matching prefix is placed first, maximizing cache hits. The method operates as a lightweight prompt-layer between retrieval and inference, leaving the retriever and serving engine unchanged.
AI.result: Across three vLLM configurations, CacheWeaver reduces median TTFT by ~20–33% relative to retrieval-order prefix caching. The greedy policy reaches 97.5% of the median TTFT gain of an oracle ordering. Answer quality in QA evaluations remains unaffected.
AI.conclusion: Significant prefix cache reuse can be recovered by inserting a simple evidence-ordering layer between retrieval and inference, without modifying the serving engine or retriever, and without compromising generation quality.

title: The Correctness Illusion in LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, LNCS format. Companion papers to follow on arXiv next week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Benchmarks for LLM-generated GPU kernels (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) score correctness through fixed-shape, small-sample allclose-style checks. The number of inputs varies between benchmarks. The shape, dtype, and tolerance are fixed for each kernel. We test that oracle empirically. We construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls and 9 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors) and re-evaluate it under op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing with a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The seeded oracle flags 9 of 9 buggy kernels and passes 15 of 15 correct controls, at zero precision cost on controls. We extend the corpus to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair) and re-run the same protocol on five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL). The verdicts are identical across all five GPUs: 10 of 10 illusions caught and 16 of 16 controls clean. The corpus result is about LLM-style transcription bugs that the allclose-on-one-shape oracle certifies as correct, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed.

AI.tldr: Existing LLM GPU kernel benchmarks rely on fixed-shape, low-sample allclose checks that miss transcription bugs. The authors propose an op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing protocol with fp64 CPU references and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances, demonstrating it catches 9/9 seeded bugs that prior oracles certified correct, with zero false positives on controls, and the verdicts replicate identically across five GPU classes.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks (KernelBench, TritonBench, GEAK) evaluate LLM-generated GPU kernels via correctness checks that are limited: they use fixed-shape inputs, small sample counts, and fixed tolerances per kernel. This leaves open the possibility that buggy kernels—especially those with subtle transcription errors—can pass these oracles. The authors aim to expose this gap by constructing a controlled corpus of known-correct and known-buggy kernels and testing whether the prevailing evaluation methodology falsely certifies bugs.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled corpus of 24 Triton and CPU stand-in kernels (15 correct controls, 9 buggy variants seeded with documented transcription errors). They re-evaluate this corpus under an op-schema-aware seeded fuzzing protocol using a high-precision (fp64) CPU reference and per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances. The corpus is then extended to 26 ops (adding a flash-attention pair), and the protocol is re-run across five GPU classes (RTX 3060, A10, L40S, A100 SXM4, H100 NVL) to test cross-hardware reproducibility of verdicts.
AI.result: The seeded oracle flags all 9 buggy kernels and passes all 15 correct controls (zero false positives). When extended to 26 ops across five GPU classes, the verdicts remain identical: 10/10 illusions caught, 16/16 controls clean. Every flagged failure replays byte-for-byte from a stored seed, ensuring reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The dominant allclose-on-one-shape evaluation paradigm in LLM kernel benchmarks systematically certifies transcription bugs as correct. The proposed fuzzing protocol provides a more rigorous, reproducible correctness standard that is hardware-agnostic and yields identical verdicts across diverse GPU architectures.

title: Benchmarking Agentic Review Systems
summary: A new class of agentic review systems are emerging as a remedy to the pressure placed on peer review systems by AI-assisted research, but it is unclear how they should be evaluated. We evaluate two open-source systems (OpenAIReview and coarse), one proprietary system (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline, across six LLMs spanning frontier and efficient models. First, we study whether AI reviews on ICLR/NeurIPS papers track with papers' quality as approximated by external signals such as citations and acceptance decisions. Every system performs above chance in pairwise accuracy, and the best is OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 at 83.0%. Second, to test whether systems can catch errors with known ground truth, we construct a perturbation benchmark that injects four categories of errors into papers across eight arXiv subject classes and measure detection recall. The strongest configuration (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) catches 71.6% of injected errors, leaving substantial room for improvement. The union of detections across six models reaches 83.3% recall, suggesting different models detect different errors and better harness design can potentially increase performance. Beyond these benchmarks, we study a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users. Votes on its comments skew positive at 1.44 to 1, and the most common complaints are about false positives and minor nitpicks. Together, by evaluating full review systems backed by state-of-the-art models on real research papers, we show that while AI reviews still have room for improvement, they can already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and earn positive feedback from real users.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AI-based peer review systems (open-source and proprietary) on their ability to assess paper quality and detect errors in academic manuscripts, finding that the best system (OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5) achieves 83% pairwise accuracy in quality judgments and 71.6% recall in error detection, with positive real-world user feedback but room for improvement.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted research is placing growing pressure on traditional peer review systems, prompting the emergence of agentic AI review systems. However, there is no established methodology for evaluating these systems, making it unclear how well they actually perform.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three review systems — two open-source (OpenAIReview, coarse), one proprietary (Reviewer3), and a zero-shot baseline — across six LLMs. Evaluation proceeds along three axes: (1) correlating AI review scores with external quality signals (citations, acceptance decisions) on ICLR/NeurIPS papers using pairwise accuracy; (2) constructing a perturbation benchmark injecting four error categories into papers across eight arXiv subjects, measuring detection recall; and (3) analyzing a public deployment of OpenAIReview with real users, tracking vote ratios and qualitative complaints.
AI.result: All systems perform above chance on pairwise accuracy, with OpenAIReview + GPT-5.5 reaching 83.0%. On error detection, the same configuration achieves 71.6% recall, while the union across six models reaches 83.3%, indicating complementarity. In the public deployment, votes skew positive (1.44:1), with common complaints being false positives and minor nitpicks.
AI.conclusion: AI review systems already track human quality judgments well, catch important errors, and receive positive user feedback, though substantial room for improvement remains — particularly through better ensemble design that leverages complementary detection strengths across models.

title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
summary: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 77.1\% exact match accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases accuracy to 80.5\% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

AI.tldr: MortarBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM-based mortgage loan origination agents. Current LLMs achieve at most 77.1% accuracy and exhibit bias against non-English names. The authors introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework that boosts accuracy to 80.5% while reducing bias and improving risk management.
AI.motivation: Firms are increasingly deploying AI agents for loan origination despite the absence of any public benchmark. This lack of standardized evaluation makes it impossible to assess model reliability, fairness, and risk management capabilities in a high-stakes financial domain.
AI.method: The authors present MortarBench, built on a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline that generates realistic examples with broad edge-case coverage matching real-world distributions. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark. They then propose CRIT, a confidence calibration framework designed to improve accuracy, steering of risk management decisions, and bias mitigation.
AI.result: Closed-source LLMs achieve at most 77.1% exact match accuracy on MortarBench. Systematic biases were discovered against applicants with non-English names. The CRIT framework raises accuracy to 80.5% while simultaneously improving risk management steering and reducing the foreignness-related bias.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are insufficiently reliable for autonomous loan origination. The CRIT framework demonstrates that confidence calibration can meaningfully improve accuracy, fairness, and risk management, but significant gaps remain before safe deployment in production lending environments.

title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
summary: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a distributionally robust optimization framework for runtime monitoring of AI agents under probabilistic security policies. Unlike prior Datalog-based approaches limited to deterministic policies, it computes sound upper bounds on policy violation probability without relying on independence assumptions, outperforming existing methods on agent benchmarks while improving the security-utility trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing runtime monitoring approaches for AI agents using formal languages like Datalog are restricted to deterministic policies. In practice, security policies often involve probabilistic components (e.g., PII detectors or declassifiers with failure probabilities), and independence assumptions required by prior probabilistic Datalog inference methods are often untenable.
AI.method: A sound framework based on distributionally robust optimization that computes upper bounds on the probability of policy violation while accounting for arbitrary correlations between probabilistic predicates.
AI.result: The approach outperforms prior art on standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents, achieving a better security-utility trade-off with rigorous, sound bounds on policy violation probability.
AI.conclusion: Distributionally robust optimization provides an effective foundation for probabilistic policy enforcement in AI agent runtime monitoring, enabling sound guarantees without restrictive independence assumptions.

title: Code-Switching Reveals Language Anchoring in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Multilingual Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to handle Code-Switched (CS) inputs, yet mixing languages frequently degrades performance relative to source- or target-language monolingual counterparts. To understand this degradation, we use grammar-forced CS as a controlled diagnostic setting for locating CS representations relative to their source and target counterparts. We introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric measure that quantifies language anchoring, whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source or target language counterpart. Across diverse MLLMs, Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS stays source-anchored, whereas target-framed CS shifts target-ward and shows larger Question Answering (QA) degradation. Motivated by this representational pattern, we propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a source-side canvas from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during prefill. CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across MLLMs and CS conditions, showing that internal anchoring signals provide an actionable target for mitigating CS inference failures.

AI.tldr: Multilingual LLMs struggle with code-switched inputs, especially when the grammatical frame is target-language. The paper introduces "Anchor Bias" to measure whether code-switched representations lean toward the source or target language, revealing that target-framed CS drifts away from source anchoring and suffers worse QA performance. The proposed CANVAS method steers target-language hidden states toward source anchors during inference, effectively recovering QA performance across models and CS conditions.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs exhibit performance degradation on code-switched inputs compared to monolingual inputs, and the underlying representational mechanisms causing this degradation are poorly understood. The authors aim to diagnose this phenomenon through controlled, grammar-forced CS settings and develop an actionable intervention.
AI.method: The authors introduce Anchor Bias, a geometric metric measuring whether a CS hidden state aligns closer to its source- or target-language monolingual counterpart. They use grammar-forced CS (manipulating the syntactic frame to be source- or target-language) as a diagnostic. Based on findings, they propose CANVAS (Contextual Anchor-based Neural Vector Alignment Steering), an inference-time intervention that extracts a "source canvas" from the input and softly steers target-language hidden states toward the source anchor during the prefill phase.
AI.result: Anchor Bias reveals a consistent grammar-frame effect: source-framed CS remains source-anchored, while target-framed CS shifts toward the target language and yields larger QA degradation (F1 drop). CANVAS consistently recovers QA F1 across multiple MLLMs and CS conditions, demonstrating that internal anchoring signals can be exploited to mitigate CS inference failures.
AI.conclusion: Code-switching degradation in MLLMs is linked to a representational shift away from the source language when the grammatical frame is target-language. Anchor Bias effectively diagnoses this, and CANVAS provides a practical, inference-time steering method to correct the misalignment, validating that internal anchoring signals are actionable targets for improving multilingual robustness.

title: Learning Critical Testing Literacy Through Puzzles: an Experience Report
summary:
In this paper, we report our experiences and takeaways from workshops using puzzles to learn CTL.
  Background: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. We introduced a BoK of puzzle-based learning activities to teach CTL, based on a model of critical tester's cognition, leading to the pedagogical framework P4TEST. We conducted thirteen workshops with students, testers, teachers, and primary school pupils to assess puzzle-based teaching of critical testing literacy.
  Experience: Across eleven workshops, we used a semi-structured approach, varying puzzles, materials, and timing. In two additional workshops, we introduced workbooks and think-aloud sessions to gather more data on the learning experience.
  Observations: Participants consistently perceived themselves as experimenting while solving puzzles. Students tended to converge on solutions, while professionals continued exploring. Emotions were visible in behaviour but hard to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions revealed immediate reasoning; written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive reflection. The theme Sensemaking / reflection-in-action captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
  Reflections: Puzzles are not the intervention: the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting is. Designing that sequence more deliberately is the work ahead. We also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to customise workshops.

AI.tldr: The paper reports on thirteen workshops using puzzle-based learning to teach Critical Testing Literacy (CTL). It finds that the full sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting — not puzzles alone — constitutes the pedagogical intervention, and that different participant groups (students vs. professionals) exhibit distinct problem-solving behaviours.
AI.motivation: Software testing is important yet difficult to teach. The authors sought to explore how puzzle-based learning activities, grounded in a model of critical tester's cognition and the P4TEST pedagogical framework, can effectively develop Critical Testing Literacy (CTL) across diverse learner populations.
AI.method: The authors conducted thirteen workshops with varied participants (students, professional testers, teachers, and primary school pupils). Eleven workshops employed a semi-structured approach with variations in puzzles, materials, and timing. Two additional workshops introduced workbooks and think-aloud protocols to capture richer data on the learning experience.
AI.result: Participants consistently framed their activity as experimentation. Students converged on solutions, while professionals continued exploring beyond them. Emotions were visible in behaviour but difficult to surface through written reflection alone. Think-aloud sessions captured immediate reasoning, whereas written reflections elicited more meta-cognitive insights. The theme "Sensemaking / reflection-in-action" captured how participants framed problems, navigated dead ends, and shifted strategies.
AI.conclusion: The pedagogical intervention is not the puzzle itself but the entire sequence of solving, debriefing, and reflecting. Future work lies in deliberately designing this full sequence. The authors also developed an open-source web application with built-in analytics to support workshop customization.

title: Grounded Inference: Principles for Deterministically Encapsulated Generative Models
summary: The incorporation of generative models into traditional computational systems presents both enormous opportunity and tremendous peril. Although many early adopters have realized these perils at great expense, the field still requires foundational frameworks to de-risk incorporation of AI into traditional systems. This manuscript establishes this foundation through the definition of four specific primitives of AI blended architecture, designed to enable deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models. It further establishes two overarching anti-patterns broadly represented across industry to serve as warnings for engineers in this field. This framework was designed to enable successful integration of AI into traditional systems while providing a foundation upon which generative model providers could build the next generation of generative model interfaces.

AI.tldr: Defines four primitives for AI-blended architecture enabling deterministic encapsulation of probabilistic models, and identifies two anti-patterns to de-risk generative AI integration into traditional systems.
AI.motivation: Early adopters have suffered costly failures integrating generative models into traditional computational systems; the field lacks foundational frameworks to systematically de-risk this integration.
AI.method: Proposes a conceptual framework comprising four architectural primitives designed to deterministically encapsulate probabilistic generative models, and catalogs two overarching industry anti-patterns as cautionary guidance.
AI.result: The framework yields four defined primitives for AI-blended architecture and two identified anti-patterns, providing a structured foundation for integration and a roadmap for next-generation generative model interfaces.
AI.conclusion: A principled architectural framework based on deterministic encapsulation primitives can mitigate the risks of blending generative AI with traditional systems, while documented anti-patterns serve as critical warnings for practitioners.

title: 3D-DLP: Self-Supervised 3D Object-Centric Scene Representation Learning
summary: We introduce 3D-DLP, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning model that decomposes scene-level RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of 3D latent particles. Building on the Deep Latent Particles (DLP) framework, each particle encodes disentangled attributes, including 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance features, and represents a distinct entity in the scene. The model learns interpretable per-particle segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective. We demonstrate on both simulated and real-world datasets that the learned latent space is interpretable and controllable: by manipulating particle positions and decoding, we can generate novel scene configurations. Furthermore, we show that leveraging these compact 3D latent particles for downstream robotic manipulation improves performance over baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure. Code and videos are available at https://eubooks3003.github.io/3d-dlp.

AI.tldr: 3D-DLP extends the Deep Latent Particles framework to 3D, learning to decompose RGB-D or voxel observations into a set of disentangled 3D latent particles — each encoding keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and appearance — through self-supervised reconstruction, enabling interpretable scene manipulation and improving robotic downstream task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing object-centric representation learning methods either lack explicit 3D spatial structure or rely on memory-intensive dense 3D inputs without object-level disentanglement. There is a need for compact, interpretable 3D object-centric representations that capture disentangled entity attributes (pose, shape, appearance) to enable controllable scene generation and improve sample efficiency in downstream robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose 3D-DLP, which takes scene-level RGB-D images or voxel grids as input and learns to infer a set of 3D latent particles. Each particle is parameterized by a 3D keypoint position, bounding box dimensions, and an appearance feature vector. The model is trained end-to-end with a self-supervised reconstruction objective (encoding and then decoding back to the input), which forces the particles to learn interpretable per-particle segmentation maps and disentangled attributes without ground-truth supervision.
AI.result: The learned latent space is shown to be interpretable and controllable — manipulating particle positions and decoding produces novel, plausible scene configurations. On simulated and real-world datasets, 3D-DLP demonstrates effective scene decomposition. For downstream robotic manipulation, leveraging these compact 3D latent particles outperforms baselines that either lack explicit 3D information or use dense 3D inputs without object-centric structure.
AI.conclusion: 3D-DLP successfully learns disentangled, object-centric 3D representations in a self-supervised manner. The compact and structured latent particles not only enable interpretable scene editing but also provide a powerful representation for robotic manipulation, outperforming less structured alternatives.

title: Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.

AI.tldr: SEB introduces a runtime enforcement boundary that bridges access-control and assurance layers by consuming certificates from a Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifying execution contracts, minting short-lived scoped identities, and enforcing that only broker-mediated mutations reach production infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents lack a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at mutation time. Identity-based access control and action-certifying assurance layers are insufficient alone — neither prevents a non-deterministic reasoning process from directly mutating production, creating a gap where certified authority must be bound to runtime execution.
AI.method: SEB acts as a mediation layer between agents and infrastructure APIs. It ingests SAB-issued certificates, verifies mutation-execution contract alignment, checks temporal validity (validity windows, policy/revocation epochs), detects live-state drift, mints scoped execution identities, invokes infrastructure APIs exclusively through the broker, and produces signed decision and outcome records. Deployment enforces that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities to prevent bypass.
AI.result: A prototype was implemented and evaluated on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation speed, drift detection efficacy, and security resilience under fault injection.
AI.conclusion: Separating proposal, admission, and execution transforms certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, closing the enforcement gap for agentic infrastructure.

title: What sentiment analysis can't see: Measuring whether customers were helped, and what went wrong, across 70,000 support conversations
summary: Most companies read their customer support data at scale using sentiment analysis, which measures how customers sound rather than whether they were satisfied with the result. We tested a richer alternative on 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform: alongside tone, we used GPT-5.4 to estimate each customer's satisfaction and to flag whether they reported a concrete problem, then validated all three readings against the 1-to-5 ratings customers left on the conversations they rated. The satisfaction estimate tracked those ratings far better than sentiment did, correlating at 0.47 against 0.36 and flagging unhappy customers with far fewer false alarms. The structured read also sees what sentiment cannot: tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of conversations, a single "Neutral" label hides everything from quietly satisfied customers to ones who quietly gave up, and the largest group of all is "tolerated friction," customers who are satisfied but still reporting a fixable problem, a standing issue that no sentiment-based dashboard can surface. The broader finding is that LLM-based annotation can capture far more than the tonality of a customer's language, offering strong potential for new business metrics grounded instead in the customer's state (whether they were satisfied) and the cause of their problem extracted directly from the raw textual data of interactions and feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that LLM-based satisfaction estimation significantly outperforms traditional sentiment analysis for analyzing customer support conversations. Using GPT-5.4 on 70,450 interactions, the authors show satisfaction estimates correlate better with actual customer ratings (0.47 vs. 0.36), reveal that tone and satisfaction disagree in 44% of cases, and surface a previously invisible category—"tolerated friction"—where customers are satisfied yet still report fixable problems.
AI.motivation: Sentiment analysis, the industry standard for reading customer support data at scale, measures linguistic tone rather than actual customer satisfaction with outcomes. This creates a fundamental blind spot: companies track how customers sound, not whether their problems were resolved. The authors argue this conflation of tone with satisfaction misses critical business insights and generates false signals.
AI.method: The study analyzed 70,450 support conversations from a leading online fundraising platform. Three readings were applied to each conversation: (1) traditional sentiment analysis (tone), (2) GPT-5.4-estimated satisfaction, and (3) GPT-5.4-flagged concrete problem reports. All three were validated against 1-to-5 ratings that customers voluntarily left on a subset of conversations. The authors then compared correlations, false-alarm rates, and cases of tone-satisfaction divergence.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Satisfaction estimates correlated with ground-truth ratings at r=0.47 vs. sentiment's r=0.36, with fewer false positives for detecting unhappy customers. (2) Tone and satisfaction disagreed in 44% of conversations. (3) A "Neutral" sentiment label collapsed distinct customer states—quietly satisfied, quietly frustrated, and disengaged. (4) The largest emergent category was "tolerated friction": customers who were satisfied overall but still reported a fixable, unresolved problem—a cohort invisible to sentiment-based dashboards.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based annotation moves beyond linguistic tonality to capture the customer's actual state and the cause of their problem from raw textual data. This enables new business metrics grounded in satisfaction and problem categorization rather than mere sentiment polarity. The concept of "tolerated friction" represents a novel, actionable metric that sentiment analysis structurally cannot detect, pointing toward a richer paradigm for customer support analytics.

title: N-Version Programming with Coding Agents
summary: This paper revisits the classical concept on N-version programming in the setting of contemporary AI coding agents. Revisiting the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment, we study whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages creates diverse failure modes. Using the Knight-Leveson's, Launch Interceptor Program Specification, we evaluate 48 agent-generated implementations on a shared oracle and a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. The results show substantial common-mode failure, along the findings of Knight-Leveson. Further analysis that many of those co-occuring failures can be traced to where is specification is particularly hard or ambiguous. We also demonstrate that diversity from coding agents provides practical benefit: across majority voting three-version units, the mean failure count drops from 387.44 for single versions to 130.99 for triples, and 11,844 N-version units exhibit zero observed failures. Our original results is the strongest evidence to date that N-Version Programming with coding agents is a useful engineering strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits N-version programming using modern AI coding agents, replicating the Knight-Leveson experiment. Evaluating 48 agent-generated implementations of a missile interceptor specification against one million test inputs, it finds significant common-mode failures—often linked to specification ambiguity—but demonstrates that majority-voting across three-version units reduces mean failures from 387.44 to 130.99, with 11,844 triplets showing zero failures, providing strong evidence that N-version programming with coding agents is practically beneficial.
AI.motivation: Classical N-version programming assumed that independently developed software versions would fail independently, but the seminal Knight-Leveson experiment found significant common-mode failures, challenging this assumption. With the emergence of AI coding agents, the authors seek to re-examine whether diversity across agent systems, models, and implementation languages can produce genuinely diverse failure modes, and whether N-version programming augmented by coding agents offers practical reliability benefits.
AI.method: The authors replicate the Knight-Leveson Launch Interceptor Program Specification, generating 48 implementations using diverse combinations of AI coding agents, underlying language models, and programming languages. All implementations are evaluated against a shared oracle using a campaign of 1,000,000 randomized test inputs. They analyze failure patterns for common-mode failures, trace co-occurring failures to specification ambiguities, and test majority-voting ensembles of three-version units (triplets) to measure reliability improvements.
AI.result: Substantial common-mode failures were observed, consistent with Knight-Leveson's original findings. Many co-occurring failures traced back to portions of the specification that were particularly hard or ambiguous. However, diversity across coding agents yielded practical benefits: the mean failure count dropped from 387.44 (single versions) to 130.99 (three-version majority-voting units), and 11,844 N-version triplets exhibited zero observed failures across the entire test campaign.
AI.conclusion: The results constitute the strongest evidence to date that N-version programming with AI coding agents is a useful engineering strategy. While common-mode failures persist—particularly linked to specification quality—the practical reliability gains from diverse agent-generated implementations and majority voting are substantial and measurable.

title: Optimal Scheduling in a Question-Answering Forum of Knowledge Workers
summary: As individuals turn to the Internet to find answers to questions they may have, several Question Answering (QA) forums have evolved, where users knowledgeable in certain topics can contribute their expertise to answering these requests for information. While these are currently volunteer based, we consider a future version employing knowledge workers who are experts in certain topics. In such a system, the request-answer processes forming the queuing system may utilize schedulers that assign requests in different topics to the experts in the forum, who may be able to answer them according to their expertise levels in different topics. With this model, we calculate the capacity of the system for handling the requests while keeping the system stable, and design schedulers that achieve capacity. We also investigate how collaboration between experts in answering requests can potentially increase capacity.

AI.tldr: The paper models a QA forum with paid knowledge workers as a queuing system, calculates its capacity under stability constraints, designs capacity-achieving schedulers that assign questions to experts based on topic expertise, and explores how expert collaboration can further increase system capacity.
AI.motivation: Current QA forums rely on volunteers, but a future model may employ paid knowledge workers. Efficient scheduling of incoming questions to experts with varying topic expertise is critical to maximize throughput and maintain system stability.
AI.method: The authors model the request-answer process as a queuing system where experts have heterogeneous expertise levels across different topics. They analyze the system's capacity region (the set of arrival rates for which a stabilizing scheduler exists) and design scheduling policies that achieve this capacity. They also extend the model to incorporate collaboration among experts.
AI.result: The paper derives the capacity of the system and proposes schedulers that provably achieve capacity while maintaining stability. It also shows that collaboration between experts can potentially increase the overall capacity of the QA system.
AI.conclusion: Intelligent scheduling that accounts for heterogeneous topic expertise is essential for maximizing throughput in paid QA forums, and collaborative answering mechanisms offer additional capacity gains beyond what individual expert scheduling alone can achieve.

title: Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?
summary: Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or "intrinsic curiosity", remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its "learning progress", which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model's predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner's prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether in-context learning (ICL) in sequence models can serve as an efficient alternative to expensive gradient-based inner loops for computing intrinsic curiosity rewards. The authors prove that unbiased learning progress estimation via ICL is impossible in general MDPs but achievable in non-temporal settings like active learning. Experiments validate that ICL-driven curiosity successfully trains optimal exploration policies.
AI.motivation: Classic intrinsic curiosity methods reward agents based on learning progress — the improvement in a world model's predictions from new observations — but require computationally prohibitive inner loops of gradient descent. The authors ask whether the emergent in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by providing immediate, update-free world models for reward computation.
AI.method: The authors (1) theoretically analyze whether exploration policies can be trained using prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner; (2) prove an impossibility result for general MDPs, showing ICL-derived rewards either contain nuisance biases or cannot be implemented; (3) prove a positive result for non-temporal settings (active learning, Bayesian Experimental Design), where ICL rewards asymptotically converge to true learning progress; (4) validate findings with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments.
AI.result: In general MDPs, unbiased learning progress estimation via ICL is provably impossible. However, for non-temporal settings (active learning, Bayesian Experimental Design), ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to true learning progress. Controlled experiments confirm the ICL-driven framework trains curious policies that explore optimally.
AI.conclusion: ICL-based intrinsic rewards are a promising alternative to gradient-based approaches for automated data selection, but their applicability is theoretically limited to non-temporal domains. The work establishes both fundamental limitations and guarantees, providing a principled foundation for leveraging sequence models in curiosity-driven exploration.

title: From Efficiency to Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents NeuroImprint, a privacy attack where a malicious federated learning server corrupts PEFT adapters to covertly memorize clients' training samples in isolated neurons, enabling later reconstruction of 59-79% of fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity across multiple language models.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) in federated learning is vulnerable to a novel privacy backdoor attack, where a malicious server can stealthily extract clients' private training data by manipulating adapter parameters to act as covert memorization channels.
AI.method: NeuroImprint assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains each neuron to update at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This avoids cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing from large local batches and stateful optimizers (Adam/AdamW). Post-training, isolated per-sample updates are analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences.
AI.result: Evaluated on BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2 across four diverse fine-tuning datasets. The attack reconstructs 59% to 79% of all fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity, without degrading model utility.
AI.conclusion: PEFT-based federated learning is susceptible to NeuroImprint, a stealthy privacy backdoor that enables a malicious server to reconstruct client training data. This reveals a significant privacy vulnerability in current FL practices that rely on PEFT adapters.

title: TerraMARS: A Domain-Adapted Small-Language-Model Pipeline for Mars Terraforming Literature
summary: Researchers are interested in learning about Mars so that it may eventually become habitable for humans. To achieve this, there is a need for comprehensive knowledge of the planet's atmosphere, hydrology, surface chemistry, radiation environment, and spatial features through the scientific literature. These contain valuable information and meaningful quantitative constraints that can be used in other models and studies, such as habitability assessment and future terraforming studies. We present TerraMARS, an end-to-end information extraction pipeline that combines a domain-adapted Small Language Model to answer Mars terraforming-related questions and convert unstructured Mars science text into machine-readable structured outputs in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format. A corpus of open-access papers is collected and processed using a multistage retrieval and chunking framework. Google Gemma 3 1B was adapted to the domain using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning on Mars-specific question-answering and information extraction datasets.
