comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
summary: Key Performance Measurement (KPM) forecasting is essential for proactive network management of 5G and next-generation telecom networks. However, existing machine learning (ML) approaches face significant limitations in scalability and explainability, restricting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We propose TelcoAgent, a foundation model-based framework that enables accurate, scalable, and explainable forecasting of multiple KPMs across diverse network cells without the need for site-specific training. Specifically, the framework comprises three key components: (i) an automated three-agent pipeline that constructs a 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) knowledge graph directly from specification documents, (ii) a scalable, time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline to deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasting, and finally (iii) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that provides actionable, domain-grounded diagnostics. Evaluated using a 3-month, real-world, city-scale 5G KPM dataset from a U.S.-based network operator, TelcoAgent demonstrates high forecasting accuracy for all 7 considered KPMs per cell across 200 cells, while delivering explainable insights and actionable instructions to address network degradations.

AI.tldr: TelcoAgent is a foundation model-based framework for 5G KPM forecasting that uses a three-agent pipeline to build a 3GPP knowledge graph, a TSFM-based prediction pipeline for zero-shot forecasting, and a reasoning pipeline for explainable diagnostics—demonstrating high accuracy across 200 cells in a real-world city-scale deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing ML approaches for KPM forecasting in 5G networks suffer from poor scalability (requiring site-specific training) and lack explainability, limiting real-world adoption. There is a need for a zero-shot, scalable, and interpretable forecasting solution grounded in domain knowledge.
AI.method: TelcoAgent consists of three components: (1) an automated three-agent pipeline that extracts and structures a 3GPP knowledge graph directly from specification documents; (2) a time-series foundation model (TSFM)-based prediction pipeline enabling zero-shot, cell-agnostic forecasting; and (3) a reasoning and explanation pipeline that maps predictions to domain-grounded, actionable diagnostics for network degradation.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 3-month real-world 5G KPM dataset from a U.S. operator covering 200 cells, TelcoAgent achieved high forecasting accuracy across all 7 KPMs without site-specific training, while also generating explainable insights and actionable remediation instructions.
AI.conclusion: TelcoAgent demonstrates that foundation model-based approaches can overcome the scalability and explainability barriers of traditional ML in telecom KPM forecasting, offering accurate zero-shot predictions paired with domain-grounded, actionable diagnostics suitable for real-world network management.

title: Tracking Representation Dynamics in Large Language Models with Persistent Homology
summary: Large language models are commonly aligned through supervised fine-tuning, yet little is known about how their internal representations evolve during this process. We study alignment dynamics using persistent homology by tracking the topology of activation spaces throughout fine-tuning. Across four transformer language models ranging from 1B to 7B parameters and three alignment objectives corresponding to helpful, harmless, and mixed training data, we find that the majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training. A dense checkpoint analysis reveals a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. We further show that different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, while instruction-tuned and pretrained models exhibit qualitatively different patterns of evolution. Our results suggest that persistent homology provides a complementary perspective on alignment, revealing representation-level changes that are not apparent from behavioral metrics alone.

AI.tldr: Using persistent homology to track activation space topology during supervised fine-tuning, this paper finds that most topological reorganization in LLMs occurs early in training, with a transient peak followed by rapid stabilization. Different alignment objectives produce distinguishable topological trajectories.
AI.motivation: Little is known about how internal representations of large language models evolve during supervised fine-tuning for alignment. The authors aim to characterize these representation-level dynamics using topological methods, since behavioral metrics alone may miss important structural changes.
AI.method: Persistent homology is applied to track the topology of activation spaces throughout supervised fine-tuning across four transformer LMs (1B–7B parameters) under three alignment objectives: helpful, harmless, and mixed training data. Dense checkpoint analysis captures fine-grained temporal dynamics, and comparisons are made between instruction-tuned and pretrained models.
AI.result: The majority of topological reorganization occurs during the earliest stages of training, with a transient peak in topological activity followed by rapid stabilization. Different alignment objectives induce distinguishable topological trajectories, and instruction-tuned vs. pretrained models show qualitatively different evolution patterns.
AI.conclusion: Persistent homology offers a complementary lens on alignment, uncovering representation-level changes invisible to behavioral metrics. The early-and-rapid reorganization pattern suggests that critical representational restructuring happens almost immediately during fine-tuning.

title: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and generation abilities, but their fixed context windows limit long-term information accumulation and reuse across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems often construct memory in a coarse and unstable manner, relying on inefficient memory representations or unstable unconstrained updates. To address these challenges, we propose AtomMem, a long-term memory system designed for value-dense storage and stable memory evolution. AtomMem introduces a Fact Executor, which selectively extracts high value atomic facts from long form interactions to serve as highly efficient memory representations. Subsequently, AtomMem organizes these facts into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, capturing coherent episodic contexts and tracking dynamically evolving user attributes over time. During retrieval, the system activates an associative memory graph to connect fragmented memories. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark confirm that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks, offering a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents.

AI.tldr: AtomMem proposes a long-term memory system for LLMs that extracts high-value atomic facts, organizes them into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, and uses an associative memory graph for retrieval, achieving SOTA on the LoCoMo benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs possess strong reasoning abilities but are constrained by fixed context windows, hindering long-term information accumulation across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems suffer from coarse, unstable memory construction using inefficient representations and unconstrained updates.
AI.method: AtomMem comprises three core components: (1) a Fact Executor that selectively extracts high-value atomic facts from long-form interactions for value-dense storage; (2) hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles that organize facts into coherent episodic contexts while tracking evolving user attributes over time; and (3) an associative memory graph activated during retrieval to connect fragmented memories.
AI.result: Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark demonstrate that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: AtomMem provides a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents with effective long-term memory capabilities.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Black-Box Uncertainty Estimation Methods for Large Language Models
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, their outputs often remain unreliable and may contain hallucinations, making uncertainty estimation (UE) essential for building trustworthy LLMs. In practice, many mainstream LLMs are only accessible through restricted APIs, where internal signals such as logits and hidden states are unavailable, making black-box UE especially important. However, existing work on black-box UE for LLMs remains fragmented in methodology and lacks a unified empirical comparison. To address this gap, we present a systematic review of black-box UE methods and organize them into five categories: verbalization-based, sampling-based, explanation-based, multi-agent, and hybrid methods. We further build a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings. Our results show that no single method consistently dominates across all settings. Nevertheless, methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective, and hybrid methods that combine multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions. By releasing the benchmark data and a unified evaluation framework, we aim to facilitate reproducible comparisons and support future research, while our empirical findings provide practical guidance for developing future black-box UE methods for LLMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic review and benchmark of black-box uncertainty estimation methods for LLMs, organizing 24 methods into five categories and evaluating them across models and datasets. Key findings: no single method dominates; reasoning over answer-space candidates and hybrid approaches are generally effective.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations and unreliable outputs, making uncertainty estimation critical for trustworthiness. Many mainstream LLMs are API-restricted (black-box), precluding access to logits/hidden states. Existing black-box UE methods are fragmented with no unified empirical comparison, motivating this systematic review and benchmark.
AI.method: The authors classify black-box UE methods into five categories: (1) verbalization-based, (2) sampling-based, (3) explanation-based, (4) multi-agent, and (5) hybrid methods. They construct a unified evaluation framework and benchmark 24 representative methods across 4 models and 4 dataset settings, using standardized metrics for comparison.
AI.result: No single method consistently dominates across all settings. Methods that reason over and compare candidates in the answer space are generally effective. Hybrid methods combining multiple uncertainty signals perform well under most conditions.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a structured taxonomy of black-box UE methods, a reproducible benchmark, and practical guidance for developing future UE methods. The release of benchmark data and evaluation framework aims to foster standardized, reproducible research in this area.

title: Predicting Mergeability of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Updates
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes it cheap to train many domain- and task-specific language model adapters, but whether two adapters can be merged is usually discovered only after both have been fully trained and evaluated. This late feedback is costly: adapters that are strong in isolation can interfere destructively once their updates are combined. We ask whether this outcome can be anticipated. We formalize adapter mergeability as the degree to which an adapter preserves its single-task utility after merging, and show that it can be forecast from signals measured in the first few percent of training -- chiefly how the low-rank updates and their gradients align across tasks and how much they disturb shared representations. We package these signals into MergeProbe, a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and turns the estimate into a concrete decision: merge directly, reweight, prune, or route. On MERGE-PEFT, a five-domain benchmark spanning math, code, science, instruction following, and safety, MergeProbe attains the best average and worst-case retention among strong interference-aware merge baselines while adding far less deployment overhead than full task routing. This turns LoRA merging from a post-hoc engineering step into an anticipatory measurement problem.

AI.tldr: MergeProbe predicts whether LoRA adapters can be successfully merged using signals from early training (gradient alignment, update similarity, representation disturbance), transforming adapter merging from a trial-and-error post-hoc process into an anticipatory decision problem.
AI.motivation: Current LoRA merging is costly: adapter compatibility is only discovered after full training and evaluation. Strong individual adapters often destructively interfere when merged, wasting compute. The authors seek early, cheap signals to forecast mergeability before training completes.
AI.method: MergeProbe formalizes adapter mergeability as post-merge single-task utility retention. It extracts early-training signals — low-rank update alignment across tasks, gradient cosine similarity, and perturbation of shared representations — within the first few percent of training. These signals feed a lightweight predictor that estimates pairwise and set-level retention and outputs a concrete action: merge directly, reweight contributions, prune conflicting parameters, or route between adapters at inference time.
AI.result: On the MERGE-PEFT benchmark spanning math, code, science, instruction following, and safety domains, MergeProbe achieves the best average and worst-case retention compared to strong interference-aware merging baselines, while incurring substantially less deployment overhead than full task routing.
AI.conclusion: LoRA adapter mergeability can be reliably forecast from early-training signals, enabling anticipatory merge decisions. MergeProbe turns merging from a post-hoc engineering step into a measurement problem, offering a practical, low-overhead solution for multi-adapter deployment.

title: Prompt, Plan, Extract: Zero-Shot Agentic LLMs Workflows for Lung Pathology Extraction from Clinical Narratives
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Affiliations: (1) Department of Health Outcomes and Biomedical Informatics, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (2) Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care and Sleep Medicine, Department of Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA; (3) College of Nursing, Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA
summary: Information extraction from pathology reports is essential for cancer staging, tumor registry population. Yet key data remains embedded in narrative reports, making manual extraction labor-intensive and error-prone. Traditional supervised Natural Language Processing pipelines address this through fully supervised Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction, but require expensive manual annotation and suffer cascading failures when upstream entities are missed. In this study, we developed a zero-shot, agentic workflow, and evaluated five open-source generative Large Language Models (LLMs) to populate 13 College of American Pathologists synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports. We compared them against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline using a novel, registry-aligned evaluation framework. The baseline achieved Micro-F1of 0.960, while the best zero-shot model (GPT-OSS-20B) achieved Micro-F1 of 0.893 (recall: 0.949), accurately extracting complex relations like Pathologic Stage without task-specific training. These results suggest that open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs are a low-cost solution for extracting lung pathology information.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot, agentic LLM workflow using open-source generative models extracts 13 CAP synoptic fields from lung pathology reports, achieving Micro-F1 of 0.893 (GPT-OSS-20B) versus 0.960 for a supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline, demonstrating a viable low-cost alternative without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Narrative pathology reports contain critical cancer staging data, but manual extraction is costly and error-prone. Supervised NER-RE pipelines require expensive annotation and suffer cascading errors when upstream entities are missed. The authors seek a zero-shot approach that eliminates annotation costs and mitigates error propagation.
AI.method: An agentic workflow was developed employing five open-source generative LLMs to populate 13 College of American Pathologists (CAP) synoptic fields from lung resection pathology reports in a zero-shot setting. Performance was evaluated using a novel registry-aligned framework and compared against a state-of-the-art supervised GatorTron NER-RE baseline.
AI.result: The supervised baseline achieved a Micro-F1 of 0.960. The best zero-shot model, GPT-OSS-20B, achieved a Micro-F1 of 0.893 with recall of 0.949, successfully extracting complex relational fields like Pathologic Stage without any task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Open-source, zero-shot agentic LLMs represent a low-cost, effective solution for extracting structured lung pathology information from narrative reports, approaching the performance of fully supervised systems while avoiding annotation overhead and cascading pipeline failures.

title: MetaResearcher: Scaling Deep Research via Self-Reflective Reinforcement Learning in Adversarial Virtual Environments
summary: Deep research agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous information gathering and synthesis, yet their training remains constrained by the static nature of simulated environments, the limits of fact-retrieval-only task designs, and the inefficiency of outcome-based reinforcement learning. In this work, we propose MetaResearcher, a novel framework that scales deep research agent training across four synergistic dimensions. First, we introduce an Evolving Virtual World that injects temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation into the training environment, forcing agents to develop source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution skills. Second, we design Discovery-Oriented Tasks -- including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution -- that transcend simple fact retrieval and push agents toward genuine research behaviors. Third, we propose a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes for answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity, directly addressing the repetitive action loop problem observed in prior work. Fourth, we introduce a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture comprising specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative research strategies through coordinated reinforcement learning. Built upon the LiteResearcher infrastructure, MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training while targeting substantial improvements in both benchmark performance (GAIA, Xbench-DS) and epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. We present the complete framework design, training methodology, and planned experimental validation.

AI.tldr: MetaResearcher is a training framework that scales deep research agents along four dimensions: an evolving virtual world with temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation, discovery-oriented tasks beyond fact retrieval, a self-reflective meta-reward mechanism in GRPO that jointly optimizes multiple quality dimensions, and a heterogeneous multi-agent swarm architecture. Built on LiteResearcher, it aims for zero marginal API training cost while improving benchmark performance and epistemic robustness.
AI.motivation: Current deep research agent training is constrained by three key limitations: (1) static simulated environments that fail to capture real-world temporal dynamics and misinformation, (2) fact-retrieval-only task designs that do not foster genuine research behaviors like hypothesis generation, and (3) inefficient outcome-based reinforcement learning that leads to repetitive action loops. These gaps motivate a comprehensive scaling framework.
AI.method: MetaResearcher scales training across four synergistic dimensions: (1) an Evolving Virtual World that introduces temporal dynamics and adversarial misinformation to train source credibility assessment and temporal conflict resolution; (2) Discovery-Oriented Tasks including hypothesis generation and contradiction resolution that go beyond fact retrieval; (3) a Self-Reflective Meta-Reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that jointly optimizes answer correctness, search path efficiency, reflection depth, and tool call diversity; and (4) a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Swarm architecture with specialized Scout, Filter, and Synthesizer models that learn collaborative strategies via coordinated reinforcement learning. The framework is built on LiteResearcher infrastructure.
AI.result: The paper presents the complete framework design and training methodology. MetaResearcher requires zero marginal API cost for training. Planned experimental validation targets substantial improvements on GAIA and Xbench-DS benchmarks, as well as enhanced epistemic robustness under adversarial conditions. Empirical results from experiments are not yet reported.
AI.conclusion: MetaResearcher offers a comprehensive, multi-dimensional approach to scaling deep research agent training that addresses fundamental limitations of prior work. By integrating dynamic environments, discovery-oriented tasks, meta-reward optimization, and heterogeneous multi-agent collaboration within a cost-efficient infrastructure, the framework sets a new direction for training agents capable of genuine, robust research behaviors beyond simple fact retrieval.

title: Displacement Is Not Direction: Evaluating Fidelity Metrics for Quantized LLM Deployment
summary: Fidelity metrics, such as per-token KL divergence (KLD) against a high-precision reference, are often used in practice as low-cost proxies for benchmark quality. We test this practice on a 28-quant cohort of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and a 41-quant cohort of Devstral-Small-2-24B, evaluated across a suite of downstream benchmarks. We find that KLD is strongly correlated with benchmark score over the full cohort ($ρ=-0.72$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.86$ on Devstral, both with $p<0.001$). However, this relationship collapses to non-significance in the near-baseline silent zone ($ρ=+0.00$ on Qwen and $ρ=-0.24$, $p=0.36$, on Devstral). This collapse persists across 14 measurement variants, including different KLD aggregations, perplexity formulations, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, and context lengths. At the per-prompt level, KLD has only weak failure-prediction power on code, with failed-vs-passed geometric-mean ratios in $[1.08,1.22]$ across five models on LiveCodeBench, and fails as a cross-model router, achieving only $42.3\%-49.4\%$ accuracy on disagreement prompts. We trace the collapse to a structural decomposition: KLD primarily measures the volume of disagreement with the reference, with silent-zone composite $ρ=+0.94$ ($p<0.001$) on Qwen and $+0.55$ ($p=0.03$) on Devstral, while its relationship to the direction of those disagreements is weak and task-conditional.

AI.tldr: Per-token KL divergence strongly correlates with downstream benchmark quality across full quantization cohorts but fails entirely in the "silent zone" near baseline — a collapse traced to KLD measuring disagreement volume rather than direction.
AI.motivation: To rigorously test the common practice of using fidelity metrics like per-token KL divergence as low-cost proxies for downstream benchmark performance, particularly in the near-baseline region where such proxies are most needed for model selection.
AI.method: Two large-scale quantization cohort studies: 28 quants of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 41 quants of Devstral-Small-2-24B, evaluated across downstream benchmarks. The authors examined KLD-benchmark correlations across the full cohort and within the near-baseline "silent zone," tested 14 measurement variants (KLD aggregations, perplexity, top-1 agreement, calibration corpora, context lengths), assessed per-prompt failure prediction on LiveCodeBench, evaluated cross-model routing accuracy, and decomposed KLD structurally into volume and direction components.
AI.result: Full-cohort KLD-benchmark correlations are strong (Qwen ρ=−0.72, Devstral ρ=−0.86, both p<0.001). However, within the silent zone, correlations collapse to non-significance (ρ=+0.00 and ρ=−0.24, p=0.36). This collapse holds across all 14 measurement variants. KLD shows only weak per-prompt failure prediction (geometric-mean ratios 1.08–1.22) and poor cross-model routing (42.3%–49.4% accuracy). Structural decomposition reveals KLD primarily captures disagreement volume (silent-zone ρ=+0.94 on Qwen, +0.55 on Devstral), while the direction-of-disagreement component is weak and task-conditional.
AI.conclusion: KL divergence is not a reliable proxy for downstream quality in the near-baseline regime where it is most needed. Its apparent utility derives from capturing how much the model disagrees with the reference, not whether those disagreements matter. Practitioners should not rely on KLD for fine-grained model selection among high-quality candidates.

title: Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly prompted and interfaced with human-readable natural language, even when the intended reader is another model. This paper investigates whether semantic information can be encoded in compact, non-standard textual forms that sacrifice human readability while remaining recoverable by LLMs. We refer to this class of model-centric textual representations as BabelTele, approached here not as a fixed protocol but as an empirical probe into LLMs' capacity to generate and interpret such representations. Through readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires, and downstream task evaluations, we find that BabelTele can substantially depart from ordinary natural language while preserving core semantics for instruction-tuned LLMs. As a task-agnostic representational paradigm, BabelTele demonstrates high information density, maintaining 99.5% semantic fidelity even when the text volume is condensed to 27.9% of its original length. We further evaluate its semantic robustness in cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication. Results suggest that BabelTele can reduce context overhead while generally maintaining reliable downstream performance, although its effectiveness depends on the compressor-reader pair and task setting. These findings indicate that human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled, opening a path toward model-native representations in future exploration of LLM systems.

AI.tldr: This paper explores "BabelTele" — compact, non-human-readable textual representations that LLMs can encode and decode, showing that semantic information can be preserved with high fidelity (99.5%) at only 27.9% of original text length, partially decoupling human readability from model-side semantic recoverability.
AI.motivation: Current LLM communication uses human-readable natural language even when both sender and receiver are models. The authors question whether this constraint is necessary, investigating whether models can develop more efficient, model-native representational formats that sacrifice human readability while preserving semantic recoverability.
AI.method: The authors frame BabelTele as an empirical probe rather than a fixed protocol. They evaluate these compressed representations through multiple lenses: readability diagnostics, model likelihood measures, human questionnaires assessing interpretability, and downstream task evaluations measuring semantic fidelity. They further test cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent communication scenarios to assess robustness across different compressor-reader pairs and task settings.
AI.result: BabelTele representations substantially depart from natural language while preserving semantics. They achieve 99.5% semantic fidelity at 27.9% of original text volume. Cross-model transfer and agent communication experiments show generally reliable downstream performance, though effectiveness varies by compressor-reader pair and task context.
AI.conclusion: Human readability, natural-language typicality, and model-side semantic recoverability can be partially decoupled. This opens a path toward model-native representations for more efficient inter-model communication in LLM systems, reducing context overhead while maintaining performance.

title: Understanding Key Features of Time Series Foundation Models from Epidemic Forecasting
summary: Seasonal influenza infects millions of people and causes substantial morbidity and mortality in the United States each year, making accurate short-term forecasting a core public-health need. Reliable forecasts of epidemic time series can inform vaccination timing, hospital staffing, and resource allocation, yet the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using influenza-like illness surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series under both temporal and spatial generalization settings for 1-4-week-ahead prediction. We compare classical neural network architectures, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. Across tasks, we demonstrate that a mixture-of-experts model that fuses multiple pretrained forecasters achieves the strongest overall performance, indicating that heterogeneous pretrained representations provide complementary predictive information. Our results further show that numerical transformer-based models produce reliable forecasts, while pretraining provides the largest gains at longer horizons, particularly when the pretraining domain is mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. In contrast, LLM-based time series methods underperform relative to numerical forecasters in this setting. Finally, we examine hospitalization information as both an auxiliary covariate and a pretraining source. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings and clarify when additional surveillance streams enhance the robustness of multi-horizon forecasting. These findings provide actionable guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, and auxiliary-signal use for influenza preparedness.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting (1–4 weeks ahead) comparing classical neural networks, numerical transformers, pretrained time-series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasters. A mixture-of-experts fusing heterogeneous pretrained forecasters achieves the best overall performance. LLM-based methods underperform; pretraining helps most at longer horizons when aligned with influenza dynamics. Hospitalization signals offer complementary gains in selected settings.
AI.motivation: Despite the public-health importance of accurate short-term influenza forecasting, the comparative behavior of modern forecasting architectures on infectious-disease surveillance data remains insufficiently characterized, leaving practitioners without clear guidance on model selection, pretraining strategy, or auxiliary-signal use.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of regional influenza forecasting using influenza-like illness (ILI) surveillance and influenza-associated hospitalization time series. Prediction horizons span 1–4 weeks ahead under both temporal and spatial generalization settings. Compared architectures include: classical neural networks, numerical transformer-based models, pretrained time-series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasting approaches. A mixture-of-experts model fusing multiple pretrained forecasters is also assessed. Hospitalization data are examined as both an auxiliary covariate and a pretraining source.
AI.result: The mixture-of-experts model combining heterogeneous pretrained forecasters achieves the strongest overall performance. Numerical transformer-based models produce reliable forecasts. Pretraining yields the largest gains at longer horizons, especially when the pretraining domain is mechanistically aligned with influenza dynamics. LLM-based time series methods consistently underperform relative to numerical forecasters. Hospitalization signals provide complementary improvements in selected settings.
AI.conclusion: Actionable guidance is provided for influenza forecasting: (1) mixture-of-experts over heterogeneous pretrained representations is the recommended top-performing strategy; (2) pretraining on mechanistically aligned domains benefits longer-horizon prediction; (3) LLM-based forecasters are not yet competitive in this domain; (4) auxiliary hospitalization signals enhance robustness in specific multi-horizon settings.

title: The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI
comment: Published in /Handbook of Democracy in the Era of Artificial Intelligence/ edited by Evangelos Pournaras, Srijoni Majumdar, Carina Ines Hausladen, and Dirk Helbing. 2026
summary: The increasing prominence of Large Language Models (LLMs) in public discourse presents both opportunities and challenges for democratic deliberation. While red teaming strategies help mitigate specific risks, broader concerns persist regarding linguistic constraints, biases, and the sycophantic tendencies of LLMs. This chapter explores how LLMs can be used to significantly scale up and democratise deliberation, particularly in fostering inclusivity and empowering traditionally marginalised groups. Drawing on concepts from Systemic-Functional Linguistics, the chapter examines how variations across language users (for example, with respect to socio-demographic groups) and across language use (for example, with respect to communicative functions) shape participation in AI-supported deliberation. The chapter presents AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their potential to scaffold argumentation, enhance access, and reduce the influence of exclusionary linguistic norms and biases which are embedded in prestigious registers. At the same time, the chapter cautions against both overclaiming, which leads to unrealistic expectations, and underclaiming, which risks missed opportunities for AI-assisted engagement. The chapter concludes by identifying future research directions to maximise the democratic potential of AI-assisted participation while embedding ethical safeguards to counteract the reproduction of linguistic inequalities.

AI.tldr: This chapter examines how LLMs can scale democratic deliberation by making it more inclusive, while cautioning against both overclaiming and underclaiming their potential. It applies Systemic-Functional Linguistics to analyze how socio-demographic and communicative variations affect AI-supported deliberation, and calls for ethical safeguards against reproducing linguistic inequalities.
AI.motivation: While LLMs offer opportunities for public discourse, they also pose risks related to linguistic constraints, biases, and sycophancy. Beyond red-teaming, there is a need to address structural exclusion in deliberation—particularly how prestigious registers and exclusionary linguistic norms marginalize certain groups. The chapter aims to explore how AI can democratize rather than distort deliberative participation.
AI.method: The author draws on Systemic-Functional Linguistics (SFL) as an analytical framework to examine two axes of variation: (1) variation across language users (socio-demographic groups) and (2) variation across language use (communicative functions). The chapter reviews AI-driven deliberation studies and assesses their capacity to scaffold argumentation, broaden access, and mitigate exclusionary linguistic norms embedded in prestigious registers.
AI.result: AI-driven deliberation tools show promise in scaffolding argumentation, enhancing accessibility, and reducing barriers imposed by exclusionary linguistic norms. However, the chapter identifies a dual risk: overclaiming breeds unrealistic expectations, while underclaiming leads to missed opportunities for meaningful AI-assisted civic engagement.
AI.conclusion: The chapter concludes by charting future research directions aimed at maximizing the democratic potential of AI-assisted deliberation while embedding ethical safeguards to prevent the reproduction of linguistic inequalities. The balance between technological promise and critical caution is essential for equitable deliberative futures.

title: eCNNTO: A Highly Generalizable ConvNet for Accelerating Topology Optimization
summary: This work proposes an element-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to accelerate density-based Topology Optimization (TO), termed eCNNTO. TO generally undergoes a large number of iterations, where finite element analysis is performed in every iteration, leading to the efficiency bottleneck especially when dense meshes are used to achieve high-resolution designs. To address this limitation, eCNNTO is proposed to build upon Kallioras et al. (2020), where a Deep Belief Network (DBN) was trained for every element to predict its near-optimal density from its early history, thereby skipping the great majority of iterations and significantly accelerating the TO procedure. However, the method lacks spatial correlations among neighboring elements and may lead to disconnected features in the final structure. The proposed method employs CNN with residual connections to address this issue. On top of it, a novel training strategy is introduced to further enhance the optimization efficiency, where the training dataset consists of the final stage density histories rather than early ones. This change can also help reduce the required training data size. eCNNTO requires only a small dataset to train and yet it can be generalized to problems with largely different boundary conditions, loading cases, design domain geometries, mesh resolutions, as well as non-design domains. In the end, the generalization capabilities and efficiency of eCNNTO are demonstrated through a variety of examples in two and three dimensions, achieving up to 90% and 97% reduction of iterations, respectively.

AI.tldr: eCNNTO uses a CNN with residual connections to predict near-optimal element densities from final-stage density histories, dramatically accelerating topology optimization by skipping most iterations while preserving spatial correlations.
AI.motivation: Topology optimization suffers from an efficiency bottleneck due to the large number of iterations requiring finite element analysis, especially at high resolutions. Prior work (DBN-based prediction) lacked spatial correlations among elements, causing disconnected structural features.
AI.method: An element-based CNN with residual connections (eCNNTO) that predicts near-optimal density for each element. Key innovations: (1) CNN architecture captures spatial correlations among neighboring elements; (2) novel training strategy using final-stage density histories (not early histories) as training data, reducing dataset size requirements.
AI.result: eCNNTO achieved up to 90% iteration reduction in 2D and 97% in 3D problems. It generalizes across different boundary conditions, loading cases, domain geometries, mesh resolutions, and non-design domains, while requiring only a small training dataset.
AI.conclusion: eCNNTO successfully addresses the disconnected-feature limitation of prior element-wise DBN approaches while maintaining strong generalization and acceleration capabilities, making high-resolution topology optimization significantly more efficient.

title: Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport
summary: This chapter reviews recent advances in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) for modeling coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport equations. Such systems, found in applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection, feature strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior that make high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. To address this, the chapter surveys state-of-the-art SciML methods for building efficient surrogate models, including linear reduced-order techniques based on Singular Value Decomposition (such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and $β$-Variational Autoencoders ($β$-VAEs). It first covers the authors' work combining these models with High Performance Computing strategies, including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. It then presents two new contributions: surrogate modeling of turbidity currents via PINNs, and the extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows using $β$-VAEs. Governing equations and representative benchmarks, including lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, illustrate these methodologies. The chapter is intentionally long, covering both the mathematical and physical foundations of coupled fluid flow and the computational aspects of state-of-the-art modeling. Overall, it demonstrates how SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered, while substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations. Broader capabilities such as real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility depends strongly on the problem at hand.

AI.tldr: Surveys SciML methods (DMD, PINNs, β-VAEs) for building efficient surrogates of coupled incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport systems, with new contributions in PINN-based turbidity current modeling and β-VAE extraction of disentangled thermal flow modes, demonstrating substantial computational savings over full-order simulations.
AI.motivation: Coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena (e.g., turbidity currents, thermal convection) exhibit strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior, rendering high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. There is a need for efficient surrogate models that can approximate these complex systems at reduced cost.
AI.method: Reviews and applies: (1) linear reduced-order modeling via Singular Value Decomposition, specifically Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD); (2) nonlinear neural network surrogates including Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and β-Variational Autoencoders (β-VAEs); (3) integration with HPC strategies (Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening, scientific floating-point data compression). New contributions: PINN-based surrogate modeling of turbidity currents and β-VAE extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows, demonstrated on lock-exchange and Rayleigh-Bénard convection benchmarks.
AI.result: Demonstrates that SciML surrogates enable fast, accurate approximations of coupled fluid-transport systems within the considered data regimes and modeling assumptions, achieving substantial computational cost reduction relative to full-order simulations.
AI.conclusion: SciML methods provide a viable path to efficient surrogate modeling of coupled incompressible flow and transport, but capabilities like real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain open research challenges whose feasibility is problem-dependent.

title: REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection
summary: Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,427 records, 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, 4,127 surface-form patterns, and 25 languages across 9 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the highest-stakes data, including HIGH-sensitivity categories (recall 0.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task's hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: REDACT is a multilingual PII detection benchmark with 13,427 records systematically controlled across nine generation axes. Evaluating five detectors reveals aggregate F1 masks critical failure patterns: rule-based systems fail on high-stakes (HIGH-sensitivity, non-verbatim) data, while LLM-based detectors prove more robust, with sensitivity-tier assignment identified as the hardest task axis.
AI.motivation: Existing PII detection benchmarks are limited: they cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and fail to reveal which surface conditions cause detector failures. A systematically controlled, multilingual benchmark is needed for stratified evaluation beyond aggregate metrics.
AI.method: The authors construct REDACT: 13,427 records across 25 languages/9 scripts with 324,078 annotations spanning 51 entity types and 4,127 surface-form patterns. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes (domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, co-occurrence). Three entity-level metadata fields — disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier — enable stratified evaluation. Five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are evaluated on a locked, language-stratified 1,000-record sample. A reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment with three models corroborates findings.
AI.result: Aggregate F1 conceals architecture-dependent failure structures. The rule-based detector (Presidio) achieves only 0.07 recall on HIGH-sensitivity categories and performs poorly on non-verbatim disclosure forms. LLM-based detectors remain more robust, with HIGH-sensitivity tier as their strongest slice. The LLM-as-judge assessment confirms sensitivity-tier assignment is the hardest axis of the task.
AI.conclusion: Stratified evaluation is essential for PII detection; aggregate metrics obscure critical failure modes on high-stakes data. The benchmark, schema, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released to facilitate rigorous, fine-grained assessment of PII detection systems.

title: QMFOL: Benchmarking Large Language Model Reasoning via Quantifiable Monadic First-Order Logic Test Case Generation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant progress in reasoning, particularly in deductive reasoning, which is crucial for high-stakes decision-making. As models improve, evaluation benchmarks should evolve to keep pace. However, existing benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency.
  To address these issues, we propose QMFOL, an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning tasks with quantifiable and controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures using conjunction and disjunction patterns, enabling precise control over reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors. These structures are then translated into natural language via LLMs, with logical consistency ensured through round-trip verification using an external prover. Based on our framework, we build QMFOLBench, a benchmark comprising 2880 instances with 960 configurations across diverse logical and semantic dimensions. Evaluations on six large reasoning models (LRMs) and two LLMs show that performance degrades and computational overhead increases with rising logical complexity. Models perform better on True-labeled tasks than on False or Unknown ones, and exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation. Overall, QMFOL offers a scalable and reliable approach for constructing deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of reasoning capabilities in modern language models.

AI.tldr: QMFOL is an automated framework for generating monadic first-order logic reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity. It constructs formal logical structures, translates them to natural language via LLMs, and verifies consistency using an external prover. The resulting QMFOLBench (2880 instances, 960 configurations) reveals that model performance degrades with increasing logical complexity, varies by label type (True > False/Unknown), and is sensitive to semantic variation.
AI.motivation: Existing deductive reasoning benchmarks lack fine-grained control over logical complexity and struggle to balance semantic diversity with logical consistency, making it difficult to precisely evaluate LLMs' reasoning capabilities as models improve.
AI.method: The QMFOL framework generates monadic first-order logic tasks by: (1) constructing formal logical structures using conjunction/disjunction patterns to control reasoning depth, width, label types, and distractors; (2) translating these structures into natural language using LLMs; (3) ensuring logical consistency via round-trip verification with an external prover (formal→natural→formal checking).
AI.result: Evaluation on six large reasoning models and two LLMs using QMFOLBench (2880 instances, 960 configurations) shows: performance degrades and computational cost increases as logical complexity rises; models perform better on True-labeled tasks than False/Unknown; models exhibit sensitivity to semantic variation.
AI.conclusion: QMFOL provides a scalable, reliable approach for building deductive reasoning benchmarks with controllable complexity, enabling more precise evaluation of modern language models' reasoning capabilities and revealing systematic weaknesses tied to logical structure and label type.

title: The Tao of Agency: Autotelic AI, Embedded Agency and Dissolution of the Self
summary:
Most artificial intelligence systems are built on the assumption that goals are exogenous and specified by the designer. Exploring what happens when an agent begins generating its own goals opens the field of autotelic AI. Agents are expected not merely to pursue objectives but to discover them. In this article, we trace its consequences through intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness; the last of which is found to be a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Embeddedness individuates the agent at the cost of revealing that the individuation is non-unique, such that the same dynamics admit many valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self.
  The deepest problem with autotelic AI is therefore not how the agent generates goals, but how it generates and relativizes the self to which the goals are assigned. The agent must believe in its own boundary in order to act, and see through that boundary in order to understand. We consolidate these developments into a single framework and extend it along three directions: a quantum formulation in which the agent-environment cut becomes physical, a philosophical reading against non-dual contemplative traditions, and a concrete LLM-based agentic instantiation.

AI.tldr: This paper explores autotelic AI—agents that generate their own goals—arguing that the core challenge is not goal generation itself, but how agents construct and relativize the self to which goals are assigned. It introduces embeddedness as a necessary-but-insufficient condition and extends the framework through quantum formulations, non-dual philosophy, and an LLM-based implementation.
AI.motivation: Traditional AI assumes goals are externally specified by designers. The paper aims to investigate the deeper implications of autotelic agency, where agents discover or generate their own goals, and to identify the foundational problem: how an agent delineates its own boundary (self) and simultaneously sees through that boundary to understand its relativity.
AI.method: The authors trace consequences of autotelic AI through five lenses: intrinsic motivation, resource-driven priors, causal-interventional learning, homeostasis, and embeddedness. They consolidate these into a unified framework and extend it along three dimensions: (1) a quantum formulation making the agent-environment cut physical, (2) a philosophical analysis drawing on non-dual contemplative traditions, and (3) a concrete instantiation using LLM-based agents.
AI.result: Embeddedness is identified as a necessary but not sufficient condition for autotelic agency. Critically, embeddedness reveals that agent individuation is non-unique—the same underlying dynamics admit multiple valid partitions, each defining a different candidate self. The deepest problem is thus not how goals are generated, but how the self is generated and relativized.
AI.conclusion: The agent must simultaneously believe in its own boundary to act and see through that boundary to understand. This dual requirement—constructing and relativizing the self—constitutes the fundamental challenge for autotelic AI, with implications spanning physics, philosophy, and practical AI implementation.

title: On the QUEST for Uncertainty Quantification via Highest Density Regions
comment: 27 pages, of which 10 are main text. Contains 7 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm in total
summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for reliable decision-making in safety-critical applications in probabilistic machine learning. For regression problems, dominant scalar UQ approaches - notably, those based on proper scoring rules - measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk. This can lead to counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. We propose an alternative framework, in which uncertainty is characterised by the volume of the most probable subset of a distribution's support. QUEST (Quantifying Uncertainty via highest dEnSiTy regions) is a novel approach to UQ based on the concentration of Lebesgue measure at a distribution's peak(s), evaluated at one or more values of a robustness parameter $α$. We establish connections between our measures and classical statistics from information theory and economics. We show that, unlike popular alternatives based on proper scoring rules, QUEST measures of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks confirm that QUEST performs favourably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.

AI.tldr: QUEST introduces a new UQ framework based on highest density regions (HDRs), measuring uncertainty via the Lebesgue measure volume of a distribution's most probable subsets, outperforming traditional scalar measures like variance and entropy in selective prediction tasks while satisfying key axiomatic properties.
AI.motivation: Dominant scalar UQ approaches (e.g., those based on proper scoring rules) measure uncertainty via pointwise predictive risk, which yields counterintuitive results when the target statistic is not the conditional expectation. The authors aim to develop an alternative that directly captures the concentration of probability mass.
AI.method: QUEST characterizes uncertainty by the volume of highest density regions — the most probable subset of a distribution's support — parameterized by a robustness parameter α. The framework connects to concepts from information theory and economics, and defines both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty measures that satisfy desiderata such as monotonicity under distributional spread and location-shift invariance.
AI.result: QUEST measures satisfy a set of axioms adapted from the UQ literature, including monotonicity under distributional spread and invariance to location shifts. Selective prediction benchmarks demonstrate that QUEST performs favorably against standard measures such as variance and differential entropy.
AI.conclusion: QUEST provides a theoretically grounded, axiomatically sound alternative to proper-scoring-rule-based UQ methods, with strong empirical performance in selective prediction settings.

title: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
summary: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit--DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.

AI.tldr: A lightweight pronunciation assessment framework using only native speech data, combining SSL-based token surprisal with transcript-guided DTW alignment, achieving near-supervised performance on SpeechOcean762.
AI.motivation: Traditional pronunciation assessment systems rely on expensive labeled learner error data or non-native corpora. The authors aim to bypass this by using only readily available native speech resources, optionally with minimal calibration.
AI.method: The framework uses an SSL encoder with K-means codebook to discretize learner speech into tokens. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal (higher values signal phonotactic deviation). A Text2DUnit–DTW module predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens via DTW, yielding error-sensitive features. These surprisal and alignment features are fused through a simple regression model, with optional light calibration on a small set of scored utterances.
AI.result: On SpeechOcean762, Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) improved from 0.60 (unsupervised) to 0.66 with transcript guidance, approaching supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC showed consistent improvements.
AI.conclusion: Native-only training combined with transcript-guided alignment is a viable, cost-effective approach to pronunciation assessment, achieving competitive results without requiring costly labeled non-native data.

title: PhysDrift: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in Humanoid Co-Speech Motion Generation
summary: Humanoid robots require co-speech motions that are not only expressive and speech-aligned, but also physically executable under embodiment constraints. Existing co-speech generation pipelines are predominantly human-centric: motions are first generated in human-body representations such as SMPL-X and subsequently retargeted to humanoid robots. In this work, we identify a fundamental embodiment gap in this paradigm, where the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid embodiment constraints disrupts embodiment consistency during motion transfer and physical execution. Through extensive analysis, we show that although retargeting can preserve coarse motion semantics, it significantly compresses motion diversity and weakens prosody-motion synchronization, limiting expressive humanoid behaviors. To address this problem, we first propose IK-EER, a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting. Building upon the curated robot-native motion dataset, we further introduce PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech without relying on intermediate human-body representations. Unlike conventional human-centric pipelines, PhysDrift maintains embodiment consistency throughout both training and inference while incorporating physical regularization to stabilize robot motion dynamics. Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that embodiment-aware robot-native generation substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability.

AI.tldr: Human-centric co-speech motion pipelines introduce an "embodiment gap" when retargeting to humanoid robots, degrading motion diversity and prosody alignment. The authors propose IK-EER for prosody-preserving retargeting and PhysDrift, an embodiment-aware framework that directly generates executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech, bypassing human-body intermediates. Results show improved alignment, physical plausibility, and real-time capability.
AI.motivation: Existing co-speech motion generation pipelines are human-centric: they generate motions in human representations (e.g., SMPL-X) and then retarget to humanoid robots. This introduces an "embodiment gap" — the mismatch between human motion manifolds and humanoid kinematic/dynamic constraints — which disrupts embodiment consistency, compresses motion diversity, and weakens prosody-motion synchronization during transfer and physical execution.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) IK-EER: a prosody-preserving humanoid motion curation framework that jointly optimizes kinematic feasibility (via inverse kinematics) and speech-motion temporal alignment during retargeting, producing a robot-native dataset. (2) PhysDrift: an embodiment-aware co-speech motion generation framework that directly predicts executable humanoid joint trajectories from speech input, eliminating intermediate human-body representations. It incorporates physical regularization to stabilize motion dynamics and maintains embodiment consistency throughout training and inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and real-world humanoid deployment demonstrate that the embodiment-aware robot-native generation approach substantially improves speech-motion alignment, physical plausibility, motion smoothness, inference efficiency, and real-time interaction capability compared to conventional human-centric retargeting pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Bypassing human-body intermediate representations and directly generating robot-native co-speech motions with embodiment-aware training (PhysDrift) resolves the embodiment gap, yielding more expressive, physically executable, and temporally aligned humanoid co-speech behaviors suitable for real-time interaction.

title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
summary: Causal abstractions formalize when a high-level structural causal model (SCM) captures the interventional behavior of a lower-level SCM. Existing applications of this notion largely follow a hypothesis-testing paradigm: an expert proposes a candidate high-level model and then evaluates if the low-level system implements it. We study the complementary problem of learning a high-level model directly from low-level measurements. Our contributions leverage hypotheses from low-rank causal discovery, and can be summarized as follows: (1) we show that observations generated by a low-rank graph induce latents that form a causal abstraction, (2) we provide identifiability results about these latents, and (3) we propose a practical objective to learn this high-level SCM.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to learn high-level causal abstractions directly from low-level data, showing that low-rank causal graphs induce latent variables forming a valid causal abstraction, providing identifiability guarantees, and proposing a practical learning objective.
AI.motivation: Existing work on causal abstraction follows a hypothesis-testing paradigm where experts manually propose high-level models and test them against low-level systems. The complementary problem—automatically learning a high-level causal model from low-level measurements—remains unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors leverage low-rank causal discovery: they analyze how low-rank structural causal models at the observation level induce latent variable structures, prove identifiability of these latents under certain conditions, and derive a practical optimization objective to learn the abstracted high-level SCM.
AI.result: Three main contributions: (1) a proof that observations from low-rank graphs induce latents forming a causal abstraction, (2) identifiability results specifying when these latents can be uniquely recovered, and (3) a tractable learning objective for the high-level SCM.
AI.conclusion: Causal abstraction can be automated through low-rank causal discovery, moving beyond hypothesis testing toward direct learning of abstracted causal structures from data.

title: GEMS: Geometric Constraints Enable Multi-Semantic Superposition in LLMs
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code and logs are available at: https://github.com/LuLu663939/gems-multi-semantic-steering
summary: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate hidden states at inference time without retraining. Existing methods handle only single-direction injection; when multiple semantic directions are superposed without constraints, the model collapses. We show that this collapse decomposes into two independently acting sources: distributional deviation, where additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers and drive activations outside the training distribution, and directional interference, where non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. These two sources define the design constraints that any training-free multi-directional intervention must address. As one instantiation of these principles, we propose GEMS, a training-free method that maps each source to a corresponding geometric constraint: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization for directional interference. On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves accuracy at 98% (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%; on Wikitext-2, the same injection incurs only 2.2% PPL increase. Component ablation isolates the causal role of each constraint, and layer-level probes confirm that orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Qualitative steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B.

AI.tldr: Activation steering with multiple concurrent directions causes model collapse due to distributional deviation and directional interference. The authors propose GEMS, a training-free method using geometric constraints—norm preservation and real-time orthogonalization—to enable multi-directional steering without collapse, achieving strong performance on GSM8K and Wikitext-2.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods only support single-direction injection. When multiple semantic directions are combined without constraints, model performance collapses entirely. The authors aim to diagnose the root causes of this collapse and provide a principled, training-free solution for multi-directional steering.
AI.method: The authors first decompose the collapse into two independent mechanisms: (1) distributional deviation—additive perturbations accumulate in norm across layers, pushing activations outside the training distribution; (2) directional interference—non-orthogonal semantic vectors mutually dampen when superposed. GEMS addresses both via geometric constraints: norm-preserving weighted superposition and targeted attention-pathway injection for distributional deviation, and real-time orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt–based) for directional interference. Method is entirely training-free.
AI.result: On GSM8K, injecting three concurrent non-mathematical directions preserves 98% accuracy (baseline 92%), while unconstrained addition collapses to 4%. On Wikitext-2, the same multi-direction injection incurs only a 2.2% perplexity increase. Component ablation confirms each constraint's causal role; layer-level probes show orthogonalized signals survive the FFN pathway and reach the output distribution with semantic specificity. Steering effects transfer across architectures from 3B to 31B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Multi-directional activation steering fails due to two separable failure modes—norm accumulation and vector interference—both of which can be mitigated through geometric constraints without retraining. GEMS demonstrates that principled, training-free multi-concept steering is feasible and scales across model sizes.

title: Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation
summary: For embodied agents capable of physical interaction, the capability to create and understand dialog is crucial to ensure both safety and effectiveness. While DialNav~\cite{han2025dialnav} provides a framework for holistic evaluation of the dialog--execution loop in photorealistic indoor navigation, its performance remains limited by a critical scarcity of training data (2K episodes). To address this, we propose an automatic generation pipeline, and construct the \textbf{RAINbow} dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog and creates cost-efficient and high-quality dataset. Then, we introduce two additional complementary advances to unlock the data's full potential: (1) Dual-Strategy Training, a navigation training scheme to align the navigation training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop, and (2) a localization model that leverages VLN knowledge. By combining these complementary solutions, our model substantially outperforms the baseline in success rate on both \textbf{Val Seen} (58.24, \textbf{+89\%}) and \textbf{Val Unseen} (29.05, \textbf{+100\%}) splits, establishing a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: To overcome the training data scarcity limiting DialNav, the authors propose RAINbow, a 238K-episode dataset generated via an automatic pipeline from existing VLN data, and introduce Dual-Strategy Training plus a VLN-enhanced localization model, achieving +89% and +100% success rate improvements on Val Seen and Val Unseen, respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing DialNav framework for dialog-based embodied navigation suffers from a critical scarcity of training data (only ~2K episodes), severely limiting its performance. There is a need for a scalable, cost-efficient method to generate large-scale dialog-navigation training data and training strategies that can fully exploit it.
AI.method: (1) An automatic generation pipeline that converts existing Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) datasets into multi-turn dialog episodes, yielding the RAINbow dataset (238K episodes). (2) Dual-Strategy Training: a navigation training scheme that aligns model training with the dynamic dialog-navigation loop. (3) A localization model that leverages VLN knowledge to improve spatial understanding.
AI.result: The combined approach achieves state-of-the-art results on DialNav benchmarks: Val Seen success rate of 58.24 (+89% over baseline) and Val Unseen success rate of 29.05 (+100% over baseline).
AI.conclusion: Large-scale synthetic dialog data generation coupled with specialized training strategies can dramatically improve dialog-based embodied navigation, establishing a new SOTA and demonstrating the effectiveness of repurposing existing VLN resources for the dialog-navigation loop.

title: IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows
summary:
Voice agents deployed in structured workflows (customer service, healthcare scheduling, account management) must handle frequent user interruptions while maintaining progress through multi-step procedures. Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models focus on the timing of interruptions: barge-in detection, endpointing, and turn-taking dynamics. They leave unmeasured what happens after the interruption: does the agent resume the workflow at the correct step? Does it address the user's interjection? Does it avoid re-delivering content the user already heard?
  We introduce IHBench (Interruption Handling Benchmark), a benchmark that evaluates post-interruption recovery in voice agents executing state-machine-driven workflows across 10 enterprise domains. Six interruption types are injected at controlled points mid-utterance, with per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality.
  We evaluate 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and the open-weight community. Models vary widely, and recovery quality depends strongly on the interruption type. Across our experiments, closed-weight models are consistently more robust to interruptions than open-weight ones: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade roughly 3.3x more slowly as conversations grow longer, and show no audio-versus-text modality gap, whereas the open-weight models lose ground on all three. A human study validates the LLM judge against human annotators, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge indicates that recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis.

AI.tldr: IHBench evaluates voice agents' ability to resume structured workflows after interruptions, testing 27 audio-language models across 10 domains. Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight ones on task fulfillment, degrade 3.3x more slowly with longer conversations, and show no audio-text modality gap. Recovery quality emerges as a distinct capability axis separate from existing interruption-timing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for speech-capable models only measure timing aspects of interruptions (barge-in detection, endpointing, turn-taking) but ignore what happens *after* the interruption — whether the agent correctly resumes the workflow, addresses the interjection, and avoids redundant content delivery. Real-world voice agents in structured domains (customer service, healthcare, banking) critically depend on this post-interruption recovery capability.
AI.method: The authors introduce IHBench, a benchmark spanning 10 enterprise domains with state-machine-driven workflows. Six interruption types are injected mid-utterance at controlled points. Each interruption is scored on two axes: task fulfillment and recovery quality, using per-interruption evaluation rubrics generated alongside the data. 27 audio-language model configurations from OpenAI, Google, and open-weight communities are evaluated. A human study validates the LLM judge, and a cross-benchmark analysis against AudioMultiChallenge is conducted.
AI.result: Closed-weight models consistently outperform open-weight models: they win far more often on task fulfillment, degrade ~3.3x more slowly as conversations lengthen, and exhibit no audio-versus-text modality gap. Open-weight models lose ground on all three metrics. Recovery quality depends strongly on interruption type. Cross-benchmark analysis shows recovery quality is a largely distinct capability axis from what AudioMultiChallenge measures.
AI.conclusion: Post-interruption recovery is a critical and currently under-measured capability for voice agents. IHBench reveals substantial performance gaps between closed-weight and open-weight models, establishes recovery quality as a distinct evaluation axis, and provides a validated framework (including human-correlated LLM judging) for benchmarking this capability across diverse domains and interruption types.

title: Source-Grounded Data Generation for Text-to-JSON Learning
summary: From financial filings to clinical records, legacy industries rely heavily on long, unstructured documents to store high-value information. Reliably extracting this information into structured, machine-readable representations is a key prerequisite to making the contents accessible to automated systems. JSON is a natural target for such structured extraction, yet constructing reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration), a source-grounded data generation pipeline that constructs reports and JSON schema by using LLMs for scalable synthesis while validating ground-truth values against the underlying spreadsheet. Evaluations on STAGE-Eval, our source-grounded benchmark with an 851-example test set, show that STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches. This improves Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.

AI.tldr: STAGE is a data generation pipeline that creates training data for text-to-JSON extraction by grounding LLM-generated reports and JSON schemas against spreadsheet data, significantly improving extraction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Legacy industries rely on long, unstructured documents containing high-value information. Reliably extracting this into structured JSON is essential for automated processing, but building reliable and scalable text-to-JSON training data remains challenging.
AI.method: STAGE (Spreadsheet-grounded Text-to-JSON Artifact GEneration) uses LLMs to synthesize reports and JSON schemas, while validating ground-truth values against underlying spreadsheets to ensure correctness. Evaluation is performed on STAGE-Eval, a source-grounded benchmark with 851 test examples.
