AI.result: STAGE produces stronger training data than existing approaches, improving Qwen3-4B exact match from 31.37% to 74.27% and value accuracy from 45.46% to 90.69%.
AI.conclusion: Source-grounded data generation that validates against spreadsheet ground truth yields substantially more reliable text-to-JSON training data, dramatically boosting model performance on structured extraction tasks.

title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
summary: Achieving dexterous robotic manipulation in the real world heavily relies on human supervision and algorithm engineering, which becomes a central bottleneck in the pursuit of general physical intelligence. Although emerging coding agents can generate code to automate algorithm search, their successes remain largely confined in digital environments. We conjecture that the missing abstraction to automate robotics research is a repeatable feedback loop for real-world policy improvement: reset the scene, execute a policy, verify the outcome, and refine the next iteration. To bridge this gap, we introduce ENPIRE, a harness framework for coding agents that instantiates this physical feedback routine with four core modules: an Environment module (EN) for automatic reset and verification, a Policy Improvement module (PI) that launches policy refinement, a Rollout module (R) to evaluate policies with one or multiple physical robots operating in parallel, and an Evolution module (E) in which coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, improve training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This closed-loop system transforms real-world manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure, minimizing human effort while allowing fair ablations across training recipe and agent variants. Powered by ENPIRE, frontier coding agents can autonomously train a policy to achieve a 99% success rate on challenging, dexterous manipulation tasks, such as organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use, a process that further accelerates when we dispatch an agent team on a robot fleet. Our results suggest a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advancing robotics in the physical world.

AI.tldr: ENPIRE is a closed-loop framework that enables coding agents to autonomously improve real-world robotic manipulation policies through a repeatable feedback cycle of environment reset, policy execution, outcome verification, and iterative refinement, achieving 99% success on dexterous tasks with minimal human supervision.
AI.motivation: Real-world dexterous robotic manipulation research is bottlenecked by heavy reliance on human supervision and manual algorithm engineering. While coding agents can automate algorithm search in digital domains, they lack a physical feedback loop — resetting scenes, executing policies, verifying outcomes, and refining iteratively — which is the missing abstraction needed to extend their capabilities to the physical world.
AI.method: The authors propose ENPIRE, a harness framework with four modules: (1) Environment (EN) for automatic scene reset and outcome verification; (2) Policy Improvement (PI) for launching policy refinement; (3) Rollout (R) for parallel policy evaluation across multiple physical robots; and (4) Evolution (E) where coding agents analyze logs, consult literature, and improve both training infrastructure and algorithm code to address failure modes. This creates a closed-loop optimization procedure.
AI.result: Frontier coding agents powered by ENPIRE autonomously trained policies achieving 99% success rates on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks including organizing a pin box, fastening a zip tie, and tool use. Performance further accelerated when deploying an agent team across a robot fleet.
AI.conclusion: ENPIRE demonstrates a practical and scalable path toward deploying coding agents to autonomously advance robotics research in the physical world, transforming manipulation learning into a controllable optimization procedure that minimizes human effort while enabling fair ablations.

title: Comparing Linear Probes with Mahalanobis Cosine Similarity
summary: Linear probes are widely used in interpretability research and often compared by cosine similarity. The Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between two directions, which reweights the inner product by test data covariance, is a natural task-aware refinement. Ying et al. (2026) report that a probe's MCS to a reference probe trained on the out-of-distribution (OOD) data near-perfectly linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC (R^2 = 0.98). Here, we extend this empirical finding across models, layers, and concept domains, and prove this general phenomenon in closed form: For balanced classes whose projections are Gaussian, OOD AUROC and MCS to the reference probe are linear because both are sigmoid-shaped functions of the probe's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the test data. The theory also predicts when this linearity fails, which we verify empirically. MCS offers a theoretically grounded and empirically effective alternative to Euclidean cosine similarity for comparing linear probes.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that Mahalanobis cosine similarity (MCS) between a probe and an OOD reference probe linearly predicts the probe's OOD AUROC because both are sigmoid functions of the test-data signal-to-noise ratio under Gaussian class-conditional assumptions. The authors empirically validate this across models, layers, and domains, and characterize when the linear relationship breaks down.
AI.motivation: Linear probes are ubiquitous in interpretability research and typically compared via Euclidean cosine similarity, which ignores task-relevant data structure. A recent empirical finding (Ying et al., 2026) showed MCS near-perfectly predicts OOD AUROC, but lacked theoretical justification. This paper aims to provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for why MCS works and when it fails.
AI.method: The authors first extend the empirical finding of Ying et al. across diverse models, layers, and concept domains. They then derive a closed-form theoretical analysis: assuming balanced classes with Gaussian class-conditional distributions in probe projection space, both OOD AUROC and MCS to a reference probe can be expressed as sigmoid functions of the probe's SNR on the OOD test data. This shared functional form implies the observed linear relationship. The theory further predicts failure conditions (e.g., when Gaussianity or class balance is violated), which are tested empirically.
AI.result: The empirical replication confirms that MCS linearly predicts OOD AUROC with R² ≈ 0.98 across varied settings. The theoretical derivation shows both quantities are monotonic, sigmoid-shaped functions of SNR, explaining their linear coupling. Predicted failure modes — such as severe class imbalance or non-Gaussian projections — are verified experimentally, where the linear relationship degrades as theory predicts.
AI.conclusion: MCS is a theoretically grounded, task-aware similarity measure for linear probes that outperforms naive Euclidean cosine similarity. The linear relationship between MCS and OOD AUROC holds broadly under Gaussian class-conditional assumptions and breaks predictably when those assumptions are violated. This provides both practical guidance and theoretical understanding for interpretability practitioners comparing linear probes.

title: IHUBERT: Vector-Based Semantic Deduplication and Domain-Balanced Pretraining for Persian Resources
summary: Persian pretrained language models (PLMs) are still limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and by insufficient evaluation beyond standard classification and NER tasks. We present IHUBERT, a monolingual Persian PLM trained from scratch with the RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) on a 45 GB curated subset of the Sepahr-Danesh collection (about 7-8B tokens). To improve corpus quality and reduce redundancy, we employ a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline that includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for distribution balancing control across domains and registers. We additionally train a 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer on the full pretraining corpus to better capture Persian morphology and orthographic variation. IHUBERT is evaluated on seven Persian NLU benchmarks covering NER, sentiment analysis, topic classification, NLI, extractive question answering, and relation extraction, using task-standard metrics (entity-level F1, Macro-F1, EM/F1). IHUBERT achieves its strongest gains on extractive QA, ranking first on both PQuAD (F1 88.3542) and ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and attains the best result on FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). On NER and topic classification, it remains competitive (e.g., 0.8308 F1 on ParsTwiNER; 0.7953 Macro-F1 on DigiMag), while relation extraction remains the main remaining gap (0.6684 Macro-F1 on PERLEX). A controlled tokenizer ablation on the IHUBERT pretraining corpus shows that BPE yields slightly lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size, supporting our tokenization design. Overall, IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling through semantically curated large-scale pretraining and broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks.

AI.tldr: IHUBERT is a monolingual Persian RoBERTa-base model trained from scratch on 45 GB of curated data (7-8B tokens) with semantic deduplication and a 139k BPE tokenizer, achieving state-of-the-art results on extractive QA and competitive performance across seven Persian NLU benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Persian PLMs suffer from (1) scarcity of large-scale, high-quality pretraining corpora and (2) insufficient evaluation limited to standard classification and NER tasks. IHUBERT addresses both gaps through curated pretraining data and broad NLU evaluation spanning comprehension-oriented tasks.
AI.method: IHUBERT uses a RoBERTa-base encoder (125M parameters) trained from scratch on a 45 GB subset of Sepahr-Danesh. The multi-stage preprocessing pipeline includes normalization, exact and near-duplicate removal, anonymization, and vector-database-based semantic deduplication for domain/register distribution balancing. A 139k-vocabulary BPE tokenizer is trained on the full corpus. Evaluation spans seven Persian NLU benchmarks: NER (ParsTwiNER), sentiment analysis, topic classification (DigiMag), NLI (FarsTail), extractive QA (PQuAD, ParsiNLU-RC), and relation extraction (PERLEX).
AI.result: IHUBERT ranks first on PQuAD (F1 88.3542), ParsiNLU-RC (F1 49.0987), and FarsTail (Macro-F1 0.8350). It remains competitive on NER (ParsTwiNER F1 0.8308) and topic classification (DigiMag Macro-F1 0.7953). Relation extraction on PERLEX (Macro-F1 0.6684) is the main remaining gap. A tokenizer ablation shows BPE yields lower subword fragmentation than WordPiece at matched vocabulary size.
AI.conclusion: IHUBERT advances Persian language modeling by combining semantically curated large-scale pretraining with broad evaluation across both classification and comprehension-oriented tasks, with its strongest gains in extractive QA.

title: Reward as An Agent for Embodied World Models
summary: While RL has become a promising tool for refining world models, existing methods largely rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, limiting exploration, behavioral diversity, and richer dynamic discovery. In this work, we challenge this conservative paradigm. We argue that the core limitation is not exploration itself, but the lack of reliable verification strategies to support broader exploration. Without reliable verification, expanded exploration becomes highly susceptible to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without achieving genuine improvement. To evaluate this motivation, we instantiate our method in embodied world models, where physical plausibility, and task completion provide a rigorous testbed for scalable RL under complex dynamics. On the verification side, we introduce Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts. On the exploration side, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification through DynDiff-GRPO, which explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors beyond conservative rollout regimes. By unifying Reward as an Agent with DynDiff-GRPO, we enable RL on a more reliable reward foundation with substantially diversified sampling, effectively mitigating reward hacking while yielding significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, thereby demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges conservative exploration in RL-based world model refinement by introducing (1) Reward as an Agent, an agentic reward framework for robust verification under distribution shifts, and (2) DynDiff-GRPO, a diversification method that expands action-space exploration. Together they mitigate reward hacking and enable broader, more reliable exploration, yielding accuracy gains across multiple world models.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for refining world models rely on conservative rollouts near the training distribution, which limits exploration, behavioral diversity, and discovery of richer dynamics. The authors argue the core bottleneck is not exploration per se but the lack of reliable verification to support broader exploration — without which expanded exploration leads to reward hacking, where policies exploit imperfect rewards without genuine improvement.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary components: (1) Reward as an Agent — an agentic reward framework that actively evaluates generated behaviors to provide robust reward signals and mitigate reward hacking under distribution shifts; (2) Dynamic-Aware Rollout Diversification via DynDiff-GRPO — a method that explicitly expands action-space exploration to diversify trajectories, broaden state-action coverage, and encourage richer embodied behaviors. These are unified and instantiated in embodied world models where physical plausibility and task completion serve as rigorous testbeds.
AI.result: The unified approach yields significant accuracy gains across multiple open-source world models, demonstrating that broader exploration can scale successfully when grounded in robust verification, while effectively mitigating reward hacking.
AI.conclusion: Broader exploration for RL-based world model refinement is viable and beneficial when paired with reliable verification mechanisms. The combination of agentic reward verification and action-space diversification overcomes the reward hacking problem that previously constrained exploration to conservative regimes.

title: Latent Confounded Causal Discovery via Lie Bracket Geometry
summary: Recent work on Kan-Do-Calculus (KDC) has established that the boundary between passive observation and active intervention in causal inference is a category-theoretic bi-adjunction, with interventions modeled by left Kan extensions and conditioning by right Kan extensions. This paper introduces two causal discovery algorithms under latent confounding, building on the information-geometric and categorical consequences of KDC. In smooth statistical settings, Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures induce local causal vector fields; failures of these fields to close under Lie brackets become computable Frobenius residuals, which we interpret as witnesses of failed visible integrability and possible latent or unmodeled structure. Our first algorithm, BRIDGE (Bracket Residuals for Interventional Discovery and Geometric Estimation), combines an interventional density or Radon-Nikodym-ratio engine with a geometric screen that proposes a high-recall family of admissible arrows, identifies non-closing visible pairs as latent-obstruction candidates, and passes the reduced family to downstream score-based or differentiable discovery routines. The second algorithmic contribution, Spectral Kan-Do Flow Matching (SKFM), learns amortized intervention fields and factors latent curvature spectrally, exposing the direct Lie-space endpoint toward which BRIDGE points. A detailed set of experiments show that both algorithms are capable of discovering causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential space of possible DAGs by many orders of magnitude. This paper introduces a new paradigm in causal discovery, where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two causal discovery algorithms—BRIDGE and SKFM—that leverage Kan-Do-Calculus and information geometry to infer latent confounding from the geometric properties of intervention-induced flows, dramatically reducing the DAG search space.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery under latent confounding suffers from a super-exponential search space of possible DAGs. The authors exploit the categorical bi-adjunction structure of KDC—where interventions are left Kan extensions and conditioning are right Kan extensions—to derive geometric invariants that signal latent variables, offering a principled alternative to brute-force combinatorial search.
AI.method: Two algorithms are proposed: (1) BRIDGE uses Radon-Nikodym derivatives between observational and interventional measures to construct local causal vector fields, then computes Frobenius residuals (Lie bracket non-closure) as witnesses of latent structure, filtering candidate arrows for downstream discovery. (2) SKFM learns amortized intervention fields and performs spectral factorization of latent curvature, directly identifying the Lie-space structure. Both build on information-geometric consequences of KDC.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that both algorithms successfully discover causal models with latent confounders while collapsing the super-exponential DAG space by many orders of magnitude. BRIDGE provides a high-recall screening step; SKFM spectrally resolves latent curvature and exposes the direct Lie-space endpoint.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new paradigm where latent structure is inferred directly from the geometry of intervention-induced flows, grounding causal discovery in category-theoretic and differential-geometric principles rather than purely combinatorial search.

title: Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision: A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly review and revise text, including their own. A documented self-preference bias (models favoring their own generations when acting as judges) raises the question of whether models also resist valid corrections to their own writing. We test this in a setting where "valid" is decided not by another model but by a deterministic verifier: instruction-following revision on IFEval. A model writes a draft; the official IFEval checker confirms the draft violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it; the model then accepts or rejects that edit either as the genuine in-context author or as a fresh model that sees the draft neutrally. Across four mid-tier model families and 85 author-versus-fresh comparisons, we find no detectable self-preference: authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts at essentially the same rate as fresh models judging the same drafts (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). A self-skepticism hint from a smaller pilot did not replicate at scale. The one robust observation is qualitative: when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of their stated reasons are flaw-catching rather than preference, that is, about the character of rejections, not an elevated rate. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit self-preference bias when reviewing corrections to their own writing, using a deterministic IFEval verifier. Across 85 comparisons and four model families, no statistically significant self-preference was found—authors accept verified fixes at similar rates as neutral judges. The only qualitative finding: when authors reject valid fixes, 97% of justifications involve flaw-detection rather than mere preference.
AI.motivation: Prior work documents a self-preference bias in LLMs when acting as judges (favoring their own outputs). This raises the concern that models might also resist valid external corrections to their own writing, undermining their reliability in self-revision pipelines. The authors aim to test this in a rigorous setting where "correctness" is established by a deterministic verifier rather than another model's judgment.
AI.method: The study uses the IFEval benchmark: a model generates a draft, the official IFEval checker confirms it violates a constraint and that a candidate edit fixes it. The model then decides whether to accept or reject the edit under two conditions: (1) as the genuine in-context author who wrote the draft, and (2) as a fresh model seeing the same draft neutrally. Four mid-tier model families are tested across 85 author-vs-fresh comparisons. A self-skepticism hint condition (from a pilot) is also tested at scale.
AI.result: No detectable self-preference bias emerged: authors reject verified-good fixes at essentially the same rate as fresh models (gap -5.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]). The self-skepticism hint from the pilot failed to replicate at scale. Qualitatively, when authors do reject a verified-good fix, 97% of stated reasons are "flaw-catching" (identifying purported issues with the edit) rather than expressions of preference for their own text. Effects smaller than ~13 pp cannot be excluded at this sample size.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to concerns raised by the self-preference literature, LLMs do not appear to systematically resist valid corrections to their own writing in this constrained setting. The null result suggests self-preference bias may not extend to revision acceptance under deterministic verification. However, the confidence intervals leave room for effects up to ~13 pp, and the finding is limited to mid-tier models on IFEval. The qualitative pattern of rejections being framed as flaw-catching rather than preference-based is a noteworthy ancillary finding.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: Evaluates DAG Plan & Execute vs ReAct architectures across 208 enterprise scenarios at three scales, finding that scale (not task complexity) dominates performance degradation due to agent discovery noise. Introduces a Task Manager with priority inference, event merging, and preemption that reduces high-priority latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by 20+ pp at enterprise scale.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent systems assume discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at enterprise scale (200+ agents) with continuous monitoring and event-driven operation. There is a gap in understanding how orchestration architectures behave under realistic enterprise conditions.
AI.method: 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios across three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). Two architectures compared: DAG Plan and Execute (structured parallelization) and ReAct (incremental reasoning). Introduced a Task Manager component for continuous operation with priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption capabilities.
AI.result: Scale dominates orchestration performance more than task complexity. Both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan & Execute provides higher precision at small scales but suffers from overhead at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust via incremental failure handling. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent orchestration for enterprise AI requires architectures that explicitly address scale-induced discovery noise rather than optimizing for task complexity. Continuous operation mechanisms (priority inference, event merging, preemption) are essential for enterprise-grade performance.

title: SEAGAN: domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a flexible framework for learning from scientific data linked through physical, biological, or functional relationships. One promising domain is plant physiology, where measured responses often arise from multiple interacting processes whose exact separation remains difficult even with manual intervention. In plant physiology, a key example is the A-Ci curve, which relates net CO2 assimilation rate (Anet) to leaf intercellular CO2 concentration (Ci) and is used to estimate photosynthetic parameters in leaf and crop-canopy models. However, reliable estimation requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point, which remains a major source of uncertainty. Here, we formulate limitation-state identification along A-Ci curves as a graph-based node classification problem, with curve points as nodes. Domain-specific graph representations are created using distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The framework was evaluated against conventional learning baselines, graph-based architectures, and an automated fitting-based benchmark. Results on a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states show that graph-based models improve classification, particularly near biochemical transition regions. The best-performing configuration, SEAGAN (domain-Specific and Edge-Aware Graph Attention Network for Dynamic Plant Processes), integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted cross-entropy loss, achieving an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882. The results show that representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy.

AI.tldr: A-Ci curve biochemical limitation-state identification is formulated as a graph node classification problem. The proposed SEAGAN model, combining domain-specific node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention with weighted loss, achieves 0.882 accuracy, outperforming conventional baselines particularly near transition regions.
AI.motivation: Reliable estimation of photosynthetic parameters from A-Ci curves requires identifying the active biochemical limitation state at each curve point. This identification remains a major source of uncertainty, as responses arise from multiple interacting processes whose separation is difficult even with manual intervention.
AI.method: The authors formulate limitation-state identification as a graph-based node classification problem where curve points serve as nodes. Two graph construction strategies are employed: distance-based k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) and auxiliary-signal-guided (ASG) connectivity, both with edge attributes encoding pairwise relations. The proposed SEAGAN architecture integrates process-aware node features, edge attributes, kNN connectivity, and graph attention mechanisms with a weighted cross-entropy loss to handle class imbalance.
AI.result: On a large synthetic dataset with known ground-truth limitation states, graph-based models improved classification over conventional learning baselines and an automated fitting-based benchmark, particularly near biochemical transition regions. SEAGAN achieved an F1-score of 0.857 and an accuracy of 0.882, representing the best-performing configuration.
AI.conclusion: Representing A-Ci curves as graphs improves biochemical limitation-state analysis, with edge-aware attention over local kNN neighborhoods providing the most effective strategy for capturing the interacting biochemical processes in photosynthetic response curves.

title: HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization
summary: The quadratic complexity of attention poses a critical bottleneck for long-context processing, spurring interest in hybrid attention designs. Most open-source hybrid models adopt a layer-wise strategy. Yet, prior work has noted the inherent difficulty of integrating Linear Attention (LA) with Full Attention (FA), suggesting that the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. To probe this space, we conduct interpretability analysis and observe that layers exhibit block-wise functional similarity, while individual heads within the same layer display distinct functional specialization despite sharing input features. This head-level heterogeneity suggests that the head dimension provides a natural and principled granularity for fusing heterogeneous attention signals. Building on this insight, we introduce HydraHead, a novel architecture that hybridizes FA and LA along the head axis. HydraHead features two key innovations: (1) an interpretability-driven selection strategy that identifies retrieval-critical heads and preserves FA only for them, and (2) a scale-normalized fusion module that reconciles the distributional gap between FA and LA head outputs. By leveraging a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and distillation, we achieve high-performance hybrid models with minimal training overhead. Under a unified training setup, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs in long-context tasks while maintaining strong general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Crucially, trained on only 15B tokens, HydraHead achieves over 69% improvement over the baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5, a leading model of comparable size with a native context length of 256K. This highlights the significant scaling potential of head-level hybridization.

AI.tldr: HydraHead introduces head-level hybridization of Full Attention and Linear Attention, using interpretability-driven selection to keep Full Attention only for retrieval-critical heads, plus a scale-normalized fusion module. With minimal training (15B tokens), it outperforms layer-wise hybrids on long-context tasks and approaches much larger-context models at 512K length.
AI.motivation: Quadratic complexity of full attention limits long-context processing. Existing layer-wise hybrid attention models suffer from integration difficulties between Linear Attention (LA) and Full Attention (FA), and the design space of attention hybridization remains underexplored. Interpretability analysis reveals block-wise functional similarity across layers but head-level functional specialization within layers, motivating head-level rather than layer-level hybridization.
AI.method: HydraHead hybridizes FA and LA along the head dimension. Two key innovations: (1) interpretability-driven selection identifies retrieval-critical heads via attention-map analysis and preserves FA only for these heads, with remaining heads using LA; (2) a scale-normalized fusion module reconciles distributional gaps between FA and LA head outputs. Training uses a three-stage transfer pipeline with parameter reuse and knowledge distillation from a pre-trained FA model, minimizing training overhead (only 15B tokens).
AI.result: Under unified training, HydraHead outperforms other hybrid designs on long-context tasks while preserving general reasoning. With interpretability-driven head selection, it matches a 3:1 layer-wise hybrid's long-context performance at a 7:1 LA-to-FA ratio. Trained on 15B tokens, it achieves >69% improvement over baseline at 512K context length, approaching Qwen3.5 (a model with native 256K context).
AI.conclusion: Head-level hybridization is a principled and effective design dimension for attention fusion. HydraHead demonstrates strong scaling potential, suggesting that interpretability-driven, fine-grained hybridization can substantially close the gap between efficient and full-attention models on extreme long-context tasks.

title: Process-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Theorem Proving via Lean
summary: While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically has relied on a single binary verification signal, symbolic proof assistants in formal reasoning offer rich, fine-grained structured feedback. This gap between structured processes and unstructured rewards highlights the importance of feedback that is both dense and sound. In this work, we demonstrate that the Lean proof assistant itself can serve as a symbolic process oracle, supplying both outcome-level and fine-grained tactic-level verified feedback during training. Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration marks both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, yielding dense, verifier-grounded credit signals rooted in type theory. We incorporate these structured rewards into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective with first-error propagation and first-token credit methods that balances outcome- and process-level advantages. Experiments with STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 show that tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet. Beyond empirical gains, our study highlights a broader perspective: symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time, but can also act as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward reinforcement learning frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the Lean proof assistant as a process-level reward oracle for RLVR in formal theorem proving. Instead of relying on binary outcome signals, Lean's elaboration provides dense, tactic-level verified feedback (identifying both sound steps and the first failure), which is integrated into a GRPO-style RL objective. Experiments show tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines on MiniF2F and ProofNet.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR for formal reasoning relies on single binary verification signals, but proof assistants like Lean offer rich, structured, fine-grained feedback during proof construction. There is a gap between the structured process of interactive theorem proving and the unstructured (binary outcome) rewards used in RL. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging Lean as a symbolic process oracle that provides both outcome- and step-level verified feedback, yielding denser and more principled credit signals.
AI.method: Proof attempts are parsed into tactic sequences, and Lean's elaboration is used to mark both locally sound steps and the earliest failing step, producing dense, verifier-grounded feedback rooted in type theory. These structured rewards are incorporated into a GRPO-style reinforcement learning objective using first-error propagation and first-token credit assignment methods to balance outcome-level and process-level advantages. The approach is evaluated using STP-Lean and DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5.
AI.result: Tactic-level supervision outperforms outcome-only baselines in most settings, delivering improvements on benchmarks such as MiniF2F and ProofNet.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic proof assistants are not only verifiers at evaluation time but can also serve as process-level reward oracles during training. This opens a path toward RL frameworks that combine the scalability of language models with the reliability of symbolic verification for formal reasoning.

title: MassSpecGym in the Wild: Uncovering and Correcting Evaluation Pitfalls in AI-Driven Molecule Discovery
summary: Reliable benchmarking is critical for developing machine learning models for tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) based molecule discovery. Subtle issues in experimental design and model evaluation procedures can degrade the trustworthiness of such benchmarks and lead to erroneous conclusions. We conduct a thorough review of model evaluation issues in the recent MS/MS machine learning literature, using the standard MassSpecGym benchmark suite as a case study to illustrate the impact of these issues. We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption. We isolate three classes of failures: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Through extensive experimentation and code replication, we quantify the impact of these issues and show how they corrupt the evaluation standards MassSpecGym was designed to enforce. We distill our findings into recommendations generalizable to MS/MS challenges, benchmarks, and custom evaluation setups. We also release MassSpecGym v1.5, an implementation of our recommendations in the MassSpecGym benchmarking suite which addresses the failure modes identified in this audit. MassSpecGym v1.5 is publicly available at https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym.

AI.tldr: An audit of MS/MS machine learning benchmarks reveals widespread evaluation flaws — data leakage, shortcut learning, and implementation bugs — affecting 17 of 26 papers in the first year of MassSpecGym adoption. The authors quantify these issues and release MassSpecGym v1.5 to remediate them.
AI.motivation: Reliable benchmarking is essential for progress in ML-based molecule discovery from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). However, subtle experimental design and evaluation flaws can undermine benchmark trustworthiness, leading to inflated or misleading performance claims. A systematic audit was needed to identify and quantify these issues.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comprehensive review of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results. They identified failure modes through code replication and extensive experimentation, then categorized them into three classes: (i) data leakage, (ii) shortcut learning, and (iii) implementation bugs and metric divergence. Impact was quantified experimentally.
AI.result: At least 17 of 26 papers (65%) contained evaluation issues. The three failure classes were confirmed and their impact on corrupting MassSpecGym evaluation standards was quantified. The findings were distilled into generalizable recommendations for MS/MS benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: Many published MS/MS ML benchmarks suffer from serious evaluation flaws. The authors codified their corrective recommendations into MassSpecGym v1.5, a refined benchmark suite that addresses all identified failure modes, and released it publicly to improve future benchmarking rigor.

title: Residual-Space Evolutionary Optimization via Flow-based Generative Models
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026 Workshop SPIGM, 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Data editing with generative methods typically requires differentiable objectives and gradient-based search. However, these assumptions break down in flow-based settings, where edits are performed through forward and backward integration and often involve non-differentiable or black-box objectives. We introduce residual-space evolutionary optimization, a model-agnostic framework that addresses this gap by combining flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. Building on the observation that conditional flow matching (CFM) can disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals, our framework directly operates in residual space and separates two complementary search regimes: self-pollination performs local exploitation through feature-preserving residual refinement, and cross-pollination promotes broader exploration by recombining residuals across heterogeneous samples. As a proof of concept, we validate on MorphoMNIST, a benchmark dataset for counterfactual generation, and on crystal data, demonstrating that this exploration--exploitation decomposition provides a useful mechanism for balancing target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and extends beyond images to real-world scientific domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes residual-space evolutionary optimization, a framework that combines flow-based generative editing with evolutionary algorithms. It separates search into self-pollination (local exploitation) and cross-pollination (broader exploration) operating on disentangled residuals from conditional flow matching. Validated on MorphoMNIST and crystal data, it balances target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity without requiring differentiable objectives.
AI.motivation: Current generative data editing methods rely on differentiable objectives and gradient-based search, which fail in flow-based settings where edits use forward/backward integration with non-differentiable or black-box objectives. There is a gap for editing methods that work effectively under these constraints.
AI.method: The authors leverage conditional flow matching (CFM) to disentangle condition-controlled factors from instance-specific residuals. They then introduce an evolutionary optimization framework operating purely in residual space with two complementary mechanisms: (1) self-pollination — local exploitation via feature-preserving residual refinement, and (2) cross-pollination — broader exploration via recombination of residuals across heterogeneous samples. This exploration-exploitation decomposition is model-agnostic and gradient-free.
AI.result: The framework is validated on MorphoMNIST (counterfactual generation benchmark) and crystal data. Results demonstrate effective balancing of target alignment, instance preservation, and diversity, and show that the approach extends successfully beyond images to real-world scientific domains.
AI.conclusion: The exploration-exploitation decomposition provided by residual-space evolutionary optimization offers a useful mechanism for flow-based generative editing under non-differentiable objectives, with applicability across diverse domains including scientific data.

title: Hard or Just Unreached? Diagnosing the Sampling Blind Spot in Math-Reasoning Difficulty Estimation
comment: 9 pages of main paper, 4 figures and 5 tables in the main paper, with more in the appendix
summary: Math and science reasoning benchmarks rely on pass@k, the fraction of sampled chains that reach gold, as the canonical per-example difficulty signal. The same signal drives RL with verifiable rewards, math data curation, synthetic curricula, and verifier training. We show this proxy has a persistent blind spot on its hardest stratum: on the eight free-form math cells we test (GSM8K and MATH across four open-weight models), 10.3-22.9% of the examples that no sampling seed solves in six tries are instead solved at matched compute by a six-chain deterministic regime. These are greedy decoding plus five cheap residual-stream perturbations applied via activation grafting, while greedy alone solves at most 6% on these math cells. Recovery scales with the additional budget, across perturbations whose mechanistic distinctness we verify across all twelve cells (cross-kind fix-set Jaccard <= 0.47 in every setup). Activation grafting is used as an intervention on internal representations, not a decoding method; we use it purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool, and our recovered items show that the pass@k= 0 % stratum is structurally identifiable in the residual stream rather than that the unmodified model reaches them under ordinary inference.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that pass@k, the standard metric for math reasoning difficulty, misses 10-23% of solvable problems in the "hardest" stratum (pass@k=0%). Using activation grafting—a diagnostic intervention on residual streams—combined with greedy decoding, the authors recover solutions that stochastic sampling fails to find, demonstrating these problems are structurally identifiable within the model's representations.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to expose a critical blind spot in pass@k as a difficulty proxy. Since pass@k drives reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, data curation, curriculum design, and verifier training, misclassifying recoverable problems as unsolvable may distort these downstream processes and underestimate model capability.
AI.method: The authors test eight free-form math cells (GSM8K and MATH datasets across four open-weight models). For examples where no sampling seed solves within six tries (pass@6=0%), they apply a deterministic regime: greedy decoding augmented with five cheap residual-stream perturbations via activation grafting. Activation grafting modifies internal representations by transplanting activations from related contexts, used purely as a diagnostic and diversification tool rather than a decoding method. They verify the mechanistic distinctness of these perturbations across all twelve cells using cross-kind fix-set Jaccard similarity (≤0.47).
AI.result: 10.3–22.9% of examples with pass@6=0% are successfully solved by the deterministic grafting-augmented regime. In contrast, greedy decoding alone solves at most 6%. Recovery scales with additional compute budget, and the distinctness of perturbation mechanisms is confirmed (Jaccard ≤0.47 across all setups).
AI.conclusion: The pass@k=0% stratum is not uniformly unsolvable; many items are structurally identifiable in the residual stream. This finding challenges the reliability of pass@k as a gold-standard difficulty signal and suggests that representation-level diagnostics like activation grafting can uncover latent model capabilities that sampling-based metrics overlook.

title: From Texts to Scores: Tracing the Emergence of Essay Quality Representations in Large Language Models
comment: This is a preprint of a manuscript currently under peer review
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have substantially transformed Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet the internal mechanisms underlying LLM-based scoring remain poorly understood. In this work, we systematically analyze the hidden representations of eight LLMs across two English essay datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Using linear probing, cross-prompt generalization, dimensionality reduction, and neuron-level analyses, we find consistent evidence that essay quality information is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. These representations emerge progressively across layers, remain robust across prompting strategies, and partially transfer across essay prompts despite differences in scoring rubrics. In addition, nonlinear probes provide only marginal and inconsistent improvements over linear probes, suggesting that most essay quality information is already linearly decodable. We further identify individual ``essay scoring neurons'' whose activations strongly correlate with essay scores and whose behavior is sensitive to targeted intervention. Moreover, the layer-wise distribution of these neurons systematically shifts with essay length, with longer essays relying more heavily on deeper layers. Overall, our findings provide evidence that LLMs encode structured representations related to essay quality and offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM-based AES systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of eight LLMs across three essay datasets reveals that essay quality information is encoded linearly in hidden representations, emerges progressively across layers, and is robust to prompting changes. Individual "essay scoring neurons" are identified, and longer essays rely more on deeper layers.
AI.motivation: Despite significant advances in LLM-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES), the internal mechanisms by which LLMs encode and process essay quality remain poorly understood. This work aims to open the "black box" of LLM-based AES through systematic interpretability analysis.
AI.method: The authors analyze hidden representations of 8 LLMs on two English datasets (ASAP++, CSEE) and one Portuguese dataset (ENEM). Techniques include: (1) linear probing, (2) cross-prompt generalization tests, (3) dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA), (4) neuron-level analysis to identify "essay scoring neurons," (5) targeted intervention experiments, and (6) comparison of linear versus nonlinear probes.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Essay quality is encoded in a linearly accessible form within LLM representations. (2) These representations emerge progressively across layers. (3) Representations are robust across different prompting strategies. (4) Cross-prompt transfer is partial but present despite differing rubrics. (5) Nonlinear probes yield only marginal, inconsistent gains over linear probes. (6) Individual "essay scoring neurons" with strong score correlation were identified and are sensitive to intervention. (7) The layer-wise distribution of these neurons shifts with essay length—longer essays rely more on deeper layers.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode structured, linearly decodable representations of essay quality, with evidence of specialized neurons and length-dependent layer utilization. These findings advance interpretability of LLM-based AES and suggest that linear methods suffice for extracting scoring-relevant information.

title: Multi-Head Attention-Based Feature Extractor Integration with Soft Actor-Critic for Porosity Prediction and Process Parameter Optimization in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Additive manufacturing process optimization requires precise parameter control to minimize defects such as porosity. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) approaches using discrete action spaces suffer from slow convergence and susceptibility to local optima, limiting their effectiveness for high-precision manufacturing tasks. This study addresses these limitations by employing a continuous action space combined with a novel architecture that integrates a multi-head attention mechanism with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. The attention-based feature extractor enhances the agent's ability to capture subtle variations in low-dimensional input features, enabling more effective exploration-exploitation balance for navigating value spaces with local minima. We validate our approach on porosity prediction and process parameter optimization in laser powder bed fusion, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final reward values compared to standard RL methods including DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC. The proposed methodology achieves a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining stability throughout training.

AI.tldr: A novel RL approach combining continuous action space SAC with multi-head attention achieves faster convergence and higher reward (322.79 in 14 episodes) for porosity minimization in additive manufacturing compared to DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC.
AI.motivation: Discrete-action RL methods for additive manufacturing process optimization suffer from slow convergence and local optima entrapment, limiting their precision for defect minimization tasks like porosity control in laser powder bed fusion.
AI.method: Continuous action space Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm augmented with a multi-head attention mechanism as the feature extractor, designed to better capture subtle variations in low-dimensional inputs and improve exploration-exploitation balance in value landscapes with local minima.
AI.result: The attention-enhanced SAC reaches a convergence value of 322.79 within 14 episodes, demonstrating faster convergence and higher final rewards compared to DQN, PPO, TD3, and vanilla SAC, with stable training behavior.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multi-head attention with SAC in a continuous action space effectively overcomes the convergence and local-optima limitations of standard RL methods for high-precision additive manufacturing parameter optimization.

title: Convex training of Lipschitz-regularized shallow neural networks
summary: In this work, we introduce a training procedure for shallow neural networks that promotes robustness against adversarial attacks. We solve a non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program by introducing a convex restriction that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our approach can be employed as a post-processing step by taking a pre-trained network as an initial solution to then solving the convex program whose optimal network is guaranteed to be no worse than the initial one. We illustrate the improvements of our training procedure with experiments using real world datasets for regression tasks under an adversarial setting. We show numerically that solving our proposed convex program yields networks with lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that on certain datasets, networks obtained using our convex training program are both more accurate and robust with respect to adversarial attacks.

AI.tldr: A convex restriction is proposed for the non-convex Lipschitz-regularized neural network training problem, solvable to global optimality. It serves as a post-processing step from a pre-trained network, yielding improved robustness against adversarial attacks while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Training shallow neural networks that are robust to adversarial attacks is challenging due to the non-convexity of Lipschitz-regularized objectives, which makes global optimization intractable. The authors aim to develop a tractable, globally optimal training procedure that promotes adversarial robustness without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: The authors introduce a convex restriction of the non-convex Lipschitz-regularized training program. This convex surrogate can be efficiently solved to global optimality. The method is designed as a post-processing step: a pre-trained network is used as initialization, and the convex program ensures the resulting network is at least as good as the initial one. The Lipschitz regularization explicitly controls the network's sensitivity to input perturbations.
AI.result: On real-world regression datasets under adversarial settings, the convex program achieves lower objective values on the Lipschitz-regularized program compared to existing methods. On certain datasets, the resulting networks exhibit both higher accuracy and greater robustness to adversarial attacks simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convex restriction approach effectively trains shallow neural networks to be adversarially robust, providing global optimality guarantees while serving as a practical post-processing step. The method demonstrates that improved robustness need not come at the cost of accuracy.

title: MedRLM: Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence for Long-Context Clinical Reasoning, Sensor-Guided Screening, Evidence-Grounded Decision Support, and Community-to-Tertiary Referral Optimization
summary: Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous and longitudinal patient information rather than answering isolated medical questions. However, current medical large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems often rely on single-step prompting or retrieval, which can be fragile when clinical evidence is distributed across long electronic health records, medical images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. This paper proposes MedRLM, a Recursive Multimodal Health Intelligence framework for long-context clinical reasoning, sensor-guided screening, and community-to-tertiary referral support. Instead of compressing all patient information into one prompt, MedRLM treats the patient case as an external clinical environment that can be recursively inspected, decomposed, retrieved, verified, and synthesized. The framework coordinates specialized agents for clinical text, longitudinal EHR, medical imaging, physiological sensor signals, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, and referral planning. It further introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to connect patient-specific observations with retrieved evidence, standardized definitions, sensor-derived biomarkers, and referral criteria. A sensor-guided recursive triggering mechanism activates deeper reasoning when abnormal physiological or behavioral patterns are detected, while uncertainty-gated refinement supports clinician review for high-risk or low-confidence cases. We also outline a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. MedRLM aims to move medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, and workflow-aware clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: MedRLM is a recursive multimodal framework for clinical decision support that treats patient cases as external environments to be iteratively inspected by specialized agents, using sensor-guided triggering and a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory to enable auditable, workflow-aware reasoning across heterogeneous longitudinal data.
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs and RAG systems rely on single-step prompting/retrieval, which fails when clinical evidence is distributed across long EHRs, images, sensor streams, guidelines, and referral constraints. Real-world clinical decision support requires reasoning over heterogeneous, longitudinal patient information, not isolated Q&A.
AI.method: MedRLM treats patient cases as external clinical environments for recursive inspection, decomposition, retrieval, verification, and synthesis. It coordinates specialized agents (clinical text, longitudinal EHR, imaging, physiological sensors, guideline retrieval, uncertainty auditing, referral planning), introduces a Clinical Evidence Graph Memory linking patient observations with evidence and criteria, and employs sensor-guided recursive triggering for abnormal patterns plus uncertainty-gated refinement for high-risk cases.
AI.result: The paper outlines a real-data evaluation design using public and credentialed clinical datasets spanning EHR, radiology, ECG, ICU time series, and referral-proxy outcomes. No empirical results are reported in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: MedRLM aims to shift medical AI from static question answering toward auditable, multimodal, workflow-aware clinical decision support, with a focus on community-to-tertiary referral scenarios and clinician-in-the-loop review for uncertain cases.

title: LOKI: Memory-Free Null-Space Constrained Lifelong Knowledge Editing
summary: Lifelong knowledge editing aims to efficiently and sequentially update language models over time, as new knowledge becomes available or when the model makes mistakes, while preserving acceptable performance on past knowledge. One unresolved challenge is that existing methods modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge samples, reducing flexibility and increasing catastrophic forgetting. Another is requiring access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing to obtain data statistics. To address these challenges, we introduce LOKI, a novel approach that uses dynamic layer selection based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of the model weights, bypassing the requirement for previous knowledge access. We show that LOKI achieves superior performance to existing approaches across a wide variety of experiments, achieving up to a 14\% improvement in average accuracy.

AI.tldr: LOKI is a lifelong knowledge editing method that dynamically selects layers via the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) and projects gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, eliminating the need for prior knowledge access. It achieves up to 14% improvement in average accuracy over existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong knowledge editing methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they modify a fixed set of layers for all new knowledge, which reduces flexibility and exacerbates catastrophic forgetting; (2) they require access to previous knowledge and extensive pre-processing for data statistics. LOKI aims to overcome both limitations.
AI.method: LOKI employs two core innovations: (1) dynamic layer selection using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to identify which layers to update per knowledge sample; and (2) projecting gradient updates onto the null-space of model weights, which constrains updates to directions that minimally interfere with previously learned knowledge, thereby circumventing the need for explicit access to past data.
AI.result: LOKI achieves superior performance compared to existing lifelong knowledge editing approaches across diverse experiments, with up to a 14% improvement in average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic layer selection via HSIC and null-space gradient projection together form an effective strategy for lifelong knowledge editing, offering both flexibility and strong resistance to catastrophic forgetting without requiring access to prior knowledge.

title: ReNikud: Audio-Supervised Hebrew Grapheme-to-Phoneme Conversion
summary: Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion for Modern Hebrew is needed for applications like text-to-speech (TTS), but is challenging due to the language's abjad writing system, which leaves vowels largely unwritten, creating substantial ambiguity. Standard approaches first predict vowel diacritics (nikud) to produce International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, but this is limited: vocalization data is scarce and laborious to produce, it does not specify features such as lexical stress, and it reflects formal grammatical rules rather than everyday spoken pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction, meanwhile, struggles on limited data and fails to exploit the character-level alignment characteristic of abjads. Our method, ReNikud, overcomes these limitations with two key insights: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) pseudo-labeling pipeline on thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew audio, yielding phonemic transcriptions that reflect natural spoken norms without manual annotation. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias. Results on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and the new targeted MILIM benchmark for spoken Hebrew show that ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release our code and trained models to support further work on Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

AI.tldr: ReNikud introduces a G2P method for Modern Hebrew that uses weak audio supervision from ASR pseudo-labeling and a character-aligned pseudo-vocalization architecture to directly predict IPA phonemes, outperforming prior diacritic-based and sequence-to-sequence approaches on both existing and new benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern Hebrew G2P is difficult because its abjad script omits most vowels, creating ambiguity. Existing approaches relying on vowel diacritic (nikud) prediction are limited by scarce annotated data, lack of lexical stress information, and formal rather than colloquial pronunciation. Direct sequence-to-sequence IPA prediction also underperforms due to limited data and failure to exploit character-level alignment inherent to abjads.
AI.method: ReNikud combines two innovations: (1) Weak audio supervision via a phoneme-based ASR pipeline that pseudo-labels thousands of hours of unlabeled Hebrew speech, producing phonemic transcriptions reflecting natural spoken norms without manual effort. (2) A pseudo-vocalization architecture that predicts IPA phonemes at each character position, enforcing character-level alignment as an inductive bias rather than using unconstrained seq2seq.
AI.result: ReNikud surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on existing Hebrew G2P benchmarks and on the newly introduced MILIM benchmark, which is specifically designed for spoken Hebrew evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging weak audio supervision with character-aligned pseudo-vocalization effectively addresses data scarcity and script ambiguity in Hebrew G2P. The approach captures natural pronunciation norms and the authors will release code and models to facilitate further research in Hebrew TTS and speech technologies.

title: Multi-Granular Attention-Driven Reinforcement Learning Framework for Web Intelligent Enhancement Systems
comment: 2026 3rd International Conference on Integrated Intelligence and Communication Systems (ICIICS), 6 Pages
summary: From the past few years, web intelligent enhancement systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous and dynamic web data to deliver personalized, context-aware services. However, traditional machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning models often struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving web environments. In this research, a Multi-Granular Attention-based Reinforcement Web Intelligent Enhancement System (MGAR-WIES) is proposed to address the challenges by integrating semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Initially, heterogeneous web data comprising structured, semi-structured and unstructured sources are collected and preprocessed for generating unified feature representations. These representations are transformed into a dynamic semantic graph, where entities and their relationships are modeled by using graph embeddings enhanced by attention mechanisms for capturing both local relevance and global contextual dependencies. Subsequently, an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy leverages the attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized web actions like content recommendation, navigation optimization, and service adaptation. Finally, the continuous online feedback is further integrated to update graph representations and learning policies in real time by ensuring sustained adaptability and performance. The proposed MGAR-WIES acheived better results in terms of accuracy (80%) when compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MGAR-WIES, a system combining semantic graph modeling, attention mechanisms, and adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning to deliver personalized web services, achieving 80% accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML, DL, and RL models struggle with semantic understanding, adaptability, and scalability in continuously evolving, heterogeneous web environments, limiting their effectiveness for intelligent web enhancement systems.
AI.method: MGAR-WIES integrates three core components: (1) unified feature representation from heterogeneous web data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured); (2) a dynamic semantic graph with attention-enhanced graph embeddings capturing local relevance and global context; (3) an adaptive multi-agent reinforcement learning strategy that uses attention-aware semantic states to optimize personalized actions (content recommendation, navigation, service adaptation), with continuous online feedback for real-time policy and graph updates.
AI.result: MGAR-WIES achieved 80% accuracy, outperforming existing approaches (no other specific metrics or baseline comparisons are detailed in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: The integration of semantic graphs, attention mechanisms, and adaptive RL with real-time online feedback effectively addresses adaptability and semantic understanding challenges in dynamic web environments, yielding superior accuracy.

title: Pitch Spelling Jazz Lead Sheets, Solo Transcriptions, Classical Piano and Monophonic Scores
summary: We present an algorithm for pitch spelling and key estimation. Given an input in MIDI-like format, containing information on note pitches (expressed in semitones relative to the lowest reference note) and bar boundaries, it estimates the appropriate note names, a global Key Signature, and a local scale for each bar. This related information elements are evaluated jointly during two stages of optimisation. During an initial 'modal' stage, a probable scale is proposed for each bar, minimising the number of accidentals to be printed in the printed score with a shortest-path search. Then, during a second stage called 'tonal', these local scales are used to estimate the Key Signature and note names that would result in the best musical notation for the entire piece. We present evaluations conducted on datasets comprising a variety of digital musical scores: jazz lead sheets taken from the Real Book, transcriptions of recordings of jazz soli and bass lines, traditional tunes, as well as classical scores for piano and monophonic instruments. Our procedure was originally designed for use in music transcription, specifically for building digital collections of jazz solos transcribed from audio recordings, for the purposes of music analysis, teaching and the preservation of cultural heritage. This method should also prove useful for other tasks related to the processing of musical notation. Furthermore, to this end, we have defined new distances between various common jazz scales, which may be of some interest to musicological studies.

AI.tldr: A two-stage algorithm for simultaneous pitch spelling and key estimation from MIDI input: a modal stage assigns local scales per bar via shortest-path optimization to minimize accidentals, followed by a tonal stage that derives a global Key Signature and note names for optimal overall notation. Evaluated across diverse datasets (jazz, classical, traditional), with novel jazz scale distance metrics introduced.
AI.motivation: To support automatic music transcription of jazz solos from audio recordings for analysis, teaching, and cultural heritage preservation, by accurately converting MIDI pitch data (semitones) into proper musical notation with correct note names, key signatures, and local scales.
AI.method: A two-stage optimization framework: (1) Modal stage — for each bar, a probable local scale is selected via shortest-path search that minimizes the number of accidentals required in printed notation. (2) Tonal stage — the per-bar local scales are aggregated to estimate a global Key Signature and final note names that yield the best overall musical notation for the entire piece. The algorithm also introduces novel distance measures between common jazz scales.
AI.result: Evaluations were conducted on multiple datasets: jazz lead sheets (Real Book), transcriptions of jazz solos and bass lines, traditional tunes, and classical piano and monophonic scores. The method demonstrated effective pitch spelling and key estimation across these varied musical styles.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage optimization approach successfully handles pitch spelling and key estimation jointly, proving useful for music transcription pipelines, particularly for building digital collections of jazz solos. The novel jazz scale distance metrics also offer potential value for musicological research. The method generalizes beyond jazz to classical and traditional music.

title: Efficiently Representing Algorithms With Chain-of-Thought Transformers
summary: The increasing popularity of \emph{reasoning} models -- language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer -- is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the \emph{Word RAM} model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on $\bigO(\log n)$-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: \emph{Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?} For instance, can they sort $n$ items in $\bigO(n \log n)$ steps or run Dijkstra's algorithm in $\bigO(E + V \log V)$ steps? We answer affirmatively, up to poly-logarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: \emph{continuous} CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a \emph{hybrid} architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT \emph{can} efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in $n$. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a ``flat'' instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions -- in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms (e.g., sorting in O(n log n), Dijkstra's algorithm) with only poly-logarithmic overhead, far better than the quadratic overhead known for Turing machine simulations. Results are established for three settings: finite-precision transformers with hard attention, continuous CoT with vector reasoning, and hybrid transformer-RNN architectures.
AI.motivation: While existing theory shows CoT transformers can simulate Turing machines (and thus any computation), Turing machines are low-level and inefficient for algorithm design. Real algorithms are designed in the Word RAM model (random-access memory, unit-cost operations on O(log n)-bit words), which can be exponentially more efficient. The key open question is whether CoT transformers can efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms, preserving their asymptotic efficiency.
AI.method: The authors prove simulation results in three increasingly practical settings: (1) finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, (2) continuous CoT where reasoning uses vectors instead of discrete tokens, and (3) a hybrid architecture with transformer layers on top of a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In each setting, they show Word RAM algorithms can be simulated with only poly-logarithmic overhead in n (the input size), with tighter bounds (log-square or logarithmic) for restricted instruction sets like flat or multiplication-free flat instructions.
AI.result: CoT transformers can simulate any Word RAM algorithm with poly-logarithmic overhead in n. This overhead reduces to O(log² n) for flat instruction sets and merely O(log n) for multiplication-free flat instructions. This starkly contrasts with Turing machine simulations, which incur quadratic overhead relative to Word RAM.
AI.conclusion: CoT transformers are not merely Turing-complete in principle; they can efficiently simulate practical, high-level Word RAM algorithms with near-optimal overhead. This provides strong theoretical justification for the empirical success of reasoning models and chain-of-thought, showing that the transformer architecture can match the efficiency of standard algorithmic models while maintaining practical architectural constraints (finite width, log-precision, hybrid designs).

title: CzechDocs: A Multiway Parallel Dataset of Formatted Documents for Minority Languages in Czechia
summary: We present CzechDocs, a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, and PDF) covering Czech and minority languages used in Czechia-primarily Ukrainian and English, with smaller portions of Vietnamese, Russian and other languages. The dataset is designed to support the evaluation of machine translation systems that aim to preserve document formatting during translation. We provide a comparison of the most common approaches to format-preserving machine translation on a validation subset of the dataset. This validation split, together with the evaluation toolkit, is publicly released for further research. A held-out test split will be reserved for a future shared task focused on document-level translation with formatting preservation.

AI.tldr: CzechDocs is a multiway parallel dataset of formatted documents (HTML, DOCX, PDF) in Czech and minority languages, designed to evaluate format-preserving machine translation, with a publicly released validation split and a held-out test set reserved for a future shared task.
AI.motivation: Existing machine translation evaluation lacks robust benchmarks for assessing how well MT systems preserve document formatting (markup, structure) across multiple file formats. There is also a need for parallel resources covering Czech and minority languages spoken in Czechia (Ukrainian, Vietnamese, Russian, etc.).
AI.method: The authors construct CzechDocs, a multiway parallel corpus of formatted documents in three formats (HTML, DOCX, PDF) spanning Czech and several minority languages. They define a validation subset on which they benchmark common format-preserving MT approaches and release this subset along with an evaluation toolkit. A held-out test split is withheld for a planned shared task.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparative evaluation of common format-preserving machine translation methods on the validation split, demonstrating the dataset's utility for benchmarking. The validation data and toolkit are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: CzechDocs fills a gap in format-preserving MT evaluation for Czech and its minority languages.
