The public release of the validation set and toolkit, plus the reserved test split for a future shared task, establishes a foundation for reproducible research in document-level translation with formatting preservation.

title: BIM-Edit: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IFC-Based Building Information Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to computer-aided design (CAD) to generate design artifacts from textual instructions. In engineering practice, this requires more than creating new geometry, models must also understand existing scenes, edit them correctly, and preserve semantics and relations. However, many CAD benchmarks focus on creating new models rather than editing existing ones, and mostly evaluate geometric correctness. We introduce BIM-Edit, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on natural-language editing of Building Information Models (BIM) represented in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) format. BIM provides a challenging testbed because building models encode geometry together with semantic and relational structure. BIM-Edit contains 324 editing tasks spanning 11 realistic building models and 36 synthetic scenes. Tasks are expressed using three instruction categories - direct, spatial, and topological - covering both explicit and scene-grounded edits. We evaluate outputs along three dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Across evaluated LLMs, the best-performing model achieves only 49.5% average score across the three metrics, and no model fully solves more than 3.4% of tasks. These results demonstrate a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the requirements of structured engineering design workflows.

AI.tldr: BIM-Edit is a benchmark evaluating LLMs on editing Building Information Models (IFC format) via natural language. With 324 tasks across 11 real and 36 synthetic models, it measures geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency. Top models achieve only 49.5% average score, with full solves under 3.4%, revealing a large capability gap for structured CAD editing.
AI.motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks focus on generating new geometry from scratch and evaluate primarily geometric correctness. However, real engineering workflows demand that models understand, edit, and preserve semantic and relational structure within existing scenes. No benchmark adequately tests LLMs on natural-language editing of semantically rich, relationally structured engineering models.
AI.method: The authors introduce BIM-Edit, comprising 324 editing tasks on 11 realistic BIM models and 36 synthetic scenes in IFC format. Tasks fall into three instruction categories: direct (explicit parameter changes), spatial (position/arrangement edits), and topological (connectivity/relationship edits). Outputs are evaluated along three orthogonal dimensions: geometric accuracy, semantic validity, and topological consistency, using automated metrics tailored to IFC structure.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves only a 49.5% average across the three evaluation dimensions. No model fully solves more than 3.4% of the 324 tasks, indicating that even the strongest models struggle significantly with structured BIM editing.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of structured engineering design workflows. BIM-Edit highlights that semantic and relational reasoning over existing models remains a major open challenge, and the benchmark provides a rigorous testbed to drive future progress in CAD-focused LLMs.

title: Efficient Neural Network Model Selection for Few-Class Application Datasets
summary: While much effort has focused on developing and benchmarking high-performance neural networks, less attention has been given to how dataset properties, known to practitioners, can guide efficient model selection. Neural models are typically evaluated on datasets with thousands of classes, yet many real-world applications involve fewer than ten. To address this understudied but common setting, we develop a measure of classification difficulty based on data-side properties and show how it enables more efficient model selection for few-class datasets, where traditional approaches are less effective. We term this phenomenon "few-class distinctiveness". Our metric allows comparison of models and datasets 6 to 29$\times$ faster than repeated training and testing. Leveraging this insight, we extend scaled model families below the smallest published models, achieving greater efficiency at similar accuracy, for example models up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano for a mobile robot task. Targeting resource-constrained applications, we demonstrate few-class model selection across mobile robot, drone, and IoT scenarios, highlighting practical gains in efficiency without sacrificing performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "few-class distinctiveness," a data-side difficulty metric that enables efficient model selection for classification tasks with fewer than ten classes — a common but understudied setting. The metric allows 6–29× faster model-dataset comparison than repeated training, enabling the design of scaled-down models (up to 42% smaller than YOLOv5-nano) with comparable accuracy for resource-constrained applications like mobile robots, drones, and IoT devices.
AI.motivation: Existing neural network research heavily emphasizes high-performance benchmarking on large-scale datasets (e.g., thousands of classes), while neglecting the practical reality that many real-world applications involve few-class problems (fewer than ten classes). Current model selection approaches rely on costly repeated training and testing, which is inefficient. There is a need for a principled, data-side measure of classification difficulty to guide rapid model selection in few-class settings, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices.
AI.method: The authors develop a data-centric metric, termed "few-class distinctiveness," that quantifies classification difficulty directly from dataset properties without requiring model training. This metric captures how separable and distinguishable the few classes are in feature space. Using this metric, they enable rapid comparison of model-dataset compatibility — 6 to 29 times faster than traditional train-and-test cycles. They further leverage the insight to derive scaled-down model families below the smallest published architectures (e.g., shrinking YOLOv5-nano by up to 42%) while maintaining similar accuracy for few-class tasks.
AI.result: The proposed few-class distinctiveness metric achieves 6–29× speedup in model-dataset comparison versus repeated training and testing. Scaled-down models designed using this insight reach up to 42% size reduction compared to YOLOv5-nano while preserving accuracy on few-class tasks. The approach is validated across mobile robot, drone, and IoT application scenarios, demonstrating practical efficiency gains without performance degradation in resource-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Dataset-side properties, specifically few-class distinctiveness, provide a powerful and computationally efficient basis for model selection in the common yet overlooked few-class regime. By shifting focus from model-centric benchmarking to data-aware selection, practitioners can achieve substantial efficiency improvements — smaller, faster models with retained accuracy — which is critical for edge deployment. The work opens a direction for data-property-driven model design and selection beyond traditional scaling paradigms.

title: Actionable Activation Directions for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment Across Language Model Families
summary: Fine-tuning language models on insecure code induces emergent misalignment with poorly understood internal structure. We investigate whether this misalignment corresponds to a causally actionable activation-space direction shared across architectures. Across four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) finetuned identically, a difference-in-means direction achieves 99.6% separation of aligned and misaligned activations at each model's final layer. Causal steering by subtracting this direction reduces code spillover by 21-51 points, while a secure-code control confirms content specificity. Cross-architecture transfer via ridge regression maps yields large behavioral suppression (up to 46 points) but fails specificity controls as random and orthogonal directions perform comparably. We identify a two-tier specificity structure: within-model directions are causally specific and actionable; cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. An asymmetric transfer topology emerges, with Gemma and Qwen acting as geometric donors and Llama as a receiver. These findings define the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on insecure code creates a shared misalignment direction in model activations. Within the same model, subtracting this direction effectively reduces insecure code generation. Cross-model transfer shows causal effects but lacks specificity, with an asymmetric donor-receiver topology emerging across architectures.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the emergent misalignment from fine-tuning language models on insecure code corresponds to a causally actionable, architecture-agnostic activation-space direction, and to characterize the limits of cross-architecture linear correction.
AI.method: Four instruction-tuned model families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Ministral-3-3B) were identically fine-tuned on insecure code. A difference-in-means direction was computed at each model's final layer to separate aligned vs. misaligned activations. Causal steering was performed by subtracting this direction. Cross-architecture transfer used ridge regression to map directions between model pairs, with comparisons against random and orthogonal direction baselines.
AI.result: The difference-in-means direction achieved 99.6% separation at the final layer. Within-model causal steering reduced code spillover by 21–51 points, with a secure-code control confirming specificity. Cross-model transfer suppressed behavior up to 46 points but failed specificity controls, as random/orthogonal directions performed comparably. An asymmetric transfer topology emerged: Gemma and Qwen act as geometric donors, Llama as a receiver.
AI.conclusion: Within-model misalignment directions are causally specific and actionable, while cross-model directions are causally real but non-specific. These findings establish the limits of linear cross-architecture correction and recommend within-model probing for auditing misaligned models.

title: Modularity-Free Conflict-Averse Training for Generalized PINNs
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a powerful framework for solving PDEs by embedding physical laws into differentiable objectives. Despite their advances, training PINNs remains fragile: recent conflict-averse optimization schemes alleviate gradient interference between residual and boundary losses, but we show that their effectiveness deteriorates as model capacity increases. In this paper, we identify a capacity-induced failure mode, where overparameterized networks undergo functional modularity, self-partitioning into task-exclusive modules that suppress cross-objective interaction and hinder convergence toward Pareto-stationary points. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks demonstrate that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Codes are available at \url{https://github.com/heejokong/ModSync}.

AI.tldr: PINNs suffer from a capacity-induced failure mode where overparameterized networks self-partition into task-exclusive modules, hindering convergence. The authors propose ModSync, which penalizes task-exclusive connections to preserve cross-objective interaction, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing conflict-averse optimization schemes for PINNs (e.g., mitigating gradient interference between residual and boundary losses) lose effectiveness as model capacity increases. The authors aim to understand and resolve this capacity-induced training fragility.
AI.method: The authors identify functional modularity as the failure mechanism — overparameterized networks self-partition into task-exclusive subnetworks that suppress cross-objective interaction, preventing convergence to Pareto-stationary points. They propose Modular-Sparsity Synchronization (ModSync), which integrates structural optimization into conflict-averse training by penalizing task-exclusive connections while preserving interaction-promoting pathways.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks show that ModSync consistently prevents capacity-driven failures, sustains robust cross-objective coupling, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.conclusion: ModSync effectively addresses the capacity-induced failure mode in PINNs by synchronizing modular sparsity with multi-objective optimization, enabling robust training of overparameterized networks for solving PDEs.

title: OnDeFog: Online Decision Transformer under Frame Dropping
summary: In challenging real-world reinforcement learning applications, communication delays or sensor failures often cause frame dropping, in which the agent cannot receive the dropped states and associated rewards. To address the performance degradation caused by frame dropping, the Decision Transformer under Random Frame Dropping (DeFog) was developed by incorporating additional mechanisms into the decision transformer to tackle frame dropping. Although DeFog can mitigate performance degradation in frame-dropping environments, since DeFog is an offline learning method, it struggles to effectively generalize to novel states not adequately represented in the training dataset. In this study, we propose OnDeFog, which integrates the mechanisms in DeFog with the online decision transformer (ODT), an online reinforcement learning method that learns policies through direct environmental interaction. Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that our proposed OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments characterized by high dropping frame rate and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing a large amount of low-reward data.

AI.tldr: OnDeFog combines DeFog's frame-dropping robustness mechanisms with the Online Decision Transformer (ODT) to create an online RL method that generalizes better to novel states and outperforms both ODT under high frame-drop rates and DeFog on low-reward-heavy datasets.
AI.motivation: Frame dropping (caused by communication delays or sensor failures) degrades RL performance. While DeFog addresses this, it is limited as an offline method—it cannot generalize well to novel states unseen in training data. This motivates an online learning approach capable of direct environmental interaction.
AI.method: OnDeFog integrates DeFog's frame-dropping mitigation mechanisms into the Online Decision Transformer (ODT) framework. ODT learns policies through direct online interaction with the environment, enabling adaptation to novel states. The resulting method inherits DeFog's robustness to missing states/rewards while gaining ODT's online generalization capability.
AI.result: OnDeFog achieves superior performance compared to ODT in environments with high frame-dropping rates and outperforms DeFog on datasets containing substantial amounts of low-reward data, where offline methods struggle.
AI.conclusion: Integrating frame-dropping robustness mechanisms into an online decision transformer framework yields a method that is both robust to frame dropping and capable of generalizing beyond static training data, addressing key limitations of prior approaches.

title: The Register Gap: A Meaning Intelligence Framework for Nigerian Public Discourse
comment: Preprint. 12 pages, 2 tables. Supplementary materials: MIF Master Specification v2.0, Annotation Guidelines v1.0, and 30-item public calibration set with gold labels available from the author
summary: We introduce the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation and evaluation schema for Nigerian public discourse that separates surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Existing benchmarks for Nigerian languages, including NaijaSenti and AfriSenti, treat sentiment classification as a three-way polarity task (positive, negative, neutral). We argue that the dominant failure mode of AI systems on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but context failure: the same utterance carries opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situation. The MIF operationalises this insight across nine scored dimensions: register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, and recommended communications action. We construct a 30-item calibration dataset spanning Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, and code-mixed registers, and evaluate a frontier language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) under zero-shot and schema-informed prompting conditions. The headline finding is the Register Gap: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) when the model receives the MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increases by 5.4 points (73.2 to 78.6) under schema-informed prompting, with the largest practical gains in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points). We release the framework specification, annotation guidelines, and the 30-item public calibration set to support reproducibility, while retaining a private holdout corpus for contamination-protected evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Meaning Intelligence Framework (MIF), a nine-dimension annotation schema for Nigerian public discourse that distinguishes surface sentiment from true communicative intent. Testing on a 30-item calibration dataset reveals a "Register Gap": a frontier LLM improves from 33.3% to 73.3% register classification accuracy when given the MIF schema, with substantial gains in coded-subtext detection and strategic action recommendation.
AI.motivation: Existing sentiment benchmarks for Nigerian languages (NaijaSenti, AfriSenti) reduce analysis to three-way polarity (positive/negative/neutral), which fails to capture context-dependent pragmatic meaning. The core argument is that the dominant AI failure mode on Nigerian discourse is not translation failure but **context failure**: identical utterances carry opposite pragmatic force depending on speaker, audience, and situational context. No existing framework operationalises this distinction.
AI.method: The authors propose the MIF with nine scored dimensions (register, surface sentiment, true intent, irony, coded subtext, risk tier, annotator confidence, speaker emotion, recommended communications action). They construct a 30-item calibration dataset across four linguistic registers (Standard English, Nigerian English, Nigerian Pidgin, code-mixed). A frontier model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) is evaluated under two conditions: zero-shot prompting and schema-informed prompting (MIF provided in-context).
AI.result: The key finding is the **Register Gap**: zero-shot register classification accuracy is 33.3%, rising to 73.3% (+40 points) with MIF schema in-context. The composite Meaning Intelligence Score increases from 73.2 to 78.6 (+5.4 points). Largest practical gains occur in register identification, coded-subtext detection (+10 points), and strategic action recommendation (+10.3 points).
AI.conclusion: The MIF demonstrates that context-aware, multidimensional annotation schemas substantially improve LLM performance on Nigerian discourse. The framework, annotation guidelines, and 30-item calibration set are publicly released for reproducibility, with a private holdout corpus retained for contamination-protected future evaluation.

title: Implicit Semantic-Aware Communication Based on Hypergraph Reasoning
comment: This work is accepted at IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Semantic-aware communication has emerged as a transformative paradigm for next-generation communication systems, shifting the fundamental goal from transmitting bit-level symbols to reliably recovering and understanding the semantic meaning of information. Previous studies have demonstrated that representing the semantic content of source messages as graph-based structures can significantly improve communication efficiency and the accuracy of semantic inference at the receiver. However, existing solutions typically employ graphs that capture only pairwise relationships, thereby neglecting higher-order implicit correlations commonly observed in real-world scenarios, such as group interactions, multi-entity associations, and complex relational contexts. This limitation reduces semantic expressiveness and makes semantic inference susceptible to ambiguity and performance degradation, particularly under noisy or corrupted channel conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework, HISR, which leverages hypergraphs to represent complex multi-entity relationships among semantic knowledge entities. In HISR, entities and their associated higher-order relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design not only disentangles diverse semantic interactions to mitigate the over-smoothing effects commonly found in traditional graph embedding methods but also enables robust semantic inference even when partial information loss occurs during transmission. Numerical results show that the proposed HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over the state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HISR, a hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework for semantic-aware communication. Unlike conventional graph-based methods limited to pairwise relations, HISR uses hypergraphs to capture higher-order multi-entity relationships. Entities and relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces per relational context, which disentangles semantic interactions, mitigates over-smoothing, and enables robust inference under noisy channels. HISR achieves up to 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy over state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic communication systems represent semantic content using graph-based structures that only capture pairwise relationships. This neglects higher-order implicit correlations (e.g., group interactions, multi-entity associations, complex relational contexts) prevalent in real-world scenarios, leading to reduced semantic expressiveness and degraded inference accuracy under noisy or corrupted channel conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose HISR, a hypergraph-based implicit semantic reasoning framework. Semantic knowledge entities and their higher-order relations are modeled as hypergraphs. Entities and associated relations are mapped into dedicated semantic subspaces tailored to distinct relational contexts. This design disentangles diverse semantic interactions to counteract over-smoothing effects typical of conventional graph embeddings and preserves robust semantic inference capability despite partial information loss during transmission.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that HISR achieves up to a 36.6% improvement in implicit semantic interpretation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The hypergraph-based HISR framework effectively addresses the limitations of pairwise graph representations in semantic communication. By capturing higher-order relationships and employing context-specific semantic subspaces, HISR significantly enhances semantic inference accuracy and robustness, marking a meaningful advance toward reliable semantic-aware communication systems.

title: Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction
summary: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies federated bilevel optimization under performative distribution shift, formalizing the Federated Bilevel Performatively Stable (FBPS) point, and proposes two algorithms (FBi-RRM and FBi-SGD) with convergence guarantees, validated through experiments on strategic regression, meta strategic classification, and CNN-based tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing federated bilevel optimization assumes fixed client data distributions, but real-world deployments induce performativity — where decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, causing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shifts. This violates standard assumptions and motivates a new framework.
AI.method: The authors formalize the FBPS point under a decoupled-risk perspective with existence/uniqueness conditions. They propose FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method using federated hypergradient estimation with diminishing step sizes and small-sensitivity guarantees.
AI.result: Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and show improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines. CNN-based classification further demonstrates effectiveness in nonconvex neural network settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FBPS framework and algorithms effectively handle performativity in federated bilevel optimization, with both theoretical guarantees and practical validation across convex and nonconvex settings.

title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
summary: Effective Automated Essay Scoring (AES) are expected to support both reliable assessment and actionable instructional feedback. However, existing approaches often treat scoring and feedback as separate components: neural scoring models provide limited interpretability, while Large Language Model (LLM)-based feedback is typically insensitive to learners proficiency levels. To address this fragmentation, this work proposes PsyScore, a psychometrically-aware framework that integrates diagnostic assessment with instructional scaffolding through a shared latent ability representation. PsyScore comprises three key modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer that incorporates the Graded Partial Credit Model (GPCM) into a neural architecture, enabling the precise estimation of student ability while maintaining psychometric interpretability, a ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator, which conditions multi-agent feedback strategies on the diagnosed ability parameter to adapt instructional focus across different proficiency levels, and a Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation Strategy that assesses feedback quality via pairwise preference judgements and student revision simulations. Experiments on the ASAP++ dataset demonstrate that PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while providing more pedagogically aligned feedback.

AI.tldr: PsyScore integrates diagnostic assessment and instructional feedback for AES via a shared latent ability representation, combining a neural IRT scorer, ZPD-scaffolded feedback, and multi-perspective evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing AES approaches fragment scoring and feedback: neural models lack interpretability, while LLM-based feedback ignores learner proficiency levels. A unified, psychometrically-aware framework is needed.
AI.method: PsyScore has three modules: (1) Trait-Adaptive Neural IRT Scorer embedding GPCM into a neural network for ability estimation with psychometric interpretability; (2) ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback Generator using multi-agent strategies conditioned on diagnosed ability to tailor feedback by proficiency level; (3) Multi-Perspective Feedback Evaluation using pairwise preference judgments and student revision simulations.
AI.result: On the ASAP++ dataset, PsyScore achieves competitive scoring performance while delivering more pedagogically aligned feedback compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: A unified psychometric framework bridging scoring and feedback generation can maintain assessment accuracy while producing proficiency-sensitive, instructionally useful feedback.

title: Manifold Bandits: Bayesian Curriculum Learning over the Latent Geometry of Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a central approach for improving reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), where training efficiency depends critically on how problems are sampled during optimization. Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods typically prioritize prompts of intermediate difficulty, treating problem selection as a standard bandit problem with independent arms and overlooking the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. In this work, we frame problem sampling as a manifold-structured bandit problem with endogenous non-stationarity: problems are related through the model's latent representation space, and sampling decisions can steer how learning signals evolve across that space. To operationalize this perspective, we introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree and applies Bayesian learning to guide sampling. Empirically, we find that different sampling strategies induce non-trivial tradeoffs between productivity (learning signal), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). These results show that prioritizing difficulty alone is insufficient for strong downstream performance, highlighting the importance of incorporating structure and type-awareness into problem sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes RL training data sampling for LLMs as a manifold-structured bandit problem, proposing Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC) — a hierarchical, structure-aware sampling framework that balances productivity, diversity, and utility, showing that difficulty-based selection alone is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive curriculum learning methods for RL-based LLM reasoning treat problem selection as a standard bandit with independent arms, ignoring the structured, heterogeneous nature of the task space. The authors argue that problems are related through the model's latent representation (a manifold), and sampling decisions non-stationarily shape learning signals across that space — dynamics not captured by difficulty-only prioritization.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bayesian Manifold Curriculum (BMC), a structure-aware framework that: (1) organizes problems into a hierarchical task tree reflecting the latent manifold structure; (2) applies Bayesian learning (e.g., Thompson sampling or posterior-guided selection) to guide sampling across this tree; (3) frames the problem as a "manifold-structured bandit with endogenous non-stationarity," where arms (problems) are correlated through the representation space and sampling steers the evolution of learning signals.
AI.result: Different sampling strategies reveal non-trivial tradeoffs among three axes: productivity (learning signal magnitude), diversity (coverage of the task manifold), and utility (evaluation relevance). Prioritizing difficulty alone proves insufficient for strong downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: Effective problem sampling for RL-based LLM reasoning must incorporate structure and type-awareness — not just difficulty. BMC provides a principled Bayesian approach that accounts for the manifold structure of the task space, yielding better-calibrated tradeoffs across productivity, diversity, and utility.

title: CATCH-ME if you RAG: a dataset of Contextually Annotated multi-Turn Counterspeech against Hate and Misinformation Exchanges
summary: Online hate speech and misinformation frequently overlap, yet NLP research has mainly treated them in isolation. While LLMs represent a scalable solution for assisting humans in the generation of counterspeech for both threats, zero-shot models frequently generate repetitive and vague responses, underscoring the need for high-quality examples to steer model generation. However, existing counterspeech datasets against the overlap of hate and misinformation are scarce and limited to single-turn English dialogues, while real-life interactions span across multiple turns and languages. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first large-scale, expert-curated, multilingual dataset of dialogues tackling the intersection of hate and misinformation. To ensure factual grounding, the dialogues are also anchored in verified external knowledge (i.e., fact-checking articles and NGO reports) and include document- and chunk-level span annotations, making it directly applicable for RAG systems. Covering five languages and targeting hate directed at seven marginalized groups, this novel resource enables the training and evaluation of more persuasive, factually grounded counterspeech models.

AI.tldr: Introduces the first large-scale, multilingual, expert-curated dialogue dataset that jointly addresses hate speech and misinformation, with dialogues grounded in verified external knowledge and span annotations to improve counterspeech generation via RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Hate speech and misinformation frequently co-occur online, yet NLP research treats them separately. LLMs for counterspeech generation suffer from repetitive, vague zero-shot outputs and lack high-quality exemplars. Existing datasets are limited to single-turn English dialogues, failing to capture real-world multi-turn, multilingual interactions.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale, expert-curated multilingual dialogue dataset covering five languages and seven marginalized groups. Dialogues are grounded in verified external knowledge (fact-checking articles, NGO reports) with document- and chunk-level span annotations, making the resource directly compatible with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines.
AI.result: The resulting resource enables training and evaluation of counterspeech models that are more persuasive and factually grounded. The dataset bridges gaps in multilingual coverage, multi-turn dialogue structure, and knowledge anchoring absent in prior work.
AI.conclusion: A novel, fact-anchored, multilingual, multi-turn dialogue dataset fills a critical gap at the intersection of hate speech and misinformation, providing a foundation for building more effective, RAG-compatible counterspeech systems.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
summary: Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.

AI.tldr: RVS is a new evaluation metric that measures how well machine learning models comply with logical rules, independent of predictive accuracy. It handles both strict hard rules and statistical soft rules, works on any relational model, and can be computed via auto-generated SQL. Experiments on link prediction and relational regression show that models with similar accuracy can differ significantly in logical consistency.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation metrics (ranking quality, prediction error, classification accuracy) only measure predictive performance but ignore whether model outputs satisfy logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance, logical consistency is crucial, yet no standard metric exists to capture this dimension.
AI.method: The authors propose the Rule Violation Score (RVS), which quantifies rule compliance for any predictive model over a relational vocabulary. RVS distinguishes between hard rules (strict constraints that must never be violated) and soft rules (statistical regularities that should hold with high probability). The metric is dataset-agnostic and model-agnostic. Computation is automated via SQL queries generated from Horn rules, making evaluation practical and scalable.
AI.result: Evaluated on three benchmarks—knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression—across rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic models. Results show that models with comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different Rule Violation Scores, revealing behavioral differences invisible to standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: RVS fills a critical gap in model evaluation by providing a principled, automatable measure of logical consistency. It can also evaluate training data consistency and help diagnose poorly defined rules. The metric should complement—not replace—traditional accuracy metrics, enabling more holistic model assessment for high-stakes applications.

title: Learning universal approximations for partial differential equations with Physics-Informed Broad Learning System
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) play a central role in modeling complex physical, biological, and engineering systems. While traditional numerical solvers are robust, they often incur prohibitive computational costs due to mesh dependencies, whereas recent Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but frequently suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. To bridge this gap, this article proposes the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a novel backpropagation-free framework that reformulates PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization. We improved an algorithm within this framework to handle nonlinear PDEs efficiently and provide a rigorous mathematical proof establishing the universal approximation property of PIBLS for these equations. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy. This framework provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, offering a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: PIBLS reformulates PDE solving as direct least-squares optimization in a backpropagation-free framework, achieving 1–3 orders of magnitude speedup over PINNs with higher accuracy, and includes a universal approximation proof for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical PDE solvers are computationally expensive due to mesh dependencies. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative but suffer from slow convergence and optimization instability. A framework is needed that combines mesh-free flexibility with fast, stable training.
AI.method: The authors propose the Physics-Informed Broad Learning System (PIBLS), a backpropagation-free framework that casts PDE solving as a direct least-squares optimization problem. An improved algorithm is introduced within PIBLS to efficiently handle nonlinear PDEs. A rigorous mathematical proof establishes the universal approximation property of PIBLS for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.result: Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs show PIBLS is one to three orders of magnitude faster than conventional PINNs while achieving significantly higher solution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PIBLS provides a computationally efficient paradigm for scientific machine learning, serving as a practical, high-speed alternative for real-time simulation and design optimization tasks.

title: Augmenting Game AI with Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Vision paper, published in Conference on Games 2026
summary: Immersion in video games depends not only on graphics, audio, and game mechanics, but also on the quality of in-game characters. Producing believable characters, or game AI, remains a significant challenge as behavioral complexity is hard to capture with hand-coded systems. Game AI is a source of immersion and engagement; however, the limitations stemming from the challenges of creating game AI often lead to frustration and the breaking of the illusion of realism within the game. The introduction of machine learning models opens the door to creating more believable, authentic, and relatable characters in games. The promise is that they either learn from interacting with the game, or from player data, to develop true human-like behavior. In this paper, we envision more applications of reinforcement learning for game AI in the future. For this to materialize, current research limitations are prohibitive to broad deployment across game genres. Therefore, we propose a framework for training reinforcement learning models with a set of requirements in mind that are suited towards game AI and game development. We present examples of games with reinforcement learning-augmented game AI and describe the practicalities of deploying player-facing machine learning agents in modern games. Furthermore, we identify bottlenecks and hard problems in these areas, which we believe offer promising research directions to accelerate the adoption of machine learning in game AI for the video game industry.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning can create more believable game AI characters than hand-coded systems, but current limitations hinder broad deployment. The paper proposes a training framework tailored to game development requirements, presents existing RL-augmented game examples, and identifies key bottlenecks and research directions to accelerate ML adoption in the video game industry.
AI.motivation: Hand-coded game AI struggles to capture behavioral complexity, leading to player frustration and broken immersion. Machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning, promises more authentic, human-like characters by learning from gameplay or player data, but current research limitations prevent widespread commercial adoption across game genres.
AI.method: The authors take a vision/position paper approach: they (1) envision future RL applications for game AI, (2) propose a conceptual framework for training RL models with requirements suited to game AI and game development pipelines, (3) present case examples of games already using RL-augmented AI, and (4) systematically identify bottlenecks and hard problems blocking broader deployment.
AI.result: The paper identifies practical deployment challenges for player-facing ML agents in modern games, including bottlenecks that span technical, design, and production concerns. It does not present empirical results but rather a structured analysis of the current landscape and future research directions needed for industry adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning holds significant promise for transforming game AI into more believable, adaptive characters. However, bridging the gap between research and commercial deployment requires addressing identified bottlenecks — which the authors frame as promising research directions — before RL-based game AI can achieve broad, cross-genre adoption in the video game industry.

title: An Information Theoretic Framework for Graph Novelty Generation via Latent Mixture Modeling
summary: We propose an information-theoretic framework for graph novelty generation, which aims to generate data that are distinct from existing patterns while preserving global structural consistency. Our approach embeds data into a latent space, models the latent distribution using finite mixture models, and generates novel samples by imposing explicit novelty and reliability conditions formulated in terms of description length. Specifically, novelty is enforced by requiring generated samples to be poorly explained by all existing mixture components, while reliability constrains their impact on the overall mixture structure under the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero with explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that the proposed method enables principled novelty generation with quantifiable risk.

AI.tldr: A framework for generating novel graph data using information theory: samples must be poorly explained by existing mixture components (novelty) while preserving global structure under the MDL principle (reliability), with theoretical guarantees on misclassification rates.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models lack principled mechanisms to explicitly control both the novelty of generated samples and their consistency with the global structure of the data distribution. The authors aim to fill this gap with a theoretically grounded framework.
AI.method: Graph data is embedded into a latent space and modeled with finite mixture models. Novel sample generation is governed by two MDL-based conditions: (1) the novelty condition requires that no existing mixture component explains the sample well (high description length), and (2) the reliability condition ensures the sample does not destabilize the overall mixture structure when incorporated. Theoretical convergence rates for misclassification probabilities are derived.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis proves that with appropriate threshold choices, the probabilities of misclassifying non-novel or unreliable samples converge to zero at explicit rates. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark graph datasets validate the framework's ability to generate principled novelty with quantifiable risk.
AI.conclusion: The proposed information-theoretic framework provides a principled approach to graph novelty generation with formal guarantees, bridging generative modeling and MDL-based model selection for controlled novelty synthesis.

title: Beyond Global Replanning: Hierarchical Recovery for Cross-Device Agent Systems
summary: Real-world computer-use tasks often span multiple applications and devices, requiring agents to coordinate heterogeneous environments under dynamic runtime failures. Existing multi-device agent systems support task decomposition and cross-device assignment, but recovery remains largely coarse-grained: when execution fails, they typically retry the same strategy, reassign the subtask, or revise the global plan, without systematically modeling the device-local strategy space. This limits their ability to distinguish failures that can be repaired within the current device from those that require cross-device replanning. We propose \textbf{H-RePlan}, a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents with unified API--CLI--GUI execution. H-RePlan equips each device with interchangeable execution strategies and separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning through a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{HeraBench}, a fault-injected benchmark that constructs cross-device workflows over Linux and Android devices and injects strategy- and device-level failures. Experiments show that H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines, achieving higher completion, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rates while reducing the token cost required for reliable end-to-end success. These results demonstrate that scope-aware hierarchical recovery is essential for robust multi-device agent execution.

AI.tldr: H-RePlan introduces a hierarchical replanning framework for multi-device agents that separates device-local strategy recovery from global replanning, using a compact cross-layer failure abstraction. Evaluated on the new HeraBench benchmark with fault-injected cross-device workflows (Linux + Android), it significantly outperforms coarse-grained baselines in completion rate, instruction adherence, and token efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-device agent systems handle task failures via coarse-grained recovery (retry same strategy, reassign subtask, or revise global plan) without distinguishing between failures solvable within the current device versus those requiring cross-device replanning. This limits robustness in dynamic, failure-prone multi-device environments.
AI.method: The authors propose H-RePlan, a hierarchical replanning framework with two key components: (1) each device is equipped with interchangeable execution strategies (unified API-CLI-GUI), enabling device-local strategy switching; (2) a compact cross-layer failure abstraction separates device-local strategy recovery from orchestrator-level global replanning. They also introduce HeraBench, a fault-injected benchmark constructing cross-device workflows over Linux and Android, injecting both strategy-level and device-level failures.
AI.result: H-RePlan substantially outperforms single-strategy and coarse-grained multi-device baselines across metrics of completion rate, instruction adherence, and perfect-pass rate, while reducing token cost for reliable end-to-end success.
AI.conclusion: Scope-aware hierarchical recovery — distinguishing device-local repairable failures from those requiring global replanning — is essential for robust multi-device agent execution in heterogeneous, fault-prone environments.

title: Flow Map Denoisers: Traversing the Distortion-Perception Plane for Inverse Problems
summary: Image restoration faces a fundamental tradeoff: methods that minimize error produce blurry reconstructions, while those that maximize perceptual quality yield sharp but less faithful images. Existing approaches either commit to a single operating point on this distortion perception (DP) frontier or require paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning of the sampler to access different points. We show that flow map models, a recent extension of flow matching for few-step sampling that learns an average field, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers that continuously spans the DP frontier. The lookahead parameter t acts as a control knob between the MMSE and perceptual regimes. For Gaussian targets, we prove that varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier; for natural images, we observe similar behavior empirically. Within a Plug-and-Play solver, the same mechanism extends to general inverse problems, where it controls a tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency. Despite the lack of exact optimality guarantees in this setting, a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both extremes. Extensive experiments on CelebA ($128\times 128$) and AFHQ ($256\times 256$) across several linear and nonlinear inverse tasks validate our findings.

AI.tldr: Flow map models, which learn an average flow field for few-step sampling, implicitly define a one-parameter family of denoisers controlled by a "lookahead" parameter t. This parameter continuously spans the distortion-perception (DP) frontier—from MMSE (blurry) to high perceptual quality (sharp but less faithful)—without requiring paired supervision, auxiliary models, or sampler tuning. For Gaussian targets, the authors prove optimality; for natural images, empirical results match or exceed specialized baselines on CelebA and AFHQ across linear and nonlinear inverse problems.
AI.motivation: Image restoration methods face a fundamental tradeoff between distortion (faithfulness) and perceptual quality. Existing approaches either fix a single point on this DP frontier or require cumbersome paired-data supervision, auxiliary models, or hyperparameter tuning to traverse it. The authors aim to provide a simple, principled mechanism to continuously span the entire DP frontier using a single trained model with a single scalar parameter.
AI.method: The method leverages flow map models—a few-step extension of flow matching that learns an "average" flow field. The key insight is that the lookahead parameter t in flow maps implicitly acts as a control knob between MMSE denoising (t=0) and perceptual sampling (t=1). The authors prove that for Gaussian targets, varying t exactly recovers the optimal DP frontier. For natural images, the same flow map is embedded within a Plug-and-Play (PnP) solver, where t controls the tradeoff between perceptual alignment and data consistency across general inverse problems.
AI.result: For Gaussian targets, varying t provably recovers the optimal DP frontier. On natural images (CelebA 128×128, AFHQ 256×256), a single trained flow map spans the DP tradeoff across multiple linear and nonlinear inverse tasks, matching or exceeding specialized baselines at both the MMSE and perceptual extremes.
AI.conclusion: Flow map models provide a simple, unified mechanism—via the lookahead parameter t—to continuously navigate the distortion-perception tradeoff in image restoration and general inverse problems, using a single model without extra supervision or tuning, with theoretical optimality in the Gaussian case and strong empirical performance on natural images.

title: StylisticBias: A Few Human Visual Cues Drive Most Social Biases in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the non-archival workshops AI4Good and Culture x AI at ICML 2026
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in personally and societally consequential settings, yet the visual cues that shape how these models judge people remain poorly understood. Prior work often compares different (groups of) individuals, making it difficult to separate appearance effects from identity differences. We introduce StylisticBias, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute-level social bias in MLLMs. We generate 500 photorealistic base faces and create about 50 single-attribute variations per face, producing about 25K images. This design keeps identity fixed and changes one visual attribute at a time. It lets us measure how specific cues shift model judgments. We evaluate six MLLMs across 25 binary social judgment scenarios. We find that age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. We further find that about 15 attributes account for nearly 80\% of the total variation, showing that bias is concentrated in a small set of visual cues. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments that are semantically aligned with appearance, especially socioeconomic and style-related judgments. We release StylisticBias as a benchmark for fine-grained bias evaluation in multimodal models. Code and dataset: https://github.com/timo-cavelius/StylisticBias and https://hf.co/datasets/shaghayegh/stylistic-bias-dataset.

AI.tldr: StylisticBias is a controlled benchmark using 25K photorealistic face images (500 base identities × ~50 single-attribute variations) to isolate how specific visual cues like age, body type, and fashion style bias MLLM social judgments. Key finding: ~15 attributes drive 80% of bias, with semantically aligned judgments (e.g., socioeconomic) most affected.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM bias evaluations compare different individuals, conflating identity differences with appearance effects. There is a need for a controlled framework that isolates how individual visual attributes (age, clothing, body type, etc.) shift model judgments while holding identity constant.
AI.method: The authors generate 500 photorealistic base faces and systematically vary ~50 single visual attributes per face (e.g., adding glasses, changing hairstyle, altering body type), yielding ~25K images. Six MLLMs are evaluated across 25 binary social judgment scenarios (e.g., "Is this person trustworthy?"). By keeping identity fixed and changing one attribute at a time, they measure the marginal effect of each cue on judgment shifts, then analyze variance partitioning and attribute-judgment semantic alignment.
AI.result: Age and body type dominate identity-level effects, while fashion style and other visual cues drive the largest attribute-level shifts. Approximately 15 attributes account for nearly 80% of total variation, indicating bias concentration. Sensitivity is strongest in judgments semantically aligned with appearance, particularly socioeconomic and style-related judgments.
AI.conclusion: Visual bias in MLLMs is concentrated in a small set of attributes and is most pronounced when the judgment domain semantically matches the visual cue. StylisticBias provides a fine-grained, identity-controlled benchmark for auditing and mitigating such biases in multimodal models.

title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
summary: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence as "lawful amplification of rare but valid futures" and proves that recursive self-simulation is both necessary and nearly sufficient for achieving high intelligence under this measure, making intelligence quantifiable across diverse systems from passive matter to LLMs.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous, universal, and measurable definition of intelligence grounded in physical law (thermodynamics), moving beyond vague or anthropocentric notions, and to identify the architectural prerequisites for intelligent behavior.
AI.method: The authors formalize intelligence thermodynamically using the concept of "rare-valid lift" — the ratio of probability of a valid future under the system's policy versus passive dynamics. They then mathematically prove a necessity theorem (high lift implies high-fidelity internal simulation) and a near-sufficiency theorem (high-fidelity simulation plus effective policy yields near-optimal lift), grounding both in recursive self-simulation where the system models a world that includes itself.
AI.result: Two central theorems: (1) Necessity — high rare-valid lift is impossible without the internal simulation identifying rare-valid futures with high fidelity; (2) Conditional near-sufficiency — when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Together, these establish recursive self-simulation as necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible architectural feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is mathematically required for high intelligence. The thermodynamic framework provides a universal scale for measuring intelligence across all systems.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling for Stable RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns large language models by training reward models on preference data and optimizing policies to maximize predicted rewards. However, this pipeline faces two fundamental challenges: (1) reward models cannot signal when their predictions are unreliable, since they usually act as deterministic point estimators; and (2) modern group-based policy optimization can amplify unreliable reward signals, as exemplified by GRPO's uniform treatment of rewards during advantage computation. As policies explore increasingly diverse responses, these two limitations create a critical vulnerability: unreliable reward estimates may be granted disproportionate influence, triggering severe reward hacking. We propose Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM), which equips reward models with calibrated uncertainty via quantile-based conformal prediction and reweights GRPO advantages through heteroscedastic variance decomposition. Experiments across HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF demonstrate that UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality compared to standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.

AI.tldr: UARM addresses reward hacking in RLHF by equipping reward models with calibrated uncertainty via conformal prediction and reweighting GRPO advantages using heteroscedastic variance decomposition, improving calibration, reducing reward hacking, and enhancing alignment.
AI.motivation: RLHF suffers from two key issues: (1) reward models are deterministic point estimators that cannot signal prediction unreliability, and (2) group-based policy optimization (specifically GRPO) treats all rewards uniformly during advantage computation, amplifying unreliable signals. These create a vulnerability where unreliable reward estimates gain disproportionate influence, triggering reward hacking.
AI.method: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Modeling (UARM) combines two components: (1) quantile-based conformal prediction to equip reward models with calibrated uncertainty estimates, and (2) heteroscedastic variance decomposition to reweight GRPO advantages, reducing the influence of high-uncertainty reward signals during policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on HelpSteer, UltraFeedback, and PKU-SafeRLHF datasets show UARM significantly improves reward model calibration, reduces reward hacking, and enhances downstream alignment quality versus standard GRPO and uncertainty-agnostic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating calibrated uncertainty into both reward modeling and advantage computation is an effective strategy for mitigating reward hacking in RLHF-based alignment, yielding more reliable and robust policy optimization.

title: Gender Bias in LLM Hiring Decisions: Evidence from a Japanese Context and Evaluation of Mitigation Strategies
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in hiring workflows, yet most research on gender bias in LLM hiring decisions has focused on English-language, Western-format resumes. This study examines whether pro-female gender bias extends to a Japanese corporate context and evaluates two practical mitigation strategies. Using a counterfactual resume design with 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes, 12 name pairs selected on linguistically grounded gender-signal criteria, and five state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B), we conducted 43,200 API calls across baseline, prompt instruction, and privacy filter conditions. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model confirms a significant pro-female bias across all five models, replicating Western findings in a non-Western context. A prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction produces no meaningful reduction in bias. A name-reliance analysis formally identifies the candidate name as the primary gender channel: removing the name from the prompt reduces the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. An unexpected incompatibility between the privacy filter and GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate, highlights a practical deployment challenge for name anonymization in LLM-assisted recruitment pipelines.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether LLMs exhibit pro-female gender bias when evaluating Japanese-format (rirekisho) resumes, and whether prompt instructions or name anonymization can mitigate it. Across five LLMs and 43,200 API calls, a significant pro-female bias was confirmed, prompt-level gender-neutrality instructions failed to reduce it, and name removal largely eliminated the bias — though a 42% refusal rate with GPT-4o's content safety filter revealed a deployment obstacle for anonymization in practice.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM gender bias research in hiring has been limited to English-language, Western-format resumes. The authors seek to determine whether previously documented pro-female bias replicates in a Japanese corporate context using authentic Japanese resume formats (rirekisho), and to evaluate practical bias mitigation strategies that could be deployed in real hiring pipelines.
AI.method: A counterfactual resume experiment was conducted using 60 Japanese rirekisho-format resumes paired with 12 gender-signaling name pairs (selected via linguistically grounded criteria). Five LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B) were tested across three conditions — baseline, prompt-level gender-neutrality instruction, and privacy filter (name removal) — yielding 43,200 API calls. A crossed random-effects linear mixed model was used to estimate the gender effect, complemented by a name-reliance analysis to isolate the name as the primary gender channel.
AI.result: A significant pro-female bias was confirmed across all five models, replicating Western findings in the Japanese context. The gender-neutrality prompt instruction produced no meaningful bias reduction. Name-reliance analysis identified the candidate name as the primary channel for gender bias: removing the name reduced the female effect by nearly its full magnitude. However, the privacy filter (name anonymization) triggered an incompatibility with GPT-4o's content safety filter, resulting in a 42% refusal rate — a practical deployment barrier.
AI.conclusion: Pro-female gender bias in LLM hiring evaluations generalizes beyond English/Western contexts to Japanese rirekisho-format resumes. Simple prompt-based debiasing instructions are ineffective, while name anonymization effectively eliminates bias but introduces operational hurdles — such as content safety filter conflicts — that must be addressed before real-world deployment in LLM-assisted recruitment.

title: Enhancing Graph Neural Networks Using Proximity Graphs for Dust Source Emission Forecasting
summary:
Accurate prediction of dust source emissions is critical for mitigating the significant environmental and health hazards posed by dust storms. Traditional forecasting methods often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of these phenomena.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that proximity graphs enable Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively model the intricate spatial and temporal relationships between data points. Specifically, we use proximity graphs--such as Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor graph, and Yao graph--as the input for GNNs (including GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Graph Attention Networks) to perform message passing.
  Our approach highlights the effectiveness of integrating proximity graphs with GNNs for robust and accurate dust source forecasting. To emphasize the importance of proximity graph representations, we compare our method against GNNs using random graphs for message passing. The results show that GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform those with random graphs and are also far superior to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model in dust source emission forecasting.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating proximity graphs (Delaunay, Gabriel, k-NN, Yao) with GNNs (GraphSAGE, GCN, GAT) for dust source emission forecasting, demonstrating significant superiority over random-graph GNNs and LSTM baselines.
AI.motivation: Traditional dust storm forecasting methods fail to capture complex spatiotemporal dynamics of dust source emissions. There is a need for models that can effectively represent and learn the intricate spatial and temporal relationships inherent in these environmental phenomena.
AI.method: The authors use proximity graphs—Delaunay triangulation, Gabriel graph, k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) graph, and Yao graph—as input structures for GNNs. Three GNN architectures are employed: GraphSAGE, Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), and Graph Attention Networks (GAT). Message passing is performed over these proximity-based graph topologies. For comparison, GNNs using random graphs and a standard LSTM model serve as baselines.
AI.result: GNNs with proximity graphs significantly outperform GNNs using random graphs for message passing. Both proximity-graph GNN approaches are far superior to the LSTM model in dust source emission forecasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: Integrating proximity graphs with GNNs provides a robust and accurate framework for dust source emission forecasting. The choice of graph representation is critical—proximity-based graph structures effectively capture the underlying spatiotemporal dynamics that random graphs and traditional sequential models (LSTM) fail to model.

title: Navigating Unreliable Parametric and Contextual Knowledge: Explicit Knowledge Conflict Resolution for LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of language-based tasks by leveraging both extensive parametric knowledge and in-context learning ability, enabling them to incorporate external information provided in the input prompt. However, the integration of external knowledge can introduce conflicts, not only between the model's internal parametric knowledge and the external information, but also among multiple pieces of external contexts. Existing approaches typically assume that either the model or the provided context is reliable, overlooking the possibility that both sources may contain errors, and avoid conflicts by privileging one source over the other, rather than actively resolving inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework MACR for LLM knowledge conflict resolution that moves beyond the conventional binary choice paradigm and incorporates an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism based on a multi-agent reasoning approach. Specifically, we first propose an adaptive knowledge assessment and retrieval approach that employs a modified semantic entropy measure to quantify an LLM's confidence in its answer to a given query. Based on this confidence estimation, MACR either externalizes the model's internal knowledge as textual representations or retrieves relevant external knowledge when internal knowledge is insufficient, generating basic contexts for subsequent reasoning. Then we introduce an inductive multi-agent reasoning framework with three specialized agents that, respectively, induce explicit rules, analyze potential conflicts, and resolve inconsistencies across all available contexts. Empirical results demonstrate that MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks, while also providing interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.

AI.tldr: MACR proposes a multi-agent reasoning framework for resolving knowledge conflicts in LLMs, moving beyond binary source selection to actively resolve inconsistencies among both internal parametric knowledge and multiple external contexts, using adaptive confidence estimation via semantic entropy and three specialized agents for rule induction, conflict analysis, and resolution.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM knowledge conflict resolution methods treat either the model or external context as reliable (binary choice paradigm), ignoring that both sources can contain errors and that conflicts can arise among multiple external contexts. They avoid rather than actively resolve inconsistencies.
AI.method: MACR has two stages: (1) Adaptive knowledge assessment using modified semantic entropy to estimate LLM confidence, externalizing internal knowledge or retrieving external knowledge accordingly; (2) An inductive multi-agent framework with three specialized agents — one inducing explicit rules, one analyzing potential conflicts, and one resolving inconsistencies across all contexts through reasoning.
AI.result: MACR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across benchmarks and provides interpretable resolutions of explicit conflicts.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent reasoning framework with explicit conflict-resolution mechanisms and adaptive knowledge assessment is more effective than binary-choice paradigms for handling knowledge conflicts in LLMs, offering both superior performance and interpretability.

title: When, Where, and How: Adaptive Binning for Tabular Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Medical tabular data are ubiquitous in clinical research, but deep learning for tables remains underexplored because reliable labels often require costly expert adjudication, even though structured clinical variables are routinely available in tabular form. Self-supervised learning can leverage these unlabeled tables, and recent binning-based pretexts offer a promising inductive bias, but existing objectives fix a single global quantile discretization and apply feature-agnostic supervision. We propose Adaptive Binning, a training-adaptive discretization pretext for tabular SSL that couples discretization to learning through a feature-wise coarse-to-fine curriculum. Motivated by the spectral bias of neural networks and the principles of curriculum learning, our method progressively refines discretization per feature upon plateau detection and selects representation-aware splits to jointly improve value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective unifies categorical reconstruction with ordinal supervision for numerical features, and experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols show consistent gains for linear probing and fine-tuning without dataset-specific discretization tuning. We further introduce a medical tabular SSL benchmark with standardized protocols to support reproducible progress in this underexplored domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/labhai/Adaptive-Binning.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Binning proposes a self-supervised learning method for medical tabular data that uses a training-adaptive, feature-wise coarse-to-fine discretization curriculum, outperforming fixed global quantile binning on downstream linear probing and fine-tuning tasks.
AI.motivation: Medical tabular data is abundant but labeled samples are scarce due to costly expert adjudication. Existing self-supervised methods for tables use binning-based pretexts with a single fixed global quantile discretization and feature-agnostic supervision, missing the opportunity to adapt discretization to learned representations during training.
AI.method: Adaptive Binning couples discretization to representation learning through a per-feature coarse-to-fine curriculum. The method detects plateaus in training and progressively refines bin boundaries using representation-aware splits that jointly optimize value-space concentration and representation-space coherence. A heterogeneity-aware objective combines categorical reconstruction loss with ordinal supervision for numerical features. The approach is grounded in spectral bias theory and curriculum learning principles.
AI.result: Experiments on public medical tabular datasets under unified evaluation protocols demonstrate consistent improvements over fixed-binning baselines for both linear probing and fine-tuning, without requiring dataset-specific discretization tuning.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive Binning advances tabular self-supervised learning by making discretization a learned, adaptive process rather than a fixed preprocessing step. The authors also contribute a standardized medical tabular SSL benchmark to facilitate reproducible progress in the domain.
