title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
summary: Student-generated drawings are widely used in science education to assess learners' conceptual understanding in modeling-based tasks aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). However, scoring such drawings requires expert human judgment to interpret complex visual representations, making large-scale assessment costly to implement and sustain in classroom settings. In this work, we study automated scoring of student-generated scientific drawings using a vision-based model. We evaluate a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation and propose a confidence-aware scoring framework that derives response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal enables selective automation by scoring high-confidence responses automatically while deferring uncertain cases for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed approach improves scoring reliability while supporting a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk, highlighting the value of confidence-aware methods for trustworthy educational assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a confidence-aware automated scoring framework using a parameter-efficient Vision Transformer (ViT) to assess student-generated scientific drawings. The method uses test-time predictive distributions to derive response-level confidence, enabling selective automation: high-confidence responses are scored automatically while uncertain cases are deferred for human review. Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items demonstrate improved scoring reliability and a practical trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
AI.motivation: Scoring student-generated scientific drawings in NGSS-aligned modeling-based tasks requires expert human judgment, making large-scale assessment costly and unsustainable in classroom settings. Existing automated approaches lack mechanisms to handle uncertainty, which limits their trustworthiness for educational assessment.
AI.method: The authors employ a Vision Transformer (ViT) with parameter-efficient adaptation for automated scoring. They introduce a confidence-aware scoring framework that computes response-level confidence from test-time predictive distributions. This confidence signal drives selective automation: responses with high confidence are scored automatically, while low-confidence responses are deferred to human raters, creating a human-AI collaboration pipeline.
AI.result: Experiments on six NGSS-aligned middle school assessment items show that the proposed confidence-aware scoring framework improves scoring reliability compared to naive automation. The method enables a tunable trade-off between automated coverage (proportion of auto-scored responses) and scoring risk (error rate on automated decisions).
AI.conclusion: Confidence-aware methods add significant value for trustworthy educational assessment by enabling selective automation. The framework balances efficiency gains with scoring reliability, making automated assessment of complex scientific drawings more viable for real classroom deployment.

title: Neural Additive and Basis Models with Feature Selection and Interactions
comment: Accepted at PAKDD 2024. Code is available at https://github.com/shiralab/NAM-FS
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit attractive performance in various fields but often suffer from low interpretability. The neural additive model (NAM) and its variant called the neural basis model (NBM) use neural networks (NNs) as nonlinear shape functions in generalized additive models (GAMs). Both models are highly interpretable and exhibit good performance and flexibility for NN training. NAM and NBM can provide and visualize the contribution of each feature to the prediction owing to GAM-based architectures. However, when using two-input NNs to consider feature interactions or when applying them to high-dimensional datasets, training NAM and NBM becomes intractable due to the increase in the computational resources required. This paper proposes incorporating the feature selection mechanism into NAM and NBM to resolve computational bottlenecks. We introduce the feature selection layer in both models and update the selection weights during training. Our method is simple and can reduce computational costs and model sizes compared to vanilla NAM and NBM. In addition, it enables us to use two-input NNs even in high-dimensional datasets and capture feature interactions. We demonstrate that the proposed models are computationally efficient compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, and they exhibit better or comparable performance with state-of-the-art GAMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes adding a feature selection mechanism to Neural Additive Models (NAM) and Neural Basis Models (NBM) to overcome computational bottlenecks when using two-input neural networks or high-dimensional data. A trainable feature selection layer is introduced to reduce computational costs and model size while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: NAM and NBM offer strong interpretability through GAM-based architectures, but training becomes computationally intractable when incorporating feature interactions via two-input neural networks or when applied to high-dimensional datasets. There is a need to reduce computational overhead while preserving interpretability and performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce a feature selection layer integrated into both NAM and NBM architectures. The layer contains learnable selection weights that are updated during training, enabling the models to automatically identify and retain relevant features while pruning irrelevant ones. This mechanism reduces computational costs and model sizes, and enables the use of two-input neural networks even in high-dimensional settings to capture feature interactions.
AI.result: The proposed models demonstrate improved computational efficiency compared to vanilla NAM and NBM, with smaller model sizes. They achieve better or comparable predictive performance relative to state-of-the-art GAMs.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a feature selection layer into NAM and NBM effectively mitigates computational bottlenecks, enabling scalable training with two-input NNs on high-dimensional data while maintaining high interpretability and competitive performance.

title: Lagrange: An Open-Vocabulary, Energy-Based Sparse Framework for Generalized End-to-End Driving
summary: Scaling end-to-end autonomous driving to complex, open-world environments requires perceptual models that generalize to anomalous scenarios and planners that produce kinematically valid trajectories. Existing paradigms face a distinct dichotomy between representational efficiency and generalization capacity. Dense models (e.g., occupancy networks), while geometrically robust, incur critical computational bottlenecks and struggle with high-level semantic reasoning. Conversely, sparse, query-based planners are efficient but reliant on closed-set definitions, rendering them vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) events. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer open-vocabulary reasoning, their autoregressive, discrete token generation fundamentally conflicts with the continuous, high-frequency control requirements of vehicle dynamics. To address this, we propose Lagrange, an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework based on Masked Latent Fields (MLF). Rather than relying on dense volumetric reconstructions or closed-set query mechanisms, Lagrange exploits Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. We introduce an intent-driven masked cross-attention module that temporally filters irrelevant entities, decoding the attended tokens into an implicit continuous energy field defined over spatial coordinates. By framing decision-making as a Lagrangian action minimization problem spanning this energy field, we enforce strict compliance with vehicle kinematics while executing collision avoidance. Extensive offline evaluations on both standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange establishes a promising framework for robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible open-world autonomy.

AI.tldr: Lagrange proposes an open-vocabulary, computationally sparse driving framework using Masked Latent Fields (MLF) that bridges dense geometric representations and sparse query-based methods. It leverages VLMs to encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic tokens, filters them via intent-driven masked cross-attention, and formulates planning as Lagrangian action minimization over an implicit energy field, achieving kinematically feasible open-world autonomous driving.
AI.motivation: Existing end-to-end autonomous driving approaches exhibit a fundamental trade-off: dense models (e.g., occupancy networks) are geometrically robust but computationally expensive and semantically limited; sparse query-based planners are efficient but fail on out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios due to closed-set assumptions. Meanwhile, VLA models offer open-vocabulary reasoning but their autoregressive discrete token generation is incompatible with continuous vehicle control. A unified framework reconciling open-vocabulary perception, computational sparsity, and kinematically feasible planning is lacking.
AI.method: Lagrange introduces Masked Latent Fields (MLF): (1) VLMs encode class-agnostic object proposals into continuous semantic visual tokens. (2) An intent-driven masked cross-attention module temporally filters irrelevant entities. (3) The attended tokens are decoded into an implicit continuous energy field over spatial coordinates. (4) Decision-making is formulated as Lagrangian action minimization over this energy field, enforcing vehicle kinematic constraints and collision avoidance.
AI.result: Extensive offline evaluations on standard (nuScenes) and long-tail (CODA) benchmarks demonstrate that Lagrange achieves robust, interpretable, and kinematically feasible performance in open-world autonomous driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Lagrange establishes a promising framework for open-world autonomy by successfully integrating open-vocabulary semantic reasoning with continuous, kinematically valid trajectory generation, overcoming the limitations of both dense and sparse existing paradigms.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Squeeze-Excitation-like Attention
summary: We introduce SEA-PINN, a novel architecture that incorporates a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks to dynamically recalibrate the importance of neurons across layers. A key feature of SEA-PINN is its highly stable initialization. On 17 out of 20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN exhibit nearly negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, establishing a quasi-deterministic and favorable starting point for optimization. Notably, without employing Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activation functions, SEA-PINN attained competitive accuracy (83\% vs. 90\% improvement relative to FNN-PINN on the high-frequency case 7) as compared with TSA-PINN-a model specifically engineered for high-frequency problems via learnable frequencies in sinusoidal activations. Furthermore, integrating SEA-PINN into TSA-PINN boosted performance by 42.49\%. These results underscore SEA-PINN as a lightweight plug-in module that enhances nonlinear representation power, promotes more robust and efficient convergence, and strengthens the overall reliability of physics-informed learning.

AI.tldr: SEA-PINN introduces a Squeeze-Excitation-like attention mechanism into physics-informed neural networks, achieving highly stable initialization with near-zero variance across 17/20 benchmarks, competitive accuracy on high-frequency problems without Fourier features, and serves as an effective plug-and-play module that enhances convergence and reliability.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from poor initialization, unstable training dynamics, and limited capacity for high-frequency function approximation. Existing solutions like Fourier feature embeddings or periodic activations add architectural complexity. The authors aim to address these issues with a lightweight, plug-in attention mechanism that provides stable initialization and improved nonlinear representation without specialized frequency-engineering components.
AI.method: SEA-PINN integrates a Squeeze-Excitation-like channel-wise attention module into the PINN architecture. This mechanism dynamically recalibrates per-neuron importance across layers by learning channel-wise scaling factors. A key design element is a carefully crafted initialization scheme that yields highly stable, quasi-deterministic starting conditions. The approach is evaluated both as a standalone enhancement over standard FNN-PINNs and as a complementary module integrated into TSA-PINN (which uses learnable sinusoidal activation frequencies).
AI.result: On 17/20 benchmark problems, SEA-PINN showed near-negligible variance and significantly reduced initial loss, providing a quasi-deterministic optimization starting point. Without Fourier features or periodic activations, it achieved 83% improvement over FNN-PINN on a high-frequency case (case 7), compared to TSA-PINN's 90%-demonstrating competitive high-frequency capability. When integrated into TSA-PINN, performance improved by an additional 42.49%, confirming its utility as a complementary plug-in module.
AI.conclusion: SEA-PINN is a lightweight, plug-and-play attention module that enhances nonlinear representational capacity, promotes robust and efficient convergence, and improves the overall reliability of physics-informed learning. Its strong initialization properties and synergy with existing methods make it a practical enhancement for PINN architectures.

title: Leveraging systems' non-linearity to tackle the scarcity of data in the design of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems
summary: Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) allows for the efficient building of Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems (IFDS). On the other hand, DTL methods still heavily rely on large amounts of labelled data. Obtaining such an amount of data can be challenging when dealing with machines or structures faults. This document proposes a novel approach to the design of vibration-based IFDS using DTL in condition of strong data scarcity. A periodic multi-excitation level procedure leveraging intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems is used to produce images that can be conveniently analysed by pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to diagnose faults. A new data visualization method and its augmentation technique are proposed in this paper to tackle the typical lack of data encountered during the design of IFDS. Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure provides effective support for the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Proposes a deep transfer learning method for vibration-based intelligent fault diagnosis under strong data scarcity, using a periodic multi-excitation procedure combined with a novel data visualization and augmentation technique, validated on a railway pantograph.
AI.motivation: Deep transfer learning methods for fault diagnosis still require large amounts of labeled data, which are difficult to obtain for machines or structural faults. This motivates the need for effective IFDS design under conditions of strong data scarcity.
AI.method: A periodic multi-excitation level procedure that exploits intrinsic non-linearities of real-world systems to generate images. These images are analyzed using pre-trained CNNs via transfer learning. A new data visualization method and an augmentation technique are proposed to address data scarcity.
AI.result: Experimental validation on a railway pantograph structure demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DTL-based IFDS method, leveraging non-linear system excitation and novel visualization/augmentation techniques, is effective for fault diagnosis under strong data scarcity conditions.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Score Matching in Gaussian Mixtures via Reverse Fisher Divergence
summary: The score matching problem is a central training objective in modern generative modeling, diffusion models, fitting unnormalized statistical models, and inverse problems. A standard approach is to minimize the forward Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the teacher distribution. However, recent results show that even in simple Gaussian mixture model settings, this objective can lead to undesirable and initialization-dependent convergence behavior. In this paper, we study an alternative objective: the reverse Fisher divergence, where the expectation is taken with respect to the student distribution. We analyze gradient descent (GD) for fitting Gaussian mixture models and show that this change in the objective leads to significantly better optimization properties. First, when the teacher distribution is a single Gaussian and the student is a Gaussian mixture model with fixed weights and identity covariances, we prove the global convergence of GD from arbitrary initializations. Second, we extend the analysis to the case where the teacher is also a Gaussian mixture model and prove global convergence guarantees under a global random initialization scheme and a $\widetildeΩ(1)$-separation assumption on the target means. In particular, with high probability, each student component converges near its closest teacher component, and we provide conditions under which the student distribution converges in total variation distance. Our proofs rely on a new Lyapunov-based analysis of the gradient descent dynamics, showing that the reverse Fisher divergence has a much more favorable optimization landscape than the forward Fisher divergence.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes gradient descent optimization under the reverse Fisher divergence for fitting Gaussian mixture models, proving global convergence guarantees from arbitrary initializations (single Gaussian teacher) and under separation assumptions (mixture teacher), demonstrating superior optimization properties compared to the standard forward Fisher divergence used in score matching.
AI.motivation: Standard score matching using the forward Fisher divergence—where expectation is taken over the teacher distribution—can exhibit poor, initialization-dependent convergence even in simple Gaussian mixture settings. This motivates studying the reverse Fisher divergence (expectation over the student distribution) as an alternative training objective with better optimization properties.
AI.method: The authors analyze continuous-time gradient descent (GD) dynamics for minimizing reverse Fisher divergence. They develop a Lyapunov-based analysis framework to prove global convergence. Two settings are studied: (1) teacher is a single Gaussian, student is a GMM with fixed weights and identity covariances; (2) teacher is also a GMM, with global random initialization and a $\widetilde{\Omega}(1)$-separation condition on target means. Convergence is measured in parameter space and total variation distance.
AI.result: For a single Gaussian teacher, GD converges globally from any initialization. For a GMM teacher, under random initialization and mean separation, each student component converges near its closest teacher component with high probability, and the student distribution converges in total variation distance. The reverse Fisher divergence exhibits a significantly more favorable optimization landscape than the forward variant.
AI.conclusion: Switching from forward to reverse Fisher divergence dramatically improves optimization guarantees for score matching with Gaussian mixtures. The Lyapunov analysis reveals that the reverse objective's landscape enables global convergence, suggesting it is a practically and theoretically preferable alternative for training generative models.

title: SoftSkill: Behavioral Compression for Contextual Adaptation
summary: Agent skills are commonly deployed as natural-language Markdown files that encode answer policies, evidence-use habits, and task procedures. These files are readable and portable, but they are consumed indirectly: for each task instance, a frozen language model must translate a long textual artifact into generation-time behavior. This paper asks whether a natural-language skill can instead initialize a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model remains frozen. We propose SoftSkill, a frozen-backbone method that tunes such soft skills with next-token prediction and deploys them as latent behavioral priors at inference time. In our main single-round setting, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Relative to SkillOpt, SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 points on LiveMath, while replacing hundreds to thousands of Markdown skill tokens with a few virtual tokens. We further study agentic execution as a harder boundary case, where sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior. More broadly, the results suggest that some task skills are better treated not as additional Markdown to be reinterpreted at inference time, but as compact latent controls over how a frozen model enters the task.

AI.tldr: SoftSkill proposes replacing verbose natural-language Markdown skill files with compact, tunable continuous prefixes (soft skills) that steer a frozen LLM's behavior at inference time, achieving significant accuracy gains over both no-skill and full-skill baselines while using far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Agent skills are currently deployed as long natural-language Markdown files that a frozen model must re-interpret for every task instance, which is inefficient (hundreds to thousands of tokens) and relies on the model's ability to faithfully translate text into behavior. The authors ask whether these skills can instead be encoded as compact continuous context objects that directly condition the frozen model.
AI.method: SoftSkill initializes a compact continuous prefix (e.g., 32 virtual tokens) from a natural-language skill description, then fine-tunes a soft delta on top via next-token prediction while keeping the base model entirely frozen. At inference time, this learned latent prefix is prepended as a behavioral prior, replacing the original Markdown skill text. The method is evaluated in single-round settings (SearchQA, LiveMath, DocVQA) and in harder multi-step agentic execution with sparse trajectory imitation.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-4B, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix improves over no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 points on LiveMath, and 1.3 points on DocVQA. Compared to SkillOpt (full Markdown skill), SoftSkill improves accuracy by 5.2 (SearchQA) and 12.5 (LiveMath) points, while using only a few virtual tokens instead of hundreds to thousands of Markdown tokens. In agentic execution, sparse trajectory imitation provides useful signal but does not yet robustly compress long-horizon procedural behavior.
AI.conclusion: Some task skills are more effective when treated as compact latent controls over a frozen model's task entry behavior, rather than as additional Markdown text to be reinterpreted at inference time. This suggests a shift in how agent skills should be represented and deployed.

title: On the Oracle Complexity of Interpolation-Based Gradient Descent
summary: Recent work on first-order optimizers for empirical risk minimization (ERM) has suggested that smoothness of ERM loss functions in the training data, rather than in the optimization parameters, can be leveraged to improve the oracle complexity of gradient descent (GD) methods. In this paper, we propose an inexact gradient method, piecewise polynomial interpolation-based gradient descent (PPI-GD), which approximates the full gradient in each iteration by querying the first-order oracle at equidistant points in the data domain to construct polynomial interpolants of the resulting gradient samples over appropriately sized patches of the data domain. We analyze the oracle complexity of PPI-GD for strongly convex and non-convex loss functions when the data space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples, and find it to outperform several GD variants in key regimes when the loss function is sufficiently smooth. Furthermore, our analysis extends several techniques from the error analysis of bicubic spline interpolants to the setting of $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants which may be of independent interest in interpolation analysis.

AI.tldr: PPI-GD is an inexact gradient method that constructs polynomial interpolants from equidistant first-order oracle queries over patches of the data domain, achieving improved oracle complexity over standard GD variants for smooth, strongly convex and non-convex ERM when data dimension is polylogarithmic in sample size.
AI.motivation: Leverage data-space smoothness (rather than parameter-space smoothness) of ERM loss functions to improve the oracle complexity of gradient-based optimization, outperforming existing GD variants in regimes where loss functions are sufficiently smooth.
AI.method: The authors propose Piecewise Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent (PPI-GD), which partitions the data domain into patches, queries the first-order oracle at equidistant points within each patch, constructs $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolants of the gradient samples, and uses these interpolated approximations as inexact gradients in each GD iteration. Complexity analysis extends bicubic spline error analysis techniques to $d$-variate tensor product polynomial interpolation.
AI.result: PPI-GD achieves improved oracle complexity over several GD variants for both strongly convex and non-convex smooth ERM loss functions, provided the data-space dimension is bounded by a polylogarithmic function of the number of training samples.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting data-space smoothness via piecewise polynomial interpolation yields provable oracle complexity gains for gradient descent in ERM. The interpolation analysis techniques developed for $d$-variate tensor product polynomials may have broader independent interest.

title: Automating SKILL.md Generation for Computer-Using Agents via Interaction Trajectory Mining
summary: Explicit skill libraries make computer-using agents easier to inspect, but it remains unclear whether such libraries can be mined from interaction data in a way that improves downstream policies. We study this question through a three-stage pipeline that segments GUI trajectories, clusters segments into candidate skills, and trains a skill-aware policy from the resulting annotations. The mined clusters are readable on the source benchmark: five of eight clusters have at least 0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels. However, readability does not imply transfer. GRPO improves IW skill-step accuracy only from 18.5\% to 20.5\%, leaves BrowseComp+ essentially unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency priors on key source-domain metrics. We therefore present the method as a diagnostic study: trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether skill libraries mined from GUI interaction trajectories can improve downstream agent policies. The three-stage pipeline (segment, cluster, train) produces readable clusters with high purity against ground-truth labels, but these clusters fail to yield meaningful policy improvements, revealing a gap between inspectability and transfer.
AI.motivation: Explicit skill libraries enhance agent interpretability, but it is unknown whether skill structures can be automatically mined from interaction data in a way that actually benefits downstream policy learning. The work aims to diagnose this gap between skill discovery and policy improvement.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) segment GUI trajectories into sub-sequences using a boundary detector, (2) cluster these segments into candidate skill libraries in an orderless representation space, and (3) train a skill-aware policy (using GRPO) conditioned on the resulting cluster annotations. Evaluation spans source-domain purity against InteraSkill Workflows labels and downstream task accuracy on InteraSkill and BrowseComp+.
AI.result: Five of eight mined clusters achieve ≥0.95 purity against InteraSkill Workflows ground-truth labels, demonstrating readability. However, GRPO with mined skills improves InteraSkill skill-step accuracy only marginally (18.5% → 20.5%), leaves BrowseComp+ unchanged, and underperforms trivial frequency-based priors on key source-domain metrics.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory mining can expose inspectable skill structure, but the current components — boundary detector, orderless segment representation, and offline reward model — are insufficient for reliable cross-domain policy improvement. The work is framed as a diagnostic study highlighting this fundamental gap.

title: Matching Markets meet Cumulative Prospect Theory: Towards Optimal and Adversarially Robust Learning
summary: We study a multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem in the competitive setup with two-sided matching markets under a human centric decision making model. To capture human preferences, we use cumulative prospect theory (CPT) that weighs the actions of the agent in a nonlinear fashion using a ($α$-Hölder continuous) weight function. CPT has been widely used in behavioral economics and risk sensitive machine learning to emulate human preferences. We analyze the state-of-the-art learning algorithm with CPT weight distorted rewards and obtain a player optimal regret of $\mathcal{O}(K\log T \left(\frac{1}Δ\right)^{2/α})$, where $K$ denotes the number of arms, $T$ is the learning horizon, and $Δ$ represents (suitably defined) players' minimum preference gap. Noticing the dependence on $Δ$ to be sub-optimal, we further improve this regret by judiciously selecting the active set of arms during exploration, which removes the dependence on $K$ in the dominant term and achieves an improved (optimal) regret guarantees in the setting where the number of arms $K$ is significantly larger than the number of players $N$. In addition, we consider adversarial markets where the observed rewards of the agents may be corrupted. We propose and analyze algorithms for robust markets with CPT as risk sensitive measure in both settings where the total corruption budget is known and where it is unknown, and establish logarithmic player-optimal regret guarantees in both cases.

AI.tldr: This paper studies competitive multi-agent multi-armed bandits with two-sided matching, incorporating human decision-making via Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT). It provides an initial regret bound of O(K log T (1/Δ)^{2/α}), then improves it by active arm set selection to remove K-dependence. It further considers adversarial corruption, proposing robust algorithms with logarithmic regret under both known and unknown corruption budgets.
AI.motivation: Traditional bandit models assume rational, expected utility-maximizing agents, which poorly captures real human decision-making. CPT better models human preferences through nonlinear probability weighting and loss aversion. Incorporating CPT into competitive multi-agent bandits with matching markets bridges behavioral economics and online learning, yielding more realistic models for applications like online advertising, labor markets, and recommendation systems.
AI.method: The authors model a multi-agent multi-armed bandit with two-sided matching where agents' rewards are distorted by a CPT weight function (α-Hölder continuous). They first analyze a state-of-the-art learning algorithm under CPT-distorted rewards, establishing regret bounds. To improve sub-optimal Δ-dependence, they propose judicious active arm set selection during exploration, removing K-dependence when K ≫ N. For adversarial markets, they design robust algorithms for both known and unknown total corruption budgets, using CPT as a risk-sensitive measure to maintain logarithmic regret.
AI.result: (1) Initial player-optimal regret: O(K log T (1/Δ)^{2/α}). (2) Improved regret via active arm selection: removes K-dependence in the dominant term, achieving optimal guarantees when K ≫ N. (3) Robust algorithms under adversarial corruption: logarithmic player-optimal regret in both known and unknown corruption budget settings.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating CPT into competitive multi-agent bandits with matching yields tractable regret guarantees. Active arm set selection can mitigate sub-optimal dependence on the minimum preference gap Δ, and robust algorithms can handle adversarial reward corruption without sacrificing logarithmic regret. The work bridges behavioral economics and multi-agent online learning.

title: Rethinking Shrinkage Bias in LLM FP4 Pretraining: Geometric Origin, Systemic Impact, and UFP4 Recipe
summary: FP4 training promises substantial reductions in memory and computation cost for LLM pretraining, yet current FP4 hardware paths and recipes, including NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin-class systems and AMD MI350-series GPUs, remain centered on E2M1 data elements. In this study, we identify a fundamental limitation of that choice: non-uniform formats such as E2M1 inherently suffer from Shrinkage Bias, a systematic negative rounding error caused by the geometric asymmetry of their representable bins. We show that this bias accumulates multiplicatively across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), providing a unified explanation for the training instability observed in existing E2M1-based FP4 recipes. In contrast, uniform grids (E1M2/INT4) bypass this grid-geometry error and better convert the improved bucket utilization from RHT into higher quantization quality. Based on this finding, we propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit training recipe that applies RHT to all three training GEMMs while restricting stochastic rounding to dY alone. On Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B long-run pretraining, UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation than strong E2M1-based baselines, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies. Our results suggest that future accelerators should support E1M2/INT4-style uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

AI.tldr: E2M1, the current FP4 standard, suffers from "Shrinkage Bias" — a systematic negative rounding error from its non-uniform bin geometry. This bias accumulates across layers and is amplified by Random Hadamard Transform (RHT), explaining FP4 training instability. The authors propose UFP4, a uniform 4-bit recipe (E1M2/INT4) with RHT applied to all three GEMMs and stochastic rounding restricted to dY, achieving superior BF16-relative loss on models up to 124B.
AI.motivation: Current FP4 hardware (NVIDIA Blackwell/Rubin, AMD MI350) and training recipes are built around the E2M1 format, yet FP4 pretraining remains unstable. The authors aim to identify the root cause of this instability and propose a principled solution — pointing to a fundamental grid-geometry flaw in non-uniform formats that has been overlooked.
AI.method: The authors analytically identify "Shrinkage Bias" as a systematic negative rounding error inherent to non-uniform formats like E2M1, caused by geometric asymmetry of representable bins. They show this bias accumulates multiplicatively layer-over-layer and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform (RHT). They then propose UFP4: a uniform 4-bit training recipe using E1M2/INT4 grids, applying RHT to all three training GEMMs (forward, backward, update), with stochastic rounding limited solely to the output gradient (dY). Validation is performed via long-run pretraining on Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, and MoE 124B models, supported by scaling-law analysis and ablation studies.
AI.result: UFP4 consistently achieves lower BF16-relative loss degradation compared to strong E2M1-based baselines across all model scales (Dense 1.5B, MoE 7.9B, MoE 124B). Scaling-law analysis and ablation studies confirm the benefit of uniform grids + RHT-on-all-GEMMs + dY-only stochastic rounding.
AI.conclusion: The Shrinkage Bias inherent to E2M1 is a first-order obstacle to stable FP4 pretraining. Uniform 4-bit formats (E1M2/INT4) avoid this geometric error and better exploit RHT's bucket utilization improvements. The authors recommend that future AI accelerators natively support uniform 4-bit grids as first-class training primitives alongside E2M1.

title: SL-S4Wave: Self-Supervised Learning of Physiological Waveforms with Structured State Space Models
summary: Modeling long-sequence medical time series data, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), poses significant challenges due to high sampling rates, multichannel signal complexity, inherent noise, and limited labeled data. While recent self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, based on various encoder architectures such as convolutional neural networks, have been proposed to learn representations from unlabeled data, they often fall short in capturing long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. Structured state space models (S4) excel at long-sequence modeling, but existing S4 architectures fail to capture the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms. In this work, we propose SL-S4Wave, a self-supervised learning framework that combines contrastive learning with a tailored encoder built on structured state space models. The encoder incorporates multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels, enabling the capture of both fine-grained local patterns and long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SL-S4Wave (1) consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines in a challenging arrhythmia detection task, (2) achieves high performance with significantly fewer labeled examples, showcasing strong label efficiency, and (3) maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, highlighting its capacity to model complex temporal dynamics in long sequences that most existing approaches fail to efficiently model, and (4) transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types, underscoring its robust cross-domain generalization. We additionally evaluate SL-S4Wave on multiple EEG tasks, achieving superior performance over strong baselines, demonstrating generalizability of our approach beyond cardiac waveforms.

AI.tldr: SL-S4Wave is a self-supervised learning framework that integrates contrastive learning with a novel S4-based encoder featuring multi-scale global convolution, designed to effectively model noisy, high-resolution multichannel physiological waveforms like ECG and EEG by capturing both local patterns and long-range dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing SSL methods for medical time series (e.g., ECG) struggle to capture long-range dependencies and noise-invariant features. While S4 models excel at long-sequence modeling, current S4 architectures fail to handle the unique characteristics of multichannel physiological waveforms.
AI.method: The authors propose SL-S4Wave, combining contrastive self-supervised learning with a tailored S4-based encoder. The encoder employs multi-layer global convolution using multiscale subkernels to capture fine-grained local patterns alongside long-range temporal dependencies in noisy, high-resolution multichannel waveforms.
AI.result: SL-S4Wave consistently outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and SSL baselines on arrhythmia detection, achieves strong label efficiency with far fewer labeled examples, maintains robust performance on long waveform segments, and transfers effectively to unseen arrhythmia types. It also achieves superior performance on multiple EEG tasks.
AI.conclusion: SL-S4Wave is a highly effective and generalizable framework for self-supervised representation learning on multichannel physiological time series, advancing the state of the art in both cardiac and neurological signal analysis.

title: Interpretable Sperm Morphology Classification via Attention-Guided Deep Learning
summary: Male infertility is a major cause of couple infertility, often linked to abnormal sperm morphology. While deep learning models offer automated analysis, most lack interpretability, limiting their clinical adoption. This study proposes an attention-guided deep learning framework for sperm morphology classification. We combine a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to focus on key areas of the sperm head, improving both accuracy and interpretability. Evaluated on the SMIDS and HuSHem public datasets, our model achieves accuracies of 90.2% and 93.9% (macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948), outperforming SimpleCNN and standard EfficientNet-B0. Furthermore, we use Grad-CAM++ visualizations to highlight features influencing the model's decisions. The results demonstrate that this accurate and transparent framework is a practical tool for automated sperm analysis in fertility clinics.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework combining EfficientNet-B0 with CBAM attention for interpretable sperm morphology classification, achieving 90.2% and 93.9% accuracy on two public datasets with Grad-CAM++ visualizations for transparency.
AI.motivation: Male infertility is a major contributor to couple infertility, frequently associated with abnormal sperm morphology. Although deep learning models can automate sperm morphology analysis, most existing approaches lack interpretability, which hinders clinical adoption. There is a need for accurate yet transparent models that clinicians can trust.
AI.method: The authors propose an attention-guided framework that integrates a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 backbone with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The CBAM enables the model to focus on diagnostically relevant regions of the sperm head. Model decisions are visualized using Grad-CAM++ to provide post-hoc interpretability. Evaluation is performed on two public benchmark datasets: SMIDS and HuSHem.
AI.result: The proposed model achieves 90.2% accuracy on SMIDS and 93.9% on HuSHem, with macro F1 scores of 0.913 and 0.948 respectively. These results surpass both a SimpleCNN baseline and a standard EfficientNet-B0 without attention.
AI.conclusion: The attention-guided EfficientNet-B0 + CBAM framework offers both high classification accuracy and interpretability through Grad-CAM++ visualizations, making it a practical and transparent tool suitable for deployment in fertility clinics for automated sperm analysis.

title: Adversarial Bandit Optimization with Globally Bounded Perturbations to Convex Losses
summary:
We study adversarial bandit optimization in which the loss functions may be non-convex and non-smooth. In each round, the learner selects an action and observes only the loss incurred at that action. The loss consists of an underlying convex and $β$-smooth component and an adversarial perturbation that may be chosen after observing the learner's action. The perturbations are subject to a global budget controlling their cumulative magnitude over time.
  This framework extends the globally budgeted, post-action perturbation model from underlying linear losses to general convex and $β$-smooth losses. For this broader class, we establish expected regret guarantees that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget.
  To establish these guarantees, we modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that controls the additional regret caused by the perturbations. In the absence of perturbations, our results reduce to regret guarantees for the standard bandit convex optimization setting with $β$-smooth losses.

AI.tldr: This paper studies adversarial bandit optimization with non-convex, non-smooth loss functions, where an underlying convex β-smooth loss is corrupted by adversarial perturbations with a cumulative budget. The authors extend post-action perturbation models from linear to general convex β-smooth losses, providing regret guarantees that explicitly quantify the perturbation budget's effect.
AI.motivation: Standard bandit convex optimization typically assumes convex and smooth losses. However, real-world adversarial settings involve non-convex, non-smooth losses due to post-action perturbations. Prior work on globally budgeted perturbations was limited to linear losses; extending to general convex β-smooth losses captures a broader and more practical class of problems.
AI.method: The authors modify a standard bandit optimization algorithm and develop an analysis that explicitly controls the additional regret induced by adversarial perturbations. The perturbation model allows an adversary to corrupt the convex β-smooth loss after observing the learner's action, subject to a global cumulative budget constraint.
AI.result: The paper establishes expected regret guarantees for this broader class that explicitly characterize the effect of the perturbation budget. In the absence of perturbations, the results recover standard regret guarantees for bandit convex optimization with β-smooth losses, demonstrating consistency with the unperturbed setting.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully generalizes globally budgeted post-action perturbations from linear to convex β-smooth losses, with regret bounds that transparently depend on the perturbation budget. The analysis technique of modifying a standard bandit algorithm and bounding perturbation-induced regret is effective and recovers known results as a special case.

title: Context-Aware Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling of IVF Laboratory Environmental Conditions
summary: IVF pregnancy rates are routinely modeled using patient-level variables, while high-resolution laboratory environmental data remain underutilized. We show that this is a missed opportunity. Rather than relying on raw sensor averages, we engineer 55 context-aware temporal features, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed, that capture the dynamics of incubator microenvironments. On 61 weeks of data from an Asian IVF clinic, these features reduce cross-validated prediction error to 1.27%, compared to 3-5% for raw averages. We then train a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model that shares environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European clinic via partial pooling, while preserving site-specific baselines. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the model achieves R2 = 0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35-39 age group over a naive baseline, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful, transferable signal.

AI.tldr: Engineering 55 context-aware temporal features from IVF incubator environmental data, combined with a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model using partial pooling across clinics, reduces prediction error to 1.27% and achieves R²=0.86 on cross-clinic transfer, demonstrating that structured environmental monitoring contains clinically meaningful signal.
AI.motivation: IVF pregnancy rate prediction models routinely rely on patient-level variables while neglecting high-resolution laboratory environmental data. This represents a missed opportunity to capture clinically relevant microenvironmental dynamics within incubators that may affect embryo viability.
AI.method: First, 55 context-aware temporal features are engineered from sensor data, including rolling thermal stability, simultaneous temperature-humidity adherence, peak stress duration, and post-stress recovery speed. Second, a hierarchical Bayesian Beta regression model is trained with partial pooling to share environmental effects across an Asian and a Northern European IVF clinic while preserving site-specific baselines.
AI.result: The engineered features reduced cross-validated prediction error to 1.27% (vs. 3–5% for raw sensor averages) on 61 weeks of Asian clinic data. On held-out data from the Northern European clinic, the hierarchical model achieved R²=0.86 and a 64% error reduction for the 35–39 age group over a naive baseline.
AI.conclusion: Structured environmental monitoring of incubator microenvironments yields transferable, clinically meaningful signal that significantly improves IVF pregnancy rate prediction across clinics, advocating for the routine integration of high-resolution laboratory environmental features into predictive models.

title: Score Approximation for Diffusion Models on Arbitrary Low-Dimensional Structures
summary: The remarkable success of score-based diffusion models has spurred significant efforts to establish their theoretical foundations. However, existing complexity bounds for score approximation rely heavily on restrictive assumptions like Lipschitz continuous densities or smooth manifold supports, which are routinely violated by the singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters inherent to real-world perceptual data. This work establishes a universal score approximation theorem that works for any distribution supported on any compact set of upper Minkowski dimension $d$. Using a novel discrete-mixture formulation, we prove that the score function can be approximated with a ReLU network whose complexity grows exponentially only with $d$, thus breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. Combined with existing theories on accurately solving the backward diffusion SDE for arbitrary compact distributions, our work shows that diffusion models readily adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, explaining their competence in real-world generative tasks.

AI.tldr: Establishes a universal score approximation theorem for diffusion models on arbitrary compact distributions with upper Minkowski dimension d, using ReLU networks with complexity exponential only in d (not ambient dimension), thereby explaining diffusion models' success on irregular, non-smooth real-world data.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical complexity bounds for score approximation in diffusion models impose restrictive assumptions (Lipschitz continuous densities, smooth manifold supports) that are routinely violated by real-world data exhibiting singularities, sharp boundaries, and disjoint clusters. The gap between theory and practice motivates a more general framework.
AI.method: Employs a novel discrete-mixture formulation to represent arbitrary distributions supported on compact sets. Proves that score functions can be approximated by ReLU networks whose complexity scales exponentially with the upper Minkowski dimension d of the support, rather than the ambient dimension D. This is combined with existing backward diffusion SDE theory.
AI.result: The complexity bound grows exponentially only in the intrinsic dimension d (upper Minkowski dimension), breaking the exponential curse of ambient dimensionality. The theorem applies to any compactly supported distribution regardless of smoothness, covering singular and irregular data structures.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models inherently adapt to irregular, non-smooth data structures, providing a theoretical explanation for their strong empirical performance on complex real-world generative tasks without requiring restrictive smoothness assumptions.

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
summary: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how language models interpret different types of in-context compliance demonstrations for jailbreaking. By mixing benign and harmful demonstrations, the authors test three hypotheses and find that benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model, preference optimization is key to preventing harmful compliance, demonstration ordering exhibits recency bias, and models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak LMs, but the underlying mechanisms — specifically how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations — remain poorly understood. The authors aim to move beyond merely showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works.
AI.method: The authors mix benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request + helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request + helpful response) to test three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Experiments are conducted across four models, with analysis of the roles of preference optimization, demonstration ordering (recency bias), and refusal behavior in in-context learning.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable — benign demos can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. (2) Preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance. (3) Demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias. (4) Models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal.
AI.conclusion: What models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology. This work advances understanding from merely showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing the mechanisms by which it operates.

title: ADaPT: Token-Level Decoupling for Efficient Large Reasoning Models
summary: Large reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought to achieve strong performance, but applying such reasoning uniformly incurs high computational cost. Existing efficiency-oriented methods attempt to shorten or mix reasoning strategies, yet often degrade reasoning capability. We identify the root cause as sequence-level coupling between efficiency incentives and correctness optimization, which implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Adaptive Dual-Process Thinking (ADaPT), a token-level dual-process framework that explicitly decouples efficiency and correctness signals during training. ADaPT introduces a mode-selection token to control fast and slow reasoning, applying efficiency-related rewards exclusively to this token to avoid penalizing correct long reasoning while encouraging efficiency when appropriate. Moreover, ADaPT enables precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off at inference time: by adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token, a single trained model can smoothly move along the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ADaPT decouples efficiency and correctness signals at the token level via a mode-selection token, enabling continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off without penalizing correct long reasoning trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing methods that shorten or mix reasoning strategies for efficiency degrade reasoning capability because sequence-level reward coupling implicitly penalizes long but correct reasoning. The authors aim to decouple efficiency incentives from correctness optimization.
AI.method: ADaPT is a token-level dual-process framework that introduces a mode-selection token to gate fast vs. slow reasoning. During training, efficiency-related rewards are applied exclusively to this token, preserving correctness rewards for the reasoning content. At inference, adjusting the generation probability of the mode-selection token enables smooth traversal of the efficiency-performance Pareto frontier with a single model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ADaPT significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining strong reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks, achieving precise and continuous control over the efficiency-performance trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Token-level decoupling of efficiency and correctness signals is an effective strategy for building adaptive reasoning models that can be dynamically tuned along the Pareto frontier without retraining.

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
summary:
LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
  We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python.
  We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

AI.tldr: Multi-LCB extends the Python-only LiveCodeBench to 12 programming languages while preserving its contamination-aware evaluation protocol. Evaluation of 24 LLMs reveals Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and significant multilingual performance gaps.
AI.motivation: LiveCodeBench (LCB) is a widely adopted benchmark for LLM code generation but is restricted to Python, leaving unaddressed the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering.
AI.method: The authors transform Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in 11 additional languages (12 total, including Python), preserving LCB's contamination controls, evaluation protocol, and format compatibility. Multi-LCB is designed to automatically track future LCB updates.
AI.result: Evaluation of 24 LLMs across instruction and reasoning settings revealed three key findings: (1) Python overfitting — models perform disproportionately well on Python relative to other languages; (2) language-specific contamination — evidence that some models have been exposed to certain languages during training; and (3) substantial disparities in multilingual code generation performance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LCB establishes a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities for cross-language code generation.

title: Compositionality Emerges in a Narrow Depth-Connectivity Regime: Architecture Constraints and Solution Manifolds
summary: Compositionality is believed to be the foundation for generalization, enabling models to reuse meaningful primitives in novel combinations. Yet, models trained with standard gradient-based optimization rarely, and often only weakly, exhibit compositional internal structure, and it remains unclear how or why such compositionality forms. In this work, we show that compositionality emerges in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot. Along the connectivity axis, compositionality only appears in some specifically sparse networks, heavily depends on which connections remain rather than on weights' sparsity alone. Along the depth axis, compositionality emerges within a narrow, target-dependent regime, peaking at specific depths, while both shallower and deeper networks fail. When either the depth or connectivity condition is violated, gradient descent silently converges to fractured solutions rather than compositional ones. To discover and exploit this emergence, we introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate where compositionality is most likely to appear. Finally, we support these empirical findings with a theoretical framework based on compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds, explaining why compositional solutions are reachable only in a narrow depth-connectivity regime.

AI.tldr: Compositionality in neural networks emerges only within a narrow "sweet spot" defined by specific connectivity (sparse, structurally dependent) and depth (target-specific, intermediate). Outside this regime, gradient descent yields fractured solutions. The authors introduce similarity-based pruning and a depth predictor to discover and exploit this emergence, supported by theoretical analysis.
AI.motivation: Compositionality is fundamental to generalization, yet standard gradient-based training rarely produces models with compositional internal structure. The mechanisms governing when and why compositionality forms remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors systematically investigate compositionality emergence along two axes: connectivity (network sparsity and specific connection patterns) and depth. They introduce (i) similarity-based pruning (SP) to recover compositional connectivity from trained networks, and (ii) a heuristic depth predictor to estimate optimal depth for compositionality. A theoretical framework is developed using compositional sparsity, volume-ratio arguments, and feature-interference bounds.
AI.result: Compositionality emerges only in a narrow connectivity-depth sweet spot: along connectivity, it appears in specifically sparse networks where which connections remain matters more than sparsity alone; along depth, it peaks at specific, target-dependent depths, with both shallower and deeper networks failing. Violating either condition causes gradient descent to converge silently to fractured (non-compositional) solutions.
AI.conclusion: Compositionality is not a generic product of gradient-based learning but requires precise structural conditions. The proposed SP pruning and depth predictor can recover and exploit this narrow regime, and the theoretical framework explains why compositional solutions are reachable only under specific depth-connectivity constraints.

title: FlowEdit: Associative Memory for Lifelong Pronunciation Adaptation in Flow-Matching TTS
summary: Flow-matching text-to-speech systems achieve remarkable zero-shot quality but remain static after deployment: pronunciation errors on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns persist unless the model is retrained. We introduce FlowEdit, a life-long adaptation framework for frozen flow-matching TTS that learns pronunciation corrections as latent conditioning edits rather than weight updates. When corrective feedback is provided, FlowEdit optimizes a token-level perturbation in the text embedding space, then stores the correction in a Modern Hopfield Network serving as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, corrections are retrieved via soft attention with a similarity gate, enabling fuzzy morphological matching. On our curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns across 18 language families, FlowEdit reduces target-word Phoneme Error Rate by 92.7% relative to the zero-shot baseline while maintaining identical general-speech quality. Corrections complete in approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit is a life-long adaptation framework that enables frozen flow-matching TTS systems to correct pronunciation of out-of-vocabulary proper nouns by learning latent text-embedding perturbations stored in a Modern Hopfield Network, achieving 92.7% relative reduction in Phoneme Error Rate with no degradation to general speech quality.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching TTS systems produce high-quality zero-shot speech but are static post-deployment, leading to persistent mispronunciations on out-of-vocabulary proper nouns. Retraining is impractical. The authors seek a lightweight, continual adaptation mechanism that corrects these errors without modifying model weights or compromising general synthesis quality.
AI.method: FlowEdit introduces token-level perturbations in the frozen TTS model's text embedding space, optimized per corrective feedback. Corrected embeddings are stored in a Modern Hopfield Network functioning as content-addressable episodic memory. At inference, a soft-attention retrieval mechanism with a similarity gate performs fuzzy morphological matching to retrieve relevant corrections for novel inputs.
AI.result: Evaluated on a curated benchmark of 312 multilingual proper nouns spanning 18 language families, FlowEdit achieves a 92.7% relative reduction in target-word Phoneme Error Rate compared to the zero-shot baseline, while maintaining identical general speech quality. Corrections require approximately 15 seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit demonstrates that latent-space editing combined with episodic memory is an effective, efficient strategy for life-long pronunciation adaptation in frozen TTS systems, enabling rapid correction of OOV proper nouns without weight updates or quality regression.

title: Towards Graph-Based Deep Learning for Map Generalization: Insights from Building Footprints Simplification and Aggregation
summary: Map generalization remains one of the fundamental tasks in cartography, especially for the simplification and aggregation of complex building footprints. This study presents the first exploratory application of graph-based deep learning to both tasks, reformulating simplification as node movement prediction and aggregation as link prediction within a unified graph learning framework. We evaluate representative graph neural network architectures (GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE) on multi-scale building datasets, showing that GraphSAGE demonstrates relative strengths in link prediction accuracy, while also revealing persistent challenges in precise node movement prediction. Beyond quantitative performance, the results highlight that aggregation poses greater complexity and challenges than simplification, underscoring the difficulty of capturing higher-level spatial relationships in map generalization with current deep learning approaches. Although limitations such as data imbalance and the need for post-processing remain, the study provides valuable insights and methodological directions for advancing automated map generalization with deep learning approaches.

AI.tldr: First exploration of graph neural networks for map generalization, framing building simplification as node movement prediction and building aggregation as link prediction. GraphSAGE performs best on link prediction; aggregation proves more challenging than simplification.
AI.motivation: To explore whether graph-based deep learning can be applied to automated map generalization tasks — specifically building footprint simplification and aggregation — which remain fundamental yet challenging in cartography.
AI.method: A unified graph learning framework is proposed: building simplification is reformulated as a node movement prediction task, and building aggregation as a link prediction task. Three representative GNN architectures — GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE — are evaluated on multi-scale building datasets.
AI.result: GraphSAGE shows relative strengths in link prediction accuracy. However, precise node movement prediction remains a persistent challenge across all architectures. Aggregation is found to be more complex and challenging than simplification, indicating current deep learning methods struggle to capture higher-level spatial relationships.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based deep learning shows promise for automated map generalization but faces significant hurdles: data imbalance, post-processing requirements, and difficulty modeling higher-level spatial relationships. The study provides methodological directions for future research despite these limitations.

title: DeepSWIP: Quotient-WMC Counterfactuals for Neural Probabilistic Logic Programs
summary: Neurosymbolic systems such as DeepProbLog combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, but standard inference is associational. Counterfactual reasoning additionally requires a causal semantics for interventions and evidence. We introduce DeepSWIP, a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog programs. Using neural materialization, we reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, apply Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs), and compute counterfactuals by weighted model counting (WMC) over a single transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique-supported-model assumptions, DeepSWIP is exact relative to the learned materialized FCM. The standard quotient-WMC form of ProbLog conditionals identifies active neural probabilities and explains intervention cleaning, calibration sensitivity, and rare-evidence instability. Experiments on MPI3D confirm the transformation against a DeepTwin construction against 12,000 queries, as predicted and a 2.14$\times$ inference speedup from avoiding the Twin's endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment shows that neural calibration degradation biases plug-in estimates, while a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands. Code is at https://github.com/saibib/deep_SWIP.

AI.tldr: DeepSWIP introduces a single-world counterfactual semantics for DeepProbLog, enabling exact counterfactual inference via weighted model counting (WMC) on a single transformed program. It avoids the DeepTwin's endogenous duplication, achieves a 2.14× speedup, and uses AIPW estimators to address neural calibration bias.
AI.motivation: Standard inference in neurosymbolic systems like DeepProbLog is purely associational and lacks a causal semantics for interventions and counterfactual reasoning. Existing twin-network approaches duplicate endogenous variables, causing computational overhead. The authors aim to provide an efficient, exact counterfactual inference method with correctly scoped causal estimands.
AI.method: DeepSWIP extends Single World Intervention Programs (SWIPs) to DeepProbLog. It uses neural materialization to reduce fixed-context neural predicates to ordinary ProbLog choices, then applies SWIP transformations to compute counterfactuals via weighted model counting (WMC) on a single program. For estimation, it employs a correctly scoped randomized-policy AIPW (Augmented Inverse Propensity Weighting) estimator to correct for neural calibration degradation.
AI.result: Experiments on MPI3D validate exactness against DeepTwin on 12,000 queries, with a 2.14× inference speedup by avoiding endogenous duplication. A SUMO HOV experiment demonstrates that plug-in estimates suffer from neural calibration bias, while the AIPW estimator removes most first-order bias for population mean and ATE estimands.
AI.conclusion: DeepSWIP provides exact, efficient counterfactual inference for neurosymbolic programs by combining neural materialization with SWIP semantics and WMC. The AIPW estimator effectively debiases neural miscalibration, and the single-program approach avoids the computational cost of twin-network constructions.

title: Low-Energy Reduced RISC-V Instruction Subset Processor for Tsetlin Machine Inference at the Edge
comment: 6 pages, 6 Figures, Accepted in IEEE ISVLSI Conference 2026
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a logic-based machine learning approach that relies on simple bitwise operations and finite-state automata, which makes it attractive for edge AI deployments. Recent work has focused on co-processor and accelerator designs based on Tsetlin Machines (TMs). Although these designs achieve high performance, they typically depend on tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and external host processors, limiting flexibility and ease of programming. In this work, we present a domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor architecture and design flow tailored for TM inference. Leveraging the modular structure of RISC-V, we design a reduced instruction subset processor that retains programmability while targeting improved performance and lower energy consumption for TM workloads. Instruction profiling is employed to guide instruction reduction, followed by datapath and control path simplifications tailored to TM inference. Both the baseline RV32IM core and the proposed reduced core are evaluated across multiple datasets and compared with Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs), which serve as a hardware-efficient baseline due to their reliance on bitwise operations during inference. Results show that TM achieves comparable or higher accuracy (e.g., up to 88.18% on CIFAR-2 compared to 60.0% for BNN) while reducing execution time by up to 98% across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the proposed design achieves an average $29.7\times$ reduction in energy consumption, demonstrating its effectiveness for programmable and efficient edge AI systems.

AI.tldr: A domain-specific RISC-V microprocessor with a reduced instruction set is proposed for Tsetlin Machine inference, achieving up to 98% execution time reduction and 29.7× energy savings compared to a baseline RV32IM core, while outperforming Binarized Neural Networks in accuracy (88.18% vs 60.0% on CIFAR-2).
AI.motivation: Existing TM accelerator designs suffer from tightly coupled interfaces, microcode-style programming, and dependence on external host processors, which limit flexibility and ease of programming. The authors aim to address these limitations by bringing programmability and efficiency together in a RISC-V-based domain-specific processor.
AI.method: The authors design a reduced instruction subset RISC-V microprocessor tailored for TM inference. Instruction profiling guides the elimination of unnecessary instructions, followed by datapath and control path simplifications specific to TM workloads. The proposed reduced core and a baseline RV32IM core are evaluated across multiple datasets, using Binarized Neural Networks as a hardware-efficient accuracy/performance baseline.
AI.result: TMs achieve significantly higher accuracy than BNNs (88.18% vs 60.0% on CIFAR-2). Execution time is reduced by up to 98% across datasets. The proposed reduced core achieves an average 29.7× reduction in energy consumption compared to the baseline RV32IM, demonstrating substantial gains in both performance and energy efficiency.
AI.conclusion: A RISC-V-based domain-specific processor with a reduced instruction set is highly effective for TM inference, delivering superior accuracy, drastic execution time reductions, and significant energy savings, making it a compelling solution for programmable, energy-efficient edge AI systems.

title: LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents
summary: Policy-adherent tool-calling agents in customer-service domains must maintain task states across turns while calling tools and obeying domain policies. Task states consist of relevant facts, identifiers, constraints, and conditions observed through user interaction and tool calls. In standard agents, task states are not represented separately. Observations, tool returns, and policy instructions are placed in the prompt, leaving agents to reconstruct the relevant states from the prompt each time they decide what to do next. This design makes state management implicit, creating two common failure modes. An agent may retrieve the right facts but later ground its decision in stale, missing, or incorrect information; and a syntactically valid tool call may still violate a domain policy that depends on the current task state. We introduce \textsc{LedgerAgent}, an inference-time method for tool-calling agents that maintains observed task states in a separate ledger and renders the states into the prompt. The ledger is also used to check state-dependent policy constraints before environment-changing tool calls are executed, blocking policy violations. Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, \textsc{LedgerAgent} improves average pass\textasciicircum{}k over a standard prompt-based tool-calling approach, with the largest gains under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.

AI.tldr: LedgerAgent introduces a separate explicit ledger for maintaining task states in tool-calling agents, reducing failures from stale/incorrect information and policy violations by rendering states into prompts and checking constraints before executing environment-changing tool calls.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling agents store all observations, tool returns, and policy instructions in the prompt, forcing agents to implicitly reconstruct task states at each decision step. This causes two failure modes: (1) grounding decisions in stale, missing, or incorrect information despite having retrieved correct facts earlier, and (2) making syntactically valid tool calls that violate domain policies dependent on the current task state.
