AI.method: LedgerAgent is an inference-time method that maintains observed task states (facts, identifiers, constraints, conditions) in a separate explicit ledger. The ledger contents are rendered into the prompt for decision-making, and the ledger is used to check state-dependent policy constraints before executing any environment-changing tool calls, blocking violations proactively.
AI.result: Across four customer-service domains and a mixed panel of open- and closed-weight models, LedgerAgent improves average pass^k over standard prompt-based tool-calling. The largest gains are observed under stricter multi-trial consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state management via a separate ledger significantly improves the reliability and policy compliance of tool-calling agents in stateful, policy-adherent domains like customer service, particularly when evaluated under rigorous consistency requirements.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing
summary: Reservoir computing offers a lightweight framework for forecasting dynamical systems but may struggle to capture long-range dependencies due to limited representational capacity. Conventional reservoir computing recurrently uses trainable reservoirs with hyperparameter sensitivity, while the next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence at the cost of rapidly growing feature dimensions. Here, we develop Kolmogorov-Arnold Reservoir Computing (KARC), which replaces reservoirs with explicit basis-function expansions inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. We rigorously show that KARC is a lightweight design of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs), preserving the potential expressive capacity of KANs while admitting efficient closed-form training of reservoir computing. At comparable cost, KARC outperforms existing reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks including partial differential equations. It can also be integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation. This work thus establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and KANs, enabling efficient and high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting.

AI.tldr: KARC replaces reservoir computing's recurrent reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, creating a lightweight KAN variant that preserves expressive capacity while enabling closed-form training. It outperforms existing reservoir methods on PDE benchmarks and integrates with diffusion models for text-to-image generation.
AI.motivation: Conventional reservoir computing struggles with long-range dependencies and has hyperparameter sensitivity; next-generation reservoir computing removes recurrence but suffers from exploding feature dimensions. The authors aim to bridge reservoir computing and KANs to achieve efficient, high-fidelity dynamical system forecasting with principled representational capacity.
AI.method: KARC replaces the reservoir with explicit basis-function expansions derived from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. This yields a lightweight KAN architecture that retains KAN's expressive capacity while admitting the efficient closed-form (ridge regression) training characteristic of reservoir computing, avoiding both recurrence-induced hyperparameter sensitivity and feature-dimension explosion.
AI.result: At comparable computational cost, KARC outperforms both conventional and next-generation reservoir computing methods on challenging benchmarks, including partial differential equation forecasting. It is also successfully integrated with generative diffusion models for text-to-image generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: KARC establishes a principled bridge between reservoir computing and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, enabling efficient, high-fidelity forecasting of dynamical systems with both strong theoretical grounding and practical performance gains.

title: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
summary: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeech-TTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models

AI.tldr: First study adapting cross-attention attribution (DAAM) to speech diffusion TTS, analyzing how style caption tokens influence acoustic output across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps, revealing layer-wise selectivity, temporal variance patterns, and correlations with F0/energy.
AI.motivation: Style-captioned TTS systems lack interpretability: how individual natural language tokens in style captions influence acoustic output is unknown. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failures and improving controllability in expressive TTS.
AI.method: The authors propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models by adapting the DAAM (Diffusion Attentive Attribution Maps) framework to the speech domain. They apply it to CapSpeech-TTS, extracting per-token heatmaps across 25 transformer layers and 24 ODE diffusion steps. The analysis covers 3,600 (style caption, transcript) combinations — 120 style captions × 30 text transcripts — to reveal token-level waveform conditioning.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Style tokens exhibit lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global acoustic conditioning; (2) Style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) Style conditioning peaks in early ODE steps and deep layers; (4) Attention entropy bottoms out at layer 17, precisely where style importance peaks, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical processing stage.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models, providing mechanistic insights into layer-wise and step-wise style conditioning that can guide future TTS system design and failure diagnosis.

title: Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR): Function-Preserving SVD Compression for LLMs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Resource-Adaptive Foundation Model Inference (AdaptFM), Seoul, South Korea (non-archival)
summary: We present Activation- and Influence-Aware Ranks (AIR), an SVD-based LLM compression framework that guides each weight matrix's low-rank approximation with a backward-signal influence metric. Starting from the activation-aware optimum of SVD-LLM(W), AIR runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that integrates influence element-wise under a monotone-descent guarantee. AIR is layer-local and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods: alone it exceeds ACIP, and AIR+LoRA outperforms it further. AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at <=60% parameter retention, matches its quality with ~90% less calibration data, and turns parameter savings into FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency gains.

AI.tldr: AIR is an SVD-based LLM compression method that uses a backward-signal influence metric to guide low-rank approximation, achieving >18% perplexity improvement over SVD-LLM(W) at ≤60% parameter retention with minimal calibration data.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LLM compression methods like SVD-LLM(W) optimize for activation-aware reconstruction but ignore the downstream influence of weight perturbations on the model's final output. AIR aims to incorporate this backward-signal influence to produce better low-rank approximations.
AI.method: AIR computes an influence metric via backward signals, then runs a single closed-form alternating least squares (ALS) sweep that element-wise integrates this influence into the low-rank approximation, all under a monotone-descent guarantee. The method operates layer-locally and composes orthogonally with end-to-end methods like LoRA.
AI.result: AIR improves perplexity over SVD-LLM(W) by >18% at ≤60% parameter retention, matches SVD-LLM(W) quality with ~90% less calibration data, surpasses ACIP alone, and achieves further gains with LoRA. It also yields FLOP, peak-memory, and per-token latency improvements.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating backward-signal influence into activation-aware SVD compression yields significant quality improvements with minimal calibration overhead, making AIR a practical and effective layer-local compression method that composes well with other techniques.

title: Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift
summary: Calibration aligns a model's predictive uncertainty with the frequencies of its empirical outcomes and is important for understanding and trusting reported probabilities. Recent work shows that enforcing calibration at the level of individual predictors can improve ensemble accuracy and calibration, with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models showing strong empirical improvements in particular; however, the conditions under which calibration helps MoE are not well understood. In this work, we study how MoE models behave under distribution shift, focusing on how routing mechanisms interact with expert-level calibration. We show that expert calibration is sufficient to ensure calibration of the overall model under a broad class of distribution shifts in hard-routed models, but is insufficient for calibrating soft-routed models. To address this, we propose an adversarial reweighting that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift, and we demonstrate that it improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult subsets of the data, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: Expert-level calibration is sufficient for overall model calibration in hard-routed MoEs under distribution shift, but not in soft-routed ones; the authors propose adversarial reweighting to fix this, improving accuracy-calibration tradeoffs across diverse settings.
AI.motivation: While calibration at the individual predictor level improves ensemble accuracy and calibration — especially in MoE models — the theoretical conditions under which calibration benefits MoE under distribution shift are not well understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze MoE behavior under distribution shift by studying how routing mechanisms (hard vs. soft) interact with expert-level calibration. They prove sufficiency of expert calibration for hard-routed models and insufficiency for soft-routed ones. They then propose an adversarial reweighting method that penalizes calibration errors of the routed aggregate under distribution shift.
AI.result: Expert calibration guarantees overall calibration for hard-routed MoEs under a broad class of distribution shifts, but fails for soft-routed MoEs. The proposed adversarial reweighting improves the accuracy-calibration tradeoff both on average and on difficult data subsets, across model classes, prediction tasks, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: The interaction between routing and calibration is critical for MoE robustness under distribution shift. Adversarial reweighting offers a practical solution for soft-routed models, enhancing both calibration and accuracy in shifted settings.

title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Work in progress; we will continuously update the codebase and arXiv version
summary: This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents: as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context. Major components of the CoD framework include: (1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes; (2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation. We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework, including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment, as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL). Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting, and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization -- within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings -- of the elicited meta-capability. Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works, and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents. To facilitate further research and applications, we release our implementations at \url{https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Connect the Dots" (CoD), a framework for training LLMs as long-lifecycle agents that continuously explore, learn from experience, and self-update their context to improve task performance over time, using end-to-end RL with interleaved solve-and-update episodes, demonstrating out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.motivation: LLM-based AI agents deployed in real environments face long sequences of tasks and must continuously adapt by learning from their own experiences. Existing approaches lack a unified training paradigm for the meta-capability of self-improvement through context updating across extended deployments. The authors aim to fill this gap by formalizing and training for this "Connect the Dots" capability.
AI.method: The CoD framework consists of: (1) an end-to-end RL algorithm (GRPO-style with fine-grained credit assignment) operating over long rollout sequences that interleave solve-task episodes and update-context episodes; and (2) specially designed tasks and environments that incentivize the meta-capability of connecting experiences across tasks, rather than merely optimizing domain-specific or per-task performance.
AI.result: Empirical results validate that end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting is effective. The elicited meta-capability shows out-of-distribution generalization: within training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings.
AI.conclusion: The CoD framework successfully connects multiple lines of prior research and opens new avenues for advancing LLMs and AI agents with long-lifecycle self-improvement capabilities.

title: Human-AI Agent Interaction in a Business Context
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure, submitted to Springer Nature
summary: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into core business processes, understanding and designing effective interaction patterns between humans and AI agents becomes crucial for value creation. This study identifies and evaluates principles and criteria for a positive User Experience (UX) with AI agents, along with methods for its measurement. We identify user expectations and needs to facilitate adoption, build trust, and support user-centered decision-making by development teams. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative and quantitative techniques, we explore interaction patterns between humans and AI agents. The findings from this exploratory research serve as the basis to develop a survey experiment which evaluates the effectiveness of specific design elements on a larger scale. This foundational research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings.

AI.tldr: This study explores principles and criteria for designing positive user experiences with AI agents in business contexts, using mixed methods to identify interaction patterns and evaluate design elements that foster adoption, trust, and user-centered decision-making.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become embedded in core business processes, there is a pressing need to understand how to design effective human-AI interaction patterns that create value, build trust, and drive adoption.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative techniques: first, exploratory research to identify interaction patterns between humans and AI agents; second, development of a survey experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of specific design elements at scale.
AI.result: The exploratory research yielded findings on user expectations and needs regarding human-AI agent interactions, which informed the design of a subsequent large-scale survey experiment to test specific design elements.
AI.conclusion: The research provides a foundational contribution toward developing more intuitive and effective human-AI agent interactions in business settings, supporting user-centered design decisions by development teams.

title: StreamKL: Fast and Memory-Efficient KL Divergence for Boosting Attention Distillation
summary: Attention distillation, which trains one attention distribution to match another by minimizing their Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, is widely used in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training. However, existing approaches materialize both attention distributions before computing the KL reduction, incurring $O(N_QN_K)$ memory and IO costs that become prohibitive at long context lengths. We present StreamKL, the first fused GPU primitive for attention KL divergence that eliminates this quadratic materialization. StreamKL derives a novel online formulation for the coupled two-distribution KL reduction, enabling a single one-pass forward kernel that streams query-key tiles through on-chip SRAM. For the backward pass, StreamKL recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile, avoiding storage of quadratic intermediates. We further design and implement efficient GPU kernels with dedicated optimizations. Experiments show StreamKL delivers up to $43\times$ and $14\times$ speedups over baseline methods in the forward and backward passes, respectively. Most importantly, StreamKL reduces the extra HBM footprint of attention distillation from $O(N_QN_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context distillation on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: StreamKL is a fused GPU primitive that computes the KL divergence between two attention distributions in a single streaming pass, eliminating the $O(N_Q N_K)$ memory materialization and enabling long-context attention distillation on a single GPU with up to 43× forward and 14× backward speedups.
AI.motivation: Attention distillation (minimizing KL divergence between two attention distributions) is widely used but requires materializing both $N_Q \times N_K$ attention matrices before computing KL, incurring prohibitive memory and IO costs at long context lengths. Existing methods cannot scale attention distillation to long sequences on resource-constrained hardware.
AI.method: StreamKL introduces: (1) a novel online/streaming formulation that decomposes the coupled two-distribution KL divergence into a form computable in a single forward pass over query-key tiles; (2) a fused GPU kernel that streams tiles through on-chip SRAM, accumulating KL statistics without materializing full attention matrices; (3) a backward pass that recomputes attention probabilities tile-by-tile rather than storing quadratic intermediates; and (4) dedicated GPU kernel optimizations for efficiency.
AI.result: StreamKL achieves up to 43× speedup in the forward pass and 14× speedup in the backward pass compared to baseline methods. Critically, it reduces the extra HBM memory footprint from $O(N_Q N_K)$ to $O(1)$, enabling long-context attention distillation on a single GPU that was previously infeasible.
AI.conclusion: By eliminating quadratic memory materialization through a streaming, fused kernel design, StreamKL makes attention distillation scalable to long contexts, removing a key bottleneck in knowledge distillation, model compression, continual learning, and sparse-attention LLM training.

title: VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a central tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but current methods face a trade-off between simplicity and credit assignment. Group-relative methods such as GRPO avoid training a critic, but typically assign a trajectory-level advantage to every token. Actor-critic methods provide denser learning signals, but require a learned value function with its own training instability. We introduce VIMPO, a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized reinforcement learning. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence can be written in terms of policy-reference log-ratios and anchored by the terminal condition that no future reward remains at the end of a trajectory. This gives a simple value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards without training a critic. The same derivation also yields a critic-free actor advantage, allowing VIMPO to separate reward incorporation through the value loss from policy improvement through a PPO-style actor update. On mathematical RLVR benchmarks, VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with especially larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO retains a consistent advantage over GRPO, suggesting that policy-implied value optimization can provide finer credit assignment while preserving the practical simplicity of critic-free training.

AI.tldr: VIMPO is a critic-free policy optimization method that derives a value function from the policy itself using KL-regularized RL optimality conditions. It separates reward incorporation (via a simple value loss) from policy improvement (via PPO-style updates), achieving better credit assignment than GRPO without the instability of training a critic. VIMPO outperforms GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, especially under noisy rewards.
AI.motivation: Current RL methods for improving LLM reasoning face a trade-off: GRPO is simple but assigns coarse trajectory-level credit to all tokens, while actor-critic methods provide finer per-token signals but suffer from training instability due to the learned value function. The authors aim to achieve fine-grained credit assignment without the complexity and instability of training a separate critic.
AI.method: VIMPO derives a policy-implied value function from the optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL. For autoregressive generation, the resulting value recurrence is expressed in terms of policy-reference log-ratios, anchored by the terminal condition of zero future reward. This yields a critic-free value loss that incorporates outcome-level verifiable rewards and a critic-free actor advantage, enabling PPO-style policy updates without a learned critic.
AI.result: VIMPO improves over GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, with larger gains on competition-style evaluations. Under noisy rewards, VIMPO consistently outperforms GRPO, indicating better credit assignment while maintaining critic-free simplicity.
AI.conclusion: Policy-implied value optimization offers a practical middle ground: it provides finer credit assignment than trajectory-level methods like GRPO while avoiding the instability of learned critics. VIMPO demonstrates that optimality conditions of KL-regularized RL can be exploited to derive effective, critic-free value functions for LLM reasoning tasks.

title: Self-Adaptive Scale Handling for Forecasting Time Series with Scale Heterogeneity
comment: This is the full version of the paper accepted by the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF
summary: Current time series forecasting (TSF) research predominantly focuses on scale-homogeneous data, where different time series share similar numerical magnitude ranges. However, in real-world industrial scenarios such as financial product sales, different time series often differ by orders of magnitude (scale heterogeneity). Since these series share similar temporal patterns, joint modeling is desirable for better data utilization, yet existing scaling methods either compress low-scale signals (global normalization) or destroy semantic discriminability and amplify inverse-scaling errors (window-based scaling). This paper proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module that learns adaptive scale factors tailored to each input, preserving semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. AS consists of Scale Calibrating (SC), which calibrates prior mean scaling factors through neural networks, and Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply calibration or retain the original factor, avoiding over-calibration. Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay show that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their performance. The code and dataset are available at the link https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/ASTSF.

AI.tldr: Proposes a self-Adaptive Scale-handling (AS) module for time series forecasting with scale-heterogeneous data, using learned adaptive scaling factors that preserve semantic discriminability while reducing inverse-scaling errors. Demonstrated on financial sales data from Ant Fortune and Alipay.
AI.motivation: Real-world industrial time series (e.g., financial product sales) exhibit scale heterogeneity — different series differ by orders of magnitude but share similar temporal patterns. Existing scaling methods fail: global normalization compresses low-scale signals, while window-based scaling destroys semantic discriminability and amplifies inverse-scaling errors. Joint modeling is desirable for data efficiency, but no adequate scaling solution exists.
AI.method: The AS module comprises two components: (1) Scale Calibrating (SC), which uses neural networks to calibrate prior mean scaling factors, and (2) Scaling Selection (SS), which decides whether to apply the calibrated factor or retain the original, preventing over-calibration. Together they learn input-tailored adaptive scale factors that preserve semantic discriminability and reduce inverse-scaling errors. AS is model-agnostic and integrates into existing TSF architectures.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world fund sales datasets from Ant Fortune and Alipay demonstrate that AS seamlessly integrates into popular TSF models and consistently improves their forecasting performance.
AI.conclusion: The AS module effectively addresses scale heterogeneity in time series forecasting without the drawbacks of existing normalization strategies, enabling better joint modeling of disparate-scale series and yielding consistent gains across multiple backbone architectures.

title: Hierarchical Control in Multi-Agent Games: LLM-based Planning and RL Execution
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong performance in sequential decision-making, yet scaling to complex multi-agent environments remains challenging due to sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the difficulty of learning coordinated strategies. We propose a hierarchical architecture where a pretrained large language model (LLM) acts as a centralized strategic controller that selects among specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents, while RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. We evaluate this hybrid system in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and \emph{``Flat''} RL (end-to-end training without skill decomposition) baselines. The LLM+RL system achieves task performance statistically equivalent to hand-crafted BT (46.4\% vs 51.5\% win rate, $p=0.103$) while both significantly outperform Flat RL trained without skill decomposition. A user study ($n=15$) reveals that 60\% of participants perceive LLM+RL agents as the most human-like ($p=0.027$), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability. These results demonstrate that pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills, achieving competitive multi-agent coordination and superior perceived believability without manual rule engineering.

AI.tldr: A hybrid architecture combining a pretrained LLM as a strategic controller with specialized RL skill policies achieves competitive multi-agent coordination in a 2v2 game, matching hand-crafted behavior trees while being perceived as more human-like than both BT and end-to-end RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Scaling RL to complex multi-agent environments is hindered by sparse rewards, large state-action spaces, and the challenge of learning coordinated strategies. The authors aim to leverage LLM reasoning to address high-level strategic coordination while delegating low-level execution to specialized RL policies.
AI.method: A hierarchical architecture with a pretrained LLM as a centralized strategic controller that selects among pretrained, specialized RL skill policies for a team of agents. RL policies handle reactive low-level execution. Evaluated in a competitive 2v2 King of the Hill environment against behavior tree (BT) and "Flat" RL (end-to-end, no skill decomposition) baselines, plus a user study (n=15) on perceived human-likeness.
AI.result: LLM+RL achieved a 46.4% win rate vs. BT's 51.5% (statistically equivalent, p=0.103), both significantly outperforming Flat RL. In the user study, 60% of participants rated LLM+RL agents as most human-like (p=0.027), citing behavioral adaptability and tactical variability.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained LLM reasoning can effectively orchestrate pretrained RL skills for multi-agent coordination, achieving competitive performance without manual rule engineering and offering superior perceived believability.

title: Adaptive Distance-Aware Trunk Deep Operator Learning for Long-Span Roadway Bridges
summary: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated FE analysis computationally expensive for applications such as influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML approaches struggle to accurately capture these localized responses. To address this challenge, this study proposes an adaptive-trunk DeepONet for localized structural response prediction in large-scale bridge systems. The framework dynamically constructs a load-dependent learning domain using a KNN strategy, allowing the network to focus on structural influence zones. The trunk network is further enhanced using distance-aware features that encode the geometric relationship between the load and structural nodes. A physics-based full-field reconstruction is incorporated through a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation, enabling predictions at adaptive nodes to be extended to the entire structural domain. To enable scalable training, response data are generated using a reduced-order equivalent shell model that preserves the dominant global behavior while significantly reducing computational cost. The proposed framework is validated on both a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge. Results show that the method achieves FEM-level accuracy with relative errors below 5%, while reducing the total response evaluation time (including full-field reconstruction) by approximately 60x; excluding the post-processing reconstruction step, the AD-DeepONet inference is up to four orders of magnitude faster than FEM. In addition, the framework enables rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading configurations, demonstrating strong potential for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

AI.tldr: An adaptive-trunk DeepONet framework with KNN-based dynamic domain construction, distance-aware features, and stiffness-informed Schur complement reconstruction achieves FEM-level accuracy (sub-5% error) for localized bridge response prediction while being 60x faster overall and up to 10,000x faster for inference alone.
AI.motivation: Long-span roadway bridges exhibit highly localized structural responses under vehicular loading, making repeated full FEM analysis computationally prohibitive for applications like influence surface generation and structural digital twins. Existing SciML methods fail to accurately capture these localized responses.
AI.method: The proposed adaptive-trunk DeepONet (AD-DeepONet) employs: (1) a KNN strategy to dynamically construct a load-dependent learning domain around structural influence zones; (2) distance-aware features in the trunk network encoding geometric load-node relationships; (3) a stiffness-informed Schur complement formulation for physics-based full-field reconstruction from adaptive node predictions; and (4) a reduced-order equivalent shell model for scalable training data generation that preserves dominant global behavior.
AI.result: Validated on a benchmark bridge model and the real-world Mussafah Bridge, the method achieves relative errors below 5% compared to FEM, reduces total response evaluation time by approximately 60x (including full-field reconstruction), and achieves inference speeds up to four orders of magnitude (10,000x) faster than FEM when excluding post-processing.
AI.conclusion: The AD-DeepONet framework demonstrates strong potential for rapid generation of full-field responses, influence lines, and influence surfaces under arbitrary vehicular loading, making it suitable for large-scale bridge analysis and digital twin applications.

title: What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought: An Information-Theoretic Analysis
summary: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) internalizes reasoning within continuous hidden states, offering a promising alternative to verbose discrete reasoning traces. However, robust latent reasoning remains difficult because outcome supervision provides weak learning signals and leaves latent trajectories prone to semantic drift. In this work, we analyze Latent CoT from an information-theoretic perspective and identify this failure as a dual collapse: gradient attenuation along the optimization path and representational drift in the latent space. We further decompose process supervision into two complementary dimensions: Trajectory Supervision, which injects dense stepwise reasoning signals, and Space Supervision, which preserves the semantic structure of the latent manifold. Our analysis shows that rigid geometric compression can collapse the reasoning space, whereas generative reconstruction provides a more flexible semantic anchor that better preserves information capacity. To measure these effects, we introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), which quantifies the mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps. Experiments reveal a clear Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy depends on the information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. These findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision and suggest shifting from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Supervision-in-Latent-CoT}{this repository}.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) from an information-theoretic perspective, identifying a "dual collapse" problem (gradient attenuation and representational drift) under outcome supervision. It proposes decomposing process supervision into Trajectory Supervision and Space Supervision, introduces the Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to measure mutual information, and demonstrates an "Information-Performance Binding" — reasoning accuracy depends on preserving information fidelity in the latent chain.
AI.motivation: Latent CoT internalizes reasoning in continuous hidden states to avoid verbose discrete traces, but outcome supervision alone provides weak learning signals, causing latent trajectories to suffer from semantic drift. The authors aim to understand why robust latent reasoning fails and to establish principled supervision strategies.
AI.method: The authors adopt an information-theoretic framework to analyze failure modes in Latent CoT, characterizing them as dual collapse (gradient attenuation + representational drift). They decompose process supervision into two axes: (1) Trajectory Supervision — injecting dense stepwise reasoning signals along the optimization path; (2) Space Supervision — preserving semantic structure of the latent manifold, where generative reconstruction is shown superior to rigid geometric compression. They introduce the Unified Latent Probe (ULP), a metric that quantifies mutual information between latent trajectories and explicit reasoning steps.
AI.result: Experiments reveal an Information-Performance Binding: reasoning accuracy is directly tied to the amount of information fidelity preserved in the latent chain. Generative reconstruction-based space supervision preserves information capacity better than rigid geometric compression, which can collapse the reasoning space.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a principled framework for latent reasoning supervision, advocating a shift from geometric imitation toward mutual information maximization as the guiding objective for training latent CoT models.

title: Exploring the potential of AlphaEarth and TESSERA embeddings for Fine-scale Local Climate Zone Mapping: A case study across five cities in Switzerland
summary: Understanding urban spatial morphology is critical for climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable urban design, and Local Climate Zone (LCZ) mapping provides the basic framework for this. However, many cities still use coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ records, which are unsuitable for fine-scale urban research. In this study, precomputed embeddings from TESSERA (Feng et al., 2025) and AlphaEarth (Brown et al., 2025) are compared to traditional Sentinel-1/2 (S1S2) composites in five Swiss cities to see if they can upscale coarse LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net. Three experiments assess multi-city transferability, the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. We find that all datasets achieve strong performance with test data Intersection-over-Union (IoU) ranging from 0.59-0.69 and 0.77-0.82 in the first two experiments. TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings As expected, we find that the transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Overall, however, our results demonstrate the promising potential of embeddings derived from EO foundation models to reduce time consuming preprocessing, respectively, manual feature engineering tasks and to guide a universal deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow. When combined with a simple location-aware attention U-Net architecture, the embeddings enhance regional transferability and scalability, supporting the development of comprehensive and reproducible fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications Improving reference data quality remains the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: This study compares precomputed embeddings from EO foundation models (TESSERA, AlphaEarth) against traditional Sentinel-1/2 composites for upscaling coarse 100-m LCZ maps to 10-m resolution using an attention-based U-Net across five Swiss cities, finding TESSERA consistently outperforms others (IoU 0.59–0.82), though temporal transfer across years remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Many cities rely on coarse ~100-m resolution LCZ maps that are inadequate for fine-scale urban climate modeling, risk assessment, and sustainable design. The authors seek to leverage EO foundation model embeddings to upscale these maps to 10-m resolution while reducing preprocessing and manual feature engineering burdens.
AI.method: Precomputed embeddings from TESSERA and AlphaEarth are compared against Sentinel-1/2 composites as input to an attention-based U-Net for super-resolving LCZ maps from 100 m to 10 m. Three experiments evaluate: (1) multi-city transferability across five Swiss cities, (2) the impact of higher-resolution reference data, and (3) temporal robustness to year-to-year phenology changes. Performance is measured via Intersection-over-Union (IoU).
AI.result: All datasets achieve strong IoU (0.59–0.69 in the first experiment; 0.77–0.82 in the second). TESSERA consistently outperforms both S1S2 and AlphaEarth across both settings. Temporal transfer of embedding-based models from one year to another remains an open challenge. Reference data quality is identified as the strongest lever for further accuracy gains.
AI.conclusion: EO foundation model embeddings show promising potential for enabling a universal, scalable, deep learning-based LCZ mapping workflow, enhancing regional transferability and supporting the development of fine-scale LCZ maps for global urban climate applications. Embedding-based approaches reduce time-consuming preprocessing and manual feature engineering, though temporal robustness requires further work.

title: Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis using a Multimodal Approach with 3D MRI and PET
comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an irreversible neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of death worldwide. Early diagnosis plays an important part especially at the Mild Cognitive Impairment stage, where timely intervention can help slow its progression before it advances to AD. Neuroimaging data, like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, can help detect brain changes early by providing structural and functional brain changes related to the disease. Yet, many multimodal models still fuse MRI and PET with static concatenation and apply identical computation to all subjects, which limits robustness to patient/site heterogeneity and can waste computation. To address these limitations, we present the first study of combining 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies - concatenation, Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and gated self-attention - and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier that performs input-adaptive routing, activating only the most informative experts per case. Finally, we utilize Grad-CAM to visualize disease-related regions, ensuring model interpretability. Experiments are performed across three binary classification tasks (NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD). Results show that GMU achieves accuracies of 80.46 % (NC vs. MCI) and 95.47 % (NC vs. AD), while gated self-attention attains 82.08 % on MCI vs. AD. Ablations show that removing the MoE consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks. These findings underscore the value of input-adaptive, multimodal modeling for AD diagnosis by leveraging the complementary nature of MRI and PET.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multimodal Alzheimer's disease diagnosis framework combining 3D CNN feature extractors with three fusion strategies (concatenation, GMU, gated self-attention) and a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts classifier for input-adaptive routing. Tested on NC/MCI/AD classification tasks using MRI and PET, GMU achieves up to 95.47% accuracy, while ablations confirm MoE's critical contribution.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal MRI-PET fusion methods rely on static concatenation and apply uniform computation to all subjects, limiting robustness to patient and site heterogeneity and wasting computational resources. Early AD diagnosis, especially at the MCI stage, demands more adaptive and efficient approaches.
AI.method: The authors combine 3D convolutional feature extractors with three fusion strategies: (1) static concatenation, (2) Gated Multimodal Unit (GMU), and (3) gated self-attention. A sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) classifier performs input-adaptive routing, selectively activating only the most informative experts per case. Grad-CAM is employed to visualize disease-relevant brain regions for interpretability. Experiments cover three binary classification tasks: NC vs. MCI, MCI vs. AD, and NC vs. AD.
AI.result: GMU achieves 80.46% accuracy on NC vs. MCI and 95.47% on NC vs. AD. Gated self-attention attains 82.08% on MCI vs. AD. Ablation studies demonstrate that removing the MoE classifier consistently degrades accuracy across all tasks, validating its importance.
AI.conclusion: Input-adaptive multimodal modeling that leverages complementary MRI and PET information, combined with dynamic expert routing via MoE, significantly improves AD diagnosis performance. The work highlights the value of moving beyond static fusion toward subject-specific computation for neuroimaging-based diagnosis.

title: Comparative Study of Neural Surrogate Architectures for Autoregressive Prediction of Internal Battery States
summary: The Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) model resolves internal electrochemical states in lithium-ion batteries with high fidelity. However, the numerical solution of its governing equations is computationally prohibitive for real-time deployment, limiting scalability from individual cells to pack and fleet-scale applications. While machine learning surrogates can substantially reduce inference latency through GPU acceleration, most existing approaches learn solution approximations tied to specific operating conditions rather than learning generalizable state-evolution dynamics. This work presents a systematic comparison of four neural network architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators that predict full DFN internal states across a wide range of operating conditions. To ensure a controlled architectural comparison, all models are trained under a unified framework using multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning, isolating the impact of spatial inductive bias. Results demonstrate that the U-Net's multi-scale feature hierarchy achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% averaged across all internal state variables after 300-step autoregressive rollouts, while providing a 5.38x speed-up over the numerical solver. These findings highlight spatial inductive bias as a critical determinant of surrogate performance, advancing the development of surrogates for internal state observability for next-generation battery management systems and digital twins.

AI.tldr: A systematic comparison of four neural architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, FNO) as autoregressive DFN state-transition surrogates shows U-Net's multi-scale spatial inductive bias yields 3% nRMSE after 300-step rollout with 5.38× speedup over numerical solvers.
AI.motivation: The DFN model is too computationally expensive for real-time battery management, and existing ML surrogates learn operating-point-specific approximations rather than generalizable state-evolution dynamics. There is a need to identify which neural architectures best capture the spatiotemporal dynamics of full internal electrochemical states across diverse operating conditions.
AI.method: Four architectures (MLP, ResNet, U-Net, Fourier Neural Operator) are formulated as autoregressive state-transition operators predicting full DFN internal states. All models are trained under a unified framework with multi-step unrolling and current-conditioning to isolate the effect of spatial inductive bias. Performance is evaluated over 300-step autoregressive rollouts across multiple state variables.
AI.result: U-Net achieves a mean final-step nRMSE of 3% across all internal state variables after 300 autoregressive steps, with a 5.38× speed-up over the numerical DFN solver. Spatial inductive bias proves to be the critical determinant of surrogate performance.
AI.conclusion: Spatial inductive bias, particularly multi-scale feature hierarchies as in U-Net architectures, is essential for building accurate and generalizable DFN surrogates. This advances the feasibility of real-time internal state observability for battery management systems and digital twins at scale.

title: PaAno+: Multiscale Encoding and Cross-Variable Attention for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time-series anomaly detection has significant practical value for industrial and medical monitoring, as well as other critical domains. Current Transformer- and large-model-based detection approaches incur excessive computational overhead, while existing lightweight alternatives are constrained by insufficient feature extraction and inadequate modeling of dependencies across multivariate variables. To mitigate the above drawbacks, this study develops a lightweight, efficient anomaly detection model, dubbed PaAno, within the patch-oriented representation learning paradigm. In the encoder module, a multiscale feature-extraction backbone is constructed using convolutional kernels with differentiated receptive fields to capture hierarchical temporal characteristics; subsequent cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation, combined with residual connection optimization, further stabilizes feature representation learning. A cross-variable fusion attention module is embedded to explicitly characterize inter-variable correlations, empowering the model to identify anomalous patterns amid intricate operational conditions. Moreover, a novel pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting is customized to uncover intrinsic structural properties of time series, and triplet loss is leveraged to optimize the patch embedding space for enhanced feature discrimination. Extensive experiments on the TSB-AD benchmark demonstrate that the proposed PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on both univariate and multivariate tasks, yielding significant performance gains across evaluation metrics, including VUS-PR, relative to the original PaAno. Leveraging a compact network design, the presented model achieves favorable computational efficiency, enabling deployment on resource-limited terminals for real-time anomaly inference.

AI.tldr: PaAno is a lightweight patch-based anomaly detection model that uses multiscale convolutional encoders, cross-scale adaptive attention, cross-variable fusion attention, and a novel temporal patch-window sorting pretext task with triplet loss to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on TSB-AD while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for resource-constrained deployment.
AI.motivation: Transformer- and large-model anomaly detectors are computationally prohibitive, while existing lightweight alternatives suffer from insufficient temporal feature extraction and weak modeling of inter-variable dependencies in multivariate time series.
AI.method: PaAno employs: (1) a multiscale convolutional backbone with differentiated receptive fields for hierarchical temporal feature extraction; (2) cross-scale adaptive attention aggregation with residual connections for stabilized representation learning; (3) a cross-variable fusion attention module to explicitly model inter-variable correlations; (4) a pretext task based on temporal patch-window sorting to capture structural properties of time series; and (5) triplet loss to enhance patch embedding discrimination.
AI.result: PaAno achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on the TSB-AD benchmark for both univariate and multivariate tasks, with significant gains in VUS-PR and other evaluation metrics, while maintaining compact network design and favorable computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: PaAno successfully bridges the gap between detection accuracy and computational efficiency, making real-time anomaly inference feasible on resource-limited terminals without sacrificing performance.

title: Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics
summary: Perception for action suggests that representations of the world should be shaped not by visual fidelity alone, but by their relevance for actions. At the same time, latent JEPA-style world models advocate learning compact predictive states from high-dimensional observations to facilitate the prediction of future states, but end-to-end training of these models is nontrivial because representations may collapse if our only goal is to construct a latent state that is easy to predict. We introduce a sensorimotor world model (SMWM): a latent world model trained end-to-end with inverse dynamics regularization. This single regularizer addresses both issues: it prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations. By forcing latent states to preserve information about the action underlying a transition, it biases the model toward the controllable degrees of freedom of the environment while discarding uncontrollable distractors. This yields stable latent world models trained from offline, reward-free trajectories, without frozen encoders, exponential moving averages, or complex latent regularizers. Empirically, SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces and enables competitive planning performance across simple 2D and 3D control tasks.

AI.tldr: SMWM introduces a sensorimotor world model trained with inverse dynamics regularization to prevent latent collapse and induce action-aligned representations, enabling stable end-to-end training from offline, reward-free trajectories for planning in control tasks.
AI.motivation: Two key challenges: (1) perception-for-action suggests representations should prioritize action relevance over visual fidelity; (2) JEPA-style latent world models suffer from representation collapse when trained end-to-end solely to predict future states. Existing solutions rely on frozen encoders, EMA, or complex regularizers, which are cumbersome.
AI.method: Proposes SMWM, a latent world model trained end-to-end with a single regularizer: inverse dynamics prediction. The model learns a latent state from observations and predicts the next latent state (forward dynamics), while simultaneously predicting the action that caused the transition from consecutive latent states. This forces latent states to retain information about controllable degrees of freedom and discard uncontrollable distractors.
AI.result: SMWM learns compact, interpretable latent spaces without frozen encoders, EMA, or complex regularizers. It demonstrates competitive planning performance on simple 2D and 3D control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Inverse dynamics regularization is a simple yet effective single mechanism that simultaneously prevents representation collapse and induces action-aligned representations in latent world models trained end-to-end from offline, reward-free data.

title: Quantile of Means: A Bonus-Free Ensemble Method for Minimax Optimal Reinforcement Learning
summary: Optimal Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically rely on carefully constructed count-based uncertainty estimates to drive exploration. Although theoretically sound, such estimates are hard to compute in practical settings and therefore offer limited insight for designing exploration heuristics. Meanwhile, ensembling has emerged as a practical approach, but remains without theoretical justification. Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, we propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Our simple count-free approach achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration in RL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon MDPs that achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds without requiring count-based uncertainty estimates, thereby providing theoretical justification for ensemble-based exploration in reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Optimal RL algorithms rely on count-based uncertainty estimates that are theoretically sound but practically hard to compute. Ensemble methods are empirically successful but lack theoretical justification. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing theoretical grounding for ensemble-based exploration.
AI.method: Building on a recent ensemble-based method for Multi-Armed Bandits, the authors propose a quantile-based ensemble method for finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The approach is count-free and uses ensembles to drive exploration.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves optimal variance-dependent regret bounds, matching the theoretical guarantees of count-based methods while maintaining the practical advantages of ensemble approaches.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-based exploration in RL can be theoretically justified. The quantile-based ensemble method provides a simple, count-free alternative that achieves optimal regret bounds, bridging theory and practice in exploration for RL.

title: When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital: Federated Conformal Risk Control via Risk-Curve Shrinkage
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the DeCaF Workshop at MICCAI 2026
summary: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees on segmentation quality by calibrating a prediction-set threshold on held-out data. In federated deployments, the standard approach pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold. We provide the first quantification, on real multi-institutional brain tumor data (FeTS-2022, 1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), showing that this naive pooled CRC protects the average hospital but violates coverage at 40% of individual institutions, with the worst site exceeding the target false-negative rate by 7.8 percentage points. The naive alternative, per-site local CRC, largely restores coverage but inflates prediction sets by 83x, rendering them clinically useless. We propose a shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n0 smoothly trades worst-case coverage for prediction-set efficiency; leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis identifies n0=19, achieving 2.7/20 violations at 2.0x stretch. We further show that direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets fails, concentrating risk on vulnerable hospitals, and that the finite-sample correction term is essential: removing it triples violations. The marginal CRC guarantee is preserved by construction under the stated site-mixture assumption; per-site coverage is validated across four targets with three seeds. No patient-level images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site.

AI.tldr: Federated conformal risk control (CRC) with a naive pooled threshold violates per-site coverage (40% of hospitals fail), while local CRC inflates prediction sets 83×. The proposed shrinkage-based federated protocol transmits only empirical risk curves, using a single hyperparameter to trade worst-case coverage for efficiency, achieving near-nominal violation rates with modest set inflation.
AI.motivation: Standard federated CRC pools calibration scores across sites into a single threshold, but this only guarantees average coverage and can catastrophically fail at individual institutions. There is a need for a privacy-preserving federated method that maintains per-site coverage guarantees without rendering prediction sets clinically useless.
AI.method: Shrinkage-based federated CRC: each site transmits only its empirical risk curve (G scalars) to a server, which computes a shrinkage-regularized threshold per site. A single hyperparameter n₀ controls the trade-off between worst-case coverage and prediction-set efficiency. The method incorporates a finite-sample correction term and uses leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter selection. Direct Lagrangian optimization of coverage budgets is also evaluated but shown to fail.
AI.result: On FeTS-2022 (1,251 subjects, 20 institutions), naive pooled CRC violated coverage at 40% of institutions (worst site: +7.8 pp false-negative rate). Local CRC inflated sets 83×. The proposed method with n₀=19 achieved 2.7/20 violations at 2.0× stretch. Removing the finite-sample correction tripled violations. Per-site coverage validated across four targets with three seeds.
AI.conclusion: The shrinkage-based federated CRC protocol effectively balances per-site coverage guarantees with clinically usable prediction-set sizes, preserving privacy (no images, masks, or per-volume scores leave any site) while maintaining the marginal CRC guarantee under the site-mixture assumption.

title: Multi-Modal Contrastive Learning for Implicit Earth Embeddings via Location Tying
summary: Spatial prediction tasks are often limited by a lack of high-quality labelled ground-truth observations. To overcome this challenge, self-supervised pre-training is a possible solution, with contrastive learning dominant for location encoders. Those approaches usually align geographic coordinates with just one additional modality. We propose two multimodal contrastive learning architectures: Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying (MELT) and Sequential Alternating Location Training (SALT). These architectures expand this framework beyond two modalities by utilising unpaired geospatial data. Both methods are technically viable and match the performance of the strongest two-modality baseline (SATCLIP) across four downstream tasks. However, increasing the number of modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting that the chosen location encoder is the main limitation - the contrastive objective reaches its peak early, regardless of modality diversity or pre-training volume. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and presents a stronger foundation for future scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MELT and SALT, two multimodal contrastive learning architectures that extend self-supervised location encoder pre-training beyond two modalities using unpaired geospatial data. While both match the strongest two-modality baseline, increasing modalities does not consistently improve performance, suggesting the location encoder itself is the limiting factor.
AI.motivation: Spatial prediction tasks suffer from scarce high-quality labelled ground-truth data. Self-supervised pre-training with contrastive learning is a promising remedy, but existing methods typically align geographic coordinates with only one additional modality, limiting the potential richness of learned representations.
AI.method: Two architectures are proposed: (1) MELT (Multimodal Embedding via Location Tying) — ties all modalities through a shared location encoder anchor, and (2) SALT (Sequential Alternating Location Training) — alternates training between different modality pairs. Both leverage unpaired geospatial data and are benchmarked against SATCLIP across four downstream tasks.
AI.result: Both MELT and SALT match SATCLIP (the strongest two-modality baseline) in performance across all downstream tasks. However, adding more modalities does not yield consistent improvements. The contrastive objective saturates early regardless of modality diversity or pre-training data volume, pointing to the location encoder as the primary bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal contrastive pre-training with unpaired geospatial data is technically viable, but simply adding modalities offers diminishing returns. Future work should focus on improving the location encoder rather than scaling modalities. MELT provides more stable training than SALT and is recommended as the foundation for further scaling efforts.

title: Predicting gestational age at birth in the context of preterm birth from multi-modal fetal MRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA) https://melba-journal.org/2026:013
summary: Preterm birth is associated with significant mortality and a risk for lifelong morbidity. The complex multifactorial aetiology hampers accurate prediction and thus optimal care. A pipeline consisting of bespoke machine learning methods for data imputation, feature selection, and regression models to predict gestational age (GA) at birth was developed and evaluated from comprehensive multi-modal morphological and functional fetal MRI data from 333 control cases and 93 preterm birth cases. The GA at birth predictions were classified into term and preterm categories and their accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were reported. An ablation study was performed to further validate the design of the pipeline. Performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The pipeline achieves an R2 score of 0.13 and a mean absolute error of 2.74 weeks. It also achieves a 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity across folds. The predominant features selected by the pipeline include cervical length and statistics derived from placental T2* values. The confluence of fast, motion-robust and multi-modal fetal MRI techniques and machine learning prediction allowed the prediction of the gestation at birth. This information is essential for any pregnancy. To the best of our knowledge, preterm birth had only been addressed as a classification problem in the literature. Therefore, this work provides a proof of concept. Future work will increase the cohort size to allow for finer stratification within the preterm birth cohort. Our code is available at https://github.com/dfajardorojas/ml-for-preterm-birth-.

AI.tldr: A machine learning pipeline using multi-modal fetal MRI data (morphological and functional) was developed to predict gestational age at birth. Evaluated on 426 cases (333 control, 93 preterm), it achieved R²=0.13, MAE=2.74 weeks, 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, and 0.82 specificity for preterm classification. Cervical length and placental T2* statistics were the most predictive features.
AI.motivation: Preterm birth carries high mortality and lifelong morbidity risk, yet its complex multifactorial etiology hampers accurate prediction and optimal clinical care. Existing literature treats preterm birth only as a classification problem, leaving a gap for continuous gestational age prediction.
AI.method: A bespoke pipeline comprising data imputation, feature selection, and regression models was built using comprehensive multi-modal fetal MRI (morphological and functional) from 333 controls and 93 preterm cases. Gestational age predictions were dichotomized into term/preterm categories for classification metrics. An ablation study validated pipeline design, and stratified 10-fold cross-validation was used for evaluation.
AI.result: The pipeline achieved R²=0.13, MAE=2.74 weeks for regression, and 0.77 accuracy, 0.59 sensitivity, 0.82 specificity for preterm classification. Predominant predictive features were cervical length and placental T2* statistics. Ablation studies supported the pipeline architecture.
AI.conclusion: This work provides proof of concept that combining fast, motion-robust multi-modal fetal MRI with machine learning enables prediction of gestation at birth — a clinically essential parameter. It is the first to address preterm birth as a regression rather than purely classification task. Future work will expand cohort size for finer preterm stratification.

title: Computational Methods and Challenges in Cell-Free DNA Analysis for Multi-Cancer Early Detection
summary: Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is a promising avenue for non-invasive multicancer early detection (MCED), in that, it can enable multiple cancer detection simultaneously from a single blood draw, with particular sensitivity to cancers that currently lack established screening programs. Here we review the computational methods developed between 2022 and 2025 for cfDNA-based MCED. We focus on how fragmentomics and epigenetic features are extracted and analyzed to detect cancer at early stages. We first briefly outline the biological basis of cfDNA signals, then review classical statistical and machine learning approaches alongside deep learning frameworks including autoencoder-based models. For each method we discuss biological interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical integration. Furthermore, we categorize the current challenges into technical, computational, and methodological while outlining open problems in the field. This review shows that multimodal ensemble approaches have the strongest promise for clinical integration and the highest readiness. However, for better assessment of future work and side-by-side comparison, standardization of evaluation protocols and reporting results will be crucial.

AI.tldr: A review of computational methods (2022–2025) for cell-free DNA-based multi-cancer early detection, covering fragmentomic and epigenetic feature extraction, classical ML and deep learning approaches, and assessing clinical readiness—with multimodal ensembles showing greatest promise.
AI.motivation: cfDNA-based liquid biopsy enables simultaneous, non-invasive detection of multiple cancers from a single blood draw, especially for cancers lacking established screening programs. However, the computational methods for extracting and analyzing fragmentomic and epigenetic signals are rapidly evolving and require systematic review to assess their interpretability, validation, and clinical integration readiness.
AI.method: This is a literature review covering computational methods published between 2022 and 2025. The authors organize methods by: (1) biological signal basis (fragmentomics and epigenetics), (2) analytical paradigm (classical statistical/ML vs. deep learning, including autoencoder-based models), and (3) evaluation criteria (biological interpretability, validation strategy, clinical readiness). Challenges are categorized into technical, computational, and methodological dimensions.
AI.result: Multimodal ensemble approaches that integrate multiple feature types (fragmentomic + epigenetic) demonstrate the strongest promise and highest readiness for clinical integration. A critical gap identified is the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and reporting practices, which hampers fair side-by-side comparison of methods.
AI.conclusion: The field is converging toward multimodal ensemble strategies for cfDNA-based MCED. Future progress depends critically on establishing standardized benchmarks and transparent reporting to enable rigorous comparative assessment and accelerate clinical translation.

title: Effective Dimension Governs Generalization in Quantum Kernel Vision Models
summary: Recent quantum vision models-quantum vision transformers and quantum convolutional networks-report two striking but unexplained empirical phenomena: (i) ansatze with more, or more uniformly distributed, entanglement generalize better, and (ii) injecting quantum noise can improve test accuracy rather than degrade it. These observations are currently treated as curiosities, discovered by grid search and explained, if at all, by hand. We show that both are manifestations of a single, measurable quantity: the \emph{effective dimension} $d_{\rm eff}$ of the (noise-shaped) quantum feature kernel. Working primarily with quantum-kernel vision models-a quantum feature map read out by a kernel classifier-we give a spectral account in which entanglement structure and quantum noise are two knobs that move $d_{\rm eff}$; in an overfitting regime, contracting $d_{\rm eff}$ acts as ridge-like regularization. We analyze the mechanism: an \emph{exact} decomposition of the depolarized kernel $K_p=(1-p)^2K+\tfrac{p(2-p)}{D}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$ with $d_{\rm eff}(K_p)\to1$, a contraction result (and its boundary) for amplitude damping, a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition; the monotone contraction operative in our entangled experiments is verified empirically, not proven in general. Along the one-parameter depolarizing family the collapse is instead exact by construction; we use it only to confirm the kernel decomposition to machine precision and at up to $12$ qubits, not as evidence for $d_{\rm eff}$. Amplitude damping contracts $d_{\rm eff}$ and lifts test accuracy by up to $+13\%$ along an inverted-U sweet spot; the effect's sign flips between the over- and under-fitting regimes; noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. Our results organize two reported anecdotes into a single measurable principle for designing quantum-vision models.

AI.tldr: Two unexplained empirical phenomena in quantum vision models—better generalization with more/uniform entanglement and improved accuracy from quantum noise injection—are unified as manifestations of a single quantity: the effective dimension of the quantum feature kernel. Entanglement and noise act as knobs controlling this effective dimension, providing ridge-like regularization in overfitting regimes.
AI.motivation: Two striking but unexplained empirical observations in quantum vision models (better generalization with more entanglement, and accuracy gains from noise injection) are currently treated as curiosities without a principled theoretical understanding.
AI.method: The authors work with quantum-kernel vision models (quantum feature map + kernel classifier) and provide a spectral analysis centered on the effective dimension of the noise-shaped quantum feature kernel. Key analytical contributions include: an exact decomposition of the depolarized kernel, a contraction result for amplitude damping, derivation of a kernel-machine capacity bound, and a capacity/alignment risk decomposition.
AI.result: Amplitude damping contracts effective dimension and lifts test accuracy by up to +13% along an inverted-U sweet spot. The effect's sign flips between overfitting and underfitting regimes. Noise injection matches an explicit spectral-filtering frontier. The depolarizing family confirms the kernel decomposition to machine precision at up to 12 qubits.
AI.conclusion: Both empirical phenomena are organized into a single measurable principle—effective dimension—for designing quantum-vision models. Entanglement structure and quantum noise serve as controllable knobs that regulate effective dimension, acting as implicit regularization.

title: Learner-based Concept Drift Detection: Analysis and Evaluation
summary: Machine learning algorithms deployed for evolving streaming environments must handle the non-stationary data distributions, commonly referred to as concept drift. The presence of concept drift poses a major challenge for many real-world applications because it can severely degrade their predictive performance, hindering their ability to support robust decision-making. Consequently, the timely and efficient detection of drift events is critical for sustaining high accuracy over time. This study examines theoretically the concept drift characteristics and numerous drift detection algorithms across several categories. Furthermore, we evaluate their performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets exhibiting diverse streaming scenarios and drift characteristics, such as abrupt and gradual changes. This study aims to enhance understanding of the complex notion of concept drift characteristics and behavior of drift detectors, along with their applicability to diverse contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a theoretical examination of concept drift characteristics and a comprehensive evaluation of various drift detection algorithms across different categories, tested on both synthetic and real-world streaming datasets with diverse drift patterns (abrupt, gradual), aiming to clarify detector behavior and applicability.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models in streaming environments suffer performance degradation due to concept drift (non-stationary data distributions), and there is a need for better theoretical understanding of drift characteristics and systematic evaluation of detection algorithms to support robust real-world decision-making.
AI.method: The authors conduct a theoretical analysis of concept drift characteristics and categorize numerous drift detection algorithms. They then empirically evaluate these detectors on both synthetic and real-world datasets that encompass diverse streaming scenarios and drift types, including abrupt and gradual changes.
AI.result: The study delivers insights into how different drift detectors perform under varying drift characteristics and streaming contexts, highlighting the relationship between drift properties and detector behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work enhances understanding of concept drift as a complex phenomenon and clarifies the applicability of different drift detection algorithms across diverse streaming contexts, guiding practitioners in selecting appropriate detectors for specific scenarios.

title: Boundary Embedding Shaping with Adaptive Contrastive Learning for Graph Structural Disentanglement
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at aggregating neighbor information for classification, yet their performance is hindered by graph structural entanglement, where spurious correlations from semantically irrelevant neighbors contaminate node embeddings. This challenge is most acute for nodes near class boundaries in the embedding space, where amplified structural noise blurs decision boundaries and destabilizes predictions. Existing robust GNN methods largely treat all nodes uniformly, ignoring boundary vulnerabilities. In this paper, to improve classification performance, we tackle graph structural disentanglement by identifying boundary-region entanglement as the primary bottleneck and propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive learning GNN plug-in module that selectively suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries with minimal model parameter perturbation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms existing leading methods. Notably, BES boosts GCN performance by an average of 3.3% in node classification (up to 5.0% on WikiCS) and achieves superior accuracy in link prediction.
