AI.tldr: BES is a plug-in contrastive learning module for GNNs that targets boundary-region structural entanglement — where spurious neighbor correlations most harm classification — by adaptively suppressing noise near decision boundaries, yielding significant gains in node classification and link prediction.
AI.motivation: GNN performance suffers from graph structural entanglement: semantically irrelevant neighbors introduce spurious correlations that contaminate node embeddings. This problem is especially severe for nodes near class decision boundaries, where structural noise blurs separability. Existing robust GNN methods treat all nodes uniformly and overlook these boundary-specific vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), a plug-in adaptive contrastive learning module. BES identifies nodes in boundary regions of the embedding space and applies selective suppression of spurious structural noise. It operates with minimal perturbation to model parameters, making it easy to integrate into existing GNN architectures.
AI.result: BES consistently improves boundary discrimination and outperforms leading methods. It boosts GCN node classification accuracy by an average of 3.3%, with up to 5.0% improvement on WikiCS. BES also achieves superior accuracy on link prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-region structural entanglement is the primary bottleneck for GNN classification. BES effectively addresses this by adaptively shaping embeddings near decision boundaries, offering a lightweight, general-purpose solution that significantly enhances GNN robustness and accuracy.

title: Integrating national forest inventory, airborne lidar, and satellite imagery for wall-to-wall mapping of forest structure with computer vision
summary: Remote sensing is increasingly relied upon to deliver actionable science for forest and wildfire risk management across large landscapes. Wall-to-wall, annually updated maps are a persistent need for effective forest management. Many planning systems and data collections combine disparate data sources with different purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, which leads to confounding behavior in operational planning systems. We introduce the VibrantForests framework, developed and applied to map forest attributes and provide a coherent foundation for effective forest and wildfire planning. VibrantForests includes a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived samples and applied across the contiguous United States to concurrently generate estimates of canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter at 10-meter resolution. We demonstrate predictive capability spanning the full spectrum of forest conditions ranging from sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass. Results show that our model extends the range at which saturation is commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models, and reduces regression-to-mean behavior that commonly produces overestimation of forest attributes in small/sparse conditions and underestimation in large/dense conditions. The VibrantForests framework addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent wall-to-wall estimates of management-relevant attributes at annual cadence and 10m resolution.

AI.tldr: VibrantForests is a satellite-based framework that generates annual, 10m-resolution, wall-to-wall maps of five forest structure attributes across the contiguous US. Trained on lidar-derived samples, it overcomes common passive-sensor saturation and regression-to-mean biases, providing coherent estimates from sparse/low-biomass to dense/high-biomass conditions for wildfire and forest management planning.
AI.motivation: Current operational forest and wildfire planning systems rely on disparate data sources with differing purposes, vintages, and prediction quality, creating confounding behavior. There is a persistent need for wall-to-wall, annually updated, management-relevant forest attribute maps that provide coherent, consistent estimates across large landscapes.
AI.method: The VibrantForests framework uses a satellite-based forest structure model trained on lidar-derived reference samples. It concurrently estimates five forest attributes — canopy cover, canopy height, aboveground live tree biomass, basal area, and quadratic mean diameter — at 10-meter resolution, applied wall-to-wall across the contiguous United States.
AI.result: The model demonstrates predictive capability across the full spectrum of forest conditions (sparse-canopy/low-biomass to dense-canopy/high-biomass). It extends the saturation range commonly encountered in comparable passive-sensor models and reduces regression-to-mean behavior, thereby mitigating overestimation in sparse/small conditions and underestimation in dense/large conditions.
AI.conclusion: VibrantForests addresses a key limitation in large-area forest and wildfire planning by delivering coherent, wall-to-wall, annually updated estimates of management-relevant forest attributes at 10m resolution, providing a unified foundation for operational decision-making.

title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
summary: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: SLiR is a general framework for generating sound linear relaxations of neural network activation functions using only a Lipschitz constant or critical points, eliminating the need for hand-crafted per-function relaxations and enabling up to 7.8x more property verifications than prior art.
AI.motivation: Existing neural network verification methods rely on hand-crafted linear relaxations tailored to each activation function. As novel activation functions proliferate, this manual approach does not scale, creating a bottleneck for formal verification in safety- and security-critical domains. A general, automated relaxation technique is needed.
AI.method: SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) parameterizes linear relaxations by slope and computes the offset through a shifting procedure. Given only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points for an activation function, SLiR derives provably sound upper and lower bounding lines over the input domain, making it universally applicable without manual per-function design.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation demonstrates that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions. It enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art verification methods that use hand-crafted relaxations.
AI.conclusion: SLiR provides a scalable, automated alternative to hand-crafted activation function relaxations for NN verification, significantly broadening the scope of verifiable networks while improving verification performance.

title: Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions
summary: Classical approximation theorems ask for a new neural network whenever the target accuracy is improved. This paper studies the opposite possibility: can the network be chosen once and for all, and can accuracy be bought only by letting it run longer? We prove that this is possible for every continuous function on [-1,1]. More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension. The mechanism behind the construction is a new intermediate model, the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). This model retains the algorithmic freedom needed to implement polynomial approximation schemes, while remaining rigid enough to be simulated by RNNs with explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitude. The resulting convergence rates reflect the underlying polynomial approximation rates. We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

AI.tldr: Classical neural network approximation requires larger networks for better accuracy. This paper proves that a single, fixed-size ReLU recurrent neural network can uniformly approximate any continuous function on [-1,1] by simply running it longer, eliminating the need for architectural changes. The construction relies on simulating a "Turing machine with neural units" (TMNU), and lower bounds confirm runtime is an essential resource, not an artifact.
AI.motivation: To challenge the classical paradigm where improved approximation accuracy demands new, typically larger neural networks. The authors ask whether a single network with fixed architecture and weights can instead achieve arbitrary accuracy solely through increased runtime (i.e., more recurrent iterations), akin to trading time for precision in a universal approximator.
AI.method: The authors construct a fixed-weight, fixed-hidden-dimension ReLU RNN whose forward iteration simulates a novel intermediate abstraction: the Turing machine with neural units (TMNU). The TMNU provides sufficient algorithmic flexibility to implement polynomial approximation schemes (e.g., Bernstein polynomials) for any continuous function on [-1,1], while being rigid enough to yield explicit bounds on hidden dimension and weight magnitudes of the simulating RNN. Complementing this, they derive minimax lower bounds to demonstrate that runtime is a necessary resource for achieving higher accuracy in this fixed-network regime.
AI.result: For every continuous function on [-1,1], there exists a single ReLU RNN with fixed weights and hidden dimension that achieves uniform ε-approximation by running for a finite number of time steps, with convergence rates matching those of the underlying polynomial schemes. Minimax lower bounds further prove that the required runtime must grow as accuracy improves, establishing that runtime is an unavoidable resource rather than a proof artifact.
AI.conclusion: The fixed-network, variable-runtime paradigm is viable: a single ReLU RNN can serve as a universal approximator for continuous functions on [-1,1], with accuracy bought solely by additional computation time. The TMNU abstraction bridges algorithmic flexibility and neural realizability, and the lower bounds cement runtime as a fundamental resource in neural approximation theory.

title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs
summary: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

AI.tldr: QCPIKAN is a hybrid quantum-classical framework combining Chebyshev-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with parameterized quantum circuits to solve PDEs. It enforces physical constraints via the training loss, achieves exponential high-frequency error convergence, and outperforms existing quantum-classical PINNs on porous media seepage problems (single-phase flow, component transport, two-phase flow).
AI.motivation: Existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks face limitations in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking, and displacement front localization when solving complex PDEs. There is a need for a more expressive, theoretically grounded hybrid architecture that can accelerate convergence and mitigate numerical dispersion.
AI.method: The authors propose QCPIKAN, built on Chebyshev-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) layers combined with parameterized quantum circuits. Physical constraints are embedded into the training loss (physics-informed paradigm). The framework is theoretically analyzed using approximation theory to prove exponential convergence rates for high-frequency errors and effective mitigation of numerical dispersion. Validation is performed on three porous-media seepage scenarios: single-phase flow, component transport, and two-phase flow.
AI.result: QCPIKAN achieves superior performance compared to existing quantum-classical PINNs across all evaluated metrics: global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking, and displacement front localization. The theoretical analysis confirms exponential convergence and numerical dispersion mitigation.
AI.conclusion: QCPIKAN offers a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs, combining the expressive power of KAN architectures with quantum circuit capabilities under a physics-informed training regime. The framework demonstrates practical utility in porous media flow problems and holds promise for broader PDE-solving applications.

title: Constrained hybrid modelling to predict microbial dynamics and organic matter turnover in soil systems
summary: Soil microorganisms control organic matter cycling and largely determine how soil systems can cope with and mitigate climate change and environmental threats. Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is therefore critical to predict carbon cycling in soils, albeit highly challenging to inform from data. One promising approach to improve their parametrisation is the integration of genomic data, yet modelling the complex and unknown relationship between genomes and the processes the microbes are driving is an unsolved problem. In this work, we present the first hybrid modeling framework for deriving biokinetic parameter values of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model from metagenome-inferred functional traits based on DNA sequencing data. Our model predicts biokinetic parameters of the process-based model from genomic trait data with a neural network and integrates constraints from ecological theory and literature to ensure realistic behavior, even of non-observed state variables. We evaluate our method on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data, showing that our approach improves performance over multiple baselines and learns the dynamics of unmeasurable components of the process-based model effectively, even for small training datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hybrid modeling framework that uses neural networks to predict biokinetic parameters of a process-based soil organic matter model from metagenome-inferred functional traits, bridging genomic data with mechanistic soil carbon modeling.
AI.motivation: Representing microbial dynamics in process-based soil models is critical for predicting carbon cycling, yet parameterizing these models is extremely challenging. Genomic data offers a promising avenue, but the relationship between genomes and microbial process rates remains complex and poorly understood — an unsolved problem the authors aim to address.
AI.method: The authors develop a hybrid framework combining a neural network with a process-based soil organic matter turnover model. The neural network predicts biokinetic parameters from metagenome-derived functional traits (DNA sequencing data). Ecological theory and literature-based constraints are integrated to ensure realistic model behavior, including for unobserved state variables.
AI.result: The method was evaluated on synthetic genomic trait datasets of varying complexity and on real data. It outperformed multiple baselines and learned the dynamics of unmeasurable components effectively, even with small training datasets.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid modeling approach successfully links genomic information to process-based soil carbon models, demonstrating that metagenome-informed parameter estimation is feasible and robust, opening new pathways for integrating molecular data into ecosystem-scale predictions.

title: Critical Percolation as a Synthetic Data Model for Interpretability
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Neural networks learn features that reflect the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Synthetic datasets used to evaluate interpretability methods typically lack this structure, limiting their value as realistic toy models. To close this gap, we introduce a family of synthetic datasets consisting of hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in a high-dimensional data space. The percolation data consists of sparse, low-dimensional fractal clusters with a power-law size distribution. Latent variables modeling a taxonomic hierarchy generate each data point's target value. The data model is analytically tractable with known critical exponents that fix its properties without requiring hyperparameter tuning. We leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to propose an almost linear-time algorithm to jointly sample a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition, enabling data generation at arbitrary scale. Using probing experiments, we find that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations. Together, sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability make critical percolation a principled testbed for interpretability research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a family of synthetic datasets based on hierarchical functions defined over critical mean-field percolation clusters, providing sparse, fractal, analytically tractable data with power-law statistics to serve as a principled testbed for neural network interpretability research.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic datasets for evaluating interpretability methods lack the hierarchical, multi-scale structure characteristic of natural data, limiting their realism. A need exists for analytically tractable toy models that capture these structural properties.
AI.method: The authors construct synthetic datasets using hierarchical functions on critical mean-field percolation clusters embedded in high-dimensional space. They leverage a mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence to develop an almost linear-time sampling algorithm that jointly generates a random tree and its hierarchical latent decomposition. Latent variables following a taxonomic hierarchy determine target values. The model's properties are fixed by analytically known critical exponents, requiring no hyperparameter tuning.
AI.result: Probing experiments demonstrate that the model's ground-truth latent variables can be linearly decoded from neural network activations trained on this data, validating its utility for interpretability research.
AI.conclusion: The combination of sparsity, self-similarity, power-law statistics, and analytical tractability positions critical percolation as a principled and scalable testbed for interpretability research, bridging the gap between simplistic synthetic datasets and natural data.

title: On the Variance of Temporal Difference Learning and its Reduction Using Control Variates
summary: We analyze the variance of temporal difference (TD) learning using the phased setting with tabular representation, and show that one of the mechanisms behind its ability to reduce variance is by effectively aggregating over a larger number of independent trajectories. Based on this insight, we demonstrate that (1) the variance of TD is asymptotically bounded from above by Monte Carlo (MC) estimators, and (2) shorter horizon updates incurs less variance for a fixed number of samples. Beyond TD, we show that Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE), a method for estimating the advantage function, can be seen as a type of regression-adjusted control variate, which achieves a tighter bound on the variance compared to TD in the large-sample limit. Finally, we numerically illustrate the behaviors of these estimators with carefully designed environments.

AI.tldr: TD learning reduces variance by aggregating over multiple independent trajectories in the phased setting. The paper proves TD's variance is asymptotically bounded above by MC, that shorter horizons reduce variance, and that DAE achieves even tighter variance bounds as a regression-adjusted control variate.
AI.motivation: To theoretically understand the variance reduction mechanisms of temporal difference (TD) learning compared to Monte Carlo methods, and to formally characterize how methods like Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) can achieve further variance reduction.
AI.method: The authors analyze TD learning variance in the phased setting with tabular representation. They derive asymptotic variance bounds comparing TD to MC estimators, analyze the effect of update horizon length on variance, and reframe DAE as a regression-adjusted control variate to establish its tighter variance bound.
AI.result: TD variance is asymptotically bounded above by MC variance. Shorter horizon updates incur less variance for a fixed sample budget. DAE, viewed as a regression-adjusted control variate, achieves a strictly tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit.
AI.conclusion: TD's variance reduction stems from effective aggregation over independent trajectories; DAE further tightens this bound via control variate adjustment. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings.

title: Train, Retrieve, or Both? A Four-Arm Head-to-Head for Correct Statutory Citation on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act
summary: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need to be pointed at the provision of law that actually governs a question, with a correct statutory citation. We study this task on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) and its core regulation, asking the operator's question empirically: is fine-tuning enough, or is hybrid retrieval needed? We run a four-arm head-to-head on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (base zero-shot, LoRA SFT-only, RAG-only, and an SFT+RAG hybrid), scored on citation exact-match (section+subsection) over a small, human-verification-pending real eval set. The base model cannot cite the RTA and SFT-only mis-recalls sections; retrieval is essential and drives hallucination to zero by construction; and the SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. Its edge comes from SFT making provision selection more robust to the higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. Notably, this cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats a pipeline built on bigger, specialized retrieval models (a larger embedder and a cross-encoder reranker), and a larger/improved training set does not help either: strong statutory-citation performance here does not require specialized retrieval models or more data. The artifact zeroes hallucination and clears the lift-over-base bar but does not reach the aspirational 0.70 exact-match target. All results are on a small, human-verification-pending real eval set and are reported as preliminary.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or a hybrid approach is needed for correctly citing legal statutes. Testing on the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, the SFT+RAG hybrid achieved the highest citation exact-match (0.481) with zero hallucinations, outperforming base, SFT-only, and RAG-only models. Cheap retrieval (bge-small) proved sufficient, matching specialized pipelines.
AI.motivation: Self-represented tenants, landlords, and help-desk staff need accurate statutory citations to the correct legal provisions. The core empirical question is whether fine-tuning alone suffices for this task or whether hybrid retrieval-augmented generation is necessary for accurate, hallucination-free legal citation.
AI.method: A four-arm head-to-head comparison using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the base model: (1) zero-shot, (2) LoRA supervised fine-tuning only (SFT-only), (3) retrieval-augmented generation only (RAG-only), and (4) an SFT+RAG hybrid. Evaluation used citation exact-match (section+subsection) on a small, human-verification-pending real evaluation set. The hybrid used bge-small embeddings, with comparisons against larger embedders and cross-encoder rerankers.
AI.result: The base model cannot cite the RTA at all. SFT-only mis-recalls sections. RAG drives hallucination to zero by construction. The SFT+RAG hybrid scores highest at 0.481 exact-match with zero hallucinated citations. SFT makes provision selection more robust to higher-recall candidate sets that hurt zero-shot RAG. The cheap bge-small hybrid matches or beats pipelines using larger specialized retrieval models and cross-encoder rerankers. A larger training set did not improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval is essential for statutory citation; fine-tuning alone is insufficient. The SFT+RAG hybrid achieves the best performance by making provision selection robust to noisy retrieval. Strong results do not require specialized retrieval models or more data. However, the 0.481 exact-match still falls short of the aspirational 0.70 target. All findings are preliminary, based on a small, human-verification-pending eval set.

title: Judging to Improve: A De-biased VLM-as-3D-Judge Protocol for Single-Image 3D Generation
summary: A companion study established a de-biased, cross-model VLM-as-3D-judge that reliably ranks single-image-to-3D mesh quality where cheap geometry and CLIP proxies fall short. This paper asks: can that judge's preferences specialize a strong open generator, TRELLIS, on one asset class (furniture), cheaply and without human labels? Taking the judge from ranking to optimization is where the work lives. Pushing a VLM judge into the training and evaluation loop exposes failure modes ranking never triggered, so our contribution is an optimization-grade hardening of the judge: a training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) held distinct from an evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; position-bias correction; and fixes for three failure modes (image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs), with calibration evidence (clear-gap win-rate 0.83-1.0; base-vs-base ~0.5). Using this protocol as an independent evaluator, and working only from public models and data with lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation, we find our methods match the strong base rather than exceed it. Independent base samples carry essentially no learnable preference (0.94 order-flip rate), so signal must be engineered by quality-contrastive construction. Across six adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, the most targeted - conditioner repair under severe degradation - reaches parity (0.50) with the base, while no method clears the >=65% win-rate target. The result is mechanistic: clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DIT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects. Matching a strong public-data base with cheap adaptation is itself informative: exceeding it needs more than lightweight PEFT on public data, and the judge protocol is reusable.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether a VLM-as-3D-judge's preferences can cheaply specialize a strong open 3D generator (TRELLIS) on furniture assets without human labels. The core contribution is hardening the judge for optimization use — fixing position bias, image overload, geometry-hiding renders, and reference-free judging failures. Results show lightweight PEFT methods only reach parity with the base model, not exceed it, revealing that independent base samples carry little learnable preference signal.
AI.motivation: A prior companion study showed that VLM-based judges reliably rank 3D mesh quality where cheap geometry/CLIP proxies fail. The natural next step is using such a judge's preferences to specialize a generator (TRELLIS) on a specific asset class (furniture) without expensive human labels. The gap is that moving from ranking to optimization exposes failure modes that ranking never triggered, requiring the judge to be hardened for training-loop use.
AI.method: The authors harden the VLM judge for optimization through: (1) separating training judge (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) from evaluation judge (InternVL3-8B) to break circularity; (2) position-bias correction; (3) fixing three failure modes — image overload, geometry-hiding splat renders, and reference-free judging that rewards clean-but-wrong outputs. They test six PEFT adaptation methods, two input regimes, and a severity sweep, using quality-contrastive construction to engineer learnable signal. All work uses only public models and data.
AI.result: Independent base samples show a 0.94 order-flip rate (near-random), confirming no inherent learnable preference signal. Across all adaptation methods, only "conditioner repair under severe degradation" reaches parity (0.50 win-rate) with the base model. No method reaches the target of ≥65% win-rate. Clean inputs saturate the judge, flow-DiT fine-tuning washes out through the sampler, and conditioning repair is identified as the locus that moves geometry. Win-rates are directional at n=8 objects.
AI.conclusion: Matching a strong public-data base model with cheap PEFT adaptation is already informative; exceeding it requires more than lightweight PEFT on public data. The hardened judge protocol is reusable for future work. The mechanistic insight is that conditioning repair is the most promising locus for geometry improvement in flow-based 3D generators.

title: CRAX: Fast Safe Reinforcement Learning Benchmarking
summary: Safety is a core concern for deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents in real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving. While benchmarks have been central to progress in RL, existing safety benchmarks with high-fidelity 3D physics remain computationally slow, limiting large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. To address this gap, we propose CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX). Built on top of the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine with realistic 3D dynamics, CRAX leverages vectorized operations and hardware acceleration, yielding up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. The benchmark features six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each spanning three difficulty levels. Evaluating six popular safe RL methods shows that no single approach dominates across all tasks, and reveals the trade-offs between performance and safety. We find that curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer can improve performance over direct training in harder settings.

AI.tldr: CRAX is a hardware-accelerated safety benchmark for constrained RL built on MuJoCo XLA (MJX), achieving ~100x speedups over CPU-based alternatives. It features six environment suites with three difficulty levels each, and benchmarking reveals no single safe RL method dominates, while curriculum learning and safety transfer improve performance.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks for RL with high-fidelity 3D physics are computationally slow, which limits large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping. There is a need for a fast, scalable benchmark that maintains realistic dynamics while enabling efficient evaluation of safe RL methods.
AI.method: CRAX is built on the MuJoCo XLA (MJX) physics engine, leveraging JAX-based vectorized operations and hardware acceleration (GPU/TPU). It provides six environment suites and three agent-specific tasks, each with three difficulty levels. Six popular safe RL algorithms are evaluated across these tasks.
AI.result: CRAX achieves up to ~100x speedups over comparable CPU-based safety benchmarks. Benchmarking results show that no single safe RL method dominates across all tasks, revealing inherent performance-safety trade-offs. Curriculum learning across difficulty levels and safety transfer from simpler to harder settings improve performance over direct training on hard tasks.
AI.conclusion: CRAX enables rapid, large-scale experimentation in safe RL with realistic 3D dynamics. The benchmark highlights that algorithm selection is task-dependent, and that curriculum-based training strategies offer a promising direction for improving both performance and safety in constrained RL settings.

title: Towards Modality-imbalanced Federated Graph Learning: A Data Synthesis-based Approach
summary: MultiModal Federated Graph Learning (MM-FGL) offers a natural collaborative training paradigm, but its practical deployment is challenged by two granularities of modality imbalance. Client-level imbalance occurs when certain clients lack entire modalities, while node-level imbalance occurs when individual nodes exhibit missing visual or textual attributes. While several relevant studies exist, our investigation reveals that they predominantly target graph-agnostic or centralized scenarios, rendering them difficult to adapt directly. To address these challenges, we formalize modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as an implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis problem. This paradigm recovers missing modal semantics directly within the representation space, thereby maximizing alignment with the original data's semantic distribution and mitigating the high variance induced by missing modalities. To this end, we propose FedMGS (Federated Modality-aware Graph Synthesis), which integrates three core components. The availability-aware graph encoder prevents missing modalities from contaminating local structural propagation. The prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer establishes cross-client semantic anchors for unavailable modalities. The reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism regulates the impact of recovered latent representations prior to predictive readout. Extensive experiments on four tasks show that FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines with gains up to 17.41% with best efficiency-performance tradeoff.

AI.tldr: FedMGS addresses modality-imbalanced MultiModal Federated Graph Learning by synthesizing missing modal semantics in latent representation space, using an availability-aware encoder, prototype-guided synthesis, and reliability-calibrated fusion, achieving up to 17.41% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing MM-FGL methods assume balanced modalities and target graph-agnostic or centralized settings, failing to handle two granularities of modality imbalance: client-level (entire modalities missing per client) and node-level (individual nodes missing visual/textual attributes). This renders direct adaptation impractical for real-world federated graph deployments.
AI.method: FedMGS formulates modality-imbalanced MM-FGL as implicit graph-aware latent semantic representation synthesis. It comprises: (1) an availability-aware graph encoder that prevents missing modalities from corrupting local structural propagation; (2) a prototype-guided latent semantic synthesizer that establishes cross-client semantic anchors to recover unavailable modal representations; and (3) a reliability-calibrated semantic fusion mechanism that regulates the contribution of synthesized representations before final prediction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across four tasks demonstrate FedMGS consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving performance gains up to 17.41% while maintaining the best efficiency-performance tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: FedMGS effectively tackles both client-level and node-level modality imbalance in MM-FGL through latent-space semantic synthesis, avoiding direct raw-data reconstruction and demonstrating superior performance and efficiency in federated multimodal graph learning.

title: The Significance of Style Diversity in Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Generating high-utility synthetic data for intent classification typically requires human-annotated seed data, which is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings. In this paper, we propose a framework for synthetic dialogue generation that works entirely without human-annotated data, relying solely on intent definitions. Our proposed dialogue generation framework utilizes two different types of topic and style attributes to improve data diversity. Also, we propose two novel post-hoc stylization models called Univ and Exam to transform synthetic LLM-generated utterances into more varied, human-like linguistic styles. To enhance data quality, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge filtering process. Experimental results on both industrial and public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained using human-annotated training data. Crucially, the findings reveal that style diversity is more critical than topic diversity for synthetic data utility, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating style attributes during the generation process is more effective than post-hoc style adaptation.

AI.tldr: A fully unsupervised framework for generating synthetic intent classification dialogues using only intent definitions, with style diversity proving more critical than topic diversity for downstream model performance.
AI.motivation: Human-annotated seed data for intent classification is often unavailable in fast-paced industrial settings, creating a need for fully automated synthetic data generation methods that do not rely on any human annotations.
AI.method: The framework generates synthetic dialogues using only intent definitions, employing two types of topic and style attributes for diversity. Two post-hoc stylization models (Univ and Exam) transform LLM-generated utterances into more human-like linguistic styles. An LLM-as-a-judge filtering process is used to enhance data quality.
AI.result: The approach achieves up to 93.3% of the performance obtained with human-annotated training data on both industrial and public datasets. Style diversity was found to be more critical than topic diversity, as it prevents models from learning spurious stylistic correlations. Incorporating style attributes during generation proved more effective than post-hoc adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Fully unsupervised synthetic dialogue generation is viable for intent classification, with style diversity being the key factor for utility rather than topic diversity. Attribute incorporation during generation outperforms post-hoc stylization.

title: Direct Advantage Estimation for Scalable and Sample-efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) has been shown to improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its reliance on full environment observability limits its applicability in realistic settings, and its requirement to model transition probabilities incurs substantial computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. In the present work, we address both limitations. First, we extend the theoretical framework of DAE to partially observable domains with minimal modifications. Second, we reduce its computational complexity by introducing discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities. We evaluate our approach on the Arcade Learning Environment and find that DAE scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Direct Advantage Estimation (DAE) to partially observable environments and reduces its computational cost via discrete latent dynamics models, demonstrating scalability and sample efficiency on the Arcade Learning Environment.
AI.motivation: DAE improves sample efficiency in deep RL but has two key limitations: (1) it requires full environment observability, restricting real-world applicability; (2) modeling transition probabilities introduces heavy computational overhead for high-dimensional observations. The authors aim to overcome both.
AI.method: The authors (1) extend DAE's theoretical framework to partially observable domains with minimal changes, presumably adapting the advantage estimation to work with belief states or histories rather than true states; (2) introduce discrete latent dynamics models that efficiently approximate transition probabilities, reducing computational complexity compared to continuous or full-dimensional transition modeling.
AI.result: Evaluated on the Arcade Learning Environment, DAE with the proposed modifications scales effectively with function approximator capacity while retaining high sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: DAE can be successfully adapted to partially observable settings with discrete latent dynamics, preserving its sample efficiency benefits while removing the requirement for full observability and mitigating computational overhead.

title: Pseudo-Feature Padding: A Lightweight Defense Against False Data Injection in Power Grids
summary: Deep Neural Networks DNNs have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks including their application in CyberPhysical Systems CPS for detecting False Data Injection Attacks FDIA during critical operations However the unique infrastructure of CPS makes DNNs vulnerable to exploitation by attackers aiming to evade detection Additionally the distinct nature of CPS presents challenges for conventional defense mechanisms against FDIA This paper proposes an innovative defense framework that strengthens DNNs against such attacks by introducing an additional input layer that performs padding in the input samples using pseudofeature values derived from the inputs statistical distribution This padding increases the input dimensionality in a randomized and dataaware manner making adversarial attacks computationally infeasible due to the nontransferable nature of crafted perturbations and the unpredictability of the padded structure Our method is lightweight modelagnostic and requires no modifications to the core architecture making it highly deployable in realworld CPS settings We evaluated our framework on critical power grid applications such as state estimation using the IEEE 14bus 30bus 118bus and 300bus systems Experiments under adversarial settings demonstrate that our padding strategy significantly improves model robustness with negligible impact on performance and effectively mitigates attacks that would otherwise bypass conventional defenses

AI.tldr: A defense framework for DNNs in CPS against FDIA evasion attacks, using randomized, data-aware pseudo-feature padding to increase input dimensionality, making adversarial perturbations computationally infeasible. It is lightweight, model-agnostic, and validated on IEEE bus systems for power grid state estimation.
AI.motivation: DNNs used for FDIA detection in CPS are vulnerable to adversarial evasion attacks due to CPS's unique infrastructure. Conventional defense mechanisms face challenges adapting to CPS-specific constraints, creating a need for a deployable, robust defense that doesn't require architectural changes.
AI.method: An additional input layer performs padding on input samples using pseudo-feature values drawn from the input's statistical distribution. This randomized, data-aware padding increases input dimensionality, making adversarial perturbations non-transferable and the padded structure unpredictable, thus rendering attack computation infeasible.
AI.result: Evaluated on IEEE 14-bus, 30-bus, 118-bus, and 300-bus power grid state estimation systems. The padding strategy significantly improved model robustness under adversarial settings with negligible performance impact, effectively mitigating attacks that bypass conventional defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a lightweight, model-agnostic, and highly deployable defense against FDIA adversarial attacks in CPS, strengthening DNN robustness without core architecture modifications.

title: On the Redundancy of Timestep Embeddings in Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models rely heavily on explicit timestep embeddings to modulate the denoising process across various noise scales. In this work, we challenge the necessity of these temporal signals by analyzing their impact on U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures. Beyond empirical evidence, we provide a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under certain conditions, the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be achieved without explicit timestep conditioning. Our findings reveal a surprising robustness when timestep embeddings are completely removed. Extensive ablation studies on the CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets show that these time-agnostic models can maintain high structural fidelity and even surpass their conditioned counterparts in competitive metrics, including FID, precision, and recall. Our analysis suggests these architectures can implicitly infer noise scales from the corrupted input under specific assumptions, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant. This study challenges long-standing temporal conditioning paradigms and paves the way for more efficient and structurally focused generative architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the necessity of explicit timestep embeddings in diffusion models, demonstrating both theoretically and empirically that under certain conditions, time-agnostic architectures can match or surpass their time-conditioned counterparts on metrics like FID, precision, and recall.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models universally employ explicit timestep embeddings to modulate denoising across noise scales. The authors question whether this architectural component is truly necessary or merely an unchallenged convention, aiming to simplify generative architectures and deepen theoretical understanding of how diffusion models infer noise levels.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical framework proving that the global minimizer of the diffusion training objective can be attained without explicit timestep conditioning, under certain assumptions. Empirically, they conduct extensive ablation studies on CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets using both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer backbones, completely removing timestep embeddings and evaluating performance via FID, precision, and recall.
AI.result: Time-agnostic models exhibit surprising robustness: they maintain high structural fidelity and even outperform conditioned counterparts on FID, precision, and recall. The results suggest that architectures can implicitly infer noise scales directly from corrupted inputs, rendering explicit temporal conditioning redundant under the studied conditions.
AI.conclusion: The study challenges the long-standing paradigm that timestep embeddings are indispensable in diffusion models, opening the door to simpler, more efficient, and structurally focused generative architectures that forgo explicit temporal conditioning.

title: Neural network surrogates with uncertainty quantification for inverse problems in partial differential equations
summary: Inverse problems for differential equations arise throughout science and engineering, where one seeks to infer unknown model parameters from noisy or incomplete observations. Traditional numerical methods for these problems are often computationally expensive, particularly in Bayesian settings where evaluating the likelihood becomes costly for complex forward models and high-dimensional parameter spaces. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepGaLA, a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions, reducing overconfident inference when training data are limited. To evaluate the fidelity of the surrogate-induced posterior approximations in practice, we show that a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo can serve as an effective diagnostic. Across a range of numerical experiments, DeepGaLA delivers forward-model approximations with accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates, while better maintaining efficiency as parameter dimension grows. Moreover, it can incorporate differential-equation constraints, including in nonlinear settings. Overall, these results indicate that uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates can enable scalable and reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems.

AI.tldr: DeepGaLA is a neural-network surrogate for differential equation solvers that provides uncertainty-aware predictions for Bayesian inverse problems. It matches Gaussian process accuracy while scaling better with parameter dimension, supports nonlinear differential-equation constraints, and can be validated via short delayed-acceptance MCMC runs.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical methods for Bayesian inverse problems with differential equations are computationally prohibitive due to costly likelihood evaluations in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Existing surrogates either lack uncertainty quantification or scale poorly, creating a need for efficient, uncertainty-aware surrogates that maintain reliability with limited training data.
AI.method: The authors propose DeepGaLA, a neural-network-based surrogate that provides uncertainty-aware predictions. It incorporates differential-equation constraints (including nonlinear ones) into the learning process. For diagnostic validation, they employ a short run of delayed-acceptance Markov chain Monte Carlo (DA-MCMC) to assess the fidelity of surrogate-induced posterior approximations.
AI.result: DeepGaLA achieves forward-model approximation accuracy comparable to established Gaussian-process surrogates while maintaining better computational efficiency as parameter dimension increases. It successfully incorporates differential-equation constraints in nonlinear settings and prevents overconfident inference under limited training data. The DA-MCMC diagnostic effectively flags poor posterior approximations.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-quantified neural surrogates like DeepGaLA can enable scalable, reliable Bayesian inference for inverse problems in complex systems, offering a practical path forward where traditional methods become intractable.

title: Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning
summary: Continual learning (CL) systems often forget previously acquired knowledge, yet the mechanisms driving forgetting remain hard to isolate in practice because real datasets entangle many factors. We present a controlled, toy-world framework that makes these mechanisms observable and testable. Using a synthetic generator-separator pipeline, we define ground-truth latent features, build tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap, and introduce measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional overlap among features). We then study retention dynamics-the temporal change of representation strength by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) between retention, superposition, and exposure history. A complementary task-level analysis based on effective rank characterizes how representational capacity is allocated across tasks. Our controlled experiments yield three takeaways. (1) Superposition tends to increase over time with transient dips at task boundaries, suggesting boundary-specific interference rather than steady drift. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet does not inevitably cause forgetting; when representations remain strong, forgetting can be reduced despite overlap. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes. Together, these results nuance the common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting by showing that overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation. Our toy analysis provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for CL.

AI.tldr: A controlled synthetic framework is introduced to study forgetting in continual learning, revealing that superposition (feature overlap) increases over time with boundary-specific interference, but does not inevitably cause forgetting when representations remain strong. Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition yet enables broader capacity allocation.
AI.motivation: Real-world datasets entangle many factors, making it difficult to isolate the mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in continual learning systems. A controlled, observable, and testable framework is needed to disentangle these mechanisms.
AI.method: A synthetic generator-separator pipeline defines ground-truth latent features and constructs tasks with tunable sparsity and overlap. Measurable quantities for representation strength and superposition (directional feature overlap) are introduced. Retention dynamics are modeled by fitting sparse dynamical relations (via SINDy) among retention, superposition, and exposure history. Task-level effective rank is used to characterize representational capacity allocation.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Superposition increases over time with transient dips at task boundaries, indicating boundary-specific interference. (2) Higher feature sparsity induces more superposition but does not inevitably cause forgetting if representations remain strong. (3) Task-level effective rank grows with sparsity, indicating broader capacity usage under sparse regimes.
AI.conclusion: The common intuition that more superposition leads to more forgetting is nuanced: overlap interacts with representation strength and capacity allocation in complex ways. The toy framework provides falsifiable hypotheses and diagnostic tools for continual learning research.

title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: Equal advising: Daria Pugacheva and Fedor Ratnikov. Accepted to the ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI and PDEs
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage evolutionary algorithm approach for hyperparameter optimization in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), where a rapid low-fidelity screening stage identifies promising configurations, followed by full training of only the best candidates, achieving improved accuracy under fixed computational budgets.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and high sensitivity to hyperparameters due to the non-convex, multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. Traditional local or gradient-based hyperparameter search strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions, necessitating a more robust, population-based optimization approach.
AI.method: A two-stage evolutionary algorithm framework: Stage 1 performs low-fidelity training with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate hyperparameter configurations as a black-box outer-loop problem; Stage 2 selects only the most promising candidates for full training with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine solutions under fixed computational budgets.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms standard PINN training across three benchmark PDEs — Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz equations — achieving significantly lower mean error within the same computational resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary algorithms provide an effective mechanism for PINN hyperparameter optimization by combining broad exploration with targeted exploitation, overcoming the sensitivity and convergence issues inherent in standard PINN training.

title: Data Bias Mitigation under Coverage Constraints & The Price of Fairness
summary: Machine learning models have been shown to exhibit discriminatory outcomes or degraded performance for individuals at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes, such as race and gender. This stems in part from two interrelated challenges: the lack of principled measures for quantifying bias (potentially intersectional), and insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. We extend a recent bias mitigation framework to incorporate coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. Since achieving exactly zero bias for all groups may not be data efficient (meaning it may require large amounts of data), our solution trades small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency while satisfying coverage constraints. We also formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, and characterize the price of fairness, the minimum data modification cost, as a function of fairness tolerance. This is essential both for legal compliance, where regulations may mandate specific fairness thresholds, and for data governance, enabling practitioners to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification (particularly, data purchasing) costs. We evaluate our techniques on publicly available datasets, demonstrating that bias mitigation via our framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers, and that coverage constraints, while motivated by statistical considerations, are essential for preserving downstream ML performance.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a bias mitigation framework with coverage constraints to ensure sufficient representation of intersectional subgroups, trading small bias approximation errors for data efficiency. It formulates bias mitigation as an integer linear program, characterizes the "price of fairness" as a function of fairness tolerance, and demonstrates that coverage constraints preserve downstream ML performance.
AI.motivation: Existing bias mitigation approaches suffer from two key limitations: (1) a lack of principled measures for quantifying intersectional bias (bias at the intersection of multiple sensitive attributes like race and gender), and (2) insufficient representation of intersectional subgroups in training data. Moreover, achieving exactly zero bias may be data-inefficient, and practitioners lack tools to make informed trade-offs between bias reduction and data modification costs.
AI.method: The authors extend a prior bias mitigation framework by incorporating coverage constraints that enforce sufficient representation across groups, including intersectional subgroups. They formulate bias mitigation as an integer linear program (ILP) that optimizes over all mitigation strategies, allowing small approximation errors in bias for greater data efficiency. They also characterize the "price of fairness" — the minimum data modification cost as a function of fairness tolerance — enabling cost-aware trade-offs. Evaluation is performed on publicly available datasets across multiple classifiers.
AI.result: The framework preserves predictive accuracy across multiple classifiers while achieving bias mitigation. Coverage constraints, though motivated by statistical considerations, prove essential for maintaining downstream ML performance. The ILP formulation successfully characterizes the price of fairness as a function of fairness tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Coverage constraints are not merely a statistical nicety but are essential for preserving downstream ML performance in intersectional bias mitigation. The ILP-based formulation provides a principled way to navigate the trade-off between fairness tolerance and data modification costs, supporting both legal compliance and data governance decisions.

title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
summary: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

AI.tldr: ASYS is a prior-guided framework that combines LLM agents, evolutionary search, and gradient-based optimization to discover interpretable symbolic representations of PDE solutions, recovering known analytic forms and discovering new ones where none previously existed.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to understanding PDE solutions — handcrafted analysis, numerical simulation, and neural networks — fail to directly produce the interpretable mathematical structures that mathematicians rely on. There is a gap between black-box approximation and human-interpretable analytic insight.
AI.method: ASYS uses an LLM agent that translates PDE theory, problem constraints, and search experience into differentiable symbolic programs. These programs undergo evolutionary search to refine their mathematical forms, while continuous parameters are optimized via gradient descent. This constitutes automated inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression.
AI.result: Across five problems (bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, free-boundary focusing), ASYS recovered known analytic forms naturally and discovered new interpretable representations — notably a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up — in settings previously lacking closed-form descriptions.
AI.conclusion: ASYS demonstrates a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions that goes beyond handcrafted analysis, mesh-based numerics, and neural network approximations, suggesting a viable path toward automated discovery of interpretable mathematical structure in PDE systems.

title: Fisher-Geometric Sharpness and the Implicit Bias of SGD toward Flat Minima
summary: A widely held intuition in deep learning is that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly favors flat minima and that flat minima generalize better, but standard Euclidean measures of flatness such as the trace or maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, which undermines the theoretical foundations of this narrative. In this study we resolve this issue by grounding flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). We define Riemannian sharpness mathematically and prove that it is invariant under smooth, function-preserving reparametrizations, which directly addresses the critique of Dinh et al. in the paper ``Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets''.We note that this invariance is a property of the true FIM; the diagonal empirical estimator used in practice (and in all experiments below) inherits invariance only approximately, and exact invariance under arbitrary reparametrizations would require structured estimators such as K-FAC. We formalize the gradient noise of mini-batch SGD as having a covariance structure proportional to the FIM, derive the stationary distribution of the resulting stochastic differential equation, and then show that the probability mass is exponentially concentrated at Riemannian-flat minima. A PAC-Bayes generalization bound controlled explicitly by SR formally links this geometric bias to test performance. Our experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that SR reliably tracks generalization in ways that Euclidean sharpness does not, and that its scaling with $η/B$ matches the theoretical predictions. Together these results provide a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the reparametrization-invariance problem in flatness-based generalization theory by defining a Riemannian sharpness measure grounded in the Fisher Information Matrix. It proves this measure is invariant under function-preserving reparametrizations, derives that SGD concentrates probability mass at Riemannian-flat minima, and provides a PAC-Bayes bound linking this geometric bias to generalization, with experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirming the theory.
AI.motivation: The core motivation is to fix a foundational flaw in the "flat minima generalize better" narrative: standard Euclidean flatness measures (e.g., Hessian trace or max eigenvalue) are not invariant under reparametrizations that preserve the network function, as pointed out by Dinh et al. This undermines theoretical claims linking flatness to generalization. The authors seek a geometrically principled, invariant notion of flatness.
AI.method: The authors ground flatness in the Riemannian geometry of the statistical manifold induced by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). They (1) define "Riemannian sharpness" mathematically and prove its invariance under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations; (2) formalize mini-batch SGD gradient noise as having covariance proportional to the FIM; (3) derive the stationary distribution of the corresponding stochastic differential equation, showing probability mass concentrates exponentially at Riemannian-flat minima; and (4) derive a PAC-Bayes generalization bound explicitly controlled by Riemannian sharpness.
AI.result: Riemannian sharpness is proven invariant under smooth function-preserving reparametrizations, directly addressing Dinh et al.'s critique. The stationary distribution of SGD is shown to exponentially favor Riemannian-flat minima. The PAC-Bayes bound formally links Riemannian sharpness to test performance. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm that Riemannian sharpness reliably tracks generalization where Euclidean measures fail, and its scaling with η/B matches theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous, reparametrization-invariant account of why flat minima generalize, resolving a major theoretical weakness in the flatness narrative. Riemannian sharpness, grounded in the FIM, successfully replaces Euclidean measures and aligns theory with empirical observation.

title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
summary: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates 4-bit KV-cache compression for context-heavy, multi-turn agent workloads, proposing UltraQuant — an FP4 approximation path optimized for AMD GPUs — achieving 3.47× faster time-to-first-token in cache-pressured late rounds and 1.63× higher output throughput versus FP8 KV caching.
AI.motivation: Serving LLMs for context-heavy, multi-round agent workloads creates tension: long reused prefixes inflate KV-cache memory, while concurrency demands high GPU utilization. Existing FP8 KV caching (e.g., vLLM) provides a deployment baseline but leaves throughput on the table; 4-bit compression offers further memory savings, yet no prior work jointly evaluates task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput in this regime, nor has the 4-bit path been made robust and performant on real GPU hardware.
AI.method: The authors use TurboQuant-style rotation plus codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. Key design choices include: (1) asymmetric treatment of K and V tensors, (2) Walsh-Hadamard rotation for distribution shaping, (3) removal of QJL (Quasi-Johnson-Lindenstrauss) projections for simplicity/speed, and (4) block-scale quantization variants. On AMD CDNA4 GPUs, they implement optimized decode-attention kernels and introduce UltraQuant: an FP4 approximation path combining FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA (Matrix Fused Multiply-Add) support. Evaluation uses a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload measuring P50 TTFT, output throughput, task quality, and cache residency jointly.
AI.result: On the tested agentic workload, UltraQuant reduces P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47× in cache-pressured late rounds (2.3× across all rounds) and increases output throughput by 1.63× over the FP8 KV baseline, while maintaining acceptable task quality.
AI.conclusion: 4-bit KV-cache compression with the described design choices can substantially improve serving throughput and latency for multi-turn agent workloads without unacceptable quality degradation. The UltraQuant FP4 approach on AMD CDNA4 demonstrates practical viability, and the paper emphasizes that KV-cache compression must be evaluated holistically across quality, residency, and throughput — not in isolation.

title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution
summary: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

AI.tldr: MAA addresses contradictory inter-batch feedback in trace distillation by formalizing alignability/comparability conditions and accumulating signed evidence per operation via EMA with semantic identity merging, achieving SOTA in 14/16 settings while cutting token consumption ~75%.
AI.motivation: In batch-style trace distillation, memory operations receive contradictory feedback across different batches, and existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism. This prevents distinguishing genuinely effective operations from accidental hits, motivating the need for a principled accumulation framework.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the cross-batch accumulation requirement as two structural conditions: alignability and comparability. It proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA), a post-processing architecture with three components: (1) construction of differential signals to make operation-level feedback comparable across batches, (2) accumulation of signed evidence per operation using Exponential Moving Average (EMA), and (3) semantic identity merging to ensure cross-batch traceability of operations.
AI.result: MAA achieved the best results in 14 out of 16 experimental settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.
AI.conclusion: MAA provides a principled solution to the cross-batch evidence accumulation problem in trace distillation. By satisfying alignability and comparability conditions, it reliably identifies stably effective operations, delivers strong empirical performance, and offers significant efficiency gains through reduced token consumption.

title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving
summary: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.

AI.tldr: FlashRT introduces execution-state capsules — graph-bound checkpoint/restore mechanisms that snapshot complete LLM execution state (KV, recurrent, convolution, MTP states, metadata) rather than reusing only KV cache fragments. Targeting low-latency, small-batch, on-device scenarios, capsules achieve sub-millisecond GPU-resident snapshot/restore with byte-exact recovery and TTFT speedups of 3.9×–27× over cold prefill.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM serving systems optimize high-throughput, high-concurrency settings via paged/radix KV-cache reuse, but fail to address low-latency, on-device, interactive scenarios (LLM agents, speech, robot policies) where execution repeatedly branches, resets, interrupts, and re-enters under tight responsiveness budgets. These workloads require full execution-state reuse, not just KV fragments.
AI.method: FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime with an NVIDIA CUDA backend. It runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. The live state is a closed set of named buffers.
