An execution-state capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the complete execution boundary — including KV cache, recurrent state, convolution state, multi-token prediction (MTP) state, and metadata. Reuse operates at graph-bound execution-state boundaries rather than token-addressed KV fragments.
AI.result: On an RTX 5090: capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, confirming recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond. TTFT speedup over cold prefill: 3.9× at 2k tokens, scaling to 27× at 16k tokens. Correctness and structural properties also hold on Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.
AI.conclusion: Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary, latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse, enabling efficient interactive and on-device LLM workloads through complete graph-bound state management.

title: Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning
summary: Bayesian predictive inference provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, data efficiency, and robust generalization. However, exact inference is often intractable, and scalable approximations may remain computationally expensive or require restrictive modeling assumptions that degrade predictive performance. Prior-Data Fitted and in-context models have recently emerged as an amortized alternative by learning to map datasets directly to predictive distributions, but existing approaches are tightly coupled to the support of the training prior and lack explicit mechanisms for adapting to new priors at test time, resulting in limited robustness under distribution shift. We introduce a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference that explicitly represents prior information as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt its predictions across families of priors. On a suite of evaluations with increasing difficulty, including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures, our method matches oracle Bayesian predictors while being orders of magnitude faster. We further demonstrate its practical relevance on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/martianmartina/multi-task-bayesian-icl/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-task in-context learning framework for amortized hierarchical Bayesian predictive inference, where prior information is explicitly represented as a prefix of in-context datasets. A transformer trained on sequences of prior and target tasks learns to adapt predictions across families of priors, matching oracle Bayesian performance with orders-of-magnitude speedup, including under out-of-distribution priors.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inference is principled but computationally intractable. Existing amortized methods like Prior-Data Fitted Networks and in-context models are tightly coupled to the training prior and fail to adapt to new priors at test time, limiting robustness under distribution shift. There is a need for an approach that generalizes across families of priors without retraining.
AI.method: A multi-task in-context learning framework where hierarchical Bayesian structure is represented by treating prior information as a prefix context (a sequence of datasets from related prior tasks) preceding the target dataset. A transformer is trained on sequences of (prior tasks, target task) to meta-learn how to adapt its predictive distribution conditioned on this explicit prior representation, enabling test-time adaptation to novel priors.
AI.result: The method matches oracle Bayesian predictive performance across evaluations of increasing difficulty — including out-of-meta-distribution priors and priors with high-dimensional latent structures — while being orders of magnitude faster. Practical relevance is demonstrated on a real-world spatiotemporal temperature prediction benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly representing prior information as in-context prefix data enables transformers to amortize hierarchical Bayesian inference across diverse prior families, achieving both the statistical efficiency of Bayesian methods and the computational efficiency of amortized inference, with strong robustness to prior distribution shift.

title: Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy
summary: Differential privacy (DP) ensures rigorous individual-level privacy guarantees against even the most knowledgeable attackers, but its worst-case nature can impose a costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. We introduce privacy via predictability, a fine-grained framework that explicitly incorporates the attacker's core knowledge, a compromised portion of the dataset generated by a stochastic process, and a specified family of queries. Predictability measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information about unknown individuals after observing the algorithm's output, beyond what can already be inferred from the compromised data. We show that predictability and DP are generally incomparable: each can be small while the other is large. However, in the worst-case regime where all but one individual is compromised, and all binary queries are considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. More generally, predictability provides a finer-grained privacy metric tailored to specific sensitive information and specific attacker models. We introduce a general framework, using the generalized method of moments (GMM), to analyze asymptotic predictability when the compromised data is generated by a stationary, ergodic, mixing process. Using this analysis, we derive a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for ERM. Our approach is complementary to DP and can be used alongside DP to provide fine-grained privacy control.

AI.tldr: Introduces "privacy via predictability," a fine-grained framework that measures privacy leakage as the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information from algorithm outputs, beyond what compromised data already reveals. Shows incomparability with differential privacy, establishes connections to mutual-information DP in worst-case regimes, and provides a GMM-based asymptotic analysis with an application to ERM.
AI.motivation: Differential privacy provides worst-case guarantees that can impose an unnecessarily costly privacy-accuracy tradeoff. The authors aim to develop a finer-grained privacy metric that explicitly accounts for the attacker's prior knowledge (compromised data), the data-generating process, and the specific queries of interest, enabling more nuanced and potentially less costly privacy protection.
AI.method: The paper formalizes predictability as the incremental gain in an attacker's predictive ability (e.g., using a bounded loss function) after observing an algorithm's output, compared to predictions based solely on compromised data. It employs the generalized method of moments (GMM) to analyze asymptotic predictability when compromised data comes from a stationary, ergodic, mixing stochastic process, and derives a predictability-calibrated output perturbation scheme for empirical risk minimization (ERM).
AI.result: Predictability and differential privacy are shown to be generally incomparable (each can be small while the other is large). In the worst-case regime with all but one individual compromised and all binary queries considered sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. The GMM-based asymptotic analysis yields a practical perturbation scheme for ERM that is complementary to DP.
AI.conclusion: Predictability offers a complementary, finer-grained alternative to differential privacy that explicitly models attacker knowledge and specific sensitive queries. It can be used alongside DP to provide more flexible and context-aware privacy control, particularly when the data-generating process and attacker capabilities are well-characterized.

title: The Token Is a Group Element: On Lie-Algebra Attention over Matrix Lie Groups
summary: We place the attention token on the group: a token is an element $g_i$ of a matrix Lie group $G$ -- a bare transformation, with no feature payload and no external action $ρ(g)$ carrying it. To our knowledge this is the first attention construction whose tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements: their score is the closed-form algebra norm of the relative pose rather than a learned kernel, and it reaches the affine full-frame groups that every irrep- or surjective-exp-based method must exclude. We call it Lie-Algebra Attention. Once tokens are group elements, the rest follows with none of the usual representation-theoretic machinery. The relative geometry of a pair is canonical, $g_i^{-1} g_j$, so the pairwise invariant $w_{ij} = \log(g_i^{-1} g_j)$ is intrinsic rather than designed; equivariance under the diagonal $G$-action is tautological, and the cocycle condition holds automatically. The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm, $s_{ij} = -\|\log(g_i^{-1} g_j)\|_λ^2/τ$: the canonical proximity kernel under a block-weighted Frobenius inner product, with no irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernel. The construction applies to any matrix Lie group on a chosen logarithm chart containing the relative poses, including the non-compact non-abelian affine groups with scale and shear that no vector-token attention method reaches: neither the irrep tradition nor surjective-exp methods. Three sequence-completion experiments, on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2), bear this out: the closed-form score matches a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant and outperforms it on SE(2), using 50 to 80x fewer score parameters, while a vector-token baseline breaks invariance by five to twelve orders of magnitude.

AI.tldr: Proposes Lie-Algebra Attention, where tokens are bare matrix Lie group elements and attention scores are computed via the closed-form negative squared algebra norm of relative poses, eliminating learned kernels and representation-theoretic machinery while extending to non-compact affine groups.
AI.motivation: Existing attention mechanisms treat tokens as vectors with feature payloads, relying on irreducible representations, spherical harmonics, Clebsch-Gordan products, or learned kernels. These methods cannot handle non-compact non-abelian affine groups (with scale and shear). The authors aim to construct an attention mechanism where tokens are pure group elements, using the intrinsic geometry of the group manifold to define scores canonically.
AI.method: Tokens are elements g_i of a matrix Lie group G. The relative geometry is g_i^{-1} g_j, with the invariant w_{ij} = log(g_i^{-1} g_j). The attention score is the negative squared algebra norm: s_{ij} = -||log(g_i^{-1} g_j)||_λ^2 / τ, using a block-weighted Frobenius inner product. Equivariance under diagonal G-action is tautological; the cocycle condition holds automatically. The method uses a chosen logarithm chart and applies to any matrix Lie group.
AI.result: Sequence-completion experiments on SE(2), SO(3), and Aff(2) show the closed-form score matches or outperforms a learned MLP kernel on the same invariant, with 50–80× fewer score parameters, while vector-token baselines break invariance by 5–12 orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Lie-Algebra Attention demonstrates that canonical group geometry suffices for attention scoring, removing the need for learned kernels or representation theory, and uniquely extends attention to non-compact affine groups like Aff(2) that prior vector-token methods cannot handle.

title: Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction
summary:
A model is multicalibrated on a collection of group weights $G$ if it is calibrated -- i.e. unbiased even conditional on its prediction -- not just overall, but also after reweighting contexts by each $g \in G$. It is a useful property for many downstream applications and is a basic desideratum of trustworthy machine learning. Before this work, all predictors known to attain the minimax-optimal $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity rate for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors were known only with substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization is necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration was explicitly asked by [CLNR26] and implicitly in several prior works.
  We resolve this open problem by giving a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor. We then generalize the algorithm to produce optimal deterministic predictors that satisfy outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. As an application, this also gives deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors with optimal sample complexity, resolving open problems posed by [OKK25] and [BHHLZ25].

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the open problem of whether randomization is necessary for achieving minimax-optimal sample complexity in multicalibration by presenting a deterministic algorithm that attains the optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate, and further generalizes the result to outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors.
AI.motivation: Prior to this work, all predictors achieving the minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration were randomized, while deterministic predictors had substantially worse sample complexity. Whether randomization was strictly necessary was an open question explicitly raised by [CLNR26] and implicitly in earlier works.
AI.method: The authors construct a minimax-optimal multicalibration algorithm that outputs a deterministic predictor, then generalize this algorithmic framework to handle outcome indistinguishability (OI) with respect to finite or finitely covered collections of tests. The approach further yields deterministic omnipredictors and panpredictors.
AI.result: The paper provides the first deterministic predictor achieving the minimax-optimal $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ sample complexity for $\varepsilon$-multicalibration. It also extends to optimal deterministic predictors for outcome indistinguishability, omnipredictors, and panpredictors, settling multiple open problems.
AI.conclusion: Randomization is not necessary for optimal sample complexity in multicalibration. Deterministic predictors can achieve the same minimax-optimal rate, and the result generalizes broadly to related fairness and indistinguishability frameworks, resolving open problems posed by [CLNR26], [OKK25], and [BHHLZ25].

title: How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?
comment: 20 main text pages and 6 pages of references and appendices
summary: LLM reasoning transparency is a critical affordance for understanding model decisions, mitigating misuse and misalignment, and debugging surprising model behaviors. However, DiffusionGemma performs a larger fraction of its computation in a continuous latent space; does this make its reasoning less transparent? We study this question by decomposing transparency into two components: variable transparency, whether we understand intermediate snapshots of a model's computational state; and algorithmic transparency, whether we can use these snapshots to reconstruct the process by which the model arrived at its outputs. Naively, DiffusionGemma has poor variable transparency: its opaque serial depth, the amount of serial computation that occurs in between interpretable model states, seems at first 28.6X higher than the corresponding autoregressive Gemma 4 model. However, we show that we can map the information flowing between denoising steps through an interpretable token bottleneck with no decrease in downstream performance. Treating these intermediate states as interpretable reduces the opaque serial depth to just 1.1X that of Gemma 4. Algorithmic transparency is harder for diffusion models than for autoregressive models because all token predictions in the canvas can change at every denoising step, giving the model the power to implement complicated distributed algorithms during the denoising process. To begin bridging this gap, we conduct a suite of interpretability case studies, uncovering initial evidence of novel diffusion-specific phenomena such as non-chronological reasoning, token and sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Finally, we test monitorability, a key application of transparency that measures whether model outputs are useful for downstream tasks. We find that DiffusionGemma is similarly monitorable to Gemma 4.

AI.tldr: DiffusionGemma appears to have 28.6X higher opaque serial depth than autoregressive Gemma 4, but mapping information through an interpretable token bottleneck reduces this to 1.1X. Algorithmic transparency remains harder for diffusion models; case studies reveal novel phenomena like non-chronological reasoning. Monitorability is comparable between both models.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether diffusion language models (specifically DiffusionGemma), which perform most computation in continuous latent space, are inherently less transparent than autoregressive models. Transparency is critical for understanding decisions, mitigating misuse, and debugging model behavior.
AI.method: The authors decompose transparency into two components: variable transparency (understanding intermediate computational snapshots) and algorithmic transparency (reconstructing the reasoning process). They introduce an interpretable token bottleneck to map information flow between denoising steps without performance degradation, then conduct interpretability case studies to probe algorithmic transparency. Monitorability is tested as a downstream application.
AI.result: Variable transparency: naive opaque serial depth is 28.6X higher than Gemma 4, but the token bottleneck reduces this to 1.1X. Algorithmic transparency: diffusion models exhibit novel phenomena including non-chronological reasoning, token/sequence smearing, and intermediate-context reasoning. Monitorability: DiffusionGemma performs comparably to Gemma 4.
AI.conclusion: DiffusionGemma's variable transparency can be substantially recovered through an interpretable token bottleneck, making it nearly as transparent as autoregressive models in this dimension. However, algorithmic transparency remains a harder challenge due to the distributed, non-chronological nature of diffusion computation. Despite these differences, practical monitorability is comparable between the two architectures.
